text: Nationwide and worldwide First U.S. case Confirmed January 20, 2020 Pandemic declared By the World Health Organization, March 11, 2020 National emergency Declared March 13, 2020; CARES Act signed March 27, 2020 First vaccine authorization December 11, 2020 (Pfizer-BioNTech) U.S. deaths More than one million by May 2022 In December 2019, a cluster of patients in Wuhan, China, developed an unusual pneumonia-like illness. The new coronavirus was highly contagious and could spread before symptoms appeared; many infected people had no symptoms at all, while the elderly and people with other conditions were especially vulnerable. Despite a lockdown in Wuhan on January 23, 2020, the virus spread worldwide through travel. The CDC confirmed the first U.S. case on January 20, 2020. On March 11 the WHO declared a pandemic, and on March 13 the Trump administration declared a national emergency. Schools, restaurants, and offices closed; New York City’s school system shut down. New York City was devastated that spring, with mobile morgues set up to hold the dead. By April, 10 million Americans had lost their jobs; on March 27 the CARES Act was signed into law to provide relief. States competed for scarce protective equipment, and mask-wearing became politicized. By May 2020, 100,000 Americans had died. The worst wave came that winter, when nearly 3,000 Americans died each day through January and much of February 2021. The FDA authorized the first vaccine on December 11, 2020, and by late spring 2021 millions were being vaccinated. Many Americans refused vaccines, influenced by conspiracy theories or politics, and new, more contagious variants such as Delta and Omicron kept the virus spreading. Over 600,000 Americans had died by the end of summer 2021, and the official death toll crossed one million by May 2022. The pandemic moved many white-collar workers to working from home while hourly workers, often without paid sick leave, had to choose between a paycheck and their health; it also deepened political polarization over public health. With more than a million American deaths, COVID-19 was a defining experience of the early twenty-first century. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8rFg-FvZZhY 2020 Timeline: The Year Of The Covid Pandemic | NBC News NOW NBC News 15:37 2026-10-22

title: The Cuban Missile Crisis
subtitle: The October 1962 showdown in which the superpowers came closest to nuclear war
summary: In October 1962 an American U-2 spy plane photographed Soviet nuclear missile sites under construction in Cuba. In the days that followed, President John F. Kennedy and Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev faced each other in the most dangerous confrontation of the Cold War, the moment when the two superpowers came closest to nuclear conflict. Kennedy imposed a naval “quarantine” of the island; Khrushchev finally agreed to remove the missiles in exchange for an American pledge not to invade Cuba, and a secret promise to pull U.S. missiles out of Turkey.
thumbAlt: U.S. aerial reconnaissance photograph of a Soviet medium-range ballistic missile launch site at San Cristobal, Cuba, November 1, 1962
aliases: Cuban missile crisis October Crisis missile crisis
themeText: The Cold War Foreign policy and diplomacy The presidency War and the military
text: Cuba, Washington, and Moscow Discovery October 14, 1962: a U-2 photographs missile sites under construction in Cuba Quarantine Announced on national television on October 22, 1962 Closest call U.S. forces at DEFCON 2 — war involving the Strategic Air Command imminent; a U-2 shot down over Cuba on October 27 The deal Soviet missiles removed; U.S. pledge not to invade Cuba; secretly, U.S. Jupiter missiles withdrawn from Turkey (April 1963) Aftermath A White House–Kremlin “Hotline” and the 1963 treaty limiting nuclear tests The crisis brought the world to the edge of nuclear war and then pushed both superpowers to step back: they set up a direct line of communication and took the first steps toward controlling the nuclear arms race. After the failed CIA-backed Bay of Pigs invasion of April 1961, the Kennedy administration planned a covert campaign against Fidel Castro’s government, Operation Mongoose. In July 1962 Khrushchev reached a secret agreement with Castro to place Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba, both to deter another invasion and, as historians at the Miller Center note, to offset the large American lead in nuclear weapons. Along with the missiles came some 42,000 Soviet troops. Construction began in late summer. When American surveillance flights detected a general Soviet arms buildup, Kennedy publicly warned on September 4 against bringing offensive weapons into Cuba. The crisis grew out of the arms race and the Cold War rivalry over Cuba. The Soviets wanted to protect Castro’s government, to compete with China for the loyalty of revolutionaries worldwide, and to neutralize the large American advantage in nuclear weapons. The United States — which itself had nuclear missiles in Turkey aimed at the Soviet Union — declared that it would not permit offensive weapons in Cuba. Secrecy and mutual misunderstanding turned the deployment into a showdown. On October 14 a U-2 took pictures clearly showing sites for medium- and intermediate-range nuclear missiles; the next day the photographs reached the White House. Kennedy gathered his closest advisers in secret meetings. All the Joint Chiefs of Staff urged an air strike followed by an invasion; others favored stern warnings. Kennedy chose a middle course. On October 22 he announced on national television a naval “quarantine” of Cuba — a word chosen because a “blockade” would legally mean a state of war — and warned that any missile launched from Cuba would be treated as a Soviet attack on the United States, “requiring a full retaliatory response upon the Soviet Union.” Khrushchev called the quarantine an “act of aggression,” but on October 24 and 25 some Soviet ships turned back from the quarantine line. Meanwhile the missile sites neared readiness, and American forces went to DEFCON 2, meaning war involving the Strategic Air Command was imminent. On October 26 a Soviet agent approached ABC News reporter John Scali with an offer: the missiles would go if the United States promised not to invade. That night came a long, emotional letter from Khrushchev with a similar proposal, urging both sides to “untie that knot.” Hope faded the next day, October 27: a second Soviet message demanded the removal of U.S. Jupiter missiles from Turkey, and an American U-2 was shot down over Cuba. Kennedy chose to answer the first letter and ignore the second, while his brother, Attorney General Robert Kennedy, told the Soviet ambassador privately that the Turkish missiles would be removed soon — but could not be part of any public deal. On October 28 Khrushchev announced that the missiles would be dismantled and taken home. The naval quarantine stayed in place until the Soviets also agreed to remove their IL-28 bombers; the United States ended it on November 20, 1962. The Jupiter missiles left Turkey in April 1963. The outcome strengthened Kennedy’s standing at home and abroad and helped repair the damage done by the Bay of Pigs. Because the two leaders had struggled throughout the crisis to understand each other’s intentions, a direct telephone link between the White House and the Kremlin — the “Hotline” — was set up. Having looked into the abyss, both superpowers began to reconsider the nuclear arms race. In 1963 the United States, Britain, and the Soviet Union agreed to ban nuclear tests in the atmosphere, in space, and underwater — an agreement Kennedy considered his greatest accomplishment. The State Department’s historians call the crisis a singular event of the Cold War, shaped as much by miscalculation and miscommunication as by calculation, and played out largely between the White House and the Kremlin themselves. title: D-Day
subtitle: The Allied invasion of Normandy, June 6, 1944
summary: On June 6, 1944, nearly 160,000 American, British, Canadian, and other Allied troops landed along fifty miles of the heavily fortified Normandy coast of France, supported by more than 5,000 ships and 13,000 aircraft. Called Operation Overlord and commanded by General Dwight D. Eisenhower, it was the largest amphibious assault in history. More than 9,000 Allied soldiers were killed or wounded that day, but the Allies gained a foothold in western Europe that led to the liberation of France and the defeat of Nazi Germany.
thumbAlt: American soldiers wading ashore from a landing craft on Omaha Beach
aliases: Operation Overlord Normandy landings Omaha Beach Utah Beach
themeText: War and the military Foreign policy and diplomacy
text: Normandy, France Date June 6, 1944 Supreme commander General Dwight D. Eisenhower Force Nearly 160,000 troops; more than 5,000 ships and 13,000 aircraft; 23,400 airborne troops dropped overnight Beaches Utah, Omaha, Gold, Juno, and Sword Casualties More than 9,000 Allied soldiers killed or wounded on D-Day Allied planners had considered a cross-Channel assault since France fell in 1940. At the Tehran Conference in November 1943, Soviet leader Joseph Stalin pressed Britain and the United States to invade France to relieve pressure on the Eastern Front; Roosevelt agreed, and Eisenhower was named to command the operation. By May 1944 nearly 2.9 million Allied troops had gathered in southern England. A second front in the west would force Germany to fight on two sides and open a direct route to the German heartland. Before dawn on June 5, Eisenhower decided to proceed. In his Order of the Day he told the troops, “The eyes of the world are upon you.” He also wrote out, on a pad of paper, a press release to be issued if the landings failed — mistakenly dating it “July 5.” Overnight, more than a thousand transport planes dropped 23,400 American, British, and Canadian airborne troops behind the beaches. On June 6 troops came ashore on five beaches code-named Utah, Omaha, Gold, Juno, and Sword. By day’s end the Allies held a foothold on the continent. The assault phase, Operation Neptune, continued through the end of June as the Allies landed more troops and supplies. Progress across France was much slower than hoped, but Paris was liberated about two months after the landings. With the Soviet Union advancing from the east, D-Day sealed Germany’s defeat; the war in Europe ended eleven months later. The landings remain the defining image of American and Allied sacrifice in World War II. D-Day was the turning point of the war in western Europe and one of the most complex military operations ever carried out. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-KY1pDLulF4 D-Day 1: The Great Crusade | WW2 | Extra History Extra History 10:25 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RIIN0Ug8wg8 America the Story of Us: D-Day Invasion | History HISTORY 3:06 2026-10-22

title: The Dust Bowl
subtitle: Drought, dust storms, and migration on the southern Plains in the 1930s
summary: During the 1930s, years of drought combined with farming practices that had stripped the Great Plains of its protective grass, and high winds lifted the exposed soil into enormous dust storms. The worst-hit area (the western third of Kansas, southeastern Colorado, the Oklahoma Panhandle, most of the Texas Panhandle, and northeastern New Mexico) became known as the Dust Bowl. Farms failed, hundreds of thousands of people left the region, and the disaster pushed the federal government to promote soil conservation.
location: Southern Great Plains: western Kansas, southeastern Colorado, the Oklahoma Panhandle, the Texas Panhandle, and northeastern New Mexico
thumbAlt: A wall of dust approaching a town in Texas in 1935
aliases: Black Sunday black blizzards Okies Migrant Mother Soil Conservation Service
themeText: Land and environment Economy and finance Everyday life
text: Southern Great Plains: western Kansas, southeastern Colorado, the Oklahoma Panhandle, the Texas Panhandle, and northeastern New Mexico Droughts 1930–31, 1934, 1936, and 1939–40 Black Sunday April 14, 1935 Name Coined by Associated Press reporter Robert Geiger in April 1935 Relief By 1937, 21% of rural Plains families received federal emergency relief Outmigration Oklahoma lost 440,000 people, 18.4% of its 1930 population In the 1920s, low crop prices and high machinery costs pushed Plains farmers to plow marginal land, and many abandoned soil conservation practices. Plowing destroyed the native sod that had held the dry soil in place; relatively wet years had masked the danger. Drought covered almost the entire Plains for nearly a decade, in at least four distinct episodes that came too quickly for the land to recover. With the ground cover gone and few windbreaks, high winds churned the dry topsoil into storms that people called “black blizzards” or “dusters.” The disaster struck farmers already ruined by years of falling prices and foreclosures during the Great Depression. Dust storms blotted out the sun, choked people and livestock,. Some carried dirt as far east as Washington, D.C., New England, and ships on the Atlantic. The worst came on Sunday, April 14, 1935 — “Black Sunday” — when a towering wall of dust swept across the Oklahoma and Texas panhandles, turning afternoon into total darkness. The next day an Associated Press reporter, Robert Geiger, who had been caught in the storm near Boise City, Oklahoma, wrote of the “dust bowl,” and the name stuck. Crops failed across the region, and many families gave up. Hundreds of thousands headed west, especially to California; the migrants, many of them from Oklahoma, were disparagingly called “Okies.” Some states tried to keep them out, and California officials briefly blockaded the border in 1935–1936. Dorothea Lange’s 1936 photograph Migrant Mother, taken at a farmworkers’ camp in Nipomo, California, and John Steinbeck’s 1939 novel The Grapes of Wrath made the migrants’ hardship a national story. Federal drought relief began in 1932, with funds specifically for drought relief released in the fall of 1933. In March 1935 soil scientist Hugh Hammond Bennett, a Roosevelt adviser, testified to Congress on the need for better soil conservation — by one widely told account, as dust from the Plains darkened the sky over Washington — and Congress passed the Soil Conservation Act that year. A 1937 Works Progress Administration bulletin reported that 21 percent of rural Plains families were on federal relief. Near-normal rains returned by 1941, and World War II revived the farm economy. The 1930s drought remains the nation’s “drought of record.” Its lessons — soil conservation, windbreaks, and government drought planning — reduced the damage when severe drought returned to the Plains in the 1950s. The Dust Bowl was one of the worst environmental disasters in American history, a human-made catastrophe as much as a natural one, and it changed how Americans farm and manage land. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sxG6Lwkzi7c The Dust Bowl: Darkness in the Great Depression Geographics 19:21 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pJ9QOcVt1Hc The Dust Bowl and the Depression NBC News Learn 3:42 2026-10-22

title: The Election of 1800
subtitle: The first transfer of power between rival parties
summary: In 1800 the Democratic-Republicans under Thomas Jefferson defeated President John Adams and the Federalists in a bitter campaign fought largely in partisan newspapers. A flaw in the Constitution produced a tie between Jefferson and his own running mate, Aaron Burr, throwing the decision to the House of Representatives, which deadlocked through thirty-five ballots before choosing Jefferson. The result was the first peaceful transfer of power from one party to another in the United States.
location: Nationwide; decided in the House of Representatives, Washington, D.C.
thumbAlt: Campaign banner celebrating Thomas Jefferson
themeText: Parties and elections The presidency Constitution and law
text: Nationwide; decided in the House of Representatives, Washington, D.C. Electoral votes Jefferson 73, Burr 73, Adams 65, Pinckney 64 Decided by The House of Representatives, after 35 deadlocked ballots Result Jefferson president, Burr vice president Constitutional fix The Twelfth Amendment (1804) required separate electoral votes for president and vice president By 1800 the country was divided between two parties. Federalists, led by Adams and Alexander Hamilton, favored a strong national government, commercial development, and good relations with Britain. Democratic-Republicans, led by Jefferson and James Madison, championed states’ rights, farmers, and sympathy for France. Adams’s administration had grown unpopular after the Alien and Sedition Acts, a direct tax in 1798, military preparations for a possible war with France, and the use of troops against Fries’s Rebellion in Pennsylvania. The Federalists were also split. Many opposed Adams for making peace with France rather than declaring war. Hamilton wrote a letter attacking Adams’s character that was leaked to the press. To carry the crucial state of New York, the Republicans put Aaron Burr of New York on the ticket with Jefferson. The campaign was waged through party newspapers and pamphlets, with each side accusing the other of threatening the republic. When the electoral votes came in, Jefferson and Burr each had 73. Under the original Constitution, each elector cast two votes without distinguishing between president and vice president, so the tie between the two Republicans sent the election to the House, where the Federalists held a majority. For days the House deadlocked. Through thirty-five ballots, no candidate won a majority of state delegations. Hamilton, who despised Burr as unprincipled, persuaded some Federalists to cast blank ballots rather than support either man, and Jefferson was finally elected. Jefferson took office in March 1801 and, in his inaugural address, called for unity: “We are all Republicans, we are all Federalists.” Before leaving, Adams and the outgoing Federalist Congress expanded the federal judiciary and filled it with Federalist judges, setting up the conflict that produced Marbury v. Madison. Hamilton’s role in Burr’s defeat deepened the feud that ended in their 1804 duel. Jefferson later called his victory “the revolution of 1800.” Whatever its revolutionary character, the election showed that power could pass peacefully between bitterly opposed parties under the Constitution — a precedent that later generations would rely on. The Twelfth Amendment, ratified in 1804, changed the Electoral College so that electors vote separately for president and vice president. The election of 1800 established that an American government could be voted out and would leave — the foundation of the peaceful transfer of power. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ictBD6U4xU4 The American Presidential Election of 1800 Mr. Beat 3:39 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ctASCMhLFVM What Really Happened With the Political Mayhem of the Election of 1800? title: The End of the Cold War
subtitle: The fall of communism in Eastern Europe and the collapse of the Soviet Union, 1989–1991
summary: Between 1989 and 1991, the communist regimes of Eastern Europe collapsed one after another, the Berlin Wall fell, and the Soviet Union itself dissolved. Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev’s reforms, perestroika (restructuring) and glasnost (openness), and his decision not to use force to prop up allied regimes made peaceful change possible. Presidents Ronald Reagan and George H. W. Bush combined pressure with negotiation. On December 25, 1991, Gorbachev resigned and the Soviet flag came down over the Kremlin, leaving the United States the world’s only superpower.
location: Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union
thumbAlt: East and West Germans at the Brandenburg Gate in 1989
aliases: fall of the Berlin Wall collapse of the Soviet Union Gorbachev perestroika glasnost
themeText: The Cold War Foreign policy and diplomacy The presidency
text: Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union INF Treaty 1987: Reagan and Gorbachev agree to reduce nuclear arsenals Poland Solidarity wins elections, June 4, 1989 Berlin Wall Opened November 9, 1989 Failed coup August 1991, against Gorbachev Soviet Union ends December 25, 1991 By the 1980s the Soviet economy was stagnating, and a costly war in Afghanistan drained its resources. Reagan built up American forces and denounced the Soviet Union, while backing anticommunist movements worldwide. Gorbachev, who came to power in 1985, believed the Soviet system needed reform and sought to end the ruinous arms race. He met Reagan at Geneva in 1985 and Reykjavik in 1986, and the two signed the Intermediate Nuclear Forces Treaty in 1987. Gorbachev also abandoned the policy of using Soviet troops to support communist governments in Eastern Europe. Historians emphasize that the most significant causes of the collapse lay within the Soviet empire itself. In Poland, round-table talks with the banned union Solidarity led to elections on June 4, 1989, which Solidarity won overwhelmingly; by August the country had Eastern Europe’s first non-communist prime minister. Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Romania, Bulgaria, and East Germany followed. On November 9, 1989, jubilant crowds brought down the Berlin Wall. Gorbachev accepted German reunification, and a reunited Germany joined NATO. Inside the Soviet Union, reforms unraveled the system. A failed hard-line coup in August 1991 fatally weakened Gorbachev; republics declared independence, and in December the leaders of Russia, Ukraine, and Belarus formed the Commonwealth of Independent States. On December 25, 1991, Gorbachev resigned as president of the Soviet Union, and the Soviet flag was lowered over the Kremlin for the last time, replaced by the Russian tricolor. The Bush administration focused on stability and security in Russia and the other former Soviet states. The end of the Cold War left the United States as the sole superpower and seemed to many to signal the global triumph of democracy and capitalism. It reshaped American defense priorities, alliances, and politics for the decades that followed. The peaceful end of the Cold War closed a four-decade conflict that had shaped American life and lifted the threat of superpower nuclear war. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=I79TpDe3t2g The Cold War - OverSimplified (Part 1) OverSimplified 16:03 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L-K19rVDxoM George HW Bush and the End of the Cold War: Crash Course US History #44 CrashCourse 13:53 2026-10-22

title: The Erie Canal
subtitle: The 363-mile “artificial river” that linked the Great Lakes to New York City in 1825
summary: Built between 1817 and 1825, the Erie Canal ran 363 miles across upstate New York from Albany on the Hudson River to Buffalo on Lake Erie. Dug largely by hand, climbing hills through 83 locks, it was the longest artificial waterway and the greatest public works project in North America. It cut shipping costs by 90 percent, opened the interior of the continent to settlers and trade, made New York City the nation’s leading port and financial center, and launched a national canal-building boom.
thumbAlt: 1839 engraving of the Erie Canal at Lockport, New York, after a picture by W. H. Bartlett
aliases: Erie Canal Erie Canalway DeWitt Clinton Lockport
themeText: Economy and finance Science and technology Territorial expansion Cities and urban life Immigration
text: Albany to Buffalo, New York Built 1817 (begun at Rome, New York) to 1825 Size 363 miles long, 4 feet deep, 40 feet wide; 83 locks and 18 aqueducts; a 571-foot rise from Albany to Buffalo Cost $7,143,789 — repaid within ten years Speed and savings Albany to Buffalo in five days instead of two weeks by stagecoach; shipping costs cut by 90 percent Champion DeWitt Clinton, New York’s leading canal advocate Today Still in use; part of a National Historic Landmark and the Erie Canalway National Heritage Corridor (2000) The Erie Canal was the centerpiece of the transportation revolution that tied the young nation together. By connecting the Midwest to the Atlantic, it made New York the “Empire State,” linked Great Lakes farms with eastern cities and factories, and showed what public investment and engineering could achieve. In the early 1800s hauling goods overland by ox-drawn wagon was slow and expensive. Improved roads and steamboats were beginning a transportation revolution, and states and localities began connecting rivers and streams with canals. In New York, DeWitt Clinton — a former state legislator, U.S. senator, and mayor of New York City — became the canal’s most persistent and effective champion. Clinton served on the commission that made the first surveys for a canal across the state and then led the political effort that made it a reality. New York State built the canal, and it would repay its cost of more than $7 million within about ten years. Construction began at Rome, New York, in 1817. Few Americans had any experience building canals, so the project became the nation’s first practical school of civil engineering. Laborers — mostly American-born, some Irish immigrants — worked for eight years through heat, mud, and freezing cold, earning 80 cents to a dollar a day, clearing forests and digging mile after mile largely with hand tools and animal power. They invented stump-pulling machines, developed a hydraulic cement that hardened underwater, and blasted rock with hand drills and black powder. At Lockport they cut a staircase of five locks through the solid rock of the Niagara Escarpment. The canal crossed rivers on aqueducts and climbed hills through 83 locks. It opened along its full length in 1825. Packet boats carried passengers from Albany to Buffalo in five days, less than half the stagecoach time, and freight costs fell by 90 percent compared with ox-drawn wagons. Midwestern grain, lumber, and minerals flowed east to Albany and down the Hudson to New York City, while manufactured goods and settlers flowed west. The canal paid for itself in about ten years. Towns along its route — Syracuse, Rochester, Buffalo — boomed so fast that it was called the “Mother of Cities,” and their populations quadrupled between 1830 and 1850. The canal’s success set off a canal-building boom in other states and secured New York City’s place as the nation’s busiest port, largest city, and center of commerce and finance. It carried more westbound immigrants than any other canal over the Appalachians, and along its corridor ideas traveled too: abolitionism, women’s rights utopian experiments, and new religious movements flourished there. Enlarged three times, the canal system has operated continuously since 1825, longer than any other built transportation system in North America; its old towpath is now a 365-mile bike trail. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iLfGSXuHu5g 200 years on the Erie Canal CBS Sunday Morning 7:49 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mTDHeSCDqig The Erie Canal: Traversing the American Midwest Before Railroads Megaprojects 15:14 2026-10-22

title: The First Africans in Virginia
subtitle: 1619: Enslaved Angolans arrive at Point Comfort
summary: In late August 1619, the English privateer White Lion arrived at Point Comfort, Virginia, and traded about twenty Africans for food; the ship Treasurer soon brought a few more. They had been captured in west central Africa, most likely from the kingdom of Ndongo in present-day Angola, and taken from a Portuguese slave ship bound for Mexico. They were the first documented Africans in English Virginia, and their arrival is often taken as the beginning of the history of slavery in what became the United States.
thumbAlt: Howard Pyle’s 1901 illustration imagining the arrival of Africans at Jamestown in 1619
themeText: Slavery and emancipation African American history Colonial encounters
text: Point Comfort (present-day Hampton), Virginia Arrived August 1619, at Point Comfort, Virginia Ships The privateers White Lion and Treasurer Origin Probably Kimbundu-speaking people from Ndongo, in present-day Angola Status Contested — but historical evidence suggests they were often treated in ways that resemble enslavement By 1619, the Portuguese had been capturing and enslaving people in west central Africa, including from the kingdom of Ndongo, whose people raised crops and animals and mostly followed local religions. Virginia’s tobacco economy, launched in 1612, created a hunger for labor that English indentured servants only partly filled. In 1619 a Portuguese slave ship sailed from west central Africa for New Spain (Mexico) carrying captives from Ndongo. Two English privateers, the White Lion and the Treasurer, attacked it and took some of the captives. Many had probably had contact with Catholic missionaries, since Portuguese law required enslaved Africans to be baptized before reaching America. The White Lion reached Point Comfort in late August 1619, and about twenty Africans were sold in exchange for food. A few days later the Treasurer arrived and sold two or three more. Most were distributed to the households of colonial leaders. Census records from the 1620s and 1630s list Africans living at Jamestown and on plantations such as Flowerdew Hundred, many identified only by first names, among them a woman named Angelo purchased by William Peirce. The legal status of these first Africans is debated. Virginia had not yet written laws defining slavery, and some Africans, such as Anthony and Mary Johnson, gained their freedom and bought land. But the National Park Service notes that the evidence suggests they were often treated in a manner closely resembling enslavement. More captives followed: in 1628 a shipload of about 100 Angolans was sold in Virginia. Over the following decades, Virginia’s laws hardened lifelong, inherited slavery based on race, and enslaved Africans replaced indentured servants as the colony’s main labor force. The year 1619 has become a symbol of slavery’s deep roots in English America — a system that ended only with the Thirteenth Amendment in 1865. The arrival of the first Africans at Point Comfort marks the beginning of the African American experience in English North America and of the system of racial slavery that shaped the country’s economy, politics, and conflicts for nearly 250 years.

title: The Great Depression
subtitle: The deepest economic collapse in American history, 1929–1941
summary: The Great Depression was the longest and deepest economic downturn in the history of the United States and the modern industrial economy. Beginning in 1929, it brought a stock market crash, thousands of bank failures, collapsing farm prices, and unemployment that reached about a quarter of the workforce. The Federal Reserve’s own historians now say its mistakes made the slump far worse. Herbert Hoover’s reliance on voluntary action gave way to Franklin D. Roosevelt’s New Deal, which transformed the federal government, but full recovery came only with World War II.

text: Nationwide and worldwide Began August 1929, when the expansion of the 1920s ended; the stock market crashed that October Bottom March 1933, when the banking system collapsed and Roosevelt declared a national bank holiday Unemployment 24.9 percent (12,830,000 people) in 1933; Black unemployment as high as 50 percent Bank failures About 1,350 in 1930 and more than 2,200 in 1931; some 5,000 between 1929 and 1933 Money supply Fell by nearly 30 percent from the fall of 1930 to the winter of 1933 Stock market The Dow fell 89 percent from its 1929 peak by July 1932 and did not recover until 1954 The 1920s looked like an age of prosperity. Automobiles, telephones, and radios spread across the country, and ordinary men and women bought stocks, often on margin: they put down about 10 percent of the price and borrowed the rest. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose sixfold, from 63 in August 1921 to 381 in September 1929. Just after the peak, the economist Irving Fisher declared that stock prices had reached “what looks like a permanently high plateau.” Beneath the boom lay serious weaknesses. The gains were unequal: per capita income rose 10 percent for all Americans during the decade, but 75 percent for the wealthiest. By 1929, the Miller Center notes, 5 percent of Americans held nearly a third of the nation’s money and property, while more than 80 percent had no savings at all. Industrial wages stagnated while profits poured into the stock market, and the market for cars and appliances was nearing saturation. Even in good years, unemployment hovered around 7 percent. Farmers had been in trouble since 1920–1921, when prices for cotton, grain, and other crops collapsed; by the late 1920s farm incomes had shrunk to a third of the national average, and many farmers could not repay loans taken out in better times. Abroad, the international gold standard, rebuilt after World War I, made the world’s economies rigid and closely linked, so that a shock in one country spread quickly to the others. Historians and economists still debate the Depression’s causes, and most see several working together. The Miller Center lists structural weaknesses in agriculture and industry, a fragile international economy, and a speculative, unstable financial sector, all of which created a badly unequal distribution of wealth: “a consumer economy in which few consumed.” Monetary policy turned a downturn into a catastrophe. In 1928 and 1929 the Federal Reserve raised interest rates to curb stock speculation, and because of the gold standard its tight money pushed other nations into recession too. Then, when banks began to fail, the Fed did not act as a lender of last resort. Some of its leaders even believed that weak banks should be allowed to fail. Hoover’s Treasury secretary, Andrew Mellon, who sat on the Federal Reserve Board, held this “liquidationist” view. From the fall of 1930 through the winter of 1933, the money supply fell by nearly 30 percent, and prices fell with it. That deflation raised the real burden of debts and drove banks, firms, and families into bankruptcy. In 2002, Ben Bernanke, then a Federal Reserve governor, admitted publicly that the Fed’s mistakes had contributed to the “worst economic disaster in American history.” Trade policy made things worse. In June 1930 Hoover signed the Smoot-Hawley Tariff, which raised rates on farm and factory imports to historic levels. Other countries retaliated, and between 1929 and 1932 world trade fell from $36 billion to $12 billion; American exports fell by 78 percent. Some Democrats later claimed that the tariff had caused the Depression, a charge the Miller Center calls politically motivated, since the slump was already well under way. Most economists agree, however, that it deepened the crisis. The crash. On Thursday, October 24, 1929, stock prices suddenly plunged. Leading bankers met at the offices of J. P. Morgan and ostentatiously bought shares to halt the slide, but the panic resumed the next week. On Black Monday, October 28, the Dow fell nearly 13 percent, and on Black Tuesday, October 29, nearly 12 percent more. By mid-November the market had lost almost half its value. Shares of U.S. Steel fell from $262 to $22. Only about 2.5 percent of Americans had brokerage accounts, and the crash alone did not cause the Depression. But it frightened consumers, who stopped buying cars and other goods on credit, and companies like Ford cut production and laid off workers. The market kept sliding until July 1932, when the Dow closed at 41.22, 89 percent below its peak. It did not regain its 1929 level until November 1954. The bank panics. By the fall of 1930 the recession had lasted fifteen months, about as long as earlier downturns, and recovery seemed near. Then, in November 1930, the collapse of Caldwell and Company, the South’s largest financial holding company, set off a chain of failures among the banks that kept their reserves with it, and panic spread from town to town. On December 11 the Bank of United States, the fourth-largest bank in New York City, closed. More waves of panic followed in 1931 and 1932. About 1,350 banks failed in 1930 and more than 2,200 in 1931; between 1929 and 1933, some 5,000 collapsed, taking depositors’ savings with them. The Federal Reserve’s response varied by district. The Atlanta Fed rushed cash to troubled banks, and its region recovered sooner; the St. Louis Fed refused to help banks outside the system, and hundreds of them failed. Hard times. By 1933, 24.9 percent of the workforce, 12,830,000 people, were unemployed, and many who still had jobs worked only part time. Workers who kept their jobs saw their wages fall by 42.5 percent between 1929 and 1933. One in four farms went into foreclosure. Families exhausted their savings, borrowed from relatives, ran up credit at the corner store, and finally turned to charities, which were themselves running dry: by mid-1932 a quarter of New York’s private charities had closed, and relief agencies in Atlanta could give needy families only $1.30 a week. The homeless built shantytowns of packing crates and scrap metal, mockingly called “Hoovervilles,” and young people whose families could no longer feed them rode the rails in search of work. Employers were quicker to fire married women, on the assumption that they did not need to work. Black workers were generally the last hired and the first fired. In 1932, when national unemployment was about 25 percent, Black unemployment reached as high as 50 percent. The Dust Bowl. On the Great Plains, drought began in 1932 and lasted until at least 1936. Decades of plowing had stripped away the grass that held the soil, and winds whipped the exposed topsoil into dust storms that darkened the sky as far east as Washington, D.C., and the Atlantic. Ruined farmers from Oklahoma, Texas, Kansas, and Arkansas headed west to California; Oklahoma alone lost 440,000 people, 18.4 percent of its 1930 population. California, Florida, and Colorado set up “border blockades” in the winter of 1935–1936 to turn poor migrants away. Dorothea Lange’s 1936 photograph Migrant Mother, taken at a camp for farmworkers in Nipomo, California, became the era’s most famous image. Deportation. Fearing competition for scarce jobs, the Hoover administration tightened immigration rules in September 1930, and between 1930 and 1932 some 54,000 people were deported. Mexican immigrants and Mexican Americans were hit hardest. In Los Angeles, officials staged deportation raids and pressured Mexicans and Mexican Americans on relief to leave “voluntarily” for Mexico. From 1930 to 1940 the Mexican-born population of Arizona, California, New Mexico, and Texas fell from 616,998 to 377,433. Hoover’s response. Hoover was not idle, but he believed that voluntary cooperation, not federal relief, was the answer. “Any lack of confidence in the economic future and the basic strength of business in the United States is simply foolish,” he said in November 1929. He won pledges from business leaders not to cut wages, urged states and cities to expand public works, and created committees to coordinate private charity. “We cannot legislate ourselves out of a world economic depression,” he told Congress in 1931. As the crisis deepened he took steps that were radical for him: the Reconstruction Finance Corporation (1932) lent money to banks, railroads, and other businesses, and the Emergency Relief and Construction Act provided $2 billion for public works and $300 million for relief programs run by the states. Critics such as Congressman Fiorello La Guardia called the RFC a “millionaire’s dole.” The Bonus Army. In the summer of 1932, more than fifteen thousand unemployed World War I veterans and their families camped in Washington to demand early payment of a bonus that was not due until 1945. “While there were billions for bankers,” they complained, “there was nothing for the poor.” After the Senate voted the bonus down, most went home, but thousands stayed. Troops under General Douglas MacArthur drove the remaining veterans out with tear gas, bayonets, and tanks and burned their camp at Anacostia Flats. Accounts of the attack differ. The American Yawp writes that Hoover ordered the veterans out and that two marchers and a baby died. The Miller Center says that Hoover ordered a peaceful removal, that War Secretary Patrick Hurley and MacArthur exceeded their orders, and that one veteran was killed. Either way, the images helped seal Hoover’s defeat. In November 1932 voters turned Hoover out in a landslide and elected Franklin D. Roosevelt, who had promised “a new deal for the American people.” By his inauguration on March 4, 1933, the banking system had collapsed, and the Federal Reserve dates the bottom of the Depression to that month. “The only thing we have to fear is fear itself,” Roosevelt told the nation. He declared a national bank holiday, and in his first hundred days Congress passed a wave of laws that created the agencies of the New Deal. New banking laws created federal deposit insurance and reformed the financial system, and the United States left the gold standard in 1933. Recovery began in 1933 but was slow and incomplete. After the Federal Reserve doubled banks’ reserve requirements in 1936 and federal fiscal policy tightened, the economy fell in May 1937 into a sharp “recession within the Depression” that lasted until June 1938. Industrial production fell 32 percent, and unemployment rose again to 20 percent. Only when war orders and defense spending poured in did the economy return to full employment. Output grew by 49 percent from 1938 to 1942, and the Depression ended in 1941. The Great Depression changed the relationship between Americans and their government. Before it, Washington played a small role in economic life; afterward, Americans expected the federal government to protect bank deposits, regulate the stock market, provide old-age pensions and unemployment insurance, and act to prevent mass unemployment. The reforms of the 1930s, and the lessons drawn from the Fed’s failures, turned the Federal Reserve into a modern central bank. In 2002 Bernanke, speaking at a conference honoring Milton Friedman, whose research with Anna Schwartz had laid much of the blame on the Fed, promised “we won’t do it again.” The Depression also reshaped American foreign policy. It pushed the United States further into isolation during the 1930s, as Japan, Italy, and Germany began their aggressions. In the long run, the State Department’s historians conclude, the lesson that turning inward had made the crisis worse helped lead the United States to take a leading role in the world economy after World War II. The Roosevelt Library calls it a test of “the fabric of American life” that caused Americans “to doubt their abilities and their values.” The Great Depression was the worst economic disaster in American history. It discredited the belief that the economy would right itself without government help and gave rise to the New Deal and the modern federal government. Any lack of confidence in the economic future and the basic strength of business in the United States is simply foolish. Herbert Hoover November 1929, weeks after the crash The Negro was born in depression. It didn’t mean too much to him. The Great American Depression … only became official when it hit the white man. A Black pensioner interviewed by the oral historian Studs Terkel My salary could keep us going, but—I am to have a baby. A woman from Humboldt County, California writing to Eleanor Roosevelt in 1934 to ask for a job for her husband, out of work for nearly two years So, first of all, let me assert my firm belief that the only thing we have to fear is fear itself—nameless, unreasoning, unjustified terror which paralyzes needed efforts to convert retreat into advance. Franklin D. title: The Great Recession
subtitle: The financial crisis and deep recession of 2007–2009
summary: The Great Recession began in December 2007 and ended in June 2009, the longest recession since World War II. It grew out of a housing bubble fueled by risky “subprime” mortgages that were bundled into securities and sold throughout the financial system. When homeowners began to default, major financial firms such as Bear Stearns and Lehman Brothers collapsed. Home prices fell about 30 percent, stocks fell 57 percent, and unemployment peaked at 10 percent. The federal government and the Federal Reserve intervened on a massive scale to stabilize the financial system.

text: Nationwide and worldwide Dates December 2007 – June 2009 Output Real GDP fell 4.3 percent, the largest postwar decline Unemployment From 5 percent (December 2007) to a peak of 10 percent (October 2009) Housing Home prices fell about 30 percent from mid-2006 to mid-2009 Stocks S&P 500 fell 57 percent from October 2007 to March 2009 From the 1990s into the 2000s, home prices climbed, and housing-related sectors accounted for roughly 40 percent of net private job creation between 2001 and 2005. Lenders offered high-risk “subprime” mortgages and repackaged them into securities, expanding credit and bidding up prices. Decades of financial deregulation — including the repeal in the 1990s of parts of the Depression-era Glass-Steagall Act and the exemption of credit-default swaps from regulation — had loosened restraints on risky practices. The housing boom peaked in 2006. As prices fell and homeowners defaulted, losses spread through the heavily leveraged financial system, because mortgages had been bundled and resold so often that it was hard to tell who owned what. Major firms such as Bear Stearns and Lehman Brothers disappeared almost overnight. President George W. Bush signed the Emergency Economic Stabilization Act, and the government poured billions into propping up banks. The Federal Reserve cut its key interest rate from 5.25 percent in September 2007 to nearly zero by December 2008 and began buying mortgage-backed securities and other debt to support the housing market and the financial system. President Barack Obama continued the bank rescue and won an $800 billion economic stimulus, the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, in 2009. Millions lost jobs and homes. Resentment of bank bailouts fueled both the conservative Tea Party movement and the left-leaning Occupy Wall Street protests. In 2010 Congress passed the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act to prevent future meltdowns. Recovery was slow: as of 2013 unemployment was still above 7 percent. The crisis magnified rising inequality and deepened distrust of financial and political elites, shaping American politics for years afterward. The Great Recession was the longest recession since World War II, with the largest drop in output of the postwar era, and a defining event for a generation of Americans. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GPOv72Awo68 How it Happened - The 2008 Financial Crisis: Crash Course Economics #12 CrashCourse 11:24 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZZ25uZtey34 Before the Great Recession, “The Warning” (full documentary) FRONTLINE PBS | Official 54:35 2026-10-22

title: The Great Society
subtitle: Lyndon Johnson’s program to end poverty and racial injustice, 1964–1968
summary: The Great Society was President Lyndon B. Johnson’s sweeping program of domestic reform. Announced in a May 1964 speech calling for “an end to poverty and racial injustice,” it produced the most ambitious burst of legislation since the New Deal: the War on Poverty, Medicare and Medicaid, federal aid to education, food stamps, the Civil Rights and Voting Rights Acts, and an immigration law that abolished the national-origins quotas of 1924. Much of it remains in place today.
thumbAlt: President Lyndon Johnson signing the Medicare bill with Harry Truman beside him
aliases: War on Poverty Medicare Medicaid Head Start Economic Opportunity Act Hart-Celler Act Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965
themeText: The presidency Economy and finance Civil rights and citizenship Reform and protest Immigration Public health
text: Washington, D.C., and nationwide Announced May 1964, commencement speech at the University of Michigan War on Poverty Economic Opportunity Act of 1964; about $3 billion; Community Action Programs; Head Start Health Medicare and Medicaid Education Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1965, more than $1 billion Immigration Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 (Hart-Celler) abolished the 1924 quota system In an age of postwar affluence, poverty persisted in cities and rural areas, and Jim Crow still ruled the South. After John F. Kennedy’s assassination in November 1963, Johnson asked Congress to honor Kennedy’s memory by passing his tax cut and civil rights bill — and then set out his own, larger agenda. He won election in his own right by a landslide in 1964. Johnson, shaped by the New Deal and by his own family’s poverty in the Texas Hill Country, believed government could abolish poverty and racial injustice in an age of affluence. Speaking at the University of Michigan in May 1964, he challenged Americans to “enrich and elevate our national life, and to advance the quality of our American civilization.” The Economic Opportunity Act of 1964 launched the War on Poverty. Its most controversial program, Community Action, sought “maximum feasible participation” by the poor themselves in running antipoverty efforts. Congress went on to create Medicare and Medicaid to provide medical care for the elderly and the poor, the first federal food stamp program, and the Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1965, the first major federal investment in public schools. It established the National Endowment for the Arts and the National Endowment for the Humanities. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 and Voting Rights Act of 1965 effectively ended legal Jim Crow, and the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 opened the country to immigrants from around the world, reshaping its population. The War on Poverty and Community Action provoked conservative resistance and helped fuel the rise of Republicans in the South and West. The escalating Vietnam War soon overshadowed Johnson’s domestic agenda, and by 1968 his presidency was consumed by the war. Later presidents and Congresses left intact most of the Great Society — Medicare and Medicaid, food stamps, federal arts funding, and Head Start. Historians continue to debate its record: its programs kept many Americans out of poverty and secured rights for minorities, while reaction against it contributed to a conservative political counterrevolution. The Great Society expanded the federal government’s responsibility for health, education, and poverty more than any reform program since the New Deal. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UTV9a88IO1k Lyndon Johnson's GREAT SOCIETY [APUSH Review Unit 8 Topic 9] Period 8 (1945-1980) Heimler's History 4:08 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pD3Vn44F7as What Were LBJ's "Great Society" Programs? | History HISTORY 3:51 2026-10-22

title: The Haymarket Affair
subtitle: A bomb at a Chicago labor rally, May 4, 1886
summary: On May 4, 1886, about 1,500 workers rallied near Chicago’s Haymarket Square to protest police violence against strikers the day before, during a nationwide campaign for the eight-hour day. As police moved to disperse the crowd, someone threw a bomb; police and possibly others opened fire. Seven police officers and at least one civilian died. Eight anarchists were convicted of murder on little evidence linking them to the bomb; four were hanged. The affair set off a wave of anti-labor and anti-immigrant fear.
thumbAlt: Harper’s Weekly engraving of the Haymarket bombing
themeText: Labor and work Reform and protest Immigration
text: Haymarket Square, Chicago, Illinois Date May 4, 1886 Deaths Seven police officers and at least one civilian; at least 60 wounded Trial Eight men convicted August 20, 1886; seven sentenced to death Executions Four hanged November 11, 1887; one died by suicide; three later pardoned (1893) In the 1880s strikes spread as workers protested long hours and low wages, and unions launched a national campaign for the eight-hour day, centered on May 1, 1886. Chicago, a fast-growing industrial and immigrant city, was a center of both the labor movement and radical anarchist politics. On May 3, police fired on strikers at the McCormick Harvesting Machine Company, leaving one man dead and many injured. Labor activists called a protest rally for the next evening. On May 4 at 7:30 p.m., around 1,500 people gathered on Desplaines Street near Haymarket Square. Chicago’s mayor, Carter Harrison, attended as an observer and confirmed the meeting was peaceful. As the rally wound down and the mayor left, police arrived to disperse the remaining crowd. Someone threw a bomb. Chaos followed as police, and possibly some in the crowd, opened fire. Seven police officers and at least one civilian died, and at least sixty were wounded. The bomb thrower was never identified. Eight men — the “Chicago Eight,” known for their anarchist politics and pro-labor activism — were charged with murder, though some had not even attended the rally and little evidence connected them to the bomb. On August 20, 1886, a jury found them guilty, and Judge Joseph E. Gary sentenced seven to death. Two sentences were commuted to life imprisonment; Louis Lingg killed himself in his cell; and on November 11, 1887, Adolph Fischer, George Engel, Albert Parsons, and August Spies were hanged. In 1893 Illinois Governor John P. Altgeld pardoned the three surviving defendants. The affair set off a wave of xenophobia and anti-labor sentiment in Chicago and across the country, damaging the Knights of Labor and the eight-hour movement as many Americans associated labor activism with violence and foreign radicals. To many workers at home and abroad, the executed men became martyrs. Haymarket became a symbol of the bitter conflict between labor and capital in the Gilded Age — and of how fear of radicalism could override due process. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6okibrpyeUs Haymarket Strike NBC News Learn 3:40 2026-10-22

title: Independence Day (the Fourth of July)
subtitle: The nation’s birthday, celebrated since 1776 and a federal holiday since 1870
summary: Independence Day marks July 4, 1776, when the Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence. John Adams predicted the day of independence would be celebrated “with Pomp and Parade… Bonfires and Illuminations from one End of this Continent to the other,” and Americans have marked it ever since with parades, music, and public readings of the Declaration. Congress made it one of the first four federal holidays in 1870. It has also been a day for Americans to measure the nation against its founding promise, most famously in Frederick Douglass’s 1852 speech “What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?”

text: Nationwide; the Declaration was adopted in Philadelphia The date July 4, 1776: Congress adopted the final text of the Declaration, two days after voting for independence on July 2 Adams’s prediction He expected July 2 to be “the great anniversary Festival,” celebrated “with Pomp and Parade” Federal holiday Since 1870, one of the first four, with New Year’s Day, Thanksgiving, and Christmas A famous coincidence John Adams and Thomas Jefferson both died on July 4, 1826 — the fiftieth anniversary Milestones Centennial (1876), Bicentennial (1976), and the 250th anniversary in 2026 The Fourth of July is the nation’s chief civic holiday, a celebration not of a battle or a ruler but of a document and its ideas. Because the Declaration promised that all men are created equal, the day has also given every generation of reformers a stage on which to ask whether the nation is living up to its creed. By the summer of 1776, after more than a year of war, a royal proclamation declaring the colonists in “open and avowed rebellion,” and news that the king had hired German mercenaries, many Americans were convinced that Britain was treating the colonies as a foreign entity. On June 7 Richard Henry Lee of Virginia proposed in the Continental Congress that the colonies “are, and of right ought to be, free and independent States.” While Congress postponed the vote, a Committee of Five — John Adams, Benjamin Franklin, Thomas Jefferson, Robert R. Livingston, and Roger Sherman — prepared a declaration explaining the decision to the world, and Jefferson wrote the draft. The holiday grew directly out of the vote for independence. Adams believed that the occasion should be remembered “as the Day of Deliverance by solemn Acts of Devotion to God Almighty” as well as by public festivities, and Americans agreed. On July 2, 1776, Congress voted for independence, with twelve colonies in favor and New York not voting. It then debated and revised Jefferson’s draft through July 3 and into the late morning of July 4, when the Declaration was adopted. John Adams, writing to his wife on July 3, believed that July 2 would be “the most memorable Epocha, in the History of America,” and that it “ought to be solemnized with Pomp and Parade, with Shews, Games, Sports, Guns, Bells, Bonfires and Illuminations from one End of this Continent to the other from this Time forward forever more.” Americans took up his program — but celebrated July 4, the day the Declaration was adopted. For half a century after 1815 the Fourth was one of only three national holidays, along with Washington’s Birthday and the anniversary of Andrew Jackson’s victory at New Orleans. Orators used the day for causes of every kind: William Lloyd Garrison gave an address on slavery at Boston’s Park Street Church on the Fourth of July, 1829, and on July 5, 1852, Frederick Douglass asked an audience in Rochester, New York: “What, to the American slave, is your 4th of July? I answer: a day that reveals to him, more than all other days in the year, the gross injustice and cruelty to which he is the constant victim.” In 1870 Congress made Independence Day one of the first four federal holidays. The anniversary became the centerpiece of American civic life. On July 4, 1826, the fiftieth anniversary, both John Adams and Thomas Jefferson — members of the committee that prepared the Declaration, and once fierce political rivals — died. For the Centennial in 1876 the original Declaration went back to Philadelphia, where it was shown to a crowd on Independence Square on the Fourth and greeted with “cheer after cheer.” The original Declaration has been kept at the National Archives in Washington since 1952 and was first displayed there on Independence Day in 1953, and the Archives’ annual celebration — begun for the Bicentennial in 1976 — includes a public reading of the document. In 2026 the Declaration turned 250. The holiday’s deeper meaning lies in the document it honors: a statement of ideals that Americans have repeatedly invoked to demand that the nation live up to them. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yb7MI8NQLoo America the Story of Us: Declaration of Independence | History HISTORY 4:00 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iIoYdC1Gkq8 History of the 4th of July: Crash Course US History Special CrashCourse 5:28 2026-10-22

title: Indian Removal
subtitle: The forced expulsion of Native nations from the East, 1830–1850
summary: Indian removal was the federal policy of forcing Native nations east of the Mississippi River to give up their homelands and move to “Indian Territory” in what is now Oklahoma. President Andrew Jackson made it a central goal, and Congress passed the Indian Removal Act on May 28, 1830. Through coerced treaties, bribery, and the army, the government relocated about 100,000 people between 1830 and 1850, among them the Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Muscogee Creek, and Seminole nations. The best-known removal, the Cherokee Trail of Tears of 1838–1839, killed thousands. Removal opened millions of acres of rich land east of the Mississippi to white settlers.

thumbAlt: Map of the forced removal routes of the Five Tribes
aliases: Indian Removal Act Trail of Tears Treaty of New Echota Five Civilized Tribes Indian Territory
themeText: Indigenous history Territorial expansion Slavery and emancipation
text: The Southeast and Old Northwest to Indian Territory (present-day Oklahoma) Indian Removal Act Signed by Andrew Jackson, May 28, 1830 Nations removed Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Muscogee Creek, Seminole, and others from the Southeast and Old Northwest People moved About 100,000 between 1830 and 1850 (National Park Service) Treaty of New Echota Signed December 1835 by a small Cherokee faction; ratified by the Senate by one vote, May 23, 1836 Trail of Tears May 1838 to March 1839; deaths estimated from about a thousand on the march to 4,000 or more Resistance Second Seminole War, 1835–1842 From the earliest years of the republic, white settlers pressed onto Native land in the backcountry of the South. Presidents Thomas Jefferson and James Monroe suggested that southeastern nations trade their lands for territory west of the Mississippi, but they did not force the issue. The first great transfer came through war. In 1814 Andrew Jackson defeated the Red Stick Creeks at Horseshoe Bend and imposed a treaty that took more than twenty million acres, about half of present-day Alabama and a fifth of Georgia. Over the next decade Jackson helped negotiate nine of the eleven major treaties that pushed Native nations off their land. Between 1816 and 1840, the Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, and Seminole nations signed more than forty treaties ceding territory. Many of these nations adopted features of white American society in the hope of keeping what remained. The Cherokee had turned to farming, created a written language through Sequoyah’s syllabary, published a newspaper, and adopted a written constitution. Some Cherokee, like some of their white neighbors, held enslaved people. None of this protected them. State and federal governments kept pressing them to sign away more land. Settlers wanted the land, and the states wanted Native nations gone. When gold was found on Cherokee land in 1830, Georgia held lotteries to hand Cherokee land and gold rights to white settlers, and it passed laws forbidding Cherokees to conduct tribal business, testify in court against whites, or mine gold. Jackson, who had made his name fighting Native nations, held that the federal government had no right to protect the Cherokees against Georgia. He urged Congress to pass a removal law, and on May 28, 1830, he signed the Indian Removal Act. It authorized the president to exchange land west of the Mississippi for the homelands of nations that agreed to leave, to pay for their move, and to guarantee them their new land “forever.” It was the only major law passed at Jackson’s request in his eight years as president. In December 1830 he told Congress that “the benevolent policy of the Government, steadily pursued for nearly thirty years,” was “approaching to a happy consummation.” “What good man,” he asked, “would prefer a country covered with forests and ranged by a few thousand savages to our extensive Republic, studded with cities, towns, and prosperous farms?” With the act in place, the State Department’s historians write, Jackson and his followers were free to “persuade, bribe, and threaten” nations into signing removal treaties. The Choctaws and Chickasaws submitted, and the Creeks agreed under duress. An estimated 3,500 Creeks died in Alabama and on the journey west, some of them transported in chains. In the north, a short campaign in 1832 crushed resistance by Black Hawk’s band of Sauk and Fox. In Florida the Seminoles, joined by free Black people and people who had escaped slavery, fought the Second Seminole War from 1835 to 1842. An American commander called it “a negro, not an Indian War.” By the end of Jackson’s presidency almost seventy removal treaties had moved nearly 50,000 eastern Native people west. The National Park Service counts about 100,000 people removed between 1830 and 1850. The Cherokee fought in the courts. In Cherokee Nation v. Georgia (1831), Chief Justice John Marshall called the tribes “domestic dependent nations” but ruled that the Court lacked jurisdiction. The next year, in Worcester v. Georgia, the Court held that Georgia’s laws did not apply within Cherokee territory. Jackson refused to enforce the ruling. According to a much-repeated story, he said that Marshall “has made his decision; let him enforce it now if he can.” The National Park Service reports the words as something he “reportedly said.” In December 1835 federal agents met a minority faction at New Echota, Georgia. Only 300 to 500 Cherokees attended, and none were elected officials of the nation. Twenty men signed a treaty giving up all Cherokee land east of the Mississippi for $5 million and new land in Indian Territory. More than 15,000 Cherokees protested, but on May 23, 1836, the Senate ratified it by a single vote. (The State Department’s summary says Congress ratified the treaty in 1835. The National Park Service gives the Senate’s vote of May 1836.) Most Cherokees, including Principal Chief John Ross, did not believe they would really be forced out. In May 1838, under Jackson’s successor Martin Van Buren, federal troops and state militia began rounding up more than 16,000 Cherokees in Tennessee, Alabama, North Carolina, and Georgia. Families were separated, the elderly and sick forced out at gunpoint, and white looters ransacked homes as their owners were led away. Three groups sent west by water that summer suffered badly in drought. Ross then won permission from General Winfield Scott to lead the rest of the removal himself. Detachments of about a thousand people each set out on the 800-mile overland route that autumn. The National Park Service counts twelve such overland groups on one page and fourteen detachments in all on another. Heavy rains, mud, ice on the Ohio and Mississippi rivers, and short rations made the winter crossing deadly. “People feel bad when they leave Old Nation,” one survivor remembered. “Womens cry and make sad wails. Children cry and many men cry.” The last survivors reached Indian Territory in March 1839. No one knows how many died. The sources give different figures: The missionary doctor Elizur Butler, who traveled with the Cherokees, estimated more than 4,000, nearly a fifth of the nation. The National Archives says about 4,000 of 16,000. The State Department’s historians give 3,000 to 4,000 of 15,000 to 16,000. Another National Park Service page counts more than a thousand deaths on the march, with perhaps several thousand more from its consequences. The American Yawp says that of 16,000 who set out, only 10,000 completed the journey. By the 1840s, apart from a few Seminoles still resisting in Florida, no Native nation remained in the American South between the Atlantic and the Mississippi. The removed nations rebuilt in Indian Territory. In August 1839 the Cherokee elected John Ross principal chief of the reunited nation, with its capital at Tahlequah, which remains the Cherokee Nation’s headquarters today. About a thousand Cherokees who escaped the roundup in the mountains became the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians in North Carolina. The Cherokee, Choctaw, and Chickasaw built their own school systems in the West. The State Department’s historians conclude that through “coerced treaties and the contravention of treaties and judicial determination,” the government cleared the way for westward expansion. Indian removal stripped the southeastern nations of their homelands and defied the Supreme Court to do it, and the Trail of Tears became the most painful symbol of the policy. What good man would prefer a country covered with forests and ranged by a few thousand savages to our extensive Republic, studded with cities, towns, and prosperous farms? Andrew Jackson annual message to Congress, December 6, 1830 Long time we travel on way to new land. People feel bad when they leave Old Nation. Womens cry and make sad wails. Children cry and many men cry. A survivor of the Trail of Tears as recorded by the National Park Service One each day. Then all are gone. title: The Founding of Jamestown
subtitle: The first permanent English settlement in North America, 1607
summary: In May 1607, 104 English men and boys sent by the Virginia Company chose a marshy island on the James River for a settlement they named for King James I. Jamestown nearly failed, from disease, hunger, and conflict with the Powhatan peoples whose land it occupied, but survived to become the first permanent English settlement in North America. By 1619 it had brought together three continents: the first representative assembly, the first documented Africans, and tobacco grown for profit on Native land.
thumbAlt: Replicas of the ships that carried the Jamestown colonists
aliases: Virginia Company Powhatan Pocahontas Starving Time
themeText: Colonial encounters Indigenous history Economy and finance Slavery and emancipation
text: Jamestown Island, Virginia Founded May 13, 1607, by 104 English men and boys Sponsor The Virginia Company of London, a private joint-stock company Starving Time Winter 1609–10 Cash crop Tobacco, after John Rolfe introduced a new strain in 1612 1619 First representative assembly (July 30); first documented Africans arrive The Chesapeake region was home to the Powhatan Indians, an Algonquian-speaking people led by a paramount chief the English called Powhatan. Archeological evidence shows that Native people used the Jamestown site more than 10,000 years ago. England, after the failure at Roanoke, tried again with a commercial venture: the Virginia Company, whose investors wanted a return on their money. The colonists left England in December 1606 on three ships — the Susan Constant, the Godspeed, and the Discovery. They chose Jamestown for its defensibility: surrounded by water on three sides, far upriver from Spanish raiders, with deep water for ships. The site was also not inhabited by Native people, though it lay within Powhatan hunting lands. The colonists finished a triangular fort by June 15, 1607. Disease — partly from drinking salty river water — killed many in the first months. Without food sent by Powhatan, the settlement would most likely have failed. By late 1609, as the English demanded too much food during a drought, relations collapsed. In the winter of 1609–10, the “Starving Time,” colonists afraid to leave the fort ate animals, leather, and in some cases the bodies of the dead. In May 1610, survivors were about to abandon Jamestown when a new governor and supplies arrived. The colony’s fortunes changed in 1612, when John Rolfe introduced a new strain of tobacco that became the cash crop the Virginia Company had hoped for. Rolfe’s marriage in 1614 to Pocahontas, Powhatan’s daughter — who had been kidnapped by the English in 1613 and converted to Christianity — brought a period of peace. In 1619 Governor George Yeardley called the first representative legislative assembly, the beginning of representative government in what became the United States. That same year the first documented Africans were brought to Virginia and sold, and the Virginia Company shipped about 90 women to the colony to start families. Tobacco’s demand for land and labor drove expansion onto Powhatan territory. In March 1622 the paramount chief Opechancanough launched a coordinated attack that killed 350–400 colonists; another in 1644 killed a similar number. After Opechancanough’s capture and death in 1646, the Powhatan were reduced to tributary status. In 1624 the king revoked the bankrupt Virginia Company’s charter and Virginia became a royal colony. Jamestown set patterns that shaped the South and the nation: representative government for some; a plantation economy built on tobacco; the dispossession of Native peoples; and, increasingly, slavery. Bacon’s Rebellion in 1676 — frontier colonists attacking Native peoples and defying the governor — exposed tensions among poor whites, elites, and Native nations. Jamestown remained the capital until 1699, when the government moved to Williamsburg. Jamestown was where English America began, and where the contradictions of American history — self-government alongside slavery and conquest — first took shape together. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o69TvQqyGdg When is Thanksgiving?
