title: Japanese American Incarceration
subtitle: The forced removal and imprisonment of Japanese Americans during World War II
summary: After Japan attacked Pearl Harbor, the United States government forced about 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry from their homes on the West Coast and held them in camps for most of World War II. Nearly 70,000 of them were American citizens. None was charged with a crime, and none could appeal. The removal rested on Executive Order 9066, signed by President Franklin D. Roosevelt on February 19, 1942, and the Supreme Court upheld it in Korematsu v. United States (1944). In 1988 Congress acknowledged that the incarceration was a “grave injustice” caused by “racial prejudice, wartime hysteria, and a failure of political leadership.” It apologized and paid $20,000 to each survivor.
location: West Coast exclusion zones; ten War Relocation Centers in California, Arizona, Utah, Idaho, Wyoming, Colorado, and Arkansas
thumbAlt: Rows of barracks at the Manzanar War Relocation Center
aliases: Japanese American internment internment camps War Relocation Authority Civil Liberties Act of 1988 redress Executive Order 9066
themeText: Asian American history Civil rights and citizenship War and the military Constitution and law Immigration
text: West Coast exclusion zones; ten War Relocation Centers in California, Arizona, Utah, Idaho, Wyoming, Colorado, and Arkansas Executive Order 9066 Signed February 19, 1942, about ten weeks after Pearl Harbor People removed About 122,000 (National Archives); other sources give 110,000 to 120,000 Citizens Nearly 70,000, about two-thirds of those removed Camps Ten War Relocation Centers, after temporary “assembly centers” Supreme Court Korematsu v. United States, December 18, 1944, upheld the removal 6 to 3 Exclusion lifted January 2, 1945 Redress Civil Liberties Act, signed August 10, 1988: apology and $20,000 per survivor; 82,219 people received payments Between 1861 and 1940 about 275,000 Japanese immigrants came to Hawaii and the mainland United States, most of them between 1898 and 1924, when new quotas ended Asian immigration. On the West Coast they farmed marginal land, fished, and ran small businesses. In 1940 Japanese Americans controlled less than 4 percent of California’s farmland but produced more than 10 percent of the value of its farm output. They faced discrimination at every turn. Real estate agents kept them in ethnic enclaves, a 1913 California law barred immigrants who could not become citizens from owning land, and in 1922 the Supreme Court ruled in Ozawa v. United States that Japanese immigrants could be denied citizenship. The immigrant generation, the Issei, therefore remained aliens, while their American-born children, the Nisei, were citizens by birth. Japan’s attack on Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941, set off fears for national security, especially on the West Coast. The National Archives notes that these fears combined with economic competition, distrust of cultural separateness, and long-standing anti-Asian racism. Lobbyists from Western states, many of them representing competing farm interests or nativist groups, pressed Congress and the president to remove all people of Japanese descent, Issei and Nisei alike. Justice Department officials raised constitutional and ethical objections, so the army carried out the plan instead. German and Italian nationals were also interned, more than ten thousand of them, but individually and after reviews. People of Japanese descent were removed as a group. On February 19, 1942, Roosevelt signed Executive Order 9066. It authorized the secretary of war and military commanders to “prescribe military areas … from which any or all persons may be excluded.” It named no ethnic group. Lieutenant General John L. DeWitt of the Western Defense Command then imposed curfews on Japanese Americans only. On March 21 Congress made violating the military orders a crime punishable by up to a year in prison. DeWitt first asked Japanese Americans to leave the coastal zones voluntarily. Only about 7 percent complied, and officials in inland states refused to accept Japanese Americans except under guard. On March 29, 1942, he ordered the forced removal of the remaining West Coast residents of Japanese ancestry on 48 hours’ notice. The speed of the removal forced many families to sell homes, farms, and businesses in a hurry. Over the next six months about 122,000 men, women, and children were moved first to temporary “assembly centers” and then to ten fenced and guarded “relocation centers” in remote parts of six Western states and Arkansas: Manzanar and Tule Lake in California, Poston and Gila River in Arizona, Topaz in Utah, Minidoka in Idaho, Heart Mountain in Wyoming, Granada in Colorado, and Jerome and Rohwer in Arkansas. The federal courts’ educational page counts some 26 sites in all. A civilian agency, the War Relocation Authority (WRA), created on March 18, 1942, ran the camps. Its first director, Milton Eisenhower, had hoped for voluntary resettlement, but when Western governors refused to accept Japanese Americans except under guard, he reluctantly planned a network of permanent camps. Dillon Myer replaced him in June 1942. In early 1943 the government gave every adult in the camps a “loyalty questionnaire.” Question 27 asked men whether they would serve in combat wherever ordered, and question 28 asked everyone to swear allegiance to the United States and renounce any allegiance to Japan’s emperor. Many resented being asked to renounce an allegiance they had never held, and Issei, barred from American citizenship, feared being left stateless. Those judged “disloyal” were segregated at Tule Lake, where guards beat inmates and a strike in November 1943 was distorted by West Coast newspapers into a “riot.” Some Japanese Americans fought the orders in court. Fred Korematsu, a young shipyard welder from the Oakland area, refused to report, changed his name and appearance, and was arrested on May 30, 1942. “I was an American citizen,” he later said, “and I had as many rights as anyone else.” On December 18, 1944, the Supreme Court upheld his conviction 6 to 3. Justice Hugo Black wrote that racial restrictions were “immediately suspect” but that “pressing public necessity” could justify them. Korematsu, he said, was excluded “because we are at war with the Japanese Empire.” Justice Frank Murphy called the order the “legalization of racism.” Justice Robert Jackson likened the principle of military necessity the Court had accepted to “a loaded weapon.” The same day the Court decided a companion case, the Endo case, in the prisoner’s favor, but it sidestepped the constitutional question. The day before, the War Department had announced that the exclusion would end on January 2, 1945. Others served. More than 30,000 Japanese Americans fought for the United States in segregated units, while their families remained behind barbed wire. The 442nd Regimental Combat Team, formed on March 23, 1943, with the 100th Infantry Battalion from Hawaii, became the most decorated unit in American military history for its size and length of service. It suffered about 800 killed or missing, and its men won more than 4,000 Purple Hearts and 29 Distinguished Service Crosses. In France in 1944 the 442nd rescued the “Lost Battalion” of Texas soldiers at a cost of casualties several times the number of men saved. “You fought the enemy abroad and prejudice at home and you won,” President Harry Truman told the unit in July 1946. The WRA closed every camp except Tule Lake by the end of 1945, pushing inmates to resettle. Most had lost their homes and property. A congressional commission later estimated their property losses at $1.3 billion and lost income at $2.7 billion, in 1983 dollars. The Japanese American Evacuation Claims Act of 1948 paid only token amounts, because it required documents that few families still had. Encouraged by the civil rights movement, Japanese American activists began calling for redress in 1970. In 1980 Congress created the Commission on Wartime Relocation and Internment of Civilians, which heard more than 750 witnesses in twenty cities. Its 1983 report, Personal Justice Denied, gave factual and moral support for reparations. Meanwhile documents uncovered by the legal historian Peter Irons showed that officials had suppressed FBI and Federal Communications Commission reports refuting claims of Japanese American espionage. On November 10, 1983, Judge Marilyn Hall Patel overturned Korematsu’s conviction. His case, she wrote, “stands as a caution that in times of distress the shield of military necessity and national security must not be used to protect governmental actions from close scrutiny and accountability.” President Ronald Reagan signed the Civil Liberties Act on August 10, 1988, and the first redress checks, each with a signed presidential apology, were presented in October 1990. In all, 82,219 people received payments. The incarceration showed how quickly fear and racism could override constitutional rights in wartime, and the decades-long fight for redress showed how a democracy can admit a wrong. I was an American citizen, and I had as many rights as anyone else. Fred Korematsu on his decision to challenge the exclusion order I dissent, therefore, from this legalization of racism. Justice Frank Murphy dissent, Korematsu v. United States, 1944 You fought the enemy abroad and prejudice at home and you won. President Harry S. Truman to the 442nd Regimental Combat Team, July 15, 1946 It stands as a caution that in times of distress the shield of military necessity and national security must not be used to protect governmental actions from close scrutiny and accountability. title: Juneteenth
subtitle: June 19, 1865: freedom announced in Texas, now a national holiday
summary: On June 19, 1865, two and a half years after the Emancipation Proclamation, Union general Gordon Granger issued General Order No. 3 in Galveston, informing the people of Texas that all enslaved people were free. The day became known as Juneteenth, a blend of “June” and “nineteenth.” Celebrated by African American communities in Texas since 1866 and later in other states, it is the oldest known celebration of the end of slavery in the United States, and became a national holiday in 2021.
thumbAlt: The handwritten text of General Order No. 3, issued at Galveston, Texas, on June 19, 1865
aliases: Freedom Day Emancipation Day General Order No. 3
themeText: Slavery and emancipation African American history National symbols and holidays
text: Galveston, Texas Order General Order No. 3, issued by Maj. Gen. Gordon Granger Place Galveston, Texas; Granger’s troops had arrived the day before Other names Freedom Day, Emancipation Day First celebrated In African American communities in Texas, from 1866 National holiday Signed into law on June 17, 2021 General Order No. 3 came two and a half years after President Abraham Lincoln’s Emancipation Proclamation. The National Archives describes it as the federal government’s final execution and fulfillment of the Proclamation’s terms: the people it addressed were the last group of Americans to be informed that all formerly enslaved persons were free. Maj. Gen. Gordon Granger commanded the Union army’s District of Texas. His troops arrived in Galveston on June 18, 1865, and the next day he issued the order. General Order No. 3 begins: “The people of Texas are informed that, in accordance with a proclamation from the Executive of the United States, all slaves are free.” It declared an absolute equality of personal and property rights between former masters and the formerly enslaved, and turned their relationship into that of employer and hired labor. But it also advised the freedpeople to stay quietly at their present homes and work for wages, and warned that they would not be allowed to gather at military posts or be “supported in idleness.” The order made freedom official across Texas. Its closing lines, the National Archives notes, used racist language that foreshadowed how long the fight for equal rights would continue. African American communities in Texas began celebrating the day in 1866, and the celebration later spread to other states. Nearly all states and the District of Columbia came to recognize Juneteenth, and on June 17, 2021, President Joe Biden signed legislation making it a national holiday. The original handwritten order survives at the National Archives in Washington, D.C. Juneteenth marks the moment emancipation reached the last enslaved Americans in the Confederacy — and, as the nation’s oldest celebration of the end of slavery, it links the history of freedom to how Americans remember it today. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lq8TNKZVEWs What is Juneteenth, and why is it important? - Karlos K. title: The Lewis and Clark Expedition
subtitle: The Corps of Discovery crosses the continent, 1804–1806
summary: In 1804, at Thomas Jefferson’s direction, Meriwether Lewis and William Clark led a small army unit, the Corps of Discovery, up the Missouri River and across the Rocky Mountains to the Pacific Ocean, returning to St. Louis in 1806. They mapped the West, recorded its plants and animals, and met dozens of Native nations. Their success depended on Native guides and hosts, above all on Sacagawea, a Lemhi Shoshone woman, and on the labor of York, a man enslaved by Clark.
location: From St. Louis up the Missouri River, across the Rockies, to the Pacific coast and back
thumbAlt: Painting of Lewis and Clark’s party on the Columbia River
aliases: Corps of Discovery Sacagawea York Meriwether Lewis William Clark
themeText: Territorial expansion Indigenous history Science and technology
text: From St. Louis up the Missouri River, across the Rockies, to the Pacific coast and back Funding $2,500, requested by Jefferson in a confidential message to Congress, January 18, 1803 Departed May 14, 1804, near St. Louis Returned September 23, 1806, to St. Louis Distance About 8,000 miles Reached the Pacific November 1805, at the mouth of the Columbia River Even before the Louisiana Purchase, Jefferson believed the United States should stretch across the continent. In a secret message of January 18, 1803 — when the territory still belonged to France — he asked Congress for $2,500 to explore the West to the Pacific, explaining the request mainly in terms of promoting commerce. Jefferson instructed Lewis, his former private secretary, to seek a practical water route across the continent, to establish relations and trade with western Native nations, and to report on the geography, geology, astronomy, plants, animals, and climate of the West. Lewis chose William Clark as co-commander. Jefferson helped plan supplies: arms, food, medicine, scientific instruments, and gifts for Native leaders. The Corps left the St. Louis area in May 1804 and worked up the Missouri. After five months they built Fort Mandan near the Mandan villages in present-day North Dakota, 1,600 miles upriver, and wintered there. They hired the French-Canadian trader Toussaint Charbonneau and his young wife, Sacagawea, a Lemhi Shoshone who had been captured by the Hidatsa as a girl. With their two-month-old son, Jean Baptiste, she set out with the Corps in April 1805. Along the Lemhi River in present-day Idaho, her people provided horses and a guide for the crossing of the Continental Divide. York, enslaved by Clark, hunted and labored alongside the others; the National Park Service credits him as the first African American known to have crossed North America. The Corps crossed the mountains and descended the Columbia River, reaching its estuary in November 1805 — Clark wrote of the “joy” of seeing the ocean on November 7 — and wintered on the Pacific coast. On the way home in July 1806 the expedition split into groups to explore more of the Missouri and Yellowstone drainages; Sacagawea guided Clark’s party over Bozeman Pass into the Yellowstone Valley. The Corps reached St. Louis on September 23, 1806. The expedition did not find an all-water route to the Pacific, because none existed. But it brought back maps, journals, and specimens that gave the U.S. government its first detailed view of the lands west of the Mississippi, and it strengthened American claims to the Oregon Country. Lewis and Clark became national heroes, and their journey a symbol of American exploration. The route crossed the territories of more than sixty Native nations, for whom the expedition was a harbinger of traders, settlers, soldiers, and treaties that would take most of their lands. After the expedition returned, York was denied his payment and his freedom. Sacagawea returned to the Mandan and Hidatsa villages in 1806; her role, little recognized at the time, was celebrated only much later. The Lewis and Clark Expedition turned the Louisiana Purchase from lines on a treaty into a known landscape, and laid the groundwork for American expansion to the Pacific. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NVkHfn6-Zl4 10 Cool Facts About The Lewis & Clark Expedition Weird History 11:25 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UQj7BKwZxD0 The Lewis and Clark Expedition: How the USA Discovered Its Eventual Western Borders Megaprojects 20:07 2026-10-22

title: Battles of Lexington and Concord
subtitle: April 19, 1775: the first fighting of the American Revolution and “the shot heard ’round the world”
summary: Before dawn on April 19, 1775, some 700 British soldiers marched from Boston to seize the military supplies that Massachusetts patriots had stockpiled at Concord. Warned by Paul Revere, William Dawes, and other riders, local militia turned out. Shots were fired on Lexington Green (no one knows who fired first) and later at Concord’s North Bridge. On the long march back to Boston, thousands of militiamen fired on the British from behind trees, walls, and houses. By nightfall 49 colonists and 73 British soldiers were dead, and the American Revolutionary War had begun.
thumbAlt: Amos Doolittle’s 1775 engraving of British regulars firing on the militia on Lexington Green
aliases: Paul Revere’s ride Midnight ride Minute Men Minutemen North Bridge shot heard round the world Battle Road Lexington Green
themeText: War and the military Political thought
text: Lexington, Lincoln, and Concord, Massachusetts Date April 19, 1775 British goal Seize and destroy colonial arms and supplies at Concord, 18 miles from Boston Forces Some 1,700 British regulars (with reinforcements) and more than 4,000 militia Killed 49 colonists and 73 British soldiers The signal Two lanterns in the Old North Church steeple: the troops were crossing by water The fighting turned years of protest into open war. Within days, some 20,000 New England militiamen surrounded British-held Boston — the beginning of the force that became the Continental Army — and the war that followed ended with American independence. After the Boston Tea Party, Parliament punished Massachusetts. In the summer of 1774 British warships closed Boston Harbor, and the royal governor, General Thomas Gage, dissolved the elected legislature. Patriot leaders formed a Provincial Congress, which took control of the colony’s militia and began stockpiling arms, ammunition, and provisions, aiming to raise an army of 15,000 men. Isolated in Boston, Gage followed advice from London and decided to strike first. Gage ordered Lieutenant Colonel Francis Smith to march about 700 elite grenadiers and light infantry to Concord “with the utmost expedition and secrecy” and to destroy the cannon, powder, and supplies stored there. Secrecy was impossible. Dr. Joseph Warren learned of the plan and sent Paul Revere and William Dawes to warn the countryside — and John Hancock and Samuel Adams, who were staying in Lexington. Revere had arranged a signal: two lanterns in the steeple of Boston’s Old North Church if the troops crossed by water, one if by land. Two were shown. Revere rowed across the Charles River, and as he rode, other riders set out and church bells and guns sounded the alarm. Revere and Dawes reached Lexington about 12:30 a.m.; when a militia sergeant told Revere not to make so much noise, he answered, “You’ll have noise enough before long! The Regulars are coming!” Riding on toward Concord, Revere was captured by a British patrol, but Dr. Samuel Prescott escaped and carried the alarm to Concord. At about 5 a.m. the British column reached Lexington, where Captain John Parker had drawn up some 70 militiamen on the green. Parker ordered them to disperse, but a shot rang out — historians still debate who fired it — and the British fired, killing seven militiamen and mortally wounding an eighth. The troops marched on to Concord and searched for supplies, much of which had already been moved or hidden. About 400 militiamen gathered on a hill above the North Bridge; seeing smoke rising from town, they thought the soldiers were burning it and advanced. The British fired, killing Captain Isaac Davis of Acton and another minuteman, and the militia fired back — the volley later called “the shot heard ’round the world.” The British fell back. Around noon the British began the march back to Boston. Along what is now called Battle Road, militiamen from town after town attacked the column for miles from behind trees, stone walls, and buildings. Near Lexington the fleeing column met a relief force of nearly 1,000 men under Brigadier General Hugh, Earl Percy, whose cannon held off the pursuers long enough for the retreat to continue. The British reached safety near Boston that evening. Within days some 20,000 militiamen from across New England surrounded the city, beginning a siege that lasted until the British left Boston in March 1776. Both sides raced to publish their version of the day: the Massachusetts Provincial Congress sent depositions describing an unprovoked British attack to London by fast schooner, and they appeared in the newspapers before General Gage’s report arrived. Lexington and Concord began eight years of war that ended in independence. Later generations made the day a founding legend, remembered as “the shot heard ’round the world.” Minute Man National Historical Park in Lexington, Lincoln, and Concord preserves the battlefield, which is also a graveyard: many soldiers killed that day still lie within the park. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BmdWe2YUVrc American Revolution: Battles of Lexington & Concord Epic History 27:54 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jQtkw2tCLyU Lexington & Concord: The Revolutionary War in Four Minutes American Battlefield Trust 5:01 2026-10-22

title: The Assassination of Abraham Lincoln
subtitle: Ford’s Theatre, April 14, 1865
summary: On the evening of April 14, 1865, five days after Lee’s surrender at Appomattox, President Abraham Lincoln was shot in the head by the actor John Wilkes Booth while watching a play at Ford’s Theatre in Washington. He died the next morning, the first American president to be assassinated. Booth, a Confederate sympathizer, had plotted with others to kill several leaders of the government. Lincoln’s death turned the celebration of victory into national mourning and placed Andrew Johnson in charge of Reconstruction.
thumbAlt: Currier and Ives print of Lincoln’s assassination at Ford’s Theatre
themeText: The presidency War and the military
text: Ford’s Theatre, Washington, D.C. Date April 14, 1865; Lincoln died the morning of April 15 Assassin John Wilkes Booth, actor and Confederate sympathizer Other targets Secretary of State William H. Seward, Vice President Andrew Johnson, General Ulysses S. Grant Aftermath Booth was found and killed ten days later; four co-conspirators were hanged On April 3, 1865, Lincoln walked through Richmond, the fallen Confederate capital, cheered by crowds of African Americans. On April 9 Lee surrendered at Appomattox. On April 11, Lincoln publicly endorsed voting rights for some Black men. John Wilkes Booth, a member of a well-known acting family and an ardent Confederate sympathizer, had spent much of the war plotting to kidnap Lincoln as a bargaining chip for the Confederacy. When he heard Lincoln endorse Black suffrage on April 11, he conspired with accomplices to kill Lincoln, Secretary of State William Seward, Vice President Andrew Johnson, and General Grant. On April 14, Lincoln and his wife, Mary Todd Lincoln, attended a performance of the comedy Our American Cousin at Ford’s Theatre. Booth entered the presidential box and shot Lincoln point-blank in the back of the head, then leapt to the stage shouting “Sic semper tyrannis!” and escaped. Lincoln died early the next morning. After a frantic search, Booth was found hiding in a barn in rural Virginia ten days later and was killed. Four of his co-conspirators were convicted and hanged. After seven days of official mourning, Lincoln’s funeral train carried his body 1,700 miles to Springfield, Illinois, as crowds gathered in towns and cities along the way. Lincoln’s death made him a national martyr and removed the leader best positioned to guide Reconstruction. His successor, Andrew Johnson — whom Booth’s plot had also targeted — pursued a lenient policy toward the defeated South that sparked a bitter conflict with Congress. Ford’s Theatre is preserved today as part of Ford’s Theatre National Historic Site. The first assassination of an American president cut short Lincoln’s leadership at the moment of victory and profoundly shaped how the nation approached Reconstruction. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hVLM0BSqx5o What Booth Said After He Killed Lincoln Smithsonian Channel 3:15 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9ozI11aFfNQ The Assassination of Abraham Lincoln Explained Mr. Beat 13:05 2026-10-22

title: The Little Rock Nine
subtitle: The desegregation of Central High School, 1957
summary: In September 1957, nine Black students tried to enroll at all-white Central High School in Little Rock, Arkansas, under a court-ordered desegregation plan. Governor Orval Faubus sent the Arkansas National Guard to keep them out, and a white mob gathered outside. After weeks of standoff, President Dwight D. Eisenhower sent troops of the Army’s 101st Airborne Division to escort and protect the students, a dramatic use of federal power to enforce Brown v. Board of Education.
thumbAlt: Members of the Little Rock Nine with New York mayor Robert F. Wagner
aliases: Central High crisis Orval Faubus 101st Airborne
themeText: Civil rights and citizenship African American history Constitution and law The presidency
text: Little Rock, Arkansas The Nine Minnijean Brown, Terrence Roberts, Elizabeth Eckford, Ernest Green, Thelma Mothershed, Melba Pattillo, Gloria Ray, Jefferson Thomas, and Carlotta Walls Organizer Daisy Bates, president of the Arkansas NAACP Federal troops 101st Airborne Division, sent by President Eisenhower, September 1957 First Black graduate Ernest Green, May 1958 Honor NAACP Spingarn Medal, 1958 Three years after the Supreme Court ruled in Brown that segregated schools were unconstitutional, Daisy Bates, president of the Arkansas NAACP, recruited nine students to enroll at Central High. Governor Orval Faubus used state power to block the students and defy the federal courts. On September 4, 1957, the first day of school, a white mob gathered in front of Central High, and Faubus deployed the Arkansas National Guard to bar the Black students. NAACP lawyers, including Thurgood Marshall, won a federal injunction against the governor. On September 23 the students entered through a side entrance with police escorts but were rushed home as the mob grew. Martin Luther King Jr. urged Eisenhower to take “a strong forthright stand.” Aware that Little Rock was becoming an international embarrassment, Eisenhower reluctantly sent the 101st Airborne; soldiers and federalized National Guardsmen protected the students for the rest of the school year. In May 1958 Ernest Green became Central High’s first Black graduate; King attended the ceremony. That fall Faubus closed all of Little Rock’s public high schools rather than continue desegregation, but the courts soon ordered the schools reopened and desegregation resumed. Little Rock showed that the federal government would use force to uphold the Constitution against state defiance, and it made the nine students symbols of courage. Central High School is now a National Historic Site — and still an operating public high school. The Little Rock crisis was a defining test of Brown and of the federal government’s willingness to enforce it. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fPVOO5sugMY Nine from Little Rock, 1964 - Restored US National Archives 18:31 2026-10-22

title: The Louisiana Purchase
subtitle: The United States doubles in size, 1803
summary: In 1803 the United States bought the vast Louisiana territory from France for $15 million, about 828,000 square miles between the Mississippi River and the Rocky Mountains, for roughly four cents an acre. The purchase doubled the size of the country, gave it control of New Orleans and the Mississippi, and opened the way to westward expansion. It also raised hard questions: whether the Constitution allowed it, whether slavery would spread into the new lands, and what would become of the many Native nations who lived there.
location: The Mississippi River valley to the Rocky Mountains
thumbAlt: Map of the Louisiana Purchase within the present-day United States
themeText: Territorial expansion Foreign policy and diplomacy Constitution and law Indigenous history Slavery and emancipation
text: The Mississippi River valley to the Rocky Mountains Signed April 30, 1803, in Paris Price $15 million: 60 million francs plus up to 20 million francs to cover American claims against France Size 828,000 square miles — all or part of fifteen present-day states U.S. negotiators Robert Livingston and James Monroe Original goal To buy New Orleans and West Florida for up to $10 million As Americans moved west of the Appalachians, the Mississippi River and the port of New Orleans became essential outlets for western farm produce. Spain had owned Louisiana since 1762, and the Pinckney Treaty of 1795 secured Americans’ right to navigate the river and ship goods through New Orleans. Then, in 1800, Spain secretly returned Louisiana to France. Napoleon Bonaparte planned to reconquer Saint-Domingue (Haiti) from the enslaved people who had overthrown slavery there, and to use Louisiana as the granary for a revived French empire in the Americas. A powerful France at New Orleans alarmed Americans. Jefferson wrote that there was one spot on the globe whose possessor was “our natural and habitual enemy. It is New Orleans.” He sent James Monroe to join Robert Livingston in France to buy New Orleans and West Florida. Meanwhile the French army in Saint-Domingue was destroyed by yellow fever and fierce Haitian resistance, and war with Britain loomed again. Napoleon abandoned his American plans. To the Americans’ surprise, France offered not just New Orleans but all of Louisiana. Far exceeding their instructions, Livingston and Monroe agreed to buy it for $15 million and signed the treaty on April 30, 1803. Jefferson, who had always insisted on a strict reading of the Constitution, found nothing in it authorizing the purchase of territory. He considered an amendment but, given public enthusiasm and the land’s value, set his scruples aside. The Senate ratified the treaty, and the United States took possession that December. The treaty promised that the territory’s inhabitants would be incorporated into the Union and admitted to the rights of citizens. Jefferson sent the Lewis and Clark Expedition to explore the new lands. The purchase strengthened Jefferson’s popularity and weakened the Federalists, many of whom feared that new western states would reduce New England’s influence. Louisiana was the first in a long series of territorial expansions that, within fifty years, carried the United States to the Pacific. Each expansion reopened the question of whether slavery would spread west, leading to the Missouri Compromise and the crises that ended in civil war. The purchase also ignored the people who actually lived on the land: thousands of Native Americans in dozens of nations, whose rights France could not sell and who would be pushed off much of it in the decades that followed. Jefferson’s decision helped establish the principle of the federal government’s implied powers. For about four cents an acre, the Louisiana Purchase transformed the United States into a continental power — and planted the conflicts over slavery and Native land that would define the next half-century. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sMh8RCqJf9U The historical audacity of the Louisiana Purchase - Judy Walton TED-Ed 3:38 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L7PpqvuUSoA The Making of a Nation: Louisiana Purchase VOA Learning English 15:00 2026-10-22

title: March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom
subtitle: The 1963 march where King delivered “I Have a Dream”
summary: On August 28, 1963, a crowd that the King Institute puts at more than 200,000 and the National Archives at more than 250,000 gathered in Washington, D.C., for the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom. Conceived by the labor leader A. Philip Randolph and organized by Bayard Rustin in less than two months, it united the major civil rights organizations, labor unions, and churches. They demanded a strong civil rights law, voting rights, school desegregation, jobs, and fair employment. It closed at the Lincoln Memorial with Martin Luther King Jr.’s “I Have a Dream” speech. The march helped build pressure for the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965, whose provisions reflected its demands.
thumbAlt: Martin Luther King Jr. among the crowd at the March on Washington
aliases: I Have a Dream 1963 March on Washington Big Six Bayard Rustin A. Philip Randolph
themeText: Civil rights and citizenship African American history Labor and work Reform and protest
text: Lincoln Memorial, Washington, D.C. Date August 28, 1963 Crowd More than 200,000 (King Institute) or 250,000 (National Archives) Leaders The “Big Six”: Randolph, Roy Wilkins (NAACP), Whitney Young (National Urban League), King (SCLC), James Farmer (CORE), John Lewis (SNCC) Organizer Bayard Rustin, deputy director, headquartered in Harlem Route Rally at the Washington Monument, march along the National Mall, program at the Lincoln Memorial Afterward Leaders met President Kennedy and Vice President Johnson at the White House The idea had a long history. In 1941 A. Philip Randolph, head of the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters, threatened to bring 100,000 Black marchers to Washington to protest their exclusion from defense jobs. President Franklin Roosevelt responded with Executive Order 8802, which created the Fair Employment Practices Commission, and Randolph called off the march. Civil rights supporters gathered at the Lincoln Memorial for the Prayer Pilgrimage for Freedom in May 1957 and for a Youth March for Integrated Schools in October 1958. By 1963, the centennial of the Emancipation Proclamation, Black Americans still faced high unemployment, low wages, disfranchisement, and segregation. Randolph began planning in 1962. The King Institute dates his first permit letter to May 24, 1962, while the National Archives says he first proposed the march in late 1962 and got little response. In May 1963, at the height of the Birmingham campaign, King joined Randolph, James Farmer of CORE, and Charles McDew of SNCC in calling for a march, declaring, “Let the black laboring masses speak!” The next month President Kennedy asked the nation for civil rights legislation. The march’s official goals, as listed by the King Institute and the American Yawp, were a comprehensive civil rights bill ending segregation in public accommodations, protection of the right to vote, desegregation of all public schools in 1963, a federal works program to train and place unemployed workers, a federal fair employment law, and a higher minimum wage. Its full name, the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom, reflected the economic demands at its heart, which came from Randolph’s labor background. Success depended on cooperation among the “Big Six”: Randolph, Roy Wilkins of the NAACP, Whitney Young of the National Urban League, King of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, James Farmer of the Congress of Racial Equality, and John Lewis of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee. The National Archives notes that these leaders competed for funding and press coverage. Bayard Rustin, Randolph’s trusted associate, whom Randolph called “Mr. March-on-Washington,” was appointed deputy director despite the concerns of many civil rights leaders. Working from headquarters in Harlem with a small office in Washington and a core staff of 200 volunteers, Rustin put the event together in less than two months. Sponsors grew to include the NAACP, the National Urban League, the National Council of the Churches of Christ, the National Catholic Conference for Interracial Justice, and the United Auto Workers. The day began with a rally at the Washington Monument featuring celebrities and musicians. Marchers then walked the mile-long National Mall to the Lincoln Memorial for a three-hour program. Performers and speakers included Marian Anderson, Odetta, Joan Baez, Bob Dylan, Daisy Bates, Ossie Davis and Ruby Dee, Rabbi Joachim Prinz, Walter Reuther of the UAW, Roy Wilkins, Whitney Young, and John Lewis. Lewis’s prepared speech caused a crisis. It called Kennedy’s civil rights bill “too little and too late” and threatened to “march through the South, through the heart of Dixie, the way Sherman did.” Reuther, Justice Department official Burke Marshall, and Archbishop Patrick O’Boyle of Washington objected. In a caucus with King, Randolph, and SNCC’s James Forman, Lewis agreed to cut those passages, though he believed the final version was “still a strong speech, very strong.” King spoke near the end. Drawing on themes he had used in speeches for years, including an address to 150,000 people in Detroit two months earlier, he used a metaphor suggested by his adviser Clarence Jones for the unfulfilled promise of constitutional rights: “America has defaulted on this promissory note insofar as her citizens of color are concerned.” He had finished the text only at 3:30 that morning. Partway through, he set the manuscript aside and turned to a refrain he had used before: “I have a dream.” He later recalled, “I just turned aside from the manuscript altogether. I didn’t come back to it.” He closed by imagining the day when all of God’s children could sing, “Free at last! Free at last! Thank God Almighty, we are free at last!” The New York Times columnist James Reston wrote that King “touched all the themes of the day, only better than anybody else.” That afternoon the march leaders met President Kennedy and Vice President Lyndon Johnson at the White House to discuss the need for bipartisan support of civil rights legislation. Not everyone was moved. Malcolm X, who attended, mocked it as “the Farce on Washington,” the Nation of Islam condemned it, and the AFL-CIO’s executive board stayed neutral, though many member unions marched. The National Archives calls the march the largest demonstration for human rights in American history and “a rare display of unity” among civil rights organizations. The American Yawp writes that King’s speech raised the movement’s profile “to new heights and put unprecedented pressure on politicians to pass meaningful civil rights legislation.” After Kennedy’s death, Congress passed the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965, whose provisions, the King Institute notes, reflected the march’s demands. “I Have a Dream” became one of the best-known speeches in American history. The March on Washington joined the moral appeal of the civil rights movement to its economic demands. It showed the nation the movement’s size, discipline, and breadth, and it gave King’s dream of racial equality its most lasting expression. America has defaulted on this promissory note insofar as her citizens of color are concerned. Martin Luther King Jr. “I Have a Dream,” August 28, 1963 Free at last! Free at last! Thank God Almighty, we are free at last! Martin Luther King Jr. closing of “I Have a Dream,” quoting a spiritual Dr. King touched all the themes of the day, only better than anybody else. title: The Marshall Plan
subtitle: The European Recovery Program, 1948–1952
summary: The Marshall Plan was a massive American program to rebuild the war-ravaged economies of Western Europe after World War II. Proposed by Secretary of State George C. Marshall in a June 1947 speech at Harvard, it provided more than $12 billion between 1948 and 1952. American leaders saw it as both a humanitarian effort and a way to stop the spread of communism by restoring prosperity. The Soviet Union refused to take part and kept its Eastern European satellites out, deepening the division of Europe.
thumbAlt: Poster promoting the Marshall Plan
aliases: European Recovery Program Economic Cooperation Act
themeText: The Cold War Foreign policy and diplomacy Economy and finance
text: Western Europe Proposed June 5, 1947, commencement speech at Harvard University Law Economic Cooperation Act, March 1948 Aid More than $12 billion to Western Europe Soviet response Refused to participate and barred Eastern European countries; offered its own “Molotov Plan” Recognition George Marshall received the Nobel Peace Prize Two years after the war, much of Europe remained in ruins. The brutal winter of 1946–1947 halted coal production, closed factories, and brought famine close; communist parties in France and Italy won nearly a third of the seats in their parliaments. American officials feared that hunger and unemployment would make Western Europe vulnerable to communism. Coming just months after the Truman Doctrine, Marshall’s proposal argued that the United States should help restore “normal economic health to the world, without which there can be no political stability and no assured peace.” He insisted the plan was directed “not against any country” but against hunger, poverty, and chaos. Congress, spurred by fear of communist expansion and Europe’s deteriorating economy, approved the Economic Cooperation Act in March 1948. American aid poured into Western Europe for reconstruction while trade barriers were loosened. Participation by the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe was initially possible, but Stalin, suspicious of American economic domination and unwilling to open Soviet society to Westerners, refused. He saw the plan as a “Trojan Horse” and tightened his control over Eastern Europe; Poland, for instance, was rewarded with a Soviet trade agreement for boycotting the plan. The plan therefore went only to Western Europe. The Marshall Plan fueled a resurgence of European industry and investment and created markets for American goods. Moscow viewed the revival of Western Europe — especially West Germany — with suspicion, and the plan contributed to the hardening division between East and West. Economic historians debate how much the Marshall Plan itself caused Europe’s recovery, but it is widely recognized as a great humanitarian effort. It established foreign aid as a permanent tool of American foreign policy and laid groundwork for European economic integration and the NATO alliance. The Marshall Plan was one of the most ambitious and successful foreign policy initiatives in American history, binding Western Europe to the United States at the start of the Cold War. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tMXjsVLOznc What Was the Marshall Plan? | History HISTORY 3:16 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hyYdBtJZEw The Marshall Plan: Rebuilding Europe In the Shadow of Communism Megaprojects 16:49 2026-10-22

title: McCarthyism and the Second Red Scare
subtitle: Anticommunist investigations and accusations, late 1940s–1954
summary: In the early Cold War, fear of communist subversion swept the United States. Congressional committees, the FBI, loyalty boards, and private employers investigated thousands of Americans; many lost their jobs or were blacklisted for past political associations. The era takes its name from Senator Joseph McCarthy of Wisconsin, who from 1950 made sensational, unsupported charges that communists had infiltrated the government, until televised hearings in 1954 exposed his tactics and the Senate condemned him.
location: Washington, D.C., Hollywood, universities, unions, and communities nationwide
thumbAlt: Joseph Welch and Senator Joseph McCarthy at the Army-McCarthy hearings
aliases: Red Scare HUAC Hollywood Ten blacklist Army-McCarthy hearings Rosenbergs
themeText: The Cold War Civil rights and citizenship Parties and elections
text: Washington, D.C., Hollywood, universities, unions, and communities nationwide Loyalty program Truman’s Executive Order 9835, March 1947 Wheeling speech February 9, 1950: McCarthy claimed a list of 205 communists in the State Department Hollywood HUAC hearings from 1947; the “Hollywood Ten” and an industry blacklist Army-McCarthy hearings 1954, watched by some 20 million people Senate condemnation December 2, 1954, by a vote of 67–22 A small Communist Party had existed in the United States since the aftermath of the 1917 Russian Revolution; even at its peak it had only about 80,000 members. Real Soviet espionage occurred: Julius and Ethel Rosenberg were convicted of passing atomic secrets and executed in 1953, and former State Department official Alger Hiss, accused of spying, was convicted of perjury after a second trial. Combined with the Soviet atomic bomb, the communist victory in China, and the Korean War, these cases fed fears of a vast conspiracy. In March 1947, facing anticommunist pressure, President Truman created loyalty reviews for federal employees. The House Un-American Activities Committee (HUAC) investigated Hollywood beginning in 1947; between 1949 and 1954, congressional committees conducted more than one hundred investigations into subversion. The Internal Security Act of 1950 required “communist organizations” to register with the government. On February 9, 1950, in Wheeling, West Virginia, McCarthy declared he had a list of 205 State Department employees who were members of the Communist Party. He had no such list; the number changed to 57, then 81. A Senate committee called his charges “a fraud and a hoax,” but McCarthy’s accusations made him famous, and he attacked the Truman administration as “soft on communism.” The Red Scare reached far beyond McCarthy. HUAC asked witnesses, “Are you now, or have you ever been, a member of the Communist Party?” and pressed them to name others; hundreds of film artists were blacklisted. Thirty-one University of California professors were dismissed in 1950 for refusing to sign a loyalty oath. The singer and activist Paul Robeson had his passport revoked. In 1954 McCarthy took on the U.S. Army. Twenty million people watched the televised Army-McCarthy hearings, in which Army counsel Joseph Welch rebuked him: “Have you no sense of decency, sir? At long last, have you left no sense of decency?” On December 2, 1954, the Senate voted 67–22 to condemn McCarthy. He died in 1957, and by the late 1950s the worst of the Red Scare was over. The Red Scare cost many Americans their jobs and reputations and pressed the country toward conformity. Playwright Arthur Miller compared it to the Salem witch trials in The Crucible (1953). As early as June 1950, the editor Freda Kirchwey described “McCarthyism” as the means by which “a handful of men, disguised as hunters of subversion, cynically subvert the instruments of justice” for political gain. McCarthyism showed how fear of an external enemy could be turned against Americans’ own civil liberties. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N35IugBYH04 What is McCarthyism? title: The Missouri Compromise
subtitle: Congress balances slave and free states, 1820
summary: When Missouri asked to join the Union as a slave state in 1819, it set off the first great national crisis over slavery. The Missouri Compromise of 1820 admitted Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state, preserving the balance between them in the Senate, and banned slavery in the rest of the Louisiana Purchase north of latitude 36°30′. The line held for thirty-four years, but the crisis revealed how deeply slavery divided the nation. Thomas Jefferson called it “a fire bell in the night.”
thumbAlt: Map of free and slave territory under the Missouri Compromise
themeText: Slavery and emancipation Territorial expansion Constitution and law
text: Washington, D.C.; the Louisiana Territory Admitted Missouri as a slave state; Maine (separated from Massachusetts) as a free state The line No slavery in the remaining Louisiana Territory north of 36°30′ latitude, except Missouri Repealed By the Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854) Declared unconstitutional By the Supreme Court in Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857) In 1819 the Union had eleven free states and eleven slave states, giving each section equal votes in the Senate even as the North’s faster-growing population gave it a majority in the House. The Louisiana Purchase had added an immense territory with no settled rule on slavery. Missouri, settled largely by Southerners who brought enslaved people with them, applied for statehood. In February 1819, Representative James Tallmadge of New York proposed amending Missouri’s statehood bill to prohibit bringing more enslaved people into the state and to provide for the gradual emancipation of those already there. After fierce debate, the House adopted the amendment by a straight sectional vote; the Senate defeated it. Northerners attacked the expansion of slavery, and Southerners insisted Congress had no power to restrict it in a new state. The deadlock broke when Maine, long part of Massachusetts, sought statehood. Congress paired the two admissions: Missouri would enter as a slave state and Maine as a free state, preserving the balance in the Senate. Congress also prohibited slavery in the rest of the Louisiana Territory north of 36°30′, while the land south of the line — organized as Arkansas Territory — stayed open to slavery. A conference committee reported the compromise on March 1, 1820, and it became law. A second dispute erupted when Missouri submitted a constitution denying free Black people the right to live in the state; it was resolved with a further proviso, and Missouri was admitted in 1821. The compromise calmed the immediate crisis and kept the two parties of the era from splitting along sectional lines. But it established that the balance of slave and free states was a central political question, to be renegotiated with every new territory. For a generation the 36°30′ line kept an uneasy peace. It collapsed when the Mexican-American War added new lands, and Congress repealed it outright in the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854. In 1857 the Supreme Court declared in Dred Scott that Congress had never had the power to ban slavery in the territories, making the compromise retroactively unconstitutional. The question it had postponed — whether slavery would expand west — led directly to the Civil War. The Missouri Compromise was the first great bargain over slavery’s expansion, and its unraveling a generation later marked the road to disunion. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=d9hQk2Mmpcw Slavery and Missouri Compromise in early 1800s | US History | Khan Academy Khan Academy 11:00 2026-10-23 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Z-Id8pqA-O4 The Missouri Compromise Explained: US History Review Hip Hughes (HipHughes) 8:35 2026-10-23

title: Montgomery Bus Boycott
subtitle: The thirteen-month protest that launched the modern civil rights movement
summary: The Montgomery bus boycott began on December 5, 1955, four days after Rosa Parks was arrested for refusing to give up her bus seat to a white passenger. For 381 days Montgomery’s Black residents walked, shared rides, and organized carpools rather than ride segregated city buses. The protest was planned by the Women’s Political Council and E. D. Nixon and led by the Montgomery Improvement Association. Its president was a twenty-six-year-old minister, Martin Luther King Jr. It survived bombings, mass indictments, and court injunctions, and it ended in victory after the Supreme Court affirmed, in Browder v. Gayle, that bus segregation was unconstitutional. The boycott made King a national figure and showed that nonviolent mass protest could defeat Jim Crow.
thumbAlt: Rosa Parks being fingerprinted after her arrest during the Montgomery bus boycott
aliases: Montgomery Improvement Association Browder v. Gayle Women’s Political Council Holt Street Baptist Church
themeText: Civil rights and citizenship African American history Reform and protest
text: Montgomery, Alabama Spark Arrest of Rosa Parks, December 1, 1955 Began December 5, 1955; about 90 percent of Black riders stayed off the buses on the first day Leadership Montgomery Improvement Association (MIA), president Martin Luther King Jr. Carpool About 300 cars Court victory Browder v. Gayle: district court June 1956; affirmed by the Supreme Court November 13, 1956 Ended December 20, 1956, after 381 days; buses integrated the next day Montgomery’s buses were rigidly segregated. The front ten seats were reserved for white passengers, and Black riders were expected to give up seats behind them when the bus filled with white passengers. Black passengers often had to pay at the front and then re-enter by the rear door. Drivers claimed the discretion to move the line between Black and white sections. Jo Ann Robinson, an English professor at Alabama State College, was ordered off a nearly empty bus in 1949 for sitting in the fifth row. The Women’s Political Council (WPC), an organization of Black professional women founded in 1946, made bus segregation a priority after Robinson became its president in 1950. In March 1954 the council asked Mayor W. A. Gayle to end the practice of making Black riders stand over empty seats and to have buses stop at every corner in Black neighborhoods, as they did in white ones. In a May 21 letter Robinson warned that “twenty-five or more local organizations” had talked of a city-wide boycott. Earlier arrests, of fifteen-year-old Claudette Colvin and eighteen-year-old Mary Louise Smith in 1955, did not mobilize the community. The American Yawp notes that in 1953 a Black member of the Women’s Army Corps, Sarah Keys, had already challenged segregated interstate buses. On the evening of December 1, 1955, Rosa Parks, a forty-two-year-old seamstress at the Montgomery Fair department store who was active in the local NAACP, was sitting in the first row behind the white section. When the bus filled, driver James Blake ordered her row to stand. Three passengers moved; Parks did not, and she was arrested. E. D. Nixon, a Pullman porter, union leader, and former head of the local NAACP, saw her as the ideal plaintiff: “She’s morally clean, she’s reliable, nobody had nothing on her, she had the courage of her convictions.” With the white attorney Clifford Durr and his wife Virginia, he bailed her out of jail. That night Robinson, two students, and a colleague, John Cannon, mimeographed about 52,500 leaflets calling on Black residents to stay off the buses on Monday, December 5. On December 2 ministers and community leaders met at King’s Dexter Avenue Baptist Church and agreed to support the one-day boycott, which also received unexpected publicity in weekend newspapers and on radio and television. On December 5 about 90 percent of Montgomery’s Black citizens stayed off the buses. That afternoon, at Mt. Zion AME Church, leaders formed the Montgomery Improvement Association to continue the protest and elected King, new to the city, as president. Nixon became treasurer. Parks later observed that King had not been in Montgomery long enough “to make any strong friends or enemies.” That evening several thousand people packed Holt Street Baptist Church and voted to continue. “If we are wrong,” King told them, “the Supreme Court of this nation is wrong. If we are wrong, the Constitution of the United States is wrong. If we are wrong, God Almighty is wrong.” The MIA’s first demands were moderate: courteous treatment, first-come, first-served seating with Black riders filling from the rear and white riders from the front, and Black drivers on mostly Black routes. When the city refused and began penalizing Black taxi drivers for helping the boycotters, the MIA built a carpool of about 300 cars, modeled on a 1953 bus boycott in Baton Rouge. Weekly mass meetings with sermons and music kept the community together, and money came from collection plates and from supporters in the North, including the fundraising group In Friendship founded by Bayard Rustin, Ella Baker, and Stanley Levison. Resistance was fierce. In early 1956 the homes of King and Nixon were bombed. King calmed the crowd outside his house: “Be calm as I and my family are. … If anything happens to me, there will be others to take my place.” (The American Yawp places the bombings of King’s and Nixon’s homes, along with four Black churches, a year into the boycott.) Police harassed Robinson, and the governor eventually ordered state police to guard boycott leaders’ homes. In February 1956 the city indicted dozens of boycott leaders under a 1921 Alabama law against conspiracies to interfere with lawful business. The King Institute’s boycott article says more than 80 were indicted and its MIA article says 89. King alone was tried, and in March he was convicted and ordered to pay $500 or serve 386 days in jail. Women sustained the movement. Robinson edited the MIA newsletter and Johnnie Carr and others ran committees. Mary Fair Burks of the WPC credited “the nameless cooks and maids who walked endless miles for a year to bring about the breach in the walls of segregation.” Rustin and Glenn Smiley advised King on Gandhian nonviolence. “Christ showed us the way,” King said, “and Gandhi in India showed it could work.” On February 1, 1956, lawyers Fred Gray and Charles Langford filed Browder v. Gayle in federal court on behalf of Aurelia Browder, Susie McDonald, Claudette Colvin, and Mary Louise Smith. Parks was not included, so that the court would decide only the constitutionality of bus segregation. In June 1956 a three-judge district court ruled 2 to 1, citing Brown v. Board of Education, that bus segregation was unconstitutional. The King Institute dates the ruling to June 5 and the National Archives to June 4. On November 13, 1956, while King sat in court defending the carpools against an injunction, he learned that the Supreme Court had affirmed the ruling. The MIA kept walking until the order arrived. On December 20, 1956, the community voted to end the boycott, and the next morning King, Ralph Abernathy, E. D. Nixon, and Glenn Smiley rode an integrated bus. “We came to see that, in the long run, it is more honorable to walk in dignity than ride in humiliation,” King said. The boycott’s combination of mass nonviolent protest and Christian ethics became the model for challenging segregation across the South. In January 1957 the MIA became one of the founding organizations of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, which King and other ministers created to coordinate civil rights efforts across the South. The American Yawp writes that the boycott not only crushed segregation on Montgomery’s buses but energized the entire civil rights movement. Parks became known as the “Mother of the Civil Rights Movement.” Robinson later called the boycott “the most beautiful memory that all of us who participated will carry to our final resting place.” Montgomery proved that ordinary people acting together could defeat Jim Crow, and it introduced Martin Luther King Jr. to the nation. If we are wrong, the Supreme Court of this nation is wrong. If we are wrong, the Constitution of the United States is wrong. If we are wrong, God Almighty is wrong. title: The New Deal
subtitle: Franklin D. Roosevelt’s programs of relief, recovery, and reform, 1933–1939
summary: The New Deal was President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s response to the Great Depression: a burst of federal programs to stabilize the banks, put the unemployed to work, raise farm prices, protect workers’ right to organize, and create a safety net for the elderly and the jobless. It did not end the Depression, and it left racial and gender inequalities largely in place. But it transformed the role of the federal government and the presidency, and it built a Democratic coalition that dominated politics for a generation.
thumbAlt: Collage of New Deal programs and posters
aliases: Hundred Days First New Deal Second New Deal alphabet agencies CCC WPA NRA AAA TVA FDIC court-packing fireside chats
themeText: Economy and finance The presidency Labor and work Reform and protest Parties and elections Civil rights and citizenship
text: Washington, D.C., and nationwide The phrase From FDR’s 1932 acceptance speech: “I pledge you, I pledge myself, to a new deal for the American people” First Hundred Days (March–June 1933) Emergency Banking Act, CCC, FERA, TVA, AAA, National Industrial Recovery Act, Securities Act, Glass-Steagall Act (FDIC) Second New Deal (1935) Works Progress Administration, Wagner Act, Social Security Act Last major measure Fair Labor Standards Act (1938): the modern minimum wage, starting at 25 cents an hour Setbacks Supreme Court rulings against the NRA (1935) and AAA (1936), the failed court-packing plan (1937), the 1937 recession Unemployment About 25 percent in 1933; still above 19 percent in 1939 By the time Roosevelt took office on March 4, 1933, the economy had collapsed. More than twelve million Americans were out of work, a quarter of the workforce, and a new wave of bank failures had hit in February. Two of every five banks open in 1929 had closed. Herbert Hoover had relied on voluntary action and loans to business, and voters had rejected him in a landslide. Roosevelt, the Democratic governor of New York, had been born to a wealthy Hudson Valley family, served as assistant secretary of the navy in World War I, and been paralyzed by polio in 1921. As governor he had told the legislature that relief was owed “not as a matter of charity, but as a matter of social duty,” and his Temporary Emergency Relief Administration came to support a tenth of the state’s families. Accepting the Democratic nomination on July 1, 1932, he declared, “I pledge you, I pledge myself, to a new deal for the American people.” Newspaper editors seized on the phrase. Hoover warned that such a program meant “the total abandonment of every principle upon which this government and the American system is founded.” The New Deal had no single blueprint. Roosevelt believed in American capitalism but thought it had to be reformed to survive, and he was a pragmatist: he would try something, and if it failed, try something else. Even the New Deal economist Alvin Hansen admitted in 1940, “I really do not know what the basic principle of the New Deal is.” Its programs rested on different, sometimes contradictory, theories of the Depression’s causes. Some blamed overproduction, some cutthroat competition, some a lack of purchasing power; John Maynard Keynes’s theory of deficit spending was not even published until 1936. Roosevelt surrounded himself with a “Brain Trust” of academic advisers and appointees such as Harry Hopkins and Frances Perkins, the first woman to serve in a cabinet. He often gave overlapping tasks to aides who disagreed with one another. The Hundred Days. “The only thing we have to fear is fear itself,” Roosevelt said in his inaugural address. Two days later he declared a national bank holiday, and Congress passed his Emergency Banking Act almost sight unseen. Federal officials would inspect every bank, reopen the sound ones, and close the rest. On March 12 he explained the plan in the first of his radio “fireside chats,” and in the following weeks Americans returned nearly $1 billion to the banks. Between March and June 1933, Congress passed a flood of laws. The Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) put 300,000 young men to work in 1,200 camps planting trees, building bridges, and cleaning beaches. The Federal Emergency Relief Administration (FERA) sent cash to state relief agencies. The Securities Act required honest information about stocks, and the Glass-Steagall Act created the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) and separated commercial from investment banking. Roosevelt also took the country off the gold standard. Planning for recovery. The heart of the early New Deal was two experiments in economic planning. The Agricultural Adjustment Act (May 1933) paid farmers to cut production in order to raise prices; more than three million farmers joined, and farm income rose by more than half between 1932 and 1935. But in the South, landowners often kept the payments, evicted their tenants and sharecroppers, and bought machinery instead, pushing the poorest farmworkers off the land. The National Industrial Recovery Act (June 1933) suspended the antitrust laws so that businesses could write more than 500 “codes of fair competition” fixing prices, wages, and production. Section 7a promised workers the right to bargain collectively, and cooperating businesses displayed the National Recovery Administration’s Blue Eagle. The codes, the National Archives concludes, “did little to help recovery, and by raising prices, they actually made the economic situation worse.” The same law created the Public Works Administration, which spent more than $3 billion on projects such as the Triborough Bridge in New York. The Tennessee Valley. On May 18, 1933, Roosevelt signed the act creating the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA), a federal corporation charged with building dams to control floods, improve navigation, and generate cheap electricity in one of the poorest regions in the country. It was the first time a federal agency was directed to develop the resources of an entire region. Its dams brought electric lights, appliances, jobs, and industry to the valley, but they also displaced thousands of families, sometimes whole towns. The Rural Electrification Administration later brought electricity to millions of farm homes. Critics and the courts. Many Americans thought the New Deal did too little. Senator Huey Long of Louisiana won a mass following for his Share Our Wealth plan to redistribute the fortunes of the rich; more than 27,000 Share Our Wealth clubs sprang up before he was assassinated in 1935. Dr. Francis Townsend campaigned for old-age pensions, and the radio priest Charles Coughlin attacked Roosevelt in broadcasts that, the American Yawp notes, were vitriolic and anti-Semitic. From the right, conservative businessmen and dissident Democrats formed the American Liberty League in 1934 to denounce the New Deal as an un-American attack on free enterprise. The Supreme Court struck hardest. On May 27, 1935, in Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States, it unanimously ruled the National Industrial Recovery Act unconstitutional, and in 1936 it struck down the AAA. The Second New Deal. Roosevelt answered by moving left. In 1935 Congress created the Works Progress Administration (WPA) with a nearly $5 billion appropriation. By 1937 it employed three million people building schools, hospitals, airports, and more than half a million miles of roads, and it hired artists, writers, and musicians as well. The National Labor Relations Act of July 5, 1935, known as the Wagner Act after its sponsor, Senator Robert Wagner of New York, guaranteed workers “the right to self-organization” and created the National Labor Relations Board to enforce it. Union membership surged: in 1937 sit-down strikers in Flint, Michigan, won recognition for the United Auto Workers from General Motors. On August 14, 1935, Roosevelt signed the Social Security Act, which created old-age pensions, unemployment insurance, and aid to dependent children and the blind. (The National Archives’ own page gives both August 14 and August 15 as the date of signing.) Roosevelt insisted that the pensions be paid from workers’ and employers’ contributions rather than general taxes. “No dole,” he said. “Mustn’t have a dole.” The second term. In 1936 Roosevelt won reelection in a landslide, losing only Maine and Vermont, and in his second inaugural vowed to help the third of the nation that was ill-housed, ill-clad, and ill-nourished. In February 1937, fearing the Court would strike down Social Security, he proposed adding a new justice for every sitting justice over a certain age, up to six in all. The American Yawp gives the age as seventy and the Miller Center as seventy-five. Critics called it “court-packing,” and the plan failed in Congress. But that spring the Court began upholding New Deal laws, including the Wagner Act in NLRB v. Jones & Laughlin Steel (1937), and it has not struck down a major New Deal law since. That same year, believing the economy had recovered, Roosevelt cut federal spending, and the economy plunged into the “Roosevelt recession.” In April 1938 he reversed course and asked Congress for a $5 billion relief and public works program. The Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 set a national minimum wage of 25 cents an hour and limited working hours. The New Deal stopped the collapse and brought partial recovery. The banking panic ended, farm incomes rose, and the WPA, CCC, and other agencies gave work to millions. But unemployment stayed high. Still above 19 percent in 1939, it remained in double digits in 1940, and stock prices had not recovered from the crash. Only the vast spending of World War II brought full employment. Politically, the tide turned. The court-packing fight and the 1937 recession helped a conservative coalition of Southern Democrats and Republicans gain ground in the 1938 elections. Roosevelt tried to purge conservative Democrats in that year’s primaries; of the ten he targeted, only one lost. By 1939 he struggled to pass new reforms, and the coming war in Europe increasingly drew his attention. Congress did pass the Reorganization Act of 1939, which created the Executive Office of the President. The New Deal changed what Americans expected from Washington. Before World War I the federal government had been, in the American Yawp’s phrase, a “government out of sight”; after the New Deal, Americans came to see it as an ally in finding work, earning a decent wage, getting a fair price for crops, or organizing a union. Social Security became the centerpiece of the American welfare state, and the floor under wages and ceiling on hours set by the Fair Labor Standards Act continue to this day. Roosevelt also reshaped the presidency: his fireside chats created a direct bond with the public, and the president became chief legislator as well as chief executive. Voter turnout jumped in 1932 and 1936, and most of the new voters stayed loyal to a Democratic coalition of liberals, urban workers, farm workers, and white Southerners well into the 1960s. The New Deal’s benefits were unequally shared. To keep the votes of Southern Democrats, Roosevelt refused to back a federal anti-lynching law or the abolition of the poll tax (“I just can’t take that risk,” he told the NAACP’s secretary), and he accepted the exclusion of farm workers and domestic servants from Social Security pensions, a decision that left out many Black and Mexican American workers. NRA codes kept lower wages for Black workers, and AAA payments helped push Black tenants and sharecroppers off the land. Many programs assumed that men were breadwinners and steered women into means-tested relief, although Roosevelt appointed Frances Perkins and the African American adviser Mary McLeod Bethune to prominent posts, and Eleanor Roosevelt became a major voice for economic and racial justice. Historians still debate when the New Deal ended. Some point to the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938; others see its spirit in wartime controls, the G.I. Bill, and a “New Deal order” that lasted until Lyndon Johnson’s Great Society. The New Deal did not end the Great Depression, but it made the federal government responsible for the economic security of ordinary Americans. It created institutions, from Social Security to the FDIC, that still shape American life. I pledge you, I pledge myself, to a new deal for the American people. Franklin D. Roosevelt accepting the Democratic presidential nomination, July 1, 1932 So, first of all, let me assert my firm belief that the only thing we have to fear is fear itself—nameless, unreasoning, unjustified terror which paralyzes needed efforts to convert retreat into advance. title: Attack on Pearl Harbor
subtitle: Japan’s surprise attack that brought the United States into World War II
summary: On the morning of December 7, 1941, Japanese planes attacked the U.S. Pacific Fleet at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii. In less than two hours the fleet was devastated and more than 3,500 Americans were killed or wounded, about 2,400 of them killed. The next day President Franklin D. Roosevelt called December 7 “a date which will live in infamy,” and Congress declared war on Japan. The attack ended American isolationism and brought the United States into World War II.
thumbAlt: The battleship USS Arizona burning after the Japanese attack
aliases: Day of Infamy USS Arizona
themeText: War and the military Foreign policy and diplomacy The presidency
text: Pearl Harbor, Oahu, Hawaii Date Morning of December 7, 1941 Casualties More than 3,500 Americans killed or wounded; about 2,400 killed USS Arizona 1,177 crew members killed; the sunken ship is the resting place of more than 900 Declaration of war December 8, 1941; one dissenting vote, Rep. Jeannette Rankin of Montana Memorial USS Arizona Memorial, dedicated 1962 Through the late 1930s Japan waged a brutal war in China. The United States aided China and gradually cut off the oil, steel, and other materials Japan’s military depended on, while demanding that Japan withdraw from China. Japan joined the Tripartite Pact with Germany and Italy in September 1940 and moved into French Indochina. After the United States imposed a full embargo and froze Japanese assets, negotiations stalled. Facing severe shortages, unwilling to leave China, and convinced that American officials opposed further talks, Japan’s leaders decided to strike first. Their planners hoped to destroy enough battleships and aircraft carriers to cripple American naval power while Japan seized resource-rich territories in Southeast Asia. U.S. leaders, still hoping for a settlement and doubting Japan could attack American territory, were caught by surprise. Japanese aircraft struck the fleet at anchor. The battleship USS Arizona was sunk with the loss of 1,177 crew members; more than 900 of them remain entombed in the ship. Japan also attacked Hong Kong, the Philippines, and other American and European holdings across the Pacific. Late that afternoon, Roosevelt dictated his request for a declaration of war, revising the first line from “a date which will live in world history” to “a date which will live in infamy.” He delivered it to a joint session of Congress at 12:30 p.m. on December 8. The Senate voted unanimously for war; in the House, only Jeannette Rankin of Montana voted no. Roosevelt signed the declaration that afternoon. Germany and Italy, Japan’s allies, declared war on the United States on December 11, and within a week the United States was at war with all the Axis powers. The attack united Americans behind a massive mobilization. It also fed fear and suspicion of Japanese Americans that led, ten weeks later, to Executive Order 9066 and their mass incarceration. Pearl Harbor became a lasting symbol of national vulnerability and of the dangers of surprise attack, invoked again after the September 11 attacks in 2001. The USS Arizona Memorial, completed in 1961 and dedicated in 1962, honors all the military personnel killed in the attack. The attack on Pearl Harbor turned two regional wars into a true world war and committed the United States to global leadership. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u1EZ55_F7xk Why Japan Attacked Pearl Harbor?
