title: Woodstock
subtitle: “3 Days of Peace and Music” that came to define a generation
summary: In August 1969 nearly half a million young people gathered on Yasgur’s farm near Bethel, New York, for a music festival billed as “An Aquarian Exposition: 3 Days of Peace and Music.” Rain, mud, and shortages turned the weekend into an improvised city, and, for many, a demonstration of the counterculture’s ideals of peace and cooperation. Coming weeks after the Moon landing and amid conflict over the Vietnam War, civil rights, and sexual politics, Woodstock became shorthand for the youth culture of the 1960s.
thumbAlt: Festival-goers with a blanket tent in the crowd at Woodstock, 1969
aliases: Woodstock Music Festival Woodstock festival
themeText: Arts and popular culture Reform and protest
text: Bethel, New York When Three days in August 1969 Where Yasgur’s farm, Bethel, New York Crowd Nearly half a million people Billed as “An Aquarian Exposition: 3 Days of Peace and Music” In the 1960s protests across the country formed the backdrop for an American counterculture. Rebellion against the supposedly hidebound conservatism of the 1950s spread among the young, and the counterculture — with its music, its experiments with psychedelic drugs, and its search for personal fulfillment — increasingly reached the mainstream through popular culture and even advertising. The festival took place weeks after Americans first walked on the Moon, against the backdrop of a nation divided over the Vietnam War, civil rights, and sexual politics. PBS describes a sense of an America in transition — a handoff between generations with very different values and ideals. Over three days, a crowd of nearly half a million — rain-soaked, often hungry, many of them on drugs — turned a few acres of farmland into a swarming, impromptu city. PBS’s American Experience calls what happened “nothing less than a miracle of teamwork,” a demonstration of the “peace and love” the festival had promised. To many participants and observers the weekend seemed to validate the counterculture’s promise. The festival quickly became a legend in its own right. The American Yawp calls 1969’s Woodstock concert “shorthand for the new youth culture and its mixture of politics, protest, and personal fulfillment.” The hippies’ rise was exaggerated and short-lived, and the Vietnam War and Richard Nixon shattered much of its idealism — but the counterculture’s liberated social norms and its embrace of personal fulfillment still shape much of American culture. Woodstock is remembered as the high point of the 1960s counterculture — a symbol of a generation that challenged the values of its parents. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YV1QKaNMQRI What Was the Original Woodstock Really Like Weird History 12:09 2026-10-23

title: The Wounded Knee Massacre
subtitle: The U.S. Army kills hundreds of Lakota at Wounded Knee Creek, December 1890
summary: On December 29, 1890, soldiers of the U.S. 7th Cavalry surrounded a band of Lakota led by Spotted Elk (Big Foot) at Wounded Knee Creek on the Pine Ridge Reservation and attempted to disarm them. A shot was fired, and the soldiers opened fire with heavy weapons, killing between 150 and 300 Lakota men, women, and children. About two dozen soldiers also died, many probably from their own side’s fire. Wounded Knee marked the end of sustained armed Native resistance on the Plains.
location: Wounded Knee Creek, Pine Ridge Reservation, South Dakota
thumbAlt: The aftermath of the Wounded Knee massacre
aliases: Ghost Dance Big Foot Spotted Elk
themeText: Indigenous history War and the military Religion
text: Wounded Knee Creek, Pine Ridge Reservation, South Dakota Date December 29, 1890 Lakota dead Estimates range from about 150 to 300, many of them women and children Army dead About 25 Context Federal alarm over the Ghost Dance; the killing of Sitting Bull on December 15 By 1890 the Lakota had lost the Black Hills, their bison-based economy had collapsed, and they lived on shrinking reservations under government agents. A Paiute prophet, Wovoka, taught that if Native people lived justly and performed the Ghost Dance, their ancestors would return, the whites would vanish, and the buffalo would again roam the Plains. Members of many nations, including the Lakota, adopted the Ghost Dance. White settlers and federal officials feared the Ghost Dance meant an armed uprising, and troops were sent to the Lakota reservations. On December 15, 1890, Lakota police trying to arrest Sitting Bull at Standing Rock killed him. Fearing more violence, Spotted Elk led his band toward the Pine Ridge Agency to seek refuge. The 7th Cavalry intercepted them and escorted them to Wounded Knee Creek. On the morning of December 29, cavalrymen entered the camp to disarm the band. Tensions flared and a shot was fired — it is unclear by whom. The soldiers then fired their heavy weaponry indiscriminately into the camp. When the shooting stopped, between 150 and 300 Lakota were dead, nearly half of them women and children by one estimate. About two dozen soldiers were killed, by concealed Lakota weapons or by friendly fire. The dead were buried in a mass grave. The killings ended the Ghost Dance as a mass movement and effectively ended armed Native resistance on the Plains. Wounded Knee became a symbol of the destruction of Native nations by the United States. In 1973, activists of the American Indian Movement occupied the town of Wounded Knee for 71 days, drawing on the site’s meaning to protest treaty violations and conditions on the reservation. The massacre at Wounded Knee is remembered as the violent end of the Plains wars and as one of the gravest atrocities committed by U.S. forces against Native people. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VyF8SOSP2YM From the Trail of Tears to Wounded Knee: Ep 11 of Crash Course Native American History CrashCourse 11:07 2026-10-23

title: The Wright Brothers’ First Flight
subtitle: Kill Devil Hills, North Carolina, December 17, 1903: the first powered, controlled airplane flights
summary: On the morning of December 17, 1903, on the windswept dunes of North Carolina’s Outer Banks, the Wright brothers’ engine-powered Wright Flyer stayed aloft for twelve seconds, the first powered, controlled flight of a heavier-than-air machine carrying a person. That day Wilbur and Orville made four flights; the longest lasted 59 seconds. Two bicycle makers from Dayton, Ohio, with no formal engineering training, they succeeded because they treated flight as a scientific problem to be solved step by step.
location: Kill Devil Hills, near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina
thumbAlt: John T. Daniels’s photograph of the Wright Flyer’s first flight on December 17, 1903, with Wilbur Wright running alongside the wingtip
aliases: Wright brothers Wilbur Wright Orville Wright Kitty Hawk Wright Flyer first flight
themeText: Science and technology Everyday life
text: Kill Devil Hills, near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina First flight Morning of December 17, 1903: twelve seconds aloft Longest flight that day 59 seconds, the fourth of four flights Engine A four-cylinder, 12-horsepower gasoline engine Witnesses Four men from the nearby Kill Devil Hills Lifesaving Station; one, John T. Daniels, took the first photographs of the flights Memorial Wright Brothers National Memorial, Kill Devil Hills; Congress set aside the site in 1927 The first flights opened the age of aviation, which within a few decades transformed war, travel, and commerce. The Wrights’ methodical, experimental approach became a model of American ingenuity. Wilbur and Orville Wright ran a bicycle shop in Dayton, Ohio. Tinkering with bicycles had given them a feel for all things mechanical, and when seasonal slumps hurt their sales they turned to a much bigger problem: building a flying machine. They spent years studying the principles of flight and building gliders and other prototypes. Other inventors had flown unpiloted models — Samuel P. Langley had catapulted one from a houseboat on the Potomac in 1896 — but no one had carried a person into the air under power and control. The Wrights needed a place with strong, steady winds to give lift and soft sand for safe landings. After searching the East Coast, they chose the remote dunes near Kitty Hawk, on North Carolina’s Outer Banks. They first came in September 1900 to test gliders, returned in 1901 and 1902, and in 1903 brought a machine powered by a lightweight engine. After months of setbacks, the brothers were ready on December 17, 1903. Men from the Kill Devil Hills Lifesaving Station, about a mile away, had been helping them, ferrying visitors and moving equipment; four of the crewmen came to watch. That morning the Wright Flyer rose under its own power and flew for twelve seconds. One of the lifesavers, John T. Daniels, who had volunteered to work the camera, captured the first images of the Wrights’ success. Three more flights followed that day; the fourth and longest lasted 59 seconds. The Wrights went home to Dayton and kept testing, building more powerful models in the following years. Their achievement — study and scientific experiment, not luck, as the National Park Service stresses — solved the basic problems of powered, controlled flight. Wilbur died of typhoid fever in 1912; Orville died of a heart attack in 1948. In 1927 Congress set aside the site near Kill Devil Hill, and a tall white granite monument now stands on the hill “in commemoration of the conquest of the air”; the site is today the Wright Brothers National Memorial. The National Park Service calls their story the embodiment of “the American ideal of hard work overcoming all obstacles.” Sixty-six years after the twelve-second flight, Americans landed on the moon. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Yjccw9o1Pwk The story of the Wright Brothers CBS Sunday Morning 7:40 2026-10-23 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K499hKMabMM The Wright Brothers: First in Flight and Family Biographics 22:35 2026-10-23

title: Congress
subtitle: The legislative branch: the Senate and the House of Representatives
summary: Article I of the Constitution vests “All legislative Powers” in a Congress made up of a Senate and a House of Representatives. Members of the House are elected every two years, with seats apportioned by population; each state has two senators serving six-year terms. Congress makes the laws, levies taxes, declares war, confirms presidential appointments, and can impeach and remove officials. As the branch closest to the people, it has been the stage for many of the great debates of American history.
thumbAlt: The west front of the United States Capitol
themeText: Constitution and law Parties and elections Voting rights
text: U.S. Capitol, Washington, D.C. Constitutional basis Article I House Members “chosen every second Year by the People”; the House alone originates revenue bills and holds “the sole Power of Impeachment” Senate Two senators per state, six-year terms; tries impeachments, approves treaties and appointments Election of senators By state legislatures until the Seventeenth Amendment (1913) provided for direct election First Congress 1789 The Constitution gives every state two senators regardless of its size, while seats in the House are apportioned among the states according to population. Senators were originally chosen by state legislatures; members of the House have always been elected directly by the people. Article I, Section 8 gives Congress power “To lay and collect Taxes,” to borrow money, to regulate commerce, “To declare War,” to raise armies and a navy, and “To make all Laws which shall be necessary and proper” for carrying out its powers. Every bill must pass both houses and be presented to the president, and Congress can override a veto by two-thirds of each house. The Senate confirms or rejects nominations for federal agencies, judges, and the Supreme Court, and Congress can remove a president from office through impeachment. Political parties, which the founders had hoped to avoid, quickly organized Congress; within a decade they absorbed state and local factions in the House. Congress debated slavery’s expansion in compromises from 1820 to 1850, led Reconstruction and passed the Thirteenth, Fourteenth, and Fifteenth Amendments, and in the Progressive Era proposed the Seventeenth Amendment for direct election of senators. In the twentieth century it enacted the New Deal, the Civil Rights Act, and the Great Society, and after Vietnam and Watergate it reasserted its oversight of presidential war-making. Congress is the first branch of government in the Constitution and the institution through which Americans’ elected representatives make law, control spending, and hold presidents to account. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=n9defOwVWS8 The Bicameral Congress: Crash Course Government and Politics #2 CrashCourse 9:05 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hltv8-nzcUc What Is the Legislative Branch of the U.S. Government? | History HISTORY 4:28 2026-10-22

title: The Continental Congress
subtitle: The colonies’ revolutionary assembly, and the first national government
summary: The Continental Congress began as a meeting of colonial delegates coordinating protest against British policy and became, almost by accident, the government of a new nation. The First Continental Congress (1774) organized a boycott of British goods; the Second (1775–1781) created the Continental Army, adopted the Declaration of Independence, conducted diplomacy, and drafted the Articles of Confederation.
location: Philadelphia (and, when the British threatened, Baltimore, Lancaster, York, and other towns)
thumbAlt: Engraving of the First Continental Congress in session
themeText: Political thought War and the military Constitution and law
text: Philadelphia (and, when the British threatened, Baltimore, Lancaster, York, and other towns) First meeting September 5, 1774, in Philadelphia; twelve colonies attended (Georgia did not) Articles of Association October 20, 1774 — a coordinated boycott of British goods Second Congress Met from May 10, 1775; appointed Washington commander in chief Ended March 1, 1781, when the Articles of Confederation took effect After the Boston Tea Party, Parliament passed the Coercive Acts of 1774 — called the Intolerable Acts in the colonies — closing Boston’s port and placing Massachusetts under tighter British control. Protest groups such as the Sons of Liberty called for a boycott, but merchants were reluctant to join unless all the colonies agreed on terms and enforcement. Colonial legislatures therefore sent delegates to a general congress. It met in Philadelphia on September 5, 1774, with every colony except Georgia represented. The Congress had no legal authority of its own. Its power came from the colonial assemblies and conventions that sent delegates and from local committees that enforced its decisions. On October 20, 1774, it adopted the Articles of Association, a boycott of British goods to begin December 1 unless the Coercive Acts were repealed. It also petitioned King George III, addressed the people of Britain and the colonies, and agreed to reconvene in May 1775. By then fighting had begun at Lexington and Concord. The Second Continental Congress created the Continental Army and appointed George Washington to command it, while still sending the king the conciliatory Olive Branch Petition in July 1775 — which he refused to receive. As British authority collapsed, Congress became the de facto national government: it issued paper money, sent diplomats to Europe, negotiated the French alliance, and, in July 1776, declared independence. Congress governed without a constitution until the Articles of Confederation, which it adopted in 1777, finally took effect when Maryland ratified in March 1781. Its weakness during the war — dependent on the states for money and soldiers — shaped the debates that later produced the Constitution. Many of the men who served in it, among them Washington, Jefferson, John Adams, Franklin, and Madison, went on to lead the new republic. The Continental Congress turned thirteen separate colonies into a single political community capable of waging war, making alliances, and declaring independence — the first institution that could claim to speak for “the United States.” https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=C6rHSiN0vKk The Articles of Confederation - Becoming the United States - Extra History - Part 1 Extra History 9:30 2026-10-22

title: The Freedmen’s Bureau
subtitle: The federal agency that aided formerly enslaved people, 1865–1872
summary: Officially the Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands, the Freedmen’s Bureau was created by Congress in March 1865 to help formerly enslaved people make the transition to freedom. Led by General Oliver O. Howard, it issued food and clothing, ran hospitals, supervised labor contracts, helped found schools, legalized marriages made in slavery, and helped families reunite. Underfunded and opposed by President Andrew Johnson and white Southerners, it did most of its work between 1865 and 1868 and closed in 1872.
location: Headquarters in Washington, D.C.; offices throughout the South
thumbAlt: Alfred Waud’s drawing “The Freedmen’s Bureau”
themeText: African American history Civil rights and citizenship Reform and protest Everyday life
text: Headquarters in Washington, D.C.; offices throughout the South Created March 3, 1865, in the War Department Commissioner Maj. Gen. Oliver Otis Howard Main activity June 1865 – December 1868 Abolished 1872 Records National Archives Record Group 105 — a key source for African American genealogy During the war, Union commanders and Treasury officials handled the needs of refugees and freedpeople and the management of abandoned and confiscated land. Congress consolidated those duties on March 3, 1865, creating the Bureau in the War Department. In May, President Andrew Johnson appointed Maj. Gen. Oliver Otis Howard as commissioner, with assistant commissioners in each Southern state. The Bureau’s mission was to provide relief and help freedpeople become self-sufficient. It issued rations and clothing, operated hospitals and refugee camps, supervised labor contracts between planters and freedpeople, handled complaints and apprenticeship disputes, assisted benevolent societies in founding schools, helped legalize marriages entered into during slavery, and provided transportation to people trying to reunite with family or relocate. Later it also helped Black veterans obtain back pay and bounties. Congress passed a new Freedmen’s Bureau bill in 1866 in the face of President Johnson’s opposition; Johnson had allowed Southern states to pass black codes that essentially maintained slavery under another name. Most of the Bureau’s work ended by December 1868, and it was abolished in 1872. Its records — letters, labor contracts, marriage registers, and school reports — are now among the richest sources on the lives of African Americans in the first years of freedom. The Freedmen’s Bureau was the federal government’s first large social welfare agency, and its schools helped launch Black education in the South, even as its limited power showed how little the nation was prepared to invest in freedom. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NGPAnLDzQYY Reconstruction: Crash Course Black American History #19 CrashCourse 13:58 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wkMy0PsUZIw Freedmen: The Civil War in Four Minutes American Battlefield Trust 4:55 2026-10-22

title: The Haudenosaunee Confederacy
subtitle: The League of the Iroquois, a union of nations governed by the Great Law of Peace
summary: The Haudenosaunee (“People of the Longhouse”) are a confederacy of Native nations whose homelands lie mostly in present-day New York. According to their tradition, a prophet called the Peacemaker, with the help of Aionwatha (Hiawatha), persuaded five warring nations (the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, and Seneca) to accept the Great Law of Peace. The Tuscarora later joined as a sixth nation. The Confederacy still exists, making it one of the longest-lasting participatory governments in the world.
location: Present-day New York State and neighboring regions; today also Ontario and Quebec
thumbAlt: Six Nations chiefs at Brantford explaining their wampum belts in 1871
aliases: Iroquois Confederacy Six Nations League of the Iroquois Great Law of Peace
themeText: Indigenous history Political thought
text: Present-day New York State and neighboring regions; today also Ontario and Quebec Original nations Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, Seneca Sixth nation Tuscarora, who joined later, in the colonial era Grand Council Meets on Onondaga territory; the Onondaga are “Keepers of the Fire” Chiefs Chosen by Clan Mothers of families holding hereditary titles Name “Iroquois” was the French term; “Five” (later “Six”) Nations was the English one The Haudenosaunee describe the Confederacy as founded by the Peacemaker, sent by the Creator to spread the good mind. Traveling from community to community with Aionwatha, he persuaded the chiefs of each nation to join the Great League of Peace. He asked the Clan Mothers to present their chiefs and placed deer antlers on their heads as symbols of authority. He planted a Tree of Peace — a white pine whose Great White Roots extend in the four directions to welcome any nation that accepts the Great Peace — and asked the people to bury their weapons beneath it. He bound one arrow from each nation together to show their united strength, and recorded each law of the Great Peace in strings of wampum. The date of these events is unknown. Scholars have proposed dates ranging from the twelfth to the fifteenth century, drawing on archaeology, astronomy, and oral history; the Haudenosaunee themselves describe the Confederacy as existing since time immemorial. Each nation keeps its own council and manages its internal affairs, while the Grand Council deals with matters affecting the Confederacy as a whole. Within the metaphorical longhouse, the Mohawk, Seneca, and Onondaga sit as Elder Brothers and the Cayuga and Oneida as Younger Brothers, with the Onondaga as Keepers of the Fire. Chiefs are selected by Clan Mothers, who also hold them to their moral obligations and can remove them — a formal political role for women that European observers found striking. In the colonial era the Confederacy was a major power, controlling most of upstate New York and parts of northern Pennsylvania and balancing between the French and British empires; it allied with Britain in the French and Indian War. The American Revolution split it: the Oneida and many Tuscarora supported the Americans, while most of the other nations fought with Britain. After the war, much Haudenosaunee land was lost. The Confederacy has continued to govern and to assert its sovereignty into the present; it describes itself as still enjoying the support of the Six Nations as their representative government, even though an elective system was established in 1924. Some writers have argued that the Great Law influenced the framers of the U.S. Constitution. Historians debate how direct any such influence was, and the claim should be treated as contested. The Haudenosaunee Confederacy is a living example of Native self-government that long predates the United States, and its diplomacy and wars shaped the colonial and revolutionary history of the Northeast. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=79RApCgwZFw Hiawatha - The Great Law of Peace - Extra History - Part 1 Extra History 10:00 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D0elAQYLdfc Haudenosaunee’s Legendary Founding | Native America | Sacred Stories | PBS PBS 5:53 2026-10-22

title: Political Parties
subtitle: From Federalists and Republicans to the modern two-party system
summary: Political parties are not mentioned in the Constitution, and many founders hoped to avoid them. But parties formed almost immediately and have organized American politics ever since. The Federalists and Jefferson’s Democratic-Republicans gave way to Jacksonian Democrats and Whigs, and in the 1850s the antislavery Republican Party was born. Since then Democrats and Republicans have dominated a two-party system, even as their coalitions and ideas have shifted dramatically.
thumbAlt: Chart of the evolution of American political parties
aliases: Federalists Democratic-Republicans Whigs Democratic Party Republican Party two-party system party realignment
themeText: Parties and elections The presidency
text: First parties Federalists vs. Democratic-Republicans, 1790s Second party system Jacksonian Democrats vs. Whigs, 1830s–1850s Republican Party Founded 1854 in opposition to slavery’s expansion Major realignments Civil War era; New Deal coalition (1930s); conservative realignment (1960s–1980s) Third parties Populists (1890s) and Theodore Roosevelt’s Progressive Party (1912), among others, challenged the two major parties The founding generation tried to create a national government free of parties, but the effort proved unworkable. By the mid-1790s, Federalists led by Alexander Hamilton and Democratic-Republicans led by Jefferson and James Madison divided over the power of the national government, the economy, and foreign policy. Within a decade, the House’s historians note, parties absorbed the various state and local factions. Jefferson’s victory in the election of 1800 brought the first peaceful transfer of power between parties. Parties nominate candidates and organize voters. According to the House’s historians, parties quickly proved their worth in organizing the work of the House and in bridging the separation of powers between Congress and the president. Under Martin Van Buren, Jackson’s supporters built the Democratic Party, the first modern party, with a centralized structure and a consistent program. Jackson’s opponents organized as the Whigs in 1834. In 1854, after the Kansas-Nebraska Act, antislavery forces formed the Republican Party, which elected Abraham Lincoln in 1860. Franklin D. Roosevelt’s New Deal built a Democratic coalition of liberals, urban workers, farmers, and white Southerners that dominated politics into the 1960s. Conservative reaction against the Great Society helped Republicans rise in the South and West, and the rise of the religious right and Ronald Reagan’s victory in 1980 marked a conservative realignment. Parties are the machinery of American democracy: they turn public opinion into governing coalitions, and their realignments mark the great turning points in American political history. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VEmOUHxessE Political Parties: Crash Course Government and Politics #40 CrashCourse 9:23 2026-10-23 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZeG7r4BDtuo The Rise of POLITICAL PARTIES, Explained [APUSH Review] Heimler's History 9:46 2026-10-23

title: The Presidency
subtitle: The executive branch and the office of president
summary: Article II of the Constitution vests “the executive Power” in a president, elected for a four-year term. The president is head of state, leader of the executive branch, and commander in chief of the armed forces, and must “take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed.” From George Washington’s precedents to Franklin D. Roosevelt’s transformation of the office, the presidency has grown into the most powerful position in American government, checked by Congress, the courts, and the voters.
thumbAlt: The north and south sides of the White House
themeText: The presidency Constitution and law
text: The White House, Washington, D.C. Constitutional basis Article II Term Four years; limited to two elected terms by the Twenty-second Amendment (1951) Powers Commander in chief; makes treaties with two-thirds Senate approval; appoints judges and officers with Senate consent; may veto legislation Removal Impeachment by the House and conviction by the Senate for “Treason, Bribery, or other high Crimes and Misdemeanors” Succession The vice president becomes president if the president cannot serve The Constitutional Convention of 1787 replaced the Articles of Confederation with a Constitution that created a single executive — a president chosen by electors from each state for a four-year term, together with a vice president. George Washington became the first president in 1789. Article II makes the president “Commander in Chief of the Army and Navy” and gives the power, “by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate,” to make treaties, “provided two thirds of the Senators present concur,” and to appoint ambassadors, judges, and other officers. The president may veto bills, which Congress can override by a two-thirds vote of each house. The president is supported by the vice president and the cabinet, whose members require Senate approval. Congress may remove a president through impeachment and conviction. The office expanded in times of crisis. Abraham Lincoln used war powers to preserve the Union and issue the Emancipation Proclamation. Theodore Roosevelt and Woodrow Wilson made the president a leader of reform and of world affairs. Franklin D. Roosevelt, who won four elections, made the president a chief legislator, built the modern White House staff, and used radio fireside chats to speak directly to citizens; the Twenty-second Amendment later limited presidents to two terms. The Vietnam War and Watergate brought a backlash: Congress passed the War Powers Resolution in 1973, and in United States v. Nixon the Supreme Court held that a president must obey a subpoena; Richard Nixon became the only president to resign. The presidency has become the center of American government and politics, embodying the nation at home and abroad — and the tension between energetic leadership and constitutional limits. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=srgfqGaGcis Every President's Biggest Mistake Mr. Beat 38:43 2026-10-23 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q5SVWi9ZeB8 American Presidents: A Complete Timeline - Washington to Cleveland (1/2) Epic History 9:14 2026-10-23

title: The Supreme Court
subtitle: The highest court in the United States and the final interpreter of federal law
summary: The Supreme Court is the highest tribunal in the United States for all cases arising under the Constitution and federal law. The Constitution created it but said little about how it would work; Congress, and the justices themselves through their decisions, built the federal judiciary over time. From a weak body whose first justices complained about its lack of stature, it became, beginning with Chief Justice John Marshall, a co-equal branch that can strike down laws as unconstitutional.
location: Washington, D.C. (first met in New York City)
thumbAlt: The U.S. Supreme Court Building at dusk
themeText: Constitution and law Civil rights and citizenship
text: Washington, D.C. (first met in New York City) Created by Article III of the Constitution; organized by the Judiciary Act of 1789 First session February 1790, in the Exchange Building in New York City Size Six justices originally; the number changed six times before settling at nine in 1869 Tenure Justices serve “during good Behaviour” — effectively for life Key power Judicial review, established in Marbury v. Madison (1803) Article III of the Constitution vests “the judicial Power of the United States” in “one supreme Court” and in such lower courts as Congress creates, and provides that judges hold office during good behavior. Beyond that, the framers left the details to Congress. Establishing a federal judiciary was a high priority: the first bill introduced in the Senate became the Judiciary Act of 1789, which divided the country into thirteen judicial districts and three circuits and created a Supreme Court of a Chief Justice and five associate justices. The Court first assembled in New York in February 1790. For most of its first century the justices also had to “ride circuit,” traveling to hold court in the districts — a burden they complained about, along with the Court’s limited prestige. The Court hears a small number of cases directly (its original jurisdiction, such as disputes between states) and many more on appeal from lower federal courts and state courts on questions of federal law. Its most important power, judicial review — the authority to declare laws and government actions unconstitutional — is not stated in the Constitution. Chief Justice Marshall claimed it in Marbury v. Madison (1803), and it has since become accepted. The Court’s power has limits. It cannot enforce its rulings on its own and depends on the other branches to carry them out. Its justices are nominated by the president and confirmed by the Senate; Congress sets its size and much of its jurisdiction; and constitutional amendments can override its interpretations. Under Marshall (1801–1835) the Court established judicial review and a broad reading of federal power in cases such as McCulloch v. Maryland. Its decision in Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857), denying that Black Americans could be citizens, helped bring on the Civil War and was overturned by the Fourteenth Amendment. After Reconstruction the Court narrowed civil rights protections, upholding segregation in Plessy v. Ferguson (1896). In the 1930s it struck down early New Deal laws, then accepted broader federal economic power. Under Chief Justice Earl Warren (1953–1969) it ended legal school segregation in Brown v. Board of Education and expanded the rights of criminal defendants and voters. Since then it has remained at the center of national debates — over abortion, elections, gun rights, and the scope of federal and presidential power. The number of justices changed six times before settling at nine in 1869. Since 1790 there have been only seventeen Chief Justices, and justices have served an average of about sixteen years. The Supreme Court is where Americans have brought their deepest disputes about rights and power — slavery, segregation, voting, privacy, and the limits of government — and its interpretations of the Constitution have shaped every era of American history. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9giPmCWnepU What Is the Judicial Branch of the U.S. Government? | History HISTORY 3:09 2026-10-23 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0xnzGSV66x4 How do US Supreme Court justices get appointed? - Peter Paccone TED-Ed 4:26 2026-10-23

title: United Nations
subtitle: The international organization founded in 1945 to keep the peace
summary: The United Nations was founded in 1945 by the victorious Allies of World War II to prevent future wars through collective security and international cooperation. Unlike the League of Nations after World War I, it had strong American backing: the Senate approved the UN Charter 89 to 2. The United States is one of five permanent members of the Security Council, each holding a veto. The UN has been a central, and often contested, arena of American foreign policy ever since.
thumbAlt: The United Nations General Assembly hall
aliases: UN UN Charter Security Council General Assembly Universal Declaration of Human Rights
themeText: Foreign policy and diplomacy War and the military The Cold War The presidency
text: Charter completed in San Francisco, 1945 Founded October 24, 1945, after 29 nations ratified the Charter Charter conference San Francisco, April–June 1945, 50 nations U.S. Senate vote 89–2, July 28, 1945 Security Council Five permanent members with vetoes — the U.S., Britain, the Soviet Union, China, and France — plus elected members Human rights Universal Declaration of Human Rights adopted December 10, 1948 On January 1, 1942, 26 nations at war with the Axis signed the Declaration of the United Nations in Washington, endorsing the Atlantic Charter and pledging not to make a separate peace. Planning continued at Allied conferences: at Tehran in 1943, Roosevelt proposed an organization in which the United States, Britain, the Soviet Union, and China would enforce peace as “four policemen.” At Dumbarton Oaks in Washington in 1944, the four powers drafted a charter, and at Yalta in 1945 Roosevelt and Stalin settled the Security Council voting rules. Determined to avoid Woodrow Wilson’s failure with the League of Nations, the Roosevelt administration cultivated bipartisan support; in 1943 the Republican Party endorsed participation, and both houses of Congress overwhelmingly agreed. The Charter created a General Assembly of all member states; a Security Council with five permanent members, each holding a veto, and elected non-permanent members; an Economic and Social Council; an International Court of Justice; a Trusteeship Council to oversee certain colonial territories; and a Secretariat headed by a Secretary-General. The organization was built on the principle of collective security. Representatives of 50 nations completed the Charter in San Francisco in the spring of 1945, and the UN came into existence on October 24. Eleanor Roosevelt, appointed to the U.S. delegation by President Truman, chaired the Human Rights Commission that drafted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted in 1948. In 1950 the UN called on member states to give South Korea military assistance against the North Korean invasion, and a U.S.-led UN force fought the Korean War. The Soviet Union’s permanent seat and veto made the UN an arena of Cold War rivalry. The United Nations embodied the American commitment, after two world wars, to lead a rules-based international order rather than retreat from the world. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FnQESSTouNU The United Nations Is Created | Flashback | History HISTORY 3:48 2026-10-23 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WF6g23ydyuU Why Does the United Nations Exist? title: Abolitionism
subtitle: The movement to end slavery in the United States
summary: Abolitionism was the movement to end slavery in the United States. Early antislavery reformers, many of them Quakers, worked for gradual emancipation and an end to the slave trade. In the 1830s a new generation, led by Black activists and white evangelicals such as William Lloyd Garrison, demanded immediate, uncompensated emancipation and equal rights for Black Americans. A small and often hated minority, abolitionists used newspapers, lectures, petitions, and the Underground Railroad to make slavery the central moral question of American politics. Their cause triumphed only through the Civil War and the Thirteenth Amendment.

text: Early organizations Pennsylvania Society for Promoting the Abolition of Slavery; Benjamin Franklin, its president, petitioned the First Congress in 1790 Turn to immediatism 1831: William Lloyd Garrison’s The Liberator demands immediate emancipation National society American Anti-Slavery Society, founded 1833; about 2,000 chapters and nearly 200,000 members by 1840 Key figures Frederick Douglass, Harriet Tubman, Sojourner Truth, David Walker, Angelina and Sarah Grimké, Lucretia Mott, Wendell Phillips Achieved Thirteenth Amendment, passed by Congress January 1865 and ratified that December Early antislavery reformers sought gradual emancipation and an end to the slave trade. Many white reformers also supported “colonization,” the plan to send free Black Americans to Africa. Most Black Americans rejected colonization, insisting that America, not Africa, was their only homeland. From the 1830s the movement’s radical wing, following the lead of Black activists, demanded immediate, uncompensated emancipation, political and social equality, and citizenship for Black Americans. The American Anti-Slavery Society rested its cause “upon the Declaration of our Independence, and upon the truths of Divine Revelation,” tying abolition to both national and Christian redemption. Petitions and early societies. Quakers questioned slavery as early as the late seventeenth century and worked with British reformers against the slave trade. In February 1790, Benjamin Franklin, as president of the Pennsylvania Society for Promoting the Abolition of Slavery, signed a petition asking the First Congress to “devise means for removing the Inconsistency from the Character of the American People.” Congress tabled it, citing the Constitution’s protection of the slave trade until 1808. After the Revolution most Northern states adopted gradual emancipation laws. Immediatism. The Second Great Awakening convinced many evangelical Protestants that slavery was the most God-defying of sins. Black writers led the way. In his 1829 Appeal to the Colored Citizens of the World, David Walker exposed the hypocrisy of American claims to freedom and Christianity, attacked colonization, and warned that God’s justice would bring violence on the slaveholding nation. Walker and James Forten convinced William Lloyd Garrison, who had supported colonization and gradual abolition, that colonization was racist. In 1831 Garrison launched The Liberator in Boston, declaring in its opening editorial: “I am in earnest—I will not equivocate—I will not excuse—I will not retreat a single inch—AND I WILL BE HEARD.” He published it every week for thirty-five years. In 1833 reformers from ten states founded the American Anti-Slavery Society, which had about 2,000 chapters and nearly 200,000 members by 1840. Its strategy was “moral suasion”: convincing enslavers through appeals to conscience to free the people they held. Words and images. Using new steam presses, abolitionists flooded the free states with pamphlets and newspapers and spoke from lecture platforms across the North. In 1835 they mailed antislavery literature to Southern enslavers, and in 1836 they sent thousands of petitions to Congress. Slave narratives exposed the cruelty of bondage. Frederick Douglass’s 1845 Narrative was reprinted in nine editions and translated into several languages, and his tour of Britain won support across the Atlantic. Women in the movement. In the 1830s women formed antislavery societies in Boston, New York, and Philadelphia, raised funds, and used their right to petition. The Grimké sisters, Angelina and Sarah, daughters of a South Carolina slaveholding family, lectured to mixed audiences of men and women. When they were attacked for speaking in public, they began to argue for women’s rights as well. When the World Anti-Slavery Convention in London refused in 1840 to seat women delegates, Lucretia Mott and Elizabeth Cady Stanton resolved to fight for women’s rights, a resolve that led to the Seneca Falls Convention of 1848. Politics. In 1839 abolitionists split. Garrison and his followers held that the Constitution was a proslavery document and refused to join party politics. Others, arguing that the Constitution could be used against slavery, founded the Liberty Party under James G. Birney. Douglass, once Garrison’s ally, broke with him in 1851 and supported political action. Their work helped prepare the ground for the antislavery Republican Party of the 1850s. Resistance and escape. In the 1840s and 1850s abolitionists increasingly helped freedom seekers escape through networks known as the Underground Railroad, to the North, Canada, Mexico, and beyond, a form of civil disobedience by people of all races. After the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, armed crowds in Northern cities tried to rescue people seized under the law. A few, like John Brown, turned to violence; his raid on Harpers Ferry in 1859 convinced many Americans that slavery was pushing the nation to the brink. Abolitionists were a small minority, detested by most white Americans in the North as well as the South. Critics attacked them as fanatics who would tear the Union apart, and many were outraged that women spoke in public and that Black and white activists worked together. Northern mobs smashed abolitionist printing presses and killed the antislavery editor Elijah Lovejoy. In 1838 a mob burned the newly built Pennsylvania Hall, where the Anti-Slavery Convention of American Women was meeting. Southern states, blaming abolitionists for Nat Turner’s rebellion of 1831, purged antislavery voices from the region. In Congress, Whigs and Democrats joined in 1836 to pass the “gag rule,” which blocked all discussion of antislavery petitions in the House. Even within the movement, conflict was bitter. In 1840, when Abby Kelley was elected to the American Anti-Slavery Society’s business committee, opponents of women’s leadership left to form a rival society. Abolitionists made slavery impossible to ignore. Their example of Black and white men and women working together offered, the American Yawp writes, “a powerful, if imperfect, model of interracial coexistence.” Although immediatists remained a minority, they prepared the ground for the antislavery Republican Party, and it is hard to imagine Abraham Lincoln’s election in 1860 without them, both as allies and as radicals against whom he could appear moderate. The movement trained a generation of women activists and gave birth to the women’s rights movement. During the Civil War, the Women’s Loyal National League, led by Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony, gathered one of the largest petition drives in American history for an amendment abolishing slavery; Senator Charles Sumner presented its first 100,000 signatures in February 1864. Congress passed the Thirteenth Amendment in January 1865, and it was ratified in December. Garrison published the last issue of The Liberator on December 29, 1865. Abolitionists disagreed about tactics, whether moral persuasion, politics, or force; about whether the Constitution was proslavery; and about women’s place in the movement. Many white abolitionists also shared the racial prejudices of their time. Even Harriet Beecher Stowe’s Uncle Tom’s Cabin, which did so much for the cause, reinforced racist stereotypes. Most important, the end of slavery did not bring the equality many abolitionists had demanded. Garrison himself kept campaigning; in 1873 he declared, “I am still for immediate, unconditional, everlasting emancipation from oppression of everyone on the face of the earth.” That struggle continued through Reconstruction and long after. Abolitionists turned slavery from an accepted institution into the great moral issue of American politics. Their agitation helped bring about the political crisis of the 1850s, and the Civil War that followed ended slavery. I am in earnest—I will not equivocate—I will not excuse—I will not retreat a single inch—AND I WILL BE HEARD. William Lloyd Garrison opening editorial of The Liberator, 1831 I will be as harsh as truth, and as uncompromising as justice. On this subject, I do not wish to think, or speak, or write, with moderation. title: Red Power and the American Indian Movement
subtitle: Native activism for sovereignty and self-determination, 1960s–1970s
summary: Inspired by the civil rights movement, young Native Americans in the 1960s and 1970s launched an intertribal movement known as Red Power to protest discrimination and assert tribal sovereignty. Activists held “fish-ins” to defend treaty fishing rights, occupied Alcatraz Island for nineteen months in 1969–1971, and, led by the American Indian Movement (AIM), occupied the town of Wounded Knee, South Dakota, for months in 1973. The movement helped end the federal policy of terminating tribes and win a policy of Indian self-determination.
location: Nationwide, including Alcatraz Island, Washington, D.C., the Pacific Northwest, and Wounded Knee, South Dakota
thumbAlt: Flag of Indians of All Tribes, the group that occupied Alcatraz
aliases: Red Power AIM Indians of All Tribes fish-ins Wounded Knee occupation

text: Nationwide, including Alcatraz Island, Washington, D.C., the Pacific Northwest, and Wounded Knee, South Dakota National Indian Youth Council Founded 1961 by Native university students Fish-ins 1964, Pacific Northwest Alcatraz Occupied November 20, 1969 – June 11, 1971, by Indians of All Tribes Wounded Knee Occupied by hundreds of activists for several months in 1973 Policy change Termination ended; self-determination became federal policy Activists demanded respect for treaty rights, tribal sovereignty and self-determination, return of land, and an end to discrimination and to federal efforts to dissolve tribes. In 1961 Native university students founded the National Indian Youth Council, whose militant rhetoric and direct action began the Red Power movement. In 1964 it held “fish-ins” in the Pacific Northwest, casting nets in defiance of state laws to defend tribal fishing rights. On November 20, 1969, Indians of All Tribes, led at first by Mohawk student Richard Oakes, began occupying Alcatraz, demanding the island for an Indian university and cultural center. Activists also occupied Bureau of Indian Affairs offices in Washington. In 1973 the American Indian Movement and hundreds of others occupied Wounded Knee, site of the 1890 massacre. Federal authorities rejected the occupiers’ demands. At Alcatraz the government cut off electricity and water and eventually removed the last occupiers on June 10–11, 1971. According to the National Park Service, the Alcatraz occupation helped bring about the end of the federal termination policy and its replacement with a policy of Indian self-determination. During the occupation, President Nixon returned Blue Lake and 48,000 acres to Taos Pueblo, and the occupation of BIA offices led to more Native Americans being hired in the agency. Poverty, land claims, and conflicts over sovereignty and natural resources on reservations continued long after the 1970s. Red Power made Native Americans’ demands for sovereignty visible to the nation and reshaped federal Indian policy. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1O2LWteKuRc The Native Civil Rights Movement: Ep 15 of Crash Course Native American History CrashCourse 10:55 2026-10-22

title: The Civil Rights Movement
subtitle: The mass struggle against segregation and disfranchisement, 1950s–1960s
summary: The civil rights movement was a mass campaign by Black Americans and their allies to end legal segregation and win the right to vote in the South. Building on decades of NAACP lawsuits, it won the Supreme Court’s Brown v. Board of Education decision in 1954 and then turned to nonviolent direct action: the Montgomery bus boycott, the sit-ins, the Freedom Rides, the Birmingham campaign, the March on Washington, Freedom Summer, and the Selma marches. Its victories, the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965, dismantled Jim Crow in law and transformed American democracy.
thumbAlt: Civil rights demonstrators at a segregated public beach in Fort Lauderdale
aliases: sit-ins Freedom Rides Freedom Summer SNCC SCLC CORE NAACP Black Power nonviolence Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party Birmingham campaign
themeText: Civil rights and citizenship African American history Voting rights Reform and protest Constitution and law
text: Landmark ruling Brown v. Board of Education, May 17, 1954, decided 9–0 Key organizations NAACP (1909), CORE (1942), SCLC (1957), SNCC (1960), and local groups such as Montgomery’s Women’s Political Council Largest protest More than 200,000 people at the March on Washington, August 28, 1963 Key laws Civil Rights Act of 1964 (Senate vote 73–27); Voting Rights Act of 1965 Leaders Martin Luther King Jr., Rosa Parks, Ella Baker, John Lewis, Diane Nash, Fannie Lou Hamer, Bayard Rustin, Thurgood Marshall, and many local organizers Method Litigation, nonviolent direct action, boycotts, and voter registration The movement set out to destroy Jim Crow, the system of laws and customs that segregated Black Southerners in schools, buses, restaurants, parks, and jobs and kept most of them from voting. After World War II, the “Double V” campaign for victory over fascism abroad and racism at home, and the postwar boom, raised expectations that persistent segregation then disappointed. The demands of the 1963 March on Washington summed up the movement’s program: a comprehensive civil rights bill ending segregated public accommodations, “protection of the right to vote,” “desegregation of all public schools,” a federal jobs program, and a law “barring discrimination in all employment.” King described the ultimate end as “the creation of the beloved community,” “a society at peace with itself, a society that can live with its conscience”; by the end of his life he argued that full citizenship also required economic security. In the courts. Beginning in the early 1930s, NAACP lawyers including Charles Hamilton Houston and Thurgood Marshall chose cases on education, voting, and juries to wear away the legal foundations of segregation, first arguing that Southern states failed to provide even “equal” facilities and then, by the late 1940s, that separation itself was unconstitutional. Brown v. Board of Education combined five cases from South Carolina, Virginia, Delaware, Washington, D.C., and Kansas. In Clarendon County, South Carolina, the district spent $179 on each white student in 1950 and $43 on each Black student. On May 17, 1954, Chief Justice Earl Warren announced a unanimous decision that “separate educational facilities are inherently unequal.” But the Court’s 1955 order to desegregate “with all deliberate speed” was so vague that it left the work in the hands of segregation’s defenders. Montgomery. On December 1, 1955, Rosa Parks, a member of the NAACP, was arrested for refusing to give up her seat on a Montgomery bus. Jo Ann Robinson and the Women’s Political Council, who had pressed the city about bus segregation since 1954, called a one-day boycott and printed tens of thousands of leaflets overnight. On December 5, 90 percent of Montgomery’s Black citizens stayed off the buses, and that day the new Montgomery Improvement Association chose a twenty-six-year-old minister, Martin Luther King Jr., as its president. For thirteen months, Black residents walked or rode in a carpool of about 300 cars, while city officials indicted more than eighty leaders and segregationists bombed King’s and E. D. Nixon’s homes. The protest ended in victory on December 20, 1956, after the Supreme Court struck down bus segregation. Women such as Robinson, Johnnie Carr, and the “nameless cooks and maids who walked endless miles” sustained the boycott, and its success led King and other ministers to found the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC) in 1957. Students take the lead. On February 1, 1960, four Black students from North Carolina A&T sat down at the whites-only Woolworth lunch counter in Greensboro and refused to leave. By the end of the month sit-ins had spread to more than thirty places in seven states, and by the end of April more than 50,000 students had taken part. In Nashville, James Lawson trained students such as John Lewis, Diane Nash, and Marion Barry in Gandhian nonviolence. That April, SCLC’s Ella Baker called the student leaders to a conference at Shaw University, where they founded the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC). Baker urged them to stay independent and to build “group-centered leaders” rather than follow a single charismatic figure. In May 1961 the Congress of Racial Equality (CORE) sent interracial Freedom Riders south to test a Supreme Court ruling against segregated bus terminals. At Anniston, Alabama, a mob firebombed one of their buses, and riders were beaten in Birmingham and Montgomery. When CORE halted the rides, Nash and the Nashville students insisted on continuing: “We can’t let them stop us with violence. If we do, the movement is dead.” Students from across the country then crowded into the jails of Jackson, Mississippi, and on November 1, 1961, a federal ban on segregation in interstate bus travel took effect. Birmingham and Washington. In April 1963 SCLC joined Fred Shuttlesworth’s local movement in Birmingham with sit-ins, marches, and a boycott of downtown stores. Arrested on Good Friday, King wrote his “Letter from Birmingham Jail” in reply to eight white clergymen who had called the protests “unwise and untimely”: “For years now, I have heard the word ‘Wait!’ … This ‘Wait’ has almost always meant ‘Never.’” In May, more than a thousand Black schoolchildren marched, and the city’s public safety commissioner, Eugene “Bull” Connor, turned fire hoses and police dogs on them. The images caused international outrage and forced a settlement that removed “Whites Only” signs and began the desegregation of lunch counters. President John F. Kennedy went on national television in June to call for a civil rights bill. On August 28, 1963, more than 200,000 people joined the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom, organized by A. Philip Randolph and Bayard Rustin, where King delivered his “I Have a Dream” speech. Mississippi and Selma. In Mississippi, where violence made mass street protests nearly impossible, SNCC’s Bob Moses built a grassroots voter registration campaign. In the summer of 1964 about 1,000 volunteers, most of them white Northern college students, joined Freedom Summer. About 17,000 Black Mississippians tried to register that summer, but registrars accepted only 1,600 applications, and 41 Freedom Schools taught more than 3,000 young people. The movement’s Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party challenged the state’s all-white delegation at the Democratic National Convention, where Fannie Lou Hamer, a former sharecropper who had been fired for trying to register and savagely beaten in a Mississippi jail, testified on national television. In Selma, Alabama, where only two percent of Black residents were on the voting rolls, SNCC and SCLC launched a voting rights campaign in January 1965. On March 7, “Bloody Sunday,” state troopers clubbed and tear-gassed marchers led by John Lewis and Hosea Williams on the Edmund Pettus Bridge. Two weeks later, under federal protection, marchers walked the fifty-four miles to Montgomery, their numbers swelling to 25,000 by the final day. White Southerners fought the movement with defiance, mass arrests, economic reprisals, and terror. In August 1955, fourteen-year-old Emmett Till of Chicago was abducted and murdered in Mississippi for supposedly whistling at a white woman; an all-white jury acquitted his killers, who months later described the crime in Look magazine. His mother’s insistence on an open-casket funeral made his death national news. Desegregation met fierce resistance: in 1957 soldiers of the 101st Airborne Division had to escort nine Black students into Little Rock’s Central High School, and in 1962 two people died in rioting when James Meredith enrolled at the University of Mississippi. Alabama governor George Wallace promised “segregation now, segregation tomorrow, segregation forever” in 1963 and stood in the door of the University of Alabama to block its integration. The violence was relentless. The night after the Birmingham agreement, bombs exploded near King’s motel and at his brother’s home; on September 15, 1963, Ku Klux Klan members bombed Birmingham’s Sixteenth Street Baptist Church, killing four young girls. The civil rights leader Medgar Evers was assassinated at his home in June 1963. In June 1964 three civil rights workers, James Chaney, a Black Mississippian, and two white Northerners, Michael Schwerner and Andrew Goodman, were murdered near Philadelphia, Mississippi, by Klan members and local law officers. In 1965 a state trooper shot Jimmie Lee Jackson during a march in Marion, Alabama; local white men attacked and fatally injured the Unitarian minister James Reeb in Selma; and Klansmen shot Viola Liuzzo, a volunteer from Michigan, after the march to Montgomery. The federal government was often a reluctant ally. The Kennedy administration intervened only after mobs had attacked the Freedom Riders, and President Lyndon B. Johnson, fearing the loss of white Southern votes, backed a compromise at the 1964 convention that offered the Mississippi Freedom Democrats just two at-large seats. “We didn’t come all this way for no two seats,” Hamer replied. The FBI later made SNCC a target of its COINTELPRO program against Black militancy. The movement destroyed legal segregation. The Civil Rights Act of 1964, which Kennedy proposed and Johnson pushed through after Kennedy’s assassination, outlawed segregation in hotels, restaurants, theaters, and other public places and banned discrimination in employment. Southern senators tried to talk it to death in a filibuster before the Senate passed it 73 to 27, and Johnson signed it on July 2, 1964. The Voting Rights Act, which Johnson introduced after Selma with the words “we shall overcome,” outlawed literacy tests, sent federal examiners to register voters, and required states with a history of discrimination to clear changes to their voting rules with Washington. Johnson signed it on August 6, 1965. By the end of 1965 a quarter of a million new Black voters had been registered, one-third of them by federal examiners. Enforcement of Brown came slowly but dramatically: in 1968, about 80 percent of Black schoolchildren in the South still attended schools that were 90 to 100 percent nonwhite, but by 1972 only 25 percent did, and Southern schools became by many measures the most integrated in the nation. The movement also changed how Americans protested. Its tactics, from the boycott and the sit-in to the mass march, and its moral language, rooted in Black churches, helped inspire new movements of Native Americans, Chicanos, and women in the 1960s. In King’s own summary, “Montgomery led to the Civil Rights Act of 1957 and 1960; Birmingham inspired the Civil Rights Act of 1964; and Selma produced the voting rights legislation of 1965.” The laws of 1964 and 1965 attacked segregation by law, but not the poverty, housing discrimination, and police brutality that shaped Black life in Northern cities as well as Southern ones. Federal housing policy had itself helped create segregated neighborhoods: from the 1930s, maps “redlined” Black neighborhoods as risky, and the Federal Housing Administration and the Veterans Administration refused to back mortgages there. Days after the Voting Rights Act was signed, rioting broke out in the Watts neighborhood of Los Angeles, and riots followed in other cities every summer, most destructively in Newark and Detroit in 1967. The movement itself divided. After the 1964 convention, many SNCC activists lost faith in interracial cooperation and nonviolence. In June 1966 Stokely Carmichael, SNCC’s new chairman, began calling for “Black Power,” and SNCC and CORE soon excluded white members. Malcolm X, a Nation of Islam minister who was killed in 1965, had offered a more militant alternative to King’s approach. King, meanwhile, turned to poverty in the North and to opposition to the Vietnam War, and was planning a Poor People’s Campaign for jobs and income when he was assassinated on April 4, 1968. The Supreme Court in 2013 struck down a key provision of the Voting Rights Act requiring federal oversight of voting rules in nine states. The civil rights movement ended legal segregation in the United States, brought about the greatest change in federal protection of voting since Reconstruction, and showed how ordinary people using nonviolent mass action could change the law of a nation. We came to see that, in the long run, it is more honorable to walk in dignity than ride in humiliation.
