title: Alexander Hamilton
subtitle: First secretary of the Treasury and architect of the federal financial system
summary: Alexander Hamilton was born in the British West Indies, came to the mainland colonies as a teenager, and became one of the most influential of the nation’s founders. He served as George Washington’s aide during the Revolution, helped call the Constitutional Convention, and wrote most of the Federalist Papers in support of the Constitution. As the first secretary of the Treasury, from 1789 to 1795, he paid the Revolutionary War debts in full, had the federal government take over the states’ debts, and created the First Bank of the United States. His program and his preference for Britain divided the government and helped create the first political parties. He was killed in a duel with Vice President Aaron Burr in 1804.
thumbAlt: Portrait of Alexander Hamilton by John Trumbull
aliases: Federalist Party Report on Public Credit assumption First Bank of the United States Hamilton-Burr duel Publius
themeText: Economy and finance Constitution and law Parties and elections Immigration
text: Alexander Hamilton Charlestown, Nevis, British West Indies New York City Aide-de-camp to George Washington (1777–1781) Member of the Continental Congress Delegate to the Constitutional Convention (1787) Principal author of the Federalist Papers First secretary of the Treasury (1789–1795) Lawyer in New York City Born January 11, 1757 (or perhaps 1755), Charlestown, Nevis, British West Indies Revolution Artillery captain in 1776; aide-de-camp to Washington, March 1777 to February 1781 Constitution Helped call the Constitutional Convention; wrote most of the 85 Federalist essays Treasury First secretary of the Treasury, 1789–1795: debt funding, assumption of state debts, the Bank, excise taxes Family Married Elizabeth Schuyler during the Revolution; built The Grange in upper Manhattan, completed in 1802 Death Mortally wounded by Aaron Burr in a duel at Weehawken, New Jersey, July 11, 1804; died July 12 Hamilton designed the financial foundations of the federal government. He established the public credit of the United States, created its first national bank, and argued for a broad reading of the Constitution’s powers, a view the Supreme Court later echoed. His vision of a commercial, industrial nation tied to a strong central government, set against Jefferson’s agrarian republic, defined one of the most lasting debates in American politics. Alexander Hamilton was born in Charlestown on the Caribbean island of Nevis, in the British West Indies. The Historical Society of the New York Courts gives his birth date as January 11, 1757, “or perhaps 1755,” and the year is still disputed. His early education came from his mother and a local clergyman. As a poor orphan he worked as a clerk for a shipping company that was partly involved in the slave trade, and the National Park Service notes that he saw the cruel treatment of enslaved people on the island’s sugar plantations at first hand. Local mentors raised money to send him north. In 1772 he attended an academy in Elizabethtown, New Jersey, and then studied at King’s College, now Columbia University, in New York. When the Revolution began, Hamilton joined the Continental Army in New York in 1776 as a captain of artillery. On March 1, 1777, Washington made him an aide-de-camp, and he served on the general’s staff until February 16, 1781. During the war he married Elizabeth Schuyler, the daughter of a wealthy and influential New York family whose estates were worked by enslaved people. The Park Service notes that Hamilton had to reconcile his disapproval of slavery with his ties to the Schuylers and to Washington. After the war New York relaxed its rules for veterans who had broken off their legal studies to fight, and in July 1782 Hamilton was admitted to the bar. He opened a law office on Wall Street once the British left New York City and became one of the state’s leading lawyers. He served in the Continental Congress in 1782, 1783, and 1788. Making the Constitution. Hamilton believed the Articles of Confederation left the nation dangerously weak. In 1786 he and James Madison wrote the report of the Annapolis Convention that called on the states to send delegates to Philadelphia to revise the Articles. At the Constitutional Convention, on June 18, 1787, he offered his own plan, calling the British government “the best in the world” and proposing an executive and senators who would serve for life during good behavior. The convention did not adopt it. To win ratification in New York, he enlisted John Jay and James Madison to write a series of newspaper essays, published under the name “Publius” and now known as the Federalist Papers. Hamilton wrote most of the 85 essays, and he then helped bring New York to ratify. In the first essay he wrote that Americans would decide “whether societies of men are really capable or not of establishing good government from reflection and choice, or whether they are forever destined to depend for their political constitutions on accident and force.” The Treasury. In 1789 Washington appointed Hamilton the first secretary of the Treasury, and he built the department. He faced a chaotic treasury and heavy war debts. “The debt of the United States,” he wrote, “was the price of liberty,” and he insisted it be repaid in full. His plan had three parts. First, the federal government would assume the states’ remaining war debts, about $25 million. Second, the government would redeem Revolutionary bonds at face value, paying whoever held them. Since many veterans had sold their bonds cheaply, this meant speculators would profit, and Madison and Jefferson objected. Third, a national bank would hold federal funds and provide credit. Southerners who had already paid their own debts resisted assumption. Hamilton won it by agreeing, in a bargain struck at a dinner at Jefferson’s house, to support placing the permanent capital on the Potomac River. By the end of 1794, 98 percent of the country’s domestic debt had been converted into new federal bonds. To pay the interest he created a revenue system based on customs duties and excise taxes, including a 1791 tax on whiskey. Hamilton believed that tying the fortunes of wealthy creditors to the government would give them a stake in its success, and that a funded debt would circulate like money, as “an engine of business.” The Bank and the Constitution. Jefferson and Madison argued that the Constitution gave Congress no power to charter a bank. Hamilton answered with an opinion of some 13,000 words, arguing that every power granted to a government includes “a right to employ all the means requisite and fairly applicable” to carry it out. Washington signed the bill on February 25, 1791, creating the First Bank of the United States, which served as the Treasury’s financial agent and issued paper currency. In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), the Supreme Court under Chief Justice John Marshall unanimously upheld a later national bank, taking a similarly broad view of the powers of Congress. He also proposed a national mint, though it was placed under the State Department in 1792. Hamilton wanted a strong, energetic national government. He believed that self-interest was the “most powerful incentive of human actions” and that a wise government should harness citizens’ desire for property to serve the public good. He saw America’s future as a commercial and industrial society, in contrast to Jefferson’s nation of small farmers. The American Yawp argues that his vision proved the more enduring. He did not think government should equalize property, and he wrote that it must be “a Repository of the Rights of the wealthy.” In foreign policy he favored close commercial ties with Britain. He disapproved of slavery. In the 1780s he helped found the New York Manumission Society, which campaigned for abolition and in 1794 established the African Free School, which educated enslaved and free Black students. Hamilton’s opponents saw his program as a scheme to enrich speculators and northern financiers. Jefferson became convinced that Hamilton secretly favored monarchy and aristocracy, and the two men fought constantly inside Washington’s cabinet. Hamilton sometimes went around the secretary of state. Encyclopedia Virginia says he privately assured the British minister that the administration would not stand firm on Jefferson’s demands. Washington usually sided with Hamilton, and the quarrel helped produce the first party system, with Hamilton’s Federalists against Jefferson and Madison’s Republicans. The whiskey tax fell hardest on western farmers, and when armed farmers in western Pennsylvania attacked tax collectors in July 1794, Hamilton rode west with the militia army and oversaw the arrest and trial of rebels. Most were released or pardoned. Hamilton resigned in 1795, partly because his $3,500 salary could not support his family, but he remained Washington’s adviser and helped draft the 1796 Farewell Address. His feud with John Adams, the leader of his own party, damaged the Federalists. The Miller Center’s Jefferson essay states that in 1796 he influenced South Carolina’s electors to withhold votes from Adams. Its Adams essay is more cautious, saying that many believed he sought to do so. In October 1800 he published a pamphlet arguing that Adams should not be reelected. When Jefferson and Aaron Burr tied in the electoral vote that year, Hamilton urged the House to choose Jefferson, whom he disliked, over Burr, whom he considered an unprincipled opportunist. In 1801 Hamilton commissioned The Grange, a Federal-style country house on a 32-acre estate in upper Manhattan, named for his father’s ancestral home in Scotland. It was completed in 1802. In 1804, while arguing a libel case in Albany, he remarked at a dinner that Burr was a dangerous man who should not be trusted with power. The remark was reported in letters printed in the Albany Register, and the long bitterness between the two men came to a head. On July 11, 1804, they met in a duel at Weehawken, New Jersey. Burr mortally wounded Hamilton, who died in New York City the next day. Burr was indicted for murder, and his political career was over. Elizabeth Hamilton continued to use The Grange for thirty years after his death, and the house is now preserved as Hamilton Grange National Memorial. Hamilton’s institutions outlived him. The Treasury Department he designed, the public credit he established, and the doctrine of implied powers became lasting parts of the federal government. So did the argument he started with Jefferson over how strong the national government should be. The debt of the United States ... was the price of liberty. title: Amelia Earhart
subtitle: The first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic, who vanished over the Pacific in 1937
summary: Amelia Earhart was one of the most influential pioneers of American aviation. In 1928 she became the first woman to cross the Atlantic by air, as a passenger, and in 1932 she flew it alone, five years to the day after Charles Lindbergh. She set record after record, including the first solo flight from Hawaiʻi to California, and used her fame to argue that women could do any job that men could. On July 2, 1937, nearing the end of an attempt to fly around the world, she and her navigator, Fred Noonan, vanished near tiny Howland Island in the Pacific. No trace of them was ever found.
thumbAlt: Photograph of Amelia Earhart in 1935
aliases: Earhart Lady Lindy Queen of the Air
themeText: Women's history Science and technology Arts and popular culture
text: Amelia Mary Earhart Atchison, Kansas Disappeared near Howland Island, Pacific Ocean Aviator Author and lecturer Career adviser at Purdue University (1935–1937) First flight as passenger June 1928: the first woman to cross the Atlantic by air Solo Atlantic May 20–21, 1932, Newfoundland to Ireland — the first woman, and the second person after Lindbergh Honors The Distinguished Flying Cross, the first awarded to a woman Pacific January 11, 1935: first person to fly solo from Honolulu to Oakland Disappearance July 2, 1937, with navigator Fred Noonan, on the flight from Lae, New Guinea, to Howland Island Earhart turned aviation into a cause for women’s equality, proving in the most public way possible that women could match men in skill and daring. Her unexplained disappearance made her a lasting American legend. Amelia Mary Earhart was born in Atchison, Kansas, in 1897. As a girl she climbed trees, “belly slammed” her sled downhill, and hunted rats with a .22 rifle, and she kept a scrapbook about women succeeding in fields dominated by men. When she saw her first airplane at a state fair at about ten, she was unimpressed — “a thing of rusty wire and wood.” After high school she attended a girls’ finishing school near Philadelphia but left to work as a nurse’s aide in a Canadian military hospital during World War I; she later attended college and became a social worker at a Boston settlement house. A ride with the pilot Frank Hawks in December 1920 changed her life: “By the time I had got two or three hundred feet off the ground, I knew I had to fly.” She took her first flying lesson in January 1921 and within six months bought a bright yellow secondhand biplane she called “The Canary,” in which she set a women’s altitude record. In April 1928 the publisher George P. Putnam’s team asked her, “How would you like to be the first woman to fly the Atlantic?” In June she crossed from Newfoundland to Wales with pilots Wilmer Stultz and Louis Gordon; although she only kept the log, the flight made her world-famous as “Lady Lindy,” with a ticker-tape parade in New York and a White House reception. She married Putnam in 1931, calling the marriage a “partnership” with “dual control.” On May 20, 1932, she took off alone from Harbor Grace, Newfoundland, bound for Paris. Ice, winds, and mechanical trouble forced her down in a pasture near Londonderry, Ireland, after about fifteen hours — the first solo transatlantic flight by a woman. Congress awarded her the Distinguished Flying Cross, the first given to a woman. Three months later she became the first woman to fly solo nonstop across the United States. On January 11, 1935, she became the first person to fly solo from Honolulu to Oakland, sipping hot chocolate over the empty Pacific. That year Purdue University made her a career adviser for women students and bought her a Lockheed Electra as a “flying laboratory.” Earhart believed her flights proved that men and women were equal in “jobs requiring intelligence, coordination, speed, coolness, and willpower.” In a letter to her husband, written in case a dangerous flight proved her last, she explained: “Please know I am quite aware of the hazards. I want to do it because I want to do it. Women must try to do things as men have tried. When they fail, their failure must be but a challenge to others.” Earhart’s 1928 fame rested on a flight on which she had only kept the log, and her career was closely tied to Putnam, a publisher who had made a fortune from Charles Lindbergh’s book; she became a bestselling author and a sought-after product endorser. The cause of her disappearance has never been established. She probably tried to set the plane down on the ocean when her fuel ran out, but no proof of her fate exists, competing theories abound, and exploration teams still search for her plane. In 1937 Earhart set out to become the first woman to fly around the world. A first attempt in March ended when she damaged the plane taking off in Honolulu. On June 1 she and Noonan left Miami flying east; by June 29 they had reached Lae, New Guinea, with about 22,000 miles behind them and 7,000 to go, all over the Pacific. On July 2, approaching Howland Island, she radioed the Coast Guard cutter Itasca that she was low on fuel and could not find the island; contact was lost. A massive Navy and Coast Guard search found nothing. Purdue keeps one of the largest collections of her papers, and she remains a symbol of courage and ambition for women. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kGIIPzvK9c0 Searching for Amelia Earhart (Full Episode) | SPECIAL | National Geographic National Geographic 1:34:30 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ivbh9vEkp1g Amelia Earhart - First Woman To Fly Alone | Mini Bio | Biography Biography 3:21 2026-10-22

title: Andrew Carnegie
subtitle: Steel magnate and philanthropist of the Gilded Age
summary: Andrew Carnegie arrived in Pennsylvania as a poor thirteen-year-old Scottish immigrant and built the largest and most profitable steel company in the world. In 1901 he sold it to J. P. Morgan, who used it to create U.S. Steel, and Carnegie spent the rest of his life giving his fortune away, funding thousands of public libraries and institutions. His mills were also the scene of the violent 1892 Homestead strike, and he remains a symbol of both the opportunity and the inequality of the Gilded Age.
thumbAlt: Photograph of Andrew Carnegie
themeText: Economy and finance Science and technology Immigration Labor and work
text: Andrew Carnegie Dunfermline, Scotland Telegrapher and railroad manager Founder of Carnegie Steel Philanthropist; author of “The Gospel of Wealth” Immigrated 1848, at age 13, from Dunfermline, Scotland, to Allegheny, Pennsylvania First job Bobbin boy in a cotton mill, $1.20 a week Sold Carnegie Steel 1901, to J. P. Morgan, forming U.S. Steel Philanthropy About half of America’s public libraries had been built with his money by his death in 1919 Carnegie was born in 1835 in a one-room house in Dunfermline, Scotland, the son of a handloom weaver. When machines took over weaving in the 1840s the family was impoverished, and in 1848 his strong-willed mother led them to Allegheny, Pennsylvania. At thirteen, his schooling over, Andrew went to work as a bobbin boy in a cotton mill for $1.20 a week, twelve hours a day, six days a week. The next year he became a $2-a-week telegraph messenger, learned to read messages by ear, and was promoted to operator. A local man, Colonel James Anderson, let working boys borrow books from his library; Carnegie read all he could and resolved that if he ever became rich he would give other working boys the same chance. Thomas A. Scott of the Pennsylvania Railroad hired him as his personal telegrapher, and by 1859, at twenty-four, Carnegie ran the railroad’s Western Division. Mentored by Scott, who helped him invest — often in insider deals — Carnegie was rich by the end of the Civil War. He bet on steel. Henry Bessemer’s process, invented in 1857, made steel in large quantities at a fraction of the old cost, and Carnegie left the railroad to build mills supplying rails to the booming railroads; he shrewdly named his first steel mill after the Pennsylvania Railroad’s president, J. Edgar Thomson, and the railroad became his best customer. His method was relentless: save profits in good times, expand during depressions when construction was cheap and rivals had to sell, and keep cutting costs through new technology. He bought up sources of raw materials and shipping (vertical integration) and absorbed competitors (horizontal integration). American steel output rose from 13,000 tons in 1860 to more than 11 million in 1900 — more than England and Germany combined — and by the 1890s Carnegie Steel was the largest and most profitable steel company in the world. In 1901, after a round of golf, Carnegie agreed to sell to J. P. Morgan for $492 million; Morgan merged Carnegie Steel with other firms into U.S. Steel, the world’s largest corporation. “Congratulations on becoming the richest man in the world,” Morgan told him. Carnegie spent his last two decades giving away about 90 percent of his fortune: he built more than 2,500 libraries in the United States, Canada, Britain, and elsewhere, founded Carnegie Hall, the Carnegie Institute in Pittsburgh, and the technical schools that became part of Carnegie Mellon University, and in 1911 created Carnegie Corporation of New York, endowing it with $125 million by 1912 — the largest philanthropic trust ever established up to that time. In his 1889 essay “The Gospel of Wealth,” Carnegie argued that great fortunes were a public trust: the rich had a moral duty to use their surplus wealth during their lifetimes “to do real and permanent good in this world,” rather than leave it to their heirs. “The man who dies rich,” he wrote, “dies disgraced.” In 1892, at Carnegie’s steel mill in Homestead, Pennsylvania, the Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers struck after repeated wage cuts and occupied the mill. The plant’s operator, Henry Clay Frick, called in hundreds of Pinkerton detectives; after a pitched battle the Pinkertons surrendered, but the governor sent the state militia, broke the strike, and reopened the mill, and the union was essentially destroyed. Homestead became a symbol of the gap between Carnegie’s professed sense of social responsibility and his company’s treatment of workers. His philanthropy has also been criticized as a way of legitimizing fortunes built on low-paid labor. Carnegie died in 1919, by which time about half the public libraries in the United States had been built with his money. His foundation — renamed the Andrew Carnegie Foundation in 2026 — has funded work from the discovery of insulin to the creation of public broadcasting and Sesame Street. Historians still debate whether the titans of the Gilded Age were “robber barons” or creative industrialists; Carnegie, the bobbin boy who became the richest man in the world and then gave it away, embodies both sides of the question. Carnegie’s rise from immigrant mill boy to steel king made him the era’s emblem of the self-made man, while Homestead and his philanthropy raised enduring questions about wealth, power, and responsibility. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Dh47mM3GOjA Andrew Carnegie: Robber Baron or America’s Greatest Philanthropist? title: Andrew Jackson
subtitle: Seventh president, champion of the “common man,” and architect of Indian removal
summary: Andrew Jackson was the dominant figure in American politics between Thomas Jefferson and Abraham Lincoln. He was the first president from the West and the first “self-made man” to reach the White House. Orphaned by the Revolution, he rose as a Tennessee lawyer, planter, and enslaver, and his victory at New Orleans in 1815 made him a national hero. As president from 1829 to 1837 he cast himself as the people’s champion against privilege, destroyed the Second Bank of the United States, faced down South Carolina’s nullification of federal law, and founded the Democratic Party. He also signed the Indian Removal Act, which drove the Native nations of the Southeast from their homelands and led to the Cherokee Trail of Tears.
thumbAlt: Portrait of Andrew Jackson
aliases: Old Hickory King Andrew Jacksonian democracy Bank War spoils system Kitchen Cabinet nullification crisis
themeText: The presidency Parties and elections Indigenous history Slavery and emancipation War and the military
text: Andrew Jackson Waxhaw settlement, on the North Carolina–South Carolina border The Hermitage, near Nashville, Tennessee Tennessee congressman, senator, and judge Major general in the War of 1812 Territorial governor of Florida (1821) Seventh president (1829–1837) Founder of the Democratic Party Tennessee planter and enslaver Born March 15, 1767, Waxhaw settlement on the Carolina border (the exact birthplace is disputed) Military fame Defeated the Red Stick Creeks at Horseshoe Bend (March 1814) and the British at New Orleans (January 8, 1815) Elections Lost in the House in 1824 despite leading the vote; won 1828 (178 electoral votes to 83) and 1832 (219 to 49) Indian removal Signed the Indian Removal Act, May 28, 1830 Bank War Vetoed recharter of the Second Bank, July 10, 1832; removed federal deposits, 1833 Vetoes Twelve, more than his six predecessors combined Died June 8, 1845, at The Hermitage; buried beside Rachel Jackson turned the presidency into a direct link between the president and the voters and built the first modern mass party, while his opponents organized as the Whigs. The Miller Center calls the national two-party system his legacy. His record also includes the forced removal of Native nations and the defense of slavery, and historians remain sharply divided over him. Andrew Jackson was born on March 15, 1767, in the Waxhaw settlement, a community of Scotch-Irish immigrants on the border between North and South Carolina. His exact birthplace is disputed, but he considered himself a South Carolinian. His father died before he was born. The Revolution wiped out the rest of his family. His oldest brother, Hugh, died in patriot service. Andrew and his brother Robert, too young to be regular soldiers, fought with irregulars and were captured in 1781. Robert died of smallpox soon after their release, and their mother died of illness while trying to help nephews held on a British prison ship. At fifteen Jackson was an orphan and a hardened veteran. He read law in North Carolina, was admitted to the bar in 1787, and in 1788 went west to Nashville as public prosecutor. There he built a legal practice, traded, and began acquiring land and enslaved people. In 1791 he began living with Rachel Donelson Robards, who was separated from her husband. They married formally in 1794 after her divorce. His supporters later claimed the couple believed she was already divorced in 1791, but the Miller Center finds this unlikely, and charges of bigamy followed Jackson into his presidential campaigns. He served as a delegate to Tennessee’s constitutional convention in 1795, as the state’s first congressman, briefly as a senator, and as a judge of the superior court. In 1804 he bought The Hermitage, a cotton plantation near Nashville worked by enslaved people. Jackson’s temper led him into many quarrels. In an 1806 duel he let Charles Dickinson, a crack shot, fire first, took a bullet in the chest, and then killed him. He carried the bullet for the rest of his life. In 1802 he had won election as major general of the Tennessee militia. When the War of 1812 came, his willingness to share his men’s hardships on a march home from Natchez earned him the nickname “Old Hickory.” After Red Stick Creeks killed more than four hundred people at Fort Mims, he led Tennessee militia and Native allies into the Creek country and crushed the main Creek force at Horseshoe Bend in March 1814. Treaties he later negotiated took millions of acres from the Creeks, Choctaws, Chickasaws, and Cherokees, including nations that had fought on his side. As a U.S. major general, Jackson defended New Orleans with regulars, militia, free Black soldiers, Native Americans, and pirates. On January 8, 1815, his men shattered a frontal British assault, inflicting more than two thousand casualties. The Miller Center counts American losses in the main attack at thirteen dead and fifty-eight wounded and missing, while the American Yawp gives barely three hundred American casualties for the campaign’s defense of the city. The peace treaty had already been signed at Ghent two weeks earlier, but the victory made Jackson the nation’s greatest hero since Washington. In 1818, pursuing Seminoles, he invaded Spanish Florida on his own broad reading of his orders, seized its forts, and executed two British subjects. The episode caused an international uproar but helped persuade Spain to cede Florida in 1819. The road to the White House. In 1824 Jackson led a four-man field with 43 percent of the popular vote and 99 electoral votes, short of a majority. When the House chose John Quincy Adams and Adams named Henry Clay secretary of state, Jackson denounced a “corrupt bargain.” In 1828 he swept Adams aside with 56 percent of the vote and 178 electoral votes to 83, after a campaign full of attacks on his marriage and violent past. Rachel died on December 22, before his inauguration. In 1832 he defeated Clay with 55 percent and 219 electoral votes to 49. That campaign also introduced national nominating conventions. The people’s tribune. Jackson saw himself as the people’s defender against special interests, and he took his case directly to the voters. He replaced officeholders through “rotation in office,” which critics called the “spoils system,” after a supporter’s phrase “to the victor belong the spoils.” He vetoed road and canal bills, beginning with the Maysville Road in 1830, and used the veto more than all his predecessors combined. He relied on informal advisers, the “Kitchen Cabinet,” and remade his official cabinet in 1831 after a bitter social feud over Peggy Eaton, the wife of his secretary of war, which also deepened his break with Vice President John C. Calhoun. He was proud of paying off the national debt. Nullification. In 1832 South Carolina declared the federal tariff null and void within its borders. Jackson, though he favored lower tariffs, issued a proclamation calling the Union indivisible and warning, “Disunion by armed force is treason.” At a dinner in 1830 he had already toasted, with Calhoun looking on, “Our federal Union: It must be preserved.” Early in 1833 Congress passed a compromise tariff together with a “force bill” authorizing him to enforce the revenue laws, and South Carolina rescinded its nullification of the tariff. The Bank War. Jackson, like Jefferson, believed the Second Bank of the United States was dangerous and unconstitutional. When its supporters pushed an early recharter through Congress in 1832, he vetoed it on July 10. His veto message declared that “the rich and powerful too often bend the acts of government to their selfish purposes.” In 1833 he moved federal deposits from the Bank to state banks, firing a Treasury secretary who refused to carry out the order. The Senate censured him in March 1834, and his allies had the censure expunged in 1837. His enemies, calling him “King Andrew the First,” organized as the Whig Party. Abroad. Foreign affairs mattered less. Jackson pressed France to pay old claims for damage to American shipping after a dispute that nearly led to war, and he tried clumsily to buy Texas from Mexico. The Miller Center argues that those efforts sowed distrust that helped bring on war with Mexico a decade later. Jackson believed that republican government should be simple, frugal, and close to the people, and that government favors bred inequality. Laissez-faire, in his view, best protected economic equality and political liberty. He held the Union to be perpetual and denounced nullification and secession. His democracy, however, was for white men. The Jacksonian era opened voting to many poor white men while Black men lost voting rights. Jackson treated the controversy over slavery as a threat to his party and to sectional peace. In 1835 he called for federal suppression of the abolitionists’ “incendiary publications” mailed to the South. Indian removal. Jackson had long favored moving the eastern nations west of the Mississippi. As president he maintained that the federal government had no right to defend the Cherokees against Georgia’s encroachments. On May 28, 1830, he signed the Indian Removal Act, the only major law passed at his request during his presidency, authorizing removal treaties with nations east of the Mississippi. He described removal as a “benevolent policy” and asked, “What good man would prefer a country covered with forests and ranged by a few thousand savages to our extensive Republic, studded with cities, towns, and prosperous farms?” The Chickasaws and Choctaws submitted, the Creeks under duress, and a long war with the Seminoles began in 1835. The Supreme Court upheld Cherokee sovereignty against Georgia in Worcester v. Georgia (1832), but Jackson refused to protect the Cherokees’ treaty rights. In 1835 his government signed the Treaty of New Echota with a minority faction of the Cherokees. In 1838, under his successor Martin Van Buren, soldiers forced the remaining Cherokees west on what became known as the Trail of Tears. The National Archives says about 4,000 of some 16,000 Cherokees died; the American Yawp says that of 16,000 who set out, only 10,000 completed the journey. Slavery and violence. From his early years in Nashville Jackson bought and held enslaved people, and his cotton plantation, The Hermitage, ran on their labor. His duels and brawls marked him as a violent man, and his 1818 invasion of Florida raised charges that he defied civilian authority. Economic consequences. Jackson’s war on the Bank, his 1836 Specie Circular requiring payment in coin for public lands, and a wave of speculation were followed by the Panic of 1837, which broke just as he left office and deepened into a long depression. The American Yawp concludes that the Bank War worsened rather than solved the country’s economic problems. Jackson retired to The Hermitage in 1837 but kept advising Van Buren. In 1844 he helped replace Van Buren with James K. Polk as the Democratic nominee because Van Buren opposed annexing Texas. He died at The Hermitage on June 8, 1845, and was buried in the garden beside Rachel. He and Rachel had no children of their own. They adopted Rachel’s nephew as Andrew Jackson Jr., and they raised Lyncoya, a Native American boy orphaned in 1813, who died in 1828. Jackson’s reputation has always divided Americans. To admirers he is a symbol of American achievement and democracy. To detractors, the Miller Center writes, he is “an incipient tyrant, the closest we have yet come to an American Caesar.” Today his presidency is remembered as much for the Trail of Tears as for the expansion of popular democracy. It is to be regretted that the rich and powerful too often bend the acts of government to their selfish purposes. title: Babe Ruth
subtitle: The slugger who transformed baseball and became the most celebrated athlete of the 1920s
summary: Babe Ruth was a troubled Baltimore boy raised in a reform school who became the most celebrated athlete of his time. A star pitcher for the Boston Red Sox, he was sold to the New York Yankees in 1920 and turned the home run from a rarity into the heart of the game, hitting 54 that year, more than all but one other major league team, and 60 in 1927. Larger than life on and off the field, he embodied the boisterous 1920s, filled ballparks across the country, and retired with 714 home runs.

aliases: the Babe the Bambino the Sultan of Swat George Herman Ruth
themeText: Arts and popular culture Everyday life Cities and urban life
text: George Herman Ruth Baltimore, Maryland New York City Pitcher, Boston Red Sox (1914–1919) Outfielder, New York Yankees (1920–1934) Boston Braves (1935) One of the first five members of the Baseball Hall of Fame (1936) Career 714 home runs, a .342 batting average, and 2,214 runs batted in over 22 seasons Pitching 89 wins in six seasons with the Red Sox; a record 29⅔ straight scoreless World Series innings The sale Sold by the Red Sox to the Yankees for $100,000 after the 1919 season 60 in 1927 His single-season home run record stood for 34 years World Series titles Seven: three with Boston, four with New York Hall of Fame One of the first five players elected, in 1936 Ruth changed how baseball was played — from a game of singles and stolen bases to one built on power — and, with the help of a ravenous press, made sports stardom a national obsession. He remains the standard against which American athletic greatness is measured. George Herman Ruth was born on February 6, 1895, in Baltimore. His father ran a saloon and his mother was often ill, and by the age of six “Little George” was roaming the waterfront unsupervised, stealing, vandalizing, and drinking the dregs from beer glasses in his father’s bar. Shortly after he turned seven, his parents had a court declare him “incorrigible” and sent him to St. Mary’s Industrial School, a reform school on the city’s edge, where he lived for most of his youth. There Brother Matthias, “the father I needed and the greatest man I’ve ever known,” taught him to read and write — and to hit, by swatting fly balls the boy watched open-mouthed. Ruth copied his swing and even his quick, tiny running steps. In 1914 the owner of the minor-league Baltimore Orioles, Jack Dunn, signed him, and within five months sold him to the Boston Red Sox. Ruth was first a superb left-handed pitcher. He won 23 games in 1916 with a league-leading 1.75 earned run average, pitched all fourteen innings of a World Series victory, and helped Boston win three championships. But his hitting was too good to waste on the bench between starts, and in 1918 the Red Sox began playing him in the field; in 1919 he set a new record with 29 home runs. After that season the owner, Harry Frazee, sold him to the Yankees for $100,000 — probably the most famous transaction in baseball history. In New York Ruth hit 54 home runs in 1920, more than fourteen of the other fifteen major league teams; no one else in the American League hit more than 19. In 1921 he hit 59, with 177 runs scored and 457 total bases, records that still stand for the modern era. Huge crowds followed him everywhere, and when the Yankees opened their own ballpark in the Bronx in 1923, Yankee Stadium was called “the House that Ruth Built.” In 1927, with Lou Gehrig beside him in the lineup, he hit 60 home runs. In the 1932 World Series at Wrigley Field he hit his legendary “called shot”: whether he really pointed to the center-field bleachers before homering there will never be known, and when asked, Ruth only smiled and said, “It’s in the papers, isn’t it?” He led the league in home runs twelve times and won seven World Series in all. Ruth played for the crowd. “The fans would rather see me hit one homer to right than three doubles to left,” he said. He never forgot his own childhood: in Boston he invited busloads of orphans to his farm for picnics and ball games, sending each child home with a glove and an autographed ball. Ruth’s appetites were as famous as his home runs. He broke curfews, earned repeated suspensions, and in 1917 punched an umpire after a disputed walk. After the 1921 World Series the commissioner, Kenesaw Mountain Landis, suspended him for the first six weeks of the next season for an illegal barnstorming tour. In 1925 he reported to spring training at 256 pounds, needed surgery in April for what a sportswriter called “the bellyache heard ’round the world,” and had the worst season of his career — after which he began working out seriously. His first marriage fell apart; his estranged wife, Helen, died in a house fire in 1929, and he soon married Claire Hodgson. Ruth retired in 1935 after a partial season with the Boston Braves. In 1936 he was one of the first five players elected to the new Hall of Fame. In 1946 he was found to have cancer, though the newspapers never printed the word. On June 13, 1948, frail and shrunken, he returned to Yankee Stadium for its 25th anniversary as his number 3 was retired; he died on August 16, 1948, at fifty-three. His name became a byword for the best in any field, and “Ruthian” entered the language to mean colossal and prodigious. As one sportswriter put it, “It wasn’t that he hit more home runs than anybody else — he hit them better, higher, farther, with more theatrical timing and a more flamboyant flourish.” https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iKvA7zB2suk Babe Ruth: American Sports Icon Biographics 21:56 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0uaq2_mRu9A Who was Babe Ruth? title: Barack Obama
subtitle: Forty-fourth president and the first African American president
summary: Barack Obama was inaugurated on January 20, 2009, as the forty-fourth president and the first African American to hold the office. The son of a white mother from Kansas and a Black Kenyan father, he grew up in Hawaii and Indonesia, worked as a community organizer in Chicago, and led the Harvard Law Review before entering politics. He took office in a deep recession, won an $800 billion stimulus, and signed the Affordable Care Act, which sharply reduced the number of uninsured Americans. Abroad he withdrew most American troops from Iraq, ordered the raid that killed Osama bin Laden, and pursued agreements on Iran’s nuclear program and climate change. Republican control of Congress after 2010 blocked much of his later agenda.
thumbAlt: Official portrait of Barack Obama
aliases: Obamacare Affordable Care Act Yes We Can The Audacity of Hope Recovery Act
themeText: The presidency African American history Economy and finance Public health Parties and elections
text: Barack Hussein Obama II Hawaii Community organizer, Chicago President of the Harvard Law Review Illinois state senator (1997–2004) U.S. Senator from Illinois (2005–2008) Forty-fourth president (2009–2017) Born August 4, 1961, Hawaii Education Occidental College; Columbia University (1983); Harvard Law School, magna cum laude Before the presidency Community organizer; civil rights lawyer; Illinois state senator; U.S. senator (2005–2008) Elections 2008: defeated John McCain, 365 electoral votes to 173; 2012: defeated Mitt Romney, 332 to 206 Signature laws American Recovery and Reinvestment Act (2009); Affordable Care Act (March 23, 2010); Dodd-Frank (2010) Foreign policy Withdrawal from Iraq; killing of Osama bin Laden (May 2, 2011); Iran nuclear agreement (2015); Paris climate agreement (2015) Family Married Michelle Robinson in 1992; daughters Malia (1998) and Sasha (2001) Obama’s election was a landmark in the long history of race in American politics. His presidency also pulled the economy back from the edge of a second depression and changed the American health-care system. Several of his achievements, especially those resting on executive action, were later reversed or challenged. Barack Hussein Obama II was born in Hawaii on August 4, 1961. His parents, who had met as students at the University of Hawaii, were Ann Dunham, a white American from Kansas, and Barack Obama Sr., a Black Kenyan studying in the United States. His father left the family when Obama was two and later returned to Kenya. After his parents divorced, his mother married an Indonesian student, Lolo Soetoro, and from age six to ten Obama lived in Indonesia, attending Catholic and Muslim schools. “I was raised as an Indonesian child and a Hawaiian child and as a black child and as a white child,” he later said. He returned to Hawaii to live with his grandparents and attend the Punahou School. His mother, who admired the civil rights movement, taught him that being Black was “a great inheritance.” Obama went to Occidental College in Los Angeles and then to Columbia University in New York, graduating in political science in 1983. In Chicago he worked as a community organizer on the largely poor and Black South Side, organizing residents of the Altgeld Gardens public housing project. Concluding that “I just can’t get things done here without a law degree,” he entered Harvard Law School in 1988. He was elected president of the Harvard Law Review for 1990–91, the first African American to hold the post. The attention led to his memoir Dreams from My Father (1995). At a Chicago law firm he met Michelle Robinson, a South Side native and lawyer; they married in 1992 and had two daughters, Malia and Sasha. Back in Chicago, Obama directed a voter registration drive, practiced civil rights law, and taught at the University of Chicago Law School. He won a seat in the Illinois state senate in 1996, after challenging his predecessor’s nominating petitions, and eventually passed nearly 300 bills there. He lost a 2000 primary race for Congress by about 30 points. In October 2002 he spoke against the coming war in Iraq: “I don’t oppose all wars. … What I am opposed to is a dumb war.” In 2004 his keynote address at the Democratic National Convention, with its theme of “the audacity of hope,” made him a national figure, and he won his U.S. Senate race with 70 percent of the vote, the largest margin in Illinois history. The 2008 election. Obama announced his candidacy in February 2007. Relying heavily on the Internet and a vast grassroots network, he won the Iowa caucuses and then defeated Hillary Clinton in a long contest for the Democratic nomination. When videos of sermons by his former pastor, Jeremiah Wright, threatened his campaign, he answered with a speech on race in Philadelphia in March 2008. He became the first presidential candidate to decline public funds, which allowed him to raise nearly three-quarters of a billion dollars. The financial collapse of September 2008 turned the race. On November 4 he defeated John McCain, 53 percent to 46 percent, and 365 electoral votes to 173. “Change has come to America,” he told supporters in Chicago that night. Rescuing the economy. When Obama took office, the economy was losing jobs and unemployment was nearing 10 percent. On February 17, 2009, he signed the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, a stimulus of about $800 billion split among aid to the states, middle-class tax cuts, and infrastructure. He directed $60 billion to rescue General Motors and Chrysler. In 2010 he signed the Dodd-Frank Act to regulate Wall Street. By the time he left office, according to the Miller Center, the economy had added a net 11.3 million jobs, unemployment had fallen below 5 percent, and the annual deficit had dropped from more than $1.4 trillion to less than $600 billion. Health care. After a year of struggle and angry protests from the conservative Tea Party movement, Obama signed the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act on March 23, 2010. It survived two major Supreme Court challenges, in 2012 and 2015, although the Court made the expansion of Medicaid optional for the states. The share of adults without health insurance fell from 18 percent to 11 percent by the end of his presidency. He also appointed two Supreme Court justices, Sonia Sotomayor, the first Latina on the Court, and Elena Kagan. Foreign policy. Obama withdrew most American troops from Iraq. In Afghanistan he first increased the American force, by 17,000 troops in early 2009 according to the American Yawp, and then by a further 33,000 announced in December 2009, before beginning withdrawals. On May 2, 2011, a team of Navy SEALs killed Osama bin Laden at his hideout in Abbottabad, Pakistan. He joined NATO in backing the Libyan rebels against Muammar Qaddafi, and from 2014 he ordered air strikes against the so-called Islamic State in Iraq and Syria. In 2015, after two years of negotiations between Iran and the United States and five other nations, an agreement limited Iran’s nuclear program in exchange for lifting sanctions. He restored diplomatic relations with Cuba in December 2014 and visited Havana in 2016, and he helped bring about the 2015 Paris climate agreement. Obama described empathy as “at the heart of my moral code,” a value he learned from his mother, and he argued that government has an important role in opening opportunity to all. His politics combined liberal goals with a pragmatic, often cautious style. The Miller Center calls his foreign policy “pragmatic and piecemeal,” except for his long concern about climate change. He stressed national unity: “There’s not a black America and white America and Latino America and Asian America. There’s a United States of America.” Obama’s presidency was marked by deep partisan division. After Republicans won the House in 2010, he spent much of his time in largely unsuccessful negotiations over taxes, budgets, and the deficit. After the 2012 massacre of schoolchildren in Newtown, Connecticut, he failed to win gun control legislation, and comprehensive immigration reform also failed. Once Republicans won the Senate in 2014, he turned increasingly to executive action, including the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program for undocumented immigrants brought to the country as children. Courts blocked a broader 2014 immigration order. The Affordable Care Act remained bitterly contested. His foreign policy drew criticism from both directions. He expanded drone strikes and special operations against suspected terrorists. The bombing campaign in Libya was followed by chaos, including the 2012 attack in Benghazi that killed four Americans. He called off planned strikes on Syria after the Assad government crossed his “red line” by using chemical weapons, and he later acknowledged that his administration had underestimated the rise of the Islamic State. Obama left office on January 20, 2017, at fifty-five, with job approval of about 60 percent. A C-SPAN survey of historians that year ranked him twelfth among all presidents. The Miller Center suggests his greatest impact may lie in “the crises that did not happen”: the country avoided a second Great Depression and did not launch new large-scale wars. Some of his most notable achievements, among them the Affordable Care Act, the Paris agreement, and DACA, were soon overturned or under attack. After leaving office he and his family stayed in Washington while his younger daughter finished school, and he began work on the Obama Presidential Center on Chicago’s South Side. There’s not a liberal America and a conservative America. There’s a United States of America. title: Benjamin Franklin
subtitle: Printer, scientist, diplomat, and the Revolution’s elder statesman
summary: Benjamin Franklin rose from a Boston candlemaker’s son to become the best-known American of the eighteenth century, as a printer, writer, scientist, and statesman. In Philadelphia he published Poor Richard’s Almanack and founded a library, a fire company, a hospital, and the academy that became the University of Pennsylvania. His experiments with electricity won him international fame. He represented the colonies in London for nearly two decades, helped draft the Declaration of Independence, won the French alliance, and helped negotiate the peace with Britain. At eighty-one he was the oldest delegate to the Constitutional Convention. An enslaver earlier in life, he ended it as president of an abolition society.
thumbAlt: Portrait of Benjamin Franklin by Joseph Siffred Duplessis
aliases: Poor Richard Richard Saunders Silence Dogood Join, or Die Albany Plan lightning rod
themeText: Political thought Foreign policy and diplomacy Science and technology Slavery and emancipation
text: Benjamin Franklin Boston, Massachusetts Philadelphia, Pennsylvania Printer and publisher Scientist and inventor Deputy postmaster general for the colonies Colonial agent in London (1757–1775) Diplomat and minister to France Signer of the Declaration, the Treaty of Paris, and the Constitution President of the Pennsylvania Abolition Society Born January 17, 1706, Boston, Massachusetts Printer Published the Pennsylvania Gazette and Poor Richard’s Almanack (1732–1757) Science Showed that lightning is electrical; invented the lightning rod, the Franklin stove, bifocals, and the glass armonica London Colonial agent, 1757–1775; helped win repeal of the Stamp Act (1766) France Commissioner from 1776; first American minister received by a foreign government (1779) Signatures Declaration of Independence (1776), Treaty of Paris (1783), Constitution (1787) Died April 17, 1790, Philadelphia; buried at Christ Church Franklin signed the three documents that established the nation, the Declaration of Independence, the Treaty of Paris, and the Constitution, and the State Department’s historians call him the most distinguished scientific and literary American of the colonial era. His life became a model of the self-made American, and his civic projects, scientific work, and diplomacy helped shape both colonial society and the new nation. Benjamin Franklin was born in Boston on January 17, 1706, to Josiah Franklin, a maker of candles and soap, and Abiah Folger. Lehigh University’s exhibit calls him the tenth child, and the Library of Congress the tenth son. He had only about two years of schooling. At ten he went to work in his father’s shop. He was then apprenticed to his brother James, a printer who started the New England Courant, one of the first American newspapers. Lehigh puts the start of the apprenticeship at age thirteen, while the National Park Service dates it from 1718, when he was twelve. (The Library of Congress exhibit names the brother as a half-brother, Peter. The National Park Service and Lehigh both name James.) He taught himself by reading widely, and in 1722 he began writing for his brother’s paper under the pen name “Silence Dogood.” In 1723 Franklin struck out on his own and went to Philadelphia, where he found work as a journeyman printer. By 1730 he had his own printing shop and owned the Pennsylvania Gazette. He had a son, William, and had married Deborah Read Rogers. In 1732 he began Poor Richard’s Almanack, written under the name Richard Saunders, which became one of the colonies’ best-sellers for twenty-five years, often selling more than 10,000 copies. He became the official printer for several colonies and printed their paper money, using mica and leaf imprints to foil counterfeiters. He also launched printing partnerships from South Carolina to New York and the West Indies. Franklin turned his energy to civic improvement. He founded the Library Company, the first successful lending library in the colonies (1731), the Union Fire Company (1736), the American Philosophical Society, Pennsylvania Hospital (1751), and the Philadelphia Contributionship, the colonies’ first insurance company (1752). He pressed for paved, lighted, and patrolled streets. He also founded the academy that became the University of Pennsylvania, dated 1749 by the National Park Service and 1751 by Lehigh. As postmaster of Philadelphia and, from 1753, deputy postmaster general for North America, he improved mail routes across the colonies. Scientist and inventor. Franklin’s electrical experiments, published as Experiments and Observations on Electricity, set out a theory of positive and negative charge, argued that lightning was electrical, and proposed a tall, grounded rod to protect buildings. In 1753 the Royal Society of London awarded him its Copley Medal. He also designed a more efficient wood stove, bifocal spectacles, and the glass armonica, for which Mozart and Beethoven composed music. He charted the Gulf Stream, studied storms and the northern lights, and wrote on the causes of the common cold. At his death the French statesman Turgot wrote that “he seized the lightning from the sky and the scepter from the hand of tyrants.” Uniting the colonies. In 1754, before the French and Indian War, Franklin proposed the Albany Plan to unite the colonies for common defense. He printed the woodcut “Join, or Die,” showing the colonies as a snake cut into pieces, which later became a symbol of the Revolution. Congress did not act on a plan of confederation he presented in July 1775, but the National Park Service credits his 1754 plan with laying the groundwork for the Articles of Confederation. Agent in London. Franklin went to London in 1757 as agent of the Pennsylvania assembly and stayed, apart from one brief return, until 1775, eventually speaking for several colonies. He briefly accepted the Stamp Act of 1765 but turned against it when he learned of the anger at home, and he helped win its repeal in 1766. On January 29, 1774, he was publicly attacked before the Privy Council, largely for obtaining copies of Massachusetts governor Thomas Hutchinson’s letters, which advised restricting the colonists’ liberties. In London, the Library of Congress writes, he gradually moved from loyalty to the British Empire to revolution. Revolutionary and diplomat. Back in Philadelphia in May 1775, Franklin joined the Second Continental Congress and served on the committee that drafted the Declaration of Independence. In 1776 Congress sent him to France as one of its commissioners. The French embraced him as the embodiment of New World Enlightenment, and his image appeared on medallions, rings, and snuffboxes. His popularity and skill, together with the American victory at Saratoga, helped bring France into an alliance with the United States in 1778. In 1779 he became the first American minister received by a foreign government, and he helped negotiate the Treaty of Paris of 1783, which ended the war. When Jefferson replaced him in 1785, Jefferson told the French foreign minister, “No one can replace him, Sir; I am only his successor.” The Constitution. Back home, Franklin served as president of Pennsylvania from 1785 to 1788. At the Constitutional Convention of 1787 he was the oldest delegate. When the debates grew bitter he proposed daily prayers, and he worked to restore harmony. On the last day, September 17, his colleague James Wilson read his speech urging the delegates to sign despite their doubts, so that the new government would “astonish our enemies.” Franklin believed in self-improvement, hard work, thrift, and practical knowledge put to public use, values spread through Poor Richard’s Almanack and his many civic projects. He was a man of the Enlightenment who prized scientific inquiry and the free exchange of ideas. Through the American Philosophical Society he kept scientific correspondence going across the Atlantic even during the Revolution. In politics he favored union among the colonies and later among the states, and he called the principle that colonists could be taxed only by their own elected representatives the “prime Maxim of all free Government.” He had a sense of humor to match. In a 1784 letter to his daughter he complained that the bald eagle on a new society’s emblem looked more like a turkey, “a much more respectable Bird.” Franklin’s household held enslaved people for decades. Benjamin Franklin House records that the family bought at least seven people, among them Peter, Jemima, King, Othello, and George, and that Franklin’s Pennsylvania Gazette profited from advertisements for the sale of enslaved people and for runaways. When he went to London in 1757 he took two enslaved men, Peter and King. King escaped in 1758. The sources disagree about the end of his slaveholding. The National Park Service says he no longer owned any enslaved people when he died, while Benjamin Franklin House says the household held enslaved people until 1790. His views changed over time. In London he came under the influence of the Quaker abolitionist Anthony Benezet and of the 1772 Somerset decision against slavery in England, and he began to attack slavery anonymously. He kept publicly silent on the issue while in France. In 1787 he became president of the Pennsylvania Society for Promoting the Abolition of Slavery. The sources date that society’s founding to April 14, 1775 (National Archives and the Constitution Center) or 1774 (Benjamin Franklin House). His last public act was to sign, on February 3, 1790, the society’s petition to the First Congress asking it to “devise means for removing the Inconsistency from the Character of the American People” and end the slave trade. The House sent it to a committee, which reported that the Constitution barred Congress from prohibiting the importation or emancipation of slaves before 1808, and then tabled it. The Senate took no action. Franklin died in Philadelphia on April 17, 1790, at his house in Franklin Court, and was buried in the graveyard of Christ Church. His will left funds in trust to lend money to young tradesmen. Two trade schools, the Franklin Union in Boston and the Franklin Institute in Philadelphia, were later founded with the money, and in 1990, as he had directed, the remaining funds, then worth more than $7 million, were distributed to schools and scholarships. His house was torn down in 1812, and a steel “ghost structure” now marks its outline above the Benjamin Franklin Museum. In Paris fashionable ladies copied the fur cap he wore instead of a wig, and his image, the Library of Congress notes, introduced him to France in 1777; it has remained one of the most familiar faces of the founding era. No one can replace him, Sir; I am only his successor. title: Booker T. Washington
subtitle: Educator and the most influential Black leader of his generation
summary: Booker T. Washington was born into slavery in Virginia and became the most prominent Black educator and spokesman of his time. As the founding principal of Alabama’s Tuskegee Institute, he championed industrial and vocational education as the road to Black economic independence. His 1895 Atlanta Exposition address, which seemed to accept segregation in exchange for economic opportunity, made him famous and drew sharp criticism from W. E. B. Du Bois, who called it the “Atlanta Compromise.” In 1901 he became the first African American invited to dine at the White House.
thumbAlt: Photograph of Booker T. Washington
themeText: African American history Civil rights and citizenship Reform and protest
text: Booker Taliaferro Washington Burroughs farm, Franklin County, Virginia Tuskegee, Alabama Founding principal of Tuskegee Institute Educator and orator Political adviser Born 1856, enslaved on the Burroughs farm in Franklin County, Virginia Tuskegee Opened July 4, 1881, with 30 students Atlanta Exposition speech September 18, 1895 White House First African American invited to dine at the White House (1901) Died November 14, 1915 Washington was born in 1856 on the Burroughs farm in Franklin County, Virginia, the son of the farm’s enslaved cook, Jane; he never knew the exact date or place, writing later only that “I suspect I must have been born somewhere and at some time.” He lived with his mother and two half-siblings in the farm’s one-room kitchen cabin, carried water to the field hands, and carried the Burroughs daughters’ books to a school he was not allowed to attend. After emancipation the family moved to Malden, West Virginia, where the boy packed salt, mined coal, and worked as a butler. In the salt furnace he learned to write his first number, 18; he then persuaded his stepfather to let him attend school around his furnace shifts — and set the mine’s clock ahead an hour to get there on time. At sixteen, with a few dollars and a small satchel, he traveled more than 500 miles to Hampton Institute in Virginia. He arrived dirty, hungry, and with fifty cents; his entrance examination was to clean a classroom, and he paid his way through school as a janitor. After graduating he taught in Malden, helping his brothers reach Hampton, and in 1879 returned to Hampton as a teacher. In May 1881 Hampton’s founder, General Armstrong, received a telegram from the board of commissioners of the new Tuskegee State Normal School in Alabama: “Booker T. Washington will suit us … send him at once.” Washington arrived in June, toured the county sleeping in the homes of Black families to learn how they lived, and opened the school on July 4, 1881, with thirty students. He built Tuskegee into an institution devoted to industrial education and vocational training, winning support from white philanthropists such as Andrew Carnegie; it became a model of Black vocational education across the South. On September 18, 1895, months after Frederick Douglass’s death, Washington spoke at the Cotton States and International Exposition in Atlanta. He urged Black Southerners to “cast your bucket down” and improve their lot where they were, and told white listeners that “in all things that are purely social we can be as separate as the fingers, yet one as the hand in all things essential to mutual progress.” The speech made him famous and the leading spokesman for Black Americans. His autobiography, Up from Slavery (1901), became a classic, and that year he became the first African American invited to dine at the White House. Washington believed that economic progress must come before political and social equality. Skills, property, and self-reliance, he argued, would bring African Americans independence and self-respect even within the harsh limits of Jim Crow. He saw education as the great hunger of the freed people; of the years after emancipation he wrote that “it was a whole race trying to go to school.” Washington was praised as a race leader and condemned as an accommodationist. Critics, above all Du Bois in The Souls of Black Folk (1903), argued that he had given up the fight for voting rights and civil equality just as segregation was being written into law — the Supreme Court upheld “separate but equal” in Plessy v. Ferguson a year after the Atlanta speech. Washington used his influence and money to support Black newspapers, many of them aimed at countering Du Bois. Yet historians note that his conciliatory public posture concealed quiet efforts to aid African Americans in legal and economic struggles for justice. Du Bois himself later said: “I never thought Washington was a bad man … I believed him to be sincere, though wrong.” Washington died at Tuskegee on November 14, 1915, at the age of fifty-nine. The institute he built endures as Tuskegee University, and his birthplace is a national monument. The debate between his strategy of economic self-help and Du Bois’s demand for full civil and political rights framed the struggle over Black strategy in the early twentieth century. Washington built one of the most important Black institutions in the country and defined one side of a lasting debate over how Black Americans should pursue freedom in the age of Jim Crow. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zHn-vSTMOWE Booker T. title: Cesar Chavez
subtitle: Labor leader and co-founder of the United Farm Workers
summary: Cesar Chavez was the Mexican American labor leader who, with Dolores Huerta, built the first lasting union of farmworkers in the United States. The son of migrant laborers who had lost their Arizona farm, he founded the National Farm Workers Association in 1962, joined the great Delano grape strike of 1965, and turned it into a national boycott of table grapes. Through strikes, marches, and long public fasts, always insisting on nonviolence, he made the United Farm Workers a union and a civil rights movement at once, and became the best-known figure of the Chicano movement.

themeText: Labor and work Latino history Civil rights and citizenship Reform and protest
text: Cesar Estrada Chavez near Yuma, Arizona San Luis, Arizona Organizer, Community Service Organization Co-founder, National Farm Workers Association (1962) President, United Farm Workers Born March 31, 1927, near Yuma, Arizona Union National Farm Workers Association (1962), later the United Farm Workers Delano grape strike Began September 1965 Fasts 25 days in 1968, 24 in 1972, 36 in 1988 Died April 23, 1993, San Luis, Arizona Cesar Estrada Chavez was born on March 31, 1927, near Yuma, Arizona, and named for his grandfather Cesario. He learned about injustice early: his father agreed to clear eighty acres in exchange for the deed to forty more beside their adobe home, but the bargain was broken, and after a lawyer’s scheme the family lost the land. In 1938–1939 they moved to California, settling in a San Jose barrio called Sal Si Puedes — “Get Out If You Can” — and following the harvests from Brawley to Mendota. School was painful. Speaking only Spanish at home, Chavez was punished with a ruler across the knuckles for using it in class, saw “whites only” signs, and with his brother Richard attended thirty-seven schools. After eighth grade, in 1942, he left school to work in the fields so his mother would not have to. He served two years in the then-segregated Navy from 1946, married Helen Fabela in 1948, and raised eight children. Talks with a priest, Father Donald McDonnell, led him to read about St. Francis, Gandhi, and nonviolence; the organizer Fred Ross recruited him to the Community Service Organization (CSO), where he began by registering voters and rose to become its national director. When the CSO refused to concentrate on farmworkers, Chavez quit and in 1962 founded the National Farm Workers Association in Delano, California, with Dolores Huerta; his brother Richard designed its black Aztec eagle on a red flag. For three years he traveled from town to town, meeting workers in their homes. Grape pickers then earned about 90 cents an hour, often lived in unheated shacks, and had no toilets in the fields. In September 1965, when Filipino workers led by Larry Itliong struck Delano’s grape growers, Chavez’s association — with $100 in the bank — voted to join them, to shouts of “¡Viva la huelga!” In March 1966 Chavez led strikers on a 340-mile, 25-day march to Sacramento; on Easter morning he told 10,000 supporters at the Capitol that the grower Schenley had signed an agreement with the union. The two unions merged that summer as the United Farm Workers Organizing Committee. Volunteers fanned out to cities to organize a consumer boycott, and millions of Americans stopped buying table grapes. By 1970 the grape growers had accepted union contracts, bringing higher wages, a union hiring hall that ended contractors’ favoritism, health clinics, and a credit union; the union claimed 50,000 dues-paying members, the most ever represented in California agriculture. In 1975 California passed the Agricultural Labor Relations Act, the first U.S. law recognizing farmworkers’ right to collective bargaining. Chavez’s faith in nonviolence drew on St. Francis and Gandhi. He fasted on water for 25 days in 1968, for 24 days in 1972, and for 36 days in 1988, explaining that farmworkers were “angry and worried that we cannot win without violence” and that the fasts were a call to win “through persistence, hard work, faith and willingness to sacrifice.” He believed that “the end of all education should surely be service to others,” and his office walls were lined with books on philosophy, economics, unions, and Gandhi. His union’s rallying cry was ¡Sí se puede! — “Yes, we can!” The union’s struggle was bitter and long. One grower sprayed strikers with agricultural poisons, and the Teamsters union offered itself to growers as a conservative alternative, colluding with growers against the farmworkers. Chavez’s final fast in 1988 protested the dangers of pesticides to workers and their children. He died while defending the union against a multimillion-dollar lawsuit brought by a lettuce grower over a 1980s boycott; the judgment was later thrown out. Chavez died in his sleep on April 23, 1993, in San Luis, Arizona, not far from the farm where he was born. The farmworker movement he led with Huerta and Itliong won higher wages and better working and living conditions, and grew into a national voice for the poor and disenfranchised. His birthday, March 31, is a holiday in California, Colorado, and Texas, and his home and the union headquarters at La Paz form the César E. Chávez National Monument. Chavez showed that the most marginalized workers in America could organize, and he made the farm workers’ cause a national movement for dignity and civil rights. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ns5NMHTk-yY Cesar Chavez - American Civil Rights Activist | Mini Bio | BIO Biography 3:59 2026-10-22

title: Donald Trump
subtitle: Forty-fifth and forty-seventh president, the second ever elected to non-consecutive terms
summary: Donald Trump, a New York real estate developer and reality-television star, won the presidency in 2016 as a Republican in a surprise victory, without ever having held public office or military command. His first term brought a large tax cut, tighter immigration policies, new tariffs, and an “America First” foreign policy, along with intense partisan division and two impeachments, both ending in acquittal. He lost the 2020 election to Joe Biden, refused to concede, and his supporters attacked the Capitol on January 6, 2021. In 2024, after being convicted on state felony charges in New York, he won the presidency again, becoming only the second president elected to non-consecutive terms.
thumbAlt: Official White House portrait of President Donald Trump, 2017
aliases: Trump Donald J. Trump 45th president 47th president MAGA
themeText: The presidency Parties and elections Immigration Foreign policy and diplomacy Economy and finance
text: Donald John Trump Queens, New York City Real estate developer and businessman Television personality (*The Apprentice*) Forty-fifth president (2017–2021) Forty-seventh president (2025– ) Presidencies January 20, 2017 – January 20, 2021; second term began January 20, 2025; Republican 2016 election Won the Electoral College 304–227 while Hillary Clinton won 2.8 million more popular votes 2024 election Beat Kamala Harris 312–226 in the Electoral College and 49.9% to 48.4% in the popular vote Firsts First president with no prior public office or military leadership; first impeached twice; first convicted of a felony Non-consecutive terms The second president elected to non-consecutive terms, and the first since the nineteenth century Trump put populist nationalism — opposition to immigration and free trade and skepticism of foreign alliances — at the center of Republican politics, and he broke with long-standing norms, above all by refusing to concede the 2020 election. Because his second term is under way, this entry covers events through its beginning; historians’ assessments are still forming. Donald John Trump was born on June 14, 1946, in the borough of Queens in New York City, the fourth of five children of Mary Anne MacLeod Trump and Fred Trump, a residential real estate developer. After graduating from the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania in 1968, he took over his father’s business and expanded it into hotels, casinos, golf courses, beauty pageants, and branded products. In the 1970s and 1980s he cultivated an image as the embodiment of the high life; several of his businesses, including casinos, went through bankruptcies, but his brand remained strong. In the 2000s he starred in the reality show The Apprentice. Politically, he identified at different times as a Democrat, a Republican, an independent, and a member of the Reform Party, and he considered running for president several times. During the Obama years he became a leading promoter of the false “birther” claim that Barack Obama had not been born in the United States, which he did not abandon until September 2016. Trump announced his candidacy on June 16, 2015, at Trump Tower in Manhattan, promising to “Make America Great Again,” to build a wall on the Mexican border, and to put “America First.” He defeated sixteen major rivals for the Republican nomination and, though most polls favored Hillary Clinton, won narrow victories in Pennsylvania, Michigan, and Wisconsin to take the Electoral College. In office he signed the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017, which lowered corporate and individual tax rates and eliminated the Affordable Care Act’s individual mandate penalty, though efforts to repeal the act itself failed. He restricted immigration, including an order barring visas for citizens of several majority-Muslim countries, and new barriers were built along more than 450 miles of the southern border. Abroad he withdrew from the Paris climate agreement, the Trans-Pacific Partnership, and the Iran nuclear deal; replaced NAFTA with the United States–Mexico–Canada Agreement; imposed tariffs on Chinese goods; moved the U.S. embassy in Israel to Jerusalem; and met North Korea’s Kim Jong-un three times, becoming the first sitting president to set foot in North Korea. His administration brokered the Abraham Accords normalizing relations between Israel and the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain. When the Covid-19 pandemic struck in 2020, he declared a national emergency and signed the $2.2 trillion CARES Act, and public health experts credited his administration with speeding the development of vaccines. Trump’s “America First” program combined economic nationalism with skepticism of foreign commitments. He blamed free trade and “bad deals” for the decline of American manufacturing, favored tariffs and country-by-country agreements over multilateral ones, called for sharply reduced immigration, and argued that defending Western Europe through NATO was too expensive. He presented himself as a dealmaker and an outsider fighting a corrupt political establishment, and he communicated directly with supporters through rallies and social media. His presidency was marked by intense partisan division. Critics condemned his rhetoric about immigrants as racist; his 2018 “zero tolerance” policy separated at least 2,300 children from their parents at the border before he reversed it. Critics faulted his handling of Covid-19, during which he often downplayed the risks. The House impeached him in December 2019, and again in January 2021 after he refused to accept his defeat by Joe Biden — who won about 7 million more votes and 306 electoral votes — and his supporters stormed the Capitol on January 6. The Senate acquitted him both times. In May 2024 a New York jury convicted him on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records in connection with a hush-money payment; after his reelection he was sentenced to an unconditional discharge, and he announced an appeal. Trump’s 2024 victory over Vice President Kamala Harris made him, at seventy-eight, the oldest person ever inaugurated, and the first president since the nineteenth century elected to non-consecutive terms. He took the oath for the second time on January 20, 2025. His presidencies remain the subject of intense debate, and a full historical assessment will have to wait until his time in office is over. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PZhhCLpVAE8 Donald Trump: What Happened Before the White House?
