title: Dwight D. Eisenhower
subtitle: Commander of the D-Day invasion and thirty-fourth president, who presided over the prosperous, anxious 1950s
summary: Dwight D. Eisenhower rose in five years from an obscure lieutenant colonel to Supreme Commander of the Allied invasion of Nazi-occupied Europe on D-Day. Elected president in 1952 and 1956, “Ike” ended the Korean War, built the Interstate Highway System, and kept the country out of new wars while waging the Cold War with nuclear deterrence and CIA covert action. He sent troops to enforce school desegregation in Little Rock but never endorsed the Brown decision, and on leaving office he warned Americans against the “military-industrial complex.”
thumbAlt: Official portrait photograph of President Dwight D. Eisenhower, 1959
aliases: Ike Eisenhower General Eisenhower
themeText: The presidency War and the military The Cold War Civil rights and citizenship Foreign policy and diplomacy Economy and finance
text: Dwight David Eisenhower Denison, Texas Supreme Allied Commander, D-Day invasion (1944) Army chief of staff (1945–1948) President of Columbia University First Supreme Commander of NATO forces in Europe Thirty-fourth president (1953–1961) Presidency January 20, 1953 – January 20, 1961; Republican D-Day Gave the order — “Okay, let’s go” — for the Normandy invasion of June 6, 1944 Interstate highways Launched in 1956: a 41,000-mile network, the largest public works program in U.S. history Little Rock 1957: the first president since Reconstruction to send troops into the South to enforce federal law Farewell warning Beware the “military-industrial complex” (January 1961) Reputation Ranked 22nd by historians in 1962; 8th by 1994 Eisenhower led the largest invasion in history and then, as president, accepted the New Deal, built the interstates, and kept the Cold War from turning hot. His caution on civil rights and his reliance on covert action left problems his successors had to face. Eisenhower was born on October 14, 1890, in a house by the railroad tracks in Denison, Texas, and grew up in the small farm town of Abilene, Kansas. His father worked as a mechanic in a creamery; his mother, Ida, a Mennonite, was a religious pacifist — though she did not try to stop her son from becoming a soldier. Inspired by a friend headed for the Naval Academy, he won an appointment to West Point in 1911, where a knee injury ended his football career and his pranks, card playing, and smoking left his teachers expecting a good officer but not a great one. He graduated 61st of 164 and in 1916 married Mamie Doud. World War I ended a week before he was to sail for Europe, and his career stalled. When he and his friend George S. Patton argued in print for using tanks to break the deadlock of trench warfare, the Army threatened him with a court-martial. His luck turned under General Fox Conner, who got him into the Command and General Staff College; Eisenhower graduated first of 245 officers. He served as an aide to General John J. Pershing and then for seven stormy years to Douglas MacArthur, including in the Philippines. Huge army maneuvers in Louisiana, with more than 400,000 troops, revealed his gift for strategic planning, and days after Pearl Harbor he was called to Washington to work on war plans. He so impressed the Army chief of staff, George C. Marshall, that promotions came quickly. He commanded the Allied invasion of North Africa in November 1942, then the landings in Sicily and Italy, and in 1944 became Supreme Commander of Operation Overlord. By working patiently with Allied leaders, he held together the coalition that launched the invasion of Normandy; despite the risk of bad weather he gave the go-ahead for June 6, 1944, with a terse “Okay, let’s go.” After the war he was Army chief of staff, president of Columbia University, and the first Supreme Commander of NATO forces in Europe. Truman privately offered to run as his vice president on the Democratic ticket in 1948; Eisenhower declined, and in 1952 he declared himself a Republican and won the presidency with Richard Nixon as his running mate. Six months after taking office he agreed to an armistice in Korea, and he sent combat troops into action only once more, to Lebanon in 1958. His “Modern Republicanism” steered “down the middle of the road”: he expanded Social Security, raised the minimum wage, created the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare, built the St. Lawrence Seaway with Canada, and in 1956 launched the Interstate Highway System — enough concrete, he said, to build “six sidewalks to the moon.” Growth was strong and inflation low, and personal income rose 45 percent during his presidency. In 1957 he signed the first civil rights law since Reconstruction, and when a mob blocked the integration of Central High School in Little Rock, he sent federal troops. He also kept defense spending in check, refusing panicked demands for huge increases after the Soviets launched Sputnik in 1957. Eisenhower believed national security depended on a healthy economy as well as military strength: his “New Look” relied on nuclear weapons and air power for “more bang for the buck” instead of costly conventional forces. He insisted on spending not one penny less than security required, nor one penny more, and he warned that every gun and warship was “a theft from those who hunger and are not fed.” On race he was a gradualist who believed changes in hearts and minds mattered more than laws. In his Farewell Address he cautioned that “an immense military establishment and a large arms industry” could endanger American liberties. Eisenhower never publicly endorsed Brown v. Board of Education, and his silence may have encouraged Southern resistance; he sent troops to Little Rock to uphold the law, not because he backed integration, and when Arkansas closed its schools in 1958 he took no further action. When he left office, only 6 percent of Black students attended integrated schools. He privately despised Senator Joseph McCarthy but refused to confront him publicly — “I just won’t get into a pissing contest with that skunk” — which prolonged McCarthy’s power (see McCarthyism). He authorized CIA operations that helped topple the governments of Iran in 1953 and Guatemala in 1954, with lasting consequences, and committed American prestige to a non-Communist South Vietnam. In 1960 a U-2 spy plane was shot down over the Soviet Union, and the administration’s cover stories were exposed as lies, wrecking a planned summit. Eisenhower retired to a farm beside the Civil War battlefield at Gettysburg, where he raised Angus cattle and painted, and he advised his successors on Vietnam. He died at Walter Reed Army Hospital on March 28, 1969; his last words were “I want to go; God take me.” He was buried in Abilene. Contemporaries noted his frequent golf games and garbled press conferences, and in 1962 historians ranked him only 22nd among presidents. But when his papers opened, they revealed a leader firmly in charge who used a “hidden hand” behind the scenes, and by 1994 historians ranked him 8th. He now gets credit for preserving peace and prosperity — while historians still note the limits of his record on civil rights and covert action. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jqm98LRB8x0 The World Wars: Dwight Eisenhower | History HISTORY 3:42 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=v1FJXK4qy-k Dwight D. title: Eleanor Roosevelt
subtitle: First lady, reformer, and champion of human rights
summary: Eleanor Roosevelt transformed the role of First Lady and became, in the words later used of her, the “First Lady of the World.” An orphaned girl from a wealthy family, she grew into a political force in her own right: during Franklin D. Roosevelt’s presidency she traveled the country as his “eyes, ears and legs,” pressed the New Deal to include women and Black Americans, and wrote a daily newspaper column. After his death she represented the United States at the United Nations, where she chaired the Human Rights Commission and helped write the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
thumbAlt: Photograph of Eleanor Roosevelt
themeText: Women's history Civil rights and citizenship Reform and protest Foreign policy and diplomacy
text: Anna Eleanor Roosevelt New York City First Lady (1933–1945) Delegate to the United Nations Chair of the UN Human Rights Commission Chair of the President’s Commission on the Status of Women Born October 11, 1884, New York City Married Franklin D. Roosevelt, a fifth cousin once removed, on March 17, 1905 Column “My Day,” 1935–1962 United Nations Chaired the Human Rights Commission; Universal Declaration adopted December 10, 1948 Died November 7, 1962 Anna Eleanor Roosevelt was born on October 11, 1884, in New York City, the niece of Theodore Roosevelt. Her privileged childhood was also a sad one: her father struggled with alcoholism, and by the time she was ten her mother, her father, and a brother had died. She was raised by a harsh, critical grandmother who wounded her self-esteem. At fifteen she was sent to Allenswood, a girls’ school near London, where the headmistress, Marie Souvestre, encouraged her independence and opened her mind to social issues. Back in New York she taught immigrant children at the Rivington Street settlement house. In 1905 she married her distant cousin Franklin Delano Roosevelt; her uncle, President Theodore Roosevelt, gave the bride away. For years she lived under the thumb of her domineering mother-in-law, Sara Roosevelt, and between 1906 and 1916 she bore six children, one of whom died in infancy. Her public life began in earnest during World War I, when she volunteered with the Red Cross and in Navy hospitals. After Franklin was stricken with polio in 1921, she kept his political career alive while building her own — in the League of Women Voters, the Women’s Trade Union League, and the women’s division of the Democratic Party — and she helped establish Val-Kill Industries, a nonprofit furniture factory, and taught at a girls’ school in New York City. By 1928 she was better known publicly than her husband. In the White House she told the nation not to expect a symbol of elegance but “plain, ordinary Mrs. Roosevelt” — and became the most politically active First Lady in history. She held the first press conferences by a First Lady, admitting only women reporters; wrote her column “My Day” from 1935 until her death; traveled the country inspecting relief projects and working conditions; and lobbied her husband to appoint women, among them Frances Perkins, the first woman to head the Department of Labor. She championed racial justice, and when the Daughters of the American Revolution barred the singer Marian Anderson from their hall in 1939, she resigned from the organization and helped arrange Anderson’s concert at the Lincoln Memorial for 75,000 people. During World War II she visited England and the South Pacific to lift the morale of American troops. After Franklin’s death in 1945, President Truman appointed her a delegate to the new United Nations. As chair of its Human Rights Commission, she worked tirelessly on the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted on December 10, 1948. President Kennedy later reappointed her to the UN and asked her to chair the President’s Commission on the Status of Women. Her marriage was strained: in 1918 she discovered that Franklin had had an affair, and while she stayed in the marriage and remained his political partner, she built an increasingly independent life, often at her Val-Kill cottage. Her very public activism was itself new and unsettling for a First Lady; her resignation from the DAR came, as the National Women’s History Museum notes, “with much media fanfare.” Roosevelt believed government had a duty to the poor, minorities, and the disadvantaged, and that democracy at home and peace abroad depended on human rights for all. Initially wary of women’s suffrage, she became a determined advocate of women’s political participation. She spoke out against McCarthyism in the 1950s and urged faster federal action on housing desegregation and protection for the Freedom Riders. Roosevelt died on November 7, 1962, and is buried beside her husband at Hyde Park. The Commission on the Status of Women, which she chaired, released its groundbreaking report on sex discrimination the following year. For decades after her death she ranked at the top of polls of the most respected American women, and in 2023 she was honored on a U.S. quarter that shows the scales of justice, a tribute to her work for human rights. Eleanor Roosevelt used an unelected position to become one of the most influential reformers of the twentieth century and a founding voice of the international human rights movement. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QMBRgDErlVw Eleanor Roosevelt: Most Iconic First Lady - Fast Facts | History HISTORY 4:27 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MpI6In4fmeo Eleanor Roosevelt - The First Lady to the World Biographics 18:29 2026-10-22

title: Elizabeth Cady Stanton
subtitle: Philosopher and strategist of the women’s rights movement
summary: Elizabeth Cady Stanton was the chief philosopher of the American women’s rights movement. In 1848 she helped organize the Seneca Falls Convention and wrote its Declaration of Sentiments, which rewrote the Declaration of Independence to proclaim that “all men and women are created equal.” For half a century she supplied the ideas, and her partner Susan B. Anthony carried them across the country. A radical on marriage, divorce, and religion, she also opposed voting rights for Black men without women, a stance that split the suffrage movement.
thumbAlt: Photograph of Elizabeth Cady Stanton
themeText: Women's history Voting rights Reform and protest Religion
text: Elizabeth Cady Stanton Johnstown, New York New York City Organizer of the Seneca Falls Convention Author of the Declaration of Sentiments President of the National Woman Suffrage Association Author of *The Woman’s Bible* Partnership With Susan B. Anthony, from 1851, for more than fifty years Organizations Co-founded the National Woman Suffrage Association (1869) Writings Declaration of Sentiments (1848); History of Woman Suffrage; The Woman’s Bible Died 1902 — eighteen years before women of her social status could vote nationally Elizabeth Cady was born on November 12, 1815, in Johnstown, New York, the eighth of ten children of Margaret Livingston and Daniel Cady, a lawyer who became a state supreme court judge. Four of his five sons died in infancy, and the fifth when Elizabeth was eleven. She never forgot climbing onto her grieving father’s knee and hearing him sigh: “Oh, my daughter, I wish you were a boy!” She vowed to be all her brother had been. No American college then admitted women, so she studied at the Johnstown Academy and Emma Willard’s Troy Female Seminary, and picked up an informal legal education from the lawyers who gathered in her father’s house to talk. At a cousin’s home she met the abolitionist lecturer Henry Stanton. They married in 1840 against her family’s wishes, and she refused to promise “to obey.” The couple sailed at once to London for the World’s Anti-Slavery Convention. In London, Stanton and the Quaker abolitionist Lucretia Mott were furious that women were barred from speaking, and they resolved to hold a convention on women’s rights. In 1848 they did so at Seneca Falls, New York. Stanton’s Declaration of Sentiments listed eighteen grievances — that men had denied women the vote, “taken from her all right in property, even to the wages she earns,” and closed colleges against her — and demanded equality. That year she also petitioned for New York’s Married Women’s Property Act, which let married women keep their own property and wages. In 1851 she met Susan B. Anthony, beginning a partnership that dominated the movement for over half a century; while raising seven children, Stanton wrote the speeches and Anthony delivered them. During the Civil War the two campaigned for the Thirteenth Amendment. In 1869 they founded the National Woman Suffrage Association, which Stanton led as president, writing for its journal The Revolution. Once her children were grown, she lectured nationwide on marriage, divorce, child rearing, and women’s property. With Anthony and Matilda Joslyn Gage she wrote the first volumes of the History of Woman Suffrage (1881–1885), and in 1890 she became the first president of the reunited National American Woman Suffrage Association. Stanton believed women were entitled to full equality in law, marriage, property, education, religion, and politics, and that the vote was essential to all the rest. She insisted on women’s “self-dependence”: girls, she said in her popular lecture “Our Girls,” were raised “to revolve round some man,” never knowing “the freedom and dignity that one secures in self-dependence and self support.” In The Woman’s Bible (1895, 1898) she argued for a secular state and challenged the male-centered theology she believed kept women subordinate. Stanton and Anthony opposed the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments because they protected the voting rights of Black men but not of women, breaking with former abolitionist allies. Her advocacy centered on the concerns of propertied, upper-middle-class women, and at times she spoke against rights for men outside her class, including “natives and foreigners.” The Woman’s Bible alienated many suffragists, and the National Women’s History Museum describes her as a controversial figure who often contradicted herself over a long life. Stanton recorded her life in the memoir Eighty Years and More and died in New York City in October 1902, eighteen years before the Nineteenth Amendment gave women the vote. The agenda she set at Seneca Falls — equality in property, wages, education, marriage, and politics — guided the women’s movement well into the twentieth century. Stanton gave the women’s movement its ideas and much of its language. Her career also shows the movement’s internal conflicts over race, which shaped suffrage politics for decades. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=I2yRHfDyhVo Who Was Elizabeth Cady Stanton? title: Elvis Presley
subtitle: The “King of Rock & Roll,” who carried a blend of Black and white Southern music to a mass audience
summary: Elvis Presley, a young truck driver from Tupelo, Mississippi, began recording at a Memphis studio in the early 1950s and, in 1954, set off a musical and cultural revolution. Mixing blues, rhythm and blues, country, and gospel, he brought music rooted in Black traditions to huge white audiences, and his hip-shaking performances shocked parents as much as they thrilled teenagers. After a string of number-one hits, national television appearances, and movies, he served in the Army, spent the 1960s making films, and returned to the stage in 1969. He died at his Memphis home, Graceland, in 1977, at forty-two.
thumbAlt: Publicity photograph of Elvis Presley for the 1957 film Jailhouse Rock
aliases: Elvis The King King of Rock and Roll Elvis the Pelvis
themeText: Arts and popular culture Everyday life African American history
text: Elvis Aron Presley Tupelo, Mississippi Graceland, Memphis, Tennessee Singer Film actor U.S. Army soldier (1958–1960) First single “That’s All Right” (1954), a blues song by Arthur Crudup, recorded for Sam Phillips’s Sun Records Breakthrough “Heartbreak Hotel” (1956), his first single for RCA Victor and his first number-one hit Army Drafted in 1958 at the height of his fame; served in Germany; honorably discharged in March 1960 Movies First film, Love Me Tender (1956); for most of the 1960s he concentrated on making movies Hall of Fame Inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 1986 Presley was the figure through whom rock & roll exploded into mainstream culture. By bringing Black-influenced music to white audiences in the segregated 1950s, he helped remake American popular music and youth culture. Elvis Aron Presley was born on January 8, 1935, in a two-room house in Tupelo, Mississippi, to Vernon and Gladys Presley. His twin brother, Jessie Garon, was stillborn, so Elvis grew up an only child. In 1948 the family moved to Memphis, where he graduated from Humes High School in 1953. As a teenager he belonged to a Pentecostal church and sometimes went to all-night gospel sings; he also absorbed the rhythm and blues he heard on Memphis’s Beale Street, as well as country and bluegrass. After high school he took a job driving a truck. In 1953 and 1954 Presley cut demo records at Sun Records, whose owner, Sam Phillips, had been looking for a white singer who could perform in the style of traditionally Black music. Phillips teamed him with guitarist Scotty Moore and bassist Bill Black, and during a sluggish 1954 session Elvis started goofing around with Arthur Crudup’s rhythm-and-blues song “That’s All Right.” Phillips recorded it and released it as Elvis’s first single. His five Sun singles blended rhythm and blues with country music into the sound later called rockabilly; his singing was so close to R&B that some Southern disc jockeys felt they had to tell listeners he was white. On the road, his gyrating hips caused an uproar and earned him the nickname “Elvis the Pelvis.” Late in 1955 Phillips sold Presley’s contract to RCA Victor for $35,000, and Colonel Tom Parker became his manager. “Heartbreak Hotel” (1956) became his first number-one hit, and appearances on national television, including The Ed Sullivan Show, made him an overnight star. Hits like “Don’t Be Cruel” and “Hound Dog” — first recorded by Willie Mae “Big Mama” Thornton — followed, and in late 1956 he starred in his first film, Love Me Tender. Drafted into the Army in 1958 at the height of his fame, he had his pompadour cut and served in Friedberg, Germany, while records he had made earlier kept topping the charts. Presley drew openly on the gospel, blues, and rhythm and blues he grew up with, and he moved easily between styles — from the edgy “hillbilly cat” of the Sun years to smooth balladeer, movie idol, and caped Las Vegas showman. He was also generous: a 1961 benefit concert he gave in Hawaii raised more than $65,000 toward the USS Arizona Memorial at Pearl Harbor. To many adults in the 1950s, Presley’s provocative stage moves were scandalous, and the controversy only fed his fame. His rise also raises questions about race in American music: Sam Phillips had gone looking for a white singer who could sound like Black musicians, and some of Presley’s biggest hits, like “Hound Dog,” had first been recorded by Black artists. After the Army, he gave up live concerts for nearly a decade to make two or three movies a year — films that were popular but never won the critical respect his music did. Presley returned to live performance in 1969 with a series of shows in Las Vegas and new hits such as “In the Ghetto” and “Suspicious Minds.” He died at Graceland, his Memphis home, on August 16, 1977, at forty-two. In 1986 he was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame. “Without Elvis, there would be no Beatles,” said John Lennon, who recalled that when he first heard “Heartbreak Hotel,” his “whole life changed.” Graceland draws hundreds of thousands of visitors a year, and Presley remains, for much of the world, simply “the King.” https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5YVnP00RdHg Elvis Presley: Life and Death of the King Biographics 24:45 2026-10-22

title: Franklin D. Roosevelt
subtitle: Thirty-second president, architect of the New Deal and wartime leader
summary: Franklin D. Roosevelt led the United States through the two great crises of the twentieth century, the Great Depression and World War II, and was the only president elected four times. Born to wealth and paralyzed by polio at thirty-nine, he returned to politics and won the presidency in 1932 by promising “a new deal for the American people.” His New Deal transformed the federal government’s role in American life. As commander in chief after Pearl Harbor, he built the alliance with Britain, the Soviet Union, and China that defeated Germany and Japan. He died in April 1945, weeks before victory in Europe.

aliases: FDR fireside chats New Deal Lend-Lease arsenal of democracy four terms
themeText: The presidency Economy and finance War and the military Foreign policy and diplomacy Parties and elections
text: Franklin Delano Roosevelt Hyde Park, New York Warm Springs, Georgia New York state senator (1911–1913) Assistant Secretary of the Navy (1913–1920) Democratic vice-presidential nominee (1920) Governor of New York (1929–1932) Thirty-second president (1933–1945) Born January 30, 1882, Hyde Park, New York Spouse Eleanor Roosevelt, a distant cousin and the niece of Theodore Roosevelt, married in 1905 Polio Struck in the summer of 1921 at Campobello Island; never regained the use of his legs Presidency 1933–1945; Democrat; elected 1932, 1936, 1940, and 1944, the only president to serve more than two terms Signature programs The New Deal: banking reform, CCC, WPA, TVA, Social Security, the Wagner Act War Lend-Lease (March 1941); led the nation after Pearl Harbor (December 7, 1941) Death Cerebral hemorrhage at Warm Springs, Georgia, April 12, 1945, aged 63 Roosevelt changed what Americans expected from their government and their president. Under him the federal government took responsibility for the economic security of ordinary citizens, the Democratic Party became the nation’s majority party, and the United States emerged from World War II as a global power. Franklin Delano Roosevelt was born on January 30, 1882, at Hyde Park, New York, the only child of James Roosevelt, a wealthy landowner and businessman, and Sara Delano Roosevelt, who devoted herself to her son throughout her long life. He grew up on the family estate on the Hudson River, taught by tutors until he was fourteen, when he entered the Groton School. There he came to admire his distant cousin Theodore Roosevelt, the rising Republican star. He graduated from Harvard in three years, edited its student newspaper, the Crimson, and studied law at Columbia, passing the bar in 1907 without finishing a degree. In 1905 he married Anna Eleanor Roosevelt, a distant cousin and President Theodore Roosevelt’s niece. They had six children, five of whom survived infancy. In 1910 Roosevelt won a seat in the New York State Senate as a Democrat from Republican-dominated Dutchess County, and he became a determined opponent of the Tammany Hall machine that ran New York City’s Democratic Party. Having backed Woodrow Wilson in 1912, he became assistant secretary of the navy in 1913. He argued for a “big Navy” and, during the war in Europe, for improving American military readiness, and he was praised for helping prepare the country to enter the war. During those years he began an affair with Lucy Mercer, Eleanor’s social secretary. When Eleanor discovered it in 1918 and offered a divorce, he refused, in part because he knew a divorced man could not succeed in politics. They stayed married, but their marriage became more a political partnership than a romance, and Eleanor built an independent public life. In 1920 Roosevelt ran for vice president on the losing Democratic ticket with James Cox. In the summer of 1921, at his vacation home on Campobello Island in Canada, Roosevelt fell ill with polio. He never regained the use of his legs. Through years of painful exercise he learned to “walk” short distances with braces, canes, and aides, and he founded a center at Warm Springs, Georgia, for other polio patients. “I know that he had real fear when he was first taken ill,” Eleanor later said, “but he learned to surmount it. After that I never heard him say he was afraid of anything.” With Eleanor and his adviser Louis Howe keeping him connected to Democratic politics, he returned to public life. In 1928 he was narrowly elected governor of New York, winning by half a percentage point while Al Smith lost the presidency to Herbert Hoover. As the Depression deepened, Governor Roosevelt declared that “there is a duty on the part of government to do something about this,” and he created a state relief program for the unemployed. Election and the New Deal. At the 1932 Democratic convention in Chicago, Roosevelt broke with tradition by flying there to accept the nomination in person. In part he went to show that polio had not weakened him, and he promised “a new deal for the American people.” He swept into office in a landslide, and Democrats won large majorities in both houses of Congress. When he took office on March 4, 1933, the banking system had collapsed and unemployment exceeded a quarter of the workforce. He closed the banks temporarily, explained his plans to the nation in radio “fireside chats,” and in his first hundred days won laws creating the Civilian Conservation Corps, the Agricultural Adjustment Administration, the Tennessee Valley Authority, and federal deposit insurance. In 1935 the Second New Deal added the Works Progress Administration, the Wagner Act protecting unions, and the Social Security Act. (See the New Deal entry for details.) A new majority. In 1936 Roosevelt crushed the Republican Alf Landon, who carried only Maine and Vermont, declaring of the business and financial interests arrayed against him, “They are unanimous in their hate for me—and I welcome their hatred.” He had built the “New Deal Coalition” of Southern whites, urban Catholics and Jews, Black voters in Northern cities, union members, Midwestern farmers, and liberals, which would power the Democratic Party for thirty years. In 1940, with Europe at war, he broke George Washington’s two-term tradition and defeated Wendell Willkie with 55 percent of the vote. In 1944 he won a fourth term over Thomas Dewey, 432 electoral votes to 99. Toward war. For most of the 1930s Roosevelt’s internationalism was limited by the Depression and by isolationist feeling in Congress, which passed five Neutrality Acts between 1935 and 1939. In 1933 he established official relations with the Soviet Union and pursued a “Good Neighbor” policy toward Latin America. When war broke out in Europe in 1939, he declared the nation neutral but said he could not ask Americans to be “neutral in thought as well.” After France fell in 1940, he traded fifty old destroyers to Britain for bases. In March 1941 he won the Lend-Lease program, which made the United States the “arsenal of democracy.” After Germany invaded the Soviet Union that June, he extended Lend-Lease to the Soviets. In August 1941 he and Winston Churchill issued the Atlantic Charter, a statement of their war aims. Commander in chief. After Japan attacked Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941, Roosevelt asked Congress for war, and Germany and Italy declared war on the United States four days later. On January 1, 1942, he formed the coalition of nations fighting the Axis that he called the “United Nations.” With Churchill and Stalin he planned the war at Tehran in 1943 and the peace at Yalta in early 1945. At Tehran he and Churchill promised Stalin the invasion of France that came on D-Day, June 6, 1944. He hoped the United Nations would outlast the war as an organization for world peace. Roosevelt believed in American capitalism but thought it had to be reformed to survive, and he approached problems as a pragmatist: try something, and if it fails, try something else. He believed government had a duty to help citizens in hard times. As governor he said relief was owed “not as a matter of charity, but as a matter of social duty.” In foreign policy he was an internationalist in the tradition of Theodore Roosevelt and Woodrow Wilson, convinced that the United States had a vital role to play in the world. Roosevelt’s critics accused him of expanding federal power and the presidency beyond constitutional limits. His 1937 plan to add justices to the Supreme Court was denounced as “court-packing” and defeated, and his 1938 attempt to purge conservative Democrats in primaries largely failed. He did little to challenge segregation, fearing the loss of Southern Democratic votes. On February 19, 1942, he signed Executive Order 9066, under which some 122,000 people of Japanese descent, nearly 70,000 of them American citizens, were forcibly removed from the West Coast and confined in fenced, guarded camps in remote areas. (The American Yawp gives the number as more than 110,000.) In 1988 Congress acknowledged the injustice, apologized, and paid $20,000 to each survivor. His administration knew for much of the war that the Nazis were killing Jews, though officials probably could not conceive of the scale of the killing. Roosevelt’s policy was to win the war first, which would in turn stop the killing, and later critics argued that the United States could and should have done more to help Europe’s Jews. Roosevelt ran for a fourth term in 1944 although a medical examination early that year had found serious heart and circulatory problems. During the campaign his opponent discreetly raised the age issue. By early 1944 a medical examination had revealed serious heart and circulatory problems, and the strain of the war, the 1944 campaign, and the Yalta Conference wore him down. On April 12, 1945, while sitting for a portrait at Warm Springs, Georgia, he collapsed and died of a cerebral hemorrhage at sixty-three. (The FDR Library describes it as a massive stroke; he died two and a half hours later without regaining consciousness.) Vice President Harry Truman took the oath of office that day. Churchill later compared the news to having “been struck a physical blow.” Hundreds of thousands of mourners lined the route of the funeral train from Georgia to Washington and on to Hyde Park, where he was buried on April 15. Victory in Europe came less than a month later. Roosevelt reshaped the presidency. His fireside chats created a direct bond with the public, and the 1939 reorganization law created the Executive Office of the President, changing the shape of the White House for good. In the Miller Center’s judgment, no president except Abraham Lincoln did more to change American society and politics. I pledge you, I pledge myself, to a new deal for the American people. Franklin D. Roosevelt accepting the Democratic nomination, July 1932 So, first of all, let me assert my firm belief that the only thing we have to fear is fear itself. Franklin D. Roosevelt first inaugural address, March 4, 1933 They are unanimous in their hate for me—and I welcome their hatred. Franklin D. Roosevelt on his business and financial opponents, 1936 campaign I know that he had real fear when he was first taken ill, but he learned to surmount it. After that I never heard him say he was afraid of anything. title: Frederick Douglass
subtitle: Escaped slave, orator, editor, and the foremost Black leader of the nineteenth century
summary: Frederick Douglass escaped from slavery in Maryland in 1838 and became the most important leader of the movement for African American civil rights in the nineteenth century. His Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave (1845) became a bestseller, and his speeches, above all “What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?” (1852), made him the nation’s most famous abolitionist orator. He edited his own newspaper, supported women’s rights from the Seneca Falls Convention onward, recruited Black soldiers during the Civil War, and pressed Abraham Lincoln face to face for equal treatment. After the war he held federal office under five presidents.
thumbAlt: Photograph of Frederick Douglass
aliases: Frederick Bailey Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July? The North Star
themeText: Slavery and emancipation African American history Civil rights and citizenship Reform and protest Women's history
text: Frederick Douglass (born Frederick Augustus Washington Bailey) Talbot County, Eastern Shore of Maryland Cedar Hill, Washington, D.C. Abolitionist lecturer and author Editor of *The North Star* Recruiter of Black Union soldiers President of the Freedman’s Bank (1874) U.S. Marshal for D.C. (1877–1881) Recorder of Deeds for D.C. (1881–1886) Minister Resident and Consul General to Haiti (1889–1891) Born February 1818, Talbot County, Maryland; he later chose February 14 as his birthday Escape September 3, 1838, from Baltimore to New York, by train and boat, dressed as a sailor Autobiographies Narrative (1845), My Bondage and My Freedom (1855), Life and Times (1881) Newspaper The North Star, first issue December 3, 1847, Rochester, New York Freedom purchased 1846, for £150 raised by British supporters Offices U.S. Marshal and Recorder of Deeds for D.C.; minister to Haiti (1889–1891) Died February 20, 1895, at Cedar Hill, Washington, D.C., aged 77 Douglass turned his own life into the most powerful argument against slavery that Americans ever heard, and then spent thirty years after emancipation insisting that freedom meant nothing without citizenship, the vote, and equal rights. He judged the nation by its own founding words, and he believed in building alliances across racial and political lines to make them true. Frederick Augustus Washington Bailey was born into slavery on the Eastern Shore of Maryland in February 1818. He barely knew his mother, who was forced to work on a distant farm and died when he was about seven, and he never knew his father. He later chose February 14 as his birthday, because on his mother’s last visit she had held him on her lap and given him a heart-shaped ginger cake. Fifteen of his close relatives, including his sister Sarah, were “sold south” during his childhood. At eight he was sent to Baltimore to work for the family of Hugh Auld. Sophia Auld began teaching him the alphabet, and he went on to teach himself to read and write in the streets of the city. At twelve or thirteen he bought The Columbian Orator, a collection of speeches on natural rights and liberty. When he was fifteen his enslaver, Thomas Auld, sent him back to the Eastern Shore as a field hand. Sent in 1834 to work for Edward Covey, a “slave-breaker” who whipped him repeatedly, he finally fought back and was not whipped again. He taught other enslaved people to read, and in 1836 he and several others planned an escape. The plot was discovered, and Frederick was jailed and sent back to Baltimore, where he learned the trade of ship caulking and was savagely beaten by white apprentices. In Baltimore he met Anna Murray, a free Black woman who used her own money to help him escape. On September 3, 1838, dressed as a sailor, he boarded a northbound train, and in less than twenty-four hours he reached New York City. (The American Yawp dates his escape to 1837; the National Park Service gives September 3, 1838.) Anna joined him, and they married on September 15. They settled in New Bedford, Massachusetts, where he took the name Douglass and worked as a caulker and laborer. The couple had five children: Rosetta, Lewis, Frederick Jr., Charles, and Annie. Abolitionist. In August 1841, at an antislavery convention on Nantucket, Douglass spoke to a large, mostly white audience, and the Massachusetts Anti-Slavery Society hired him as a lecturer. He toured the North and Midwest. Mobs attacked him, as at Pendleton, Indiana, where his hand was broken in 1843, and he was thrown off a train for refusing to ride in a “Jim Crow” car. Because some audiences doubted that so polished a speaker had ever been enslaved, he published the Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave in May 1845, naming the people and places of his enslavement. The book became a bestseller, but it exposed him to recapture. He sailed for Britain in August 1845 and spent almost two years lecturing in England, Ireland, and Scotland, and in 1846 British supporters raised £150 to buy his freedom from Hugh Auld. Editor and organizer. Back in the United States, Douglass moved his family to Rochester, New York, and on December 3, 1847, published the first issue of his own newspaper, The North Star, despite the bitter opposition of his former ally William Lloyd Garrison. In 1848 he attended the first women’s rights convention at Seneca Falls and began his lifelong support for women’s suffrage. He broke with Garrison in 1851, rejecting Garrison’s view that the Constitution was a proslavery document and that abolitionists should stay out of politics. He supported the Liberty Party and later the new Republican Party. He and Anna also opened their home to freedom seekers, and Douglass acted as a “station master” of the Underground Railroad in Rochester, helping hundreds to freedom. In 1855 he published a second autobiography, My Bondage and My Freedom, which also attacked racial segregation in the North. The Fourth of July. On July 5, 1852, Douglass spoke to the Ladies’ Anti-Slavery Society of Rochester in Corinthian Hall. He insisted on speaking the day after Independence Day. “What, to the American slave, is your 4th of July?” he asked. “I answer: a day that reveals to him, more than all other days in the year, the gross injustice and cruelty to which he is the constant victim.” Yet he did not reject the nation’s founding documents; he held that the Constitution, rightly read, was not a proslavery document. John Brown. Douglass met the militant abolitionist John Brown in 1847, and Brown stayed at his Rochester home in 1858 while planning a slave revolt. In August 1859, at a stone quarry near Chambersburg, Pennsylvania, Brown told him of his plan to attack Harpers Ferry, and Douglass refused to join. After the raid, he fled to Canada to avoid arrest as an accomplice and then went on to England. The Civil War. Douglass worked to make emancipation an aim of the war and urged that Black men be allowed to fight. “We are striking the rebels with our soft white hand,” he complained, “when we should be striking them with the iron hand of the black man.” In 1863 he became a recruiter for the Union Army, and two of his sons, Lewis and Charles, joined the 54th Massachusetts Infantry; Lewis was badly wounded in the regiment’s assault on Fort Wagner in July. Angry that Black soldiers received less pay, no promotions, and no protection as prisoners of war, he stopped recruiting and went to see Lincoln at the White House. The National Park Service’s account of their meetings dates that first visit to August 10, 1863, while its chronology places it in July. “I know who you are Mr. Douglass,” Lincoln said. “Sit down. I am glad to see you.” Douglass left unconvinced on some points but respecting Lincoln’s “humane spirit,” and resumed recruiting. In August 1864, expecting to lose the election, Lincoln asked Douglass to organize a network to help enslaved people escape from the Confederate states, a plan made unnecessary by Lincoln’s reelection. At the White House reception after the second inauguration, Lincoln greeted him as “my friend Douglass” and told him, “there is no man in the country whose opinion I value more than yours.” Reconstruction and public office. After the war Douglass argued that freedom would be empty without the rights of citizenship, and he denounced President Andrew Johnson’s lenient Reconstruction policy. He saw the Thirteenth, Fourteenth, and Fifteenth Amendments adopted between 1865 and 1870. In 1872, after his Rochester home burned, he moved to Washington, D.C. He served as assistant secretary of a commission to Santo Domingo, sat on the board of Howard University, and in 1874 became president of the Freedman’s Bank shortly before it failed. Under five presidents he served as U.S. Marshal for the District of Columbia (1877–1881), Recorder of Deeds (1881–1886), and minister to Haiti (1889–1891), at a time when violence and fraud severely restricted Black political activity. He bought Cedar Hill, an estate on a hill in Anacostia overlooking the capital, and lived there until his death; the National Park Service gives the year of purchase as 1877 in one place and 1878 in another. Douglass believed that literacy was the road to freedom, a lesson he learned as a boy in Baltimore. He believed in the moral force of plain truth: “The feeling of the nation must be quickened; the conscience of the nation must be roused … the hypocrisy of the nation must be exposed.” Unlike the Garrisonians, he came to see the Constitution as an antislavery charter and political action as a legitimate weapon. He supported women’s rights throughout his life and believed in dialogue and alliances across racial and ideological lines. Douglass’s independence often put him at odds with allies. His decision to start his own newspaper and enter politics led to a bitter public split with Garrison, though the two camps renewed their friendship during the war. He was a sharp critic of Lincoln early in the war and later spoke of him with deep ambivalence. At the dedication of the Freedmen’s Memorial in 1876 he said that Lincoln had been, “in his prejudices, … a white man,” and that white Americans were Lincoln’s children while Black Americans were “at best only his step-children.” His commitment to Black voting rights strained his alliance with the women’s movement. In 1869 he broke with feminist leaders who refused to support the Fifteenth Amendment unless it also gave women the vote, arguing that the ballot was a “question of life and death” for Black men in the South. In 1872 the Equal Rights Party nominated him for vice president on Victoria Woodhull’s ticket without his knowledge or consent; he campaigned instead for Ulysses S. Grant. In 1884, two years after Anna’s death, he married Helen Pitts, a white activist from an abolitionist family who had worked as a clerk in his office. The marriage stirred controversy because she was white and twenty years younger. Douglass remained active to the end. In January 1894 he delivered his last great address, “Lessons of the Hour,” attacking the lynching of Black Southerners. On February 20, 1895, he attended a meeting of the National Council of Women in Washington, returned home to Cedar Hill, and died of a heart attack that evening, at seventy-seven. He was buried in Mount Hope Cemetery in Rochester. Helen Pitts Douglass devoted her remaining years to preserving Cedar Hill. Congress chartered the Frederick Douglass Memorial and Historical Association at her urging in 1900, and it received the property on her death in 1903. Cedar Hill is now the Frederick Douglass National Historic Site, and about 70 percent of the objects displayed there belonged to Douglass or his household. What, to the American slave, is your 4th of July? I answer: a day that reveals to him, more than all other days in the year, the gross injustice and cruelty to which he is the constant victim. Frederick Douglass “What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?”, Rochester, July 5, 1852 We are striking the rebels with our soft white hand, when we should be striking them with the iron hand of the black man which we keep chained behind us. Frederick Douglass urging the Union to enlist Black soldiers, early in the Civil War I was an ex-slave, identified with a despised race, and yet I was to meet the most exalted person in this great republic. Frederick Douglass recalling his first visit to Lincoln at the White House, 1863 You are the children of Abraham Lincoln. We are at best only his step-children. title: George Washington
subtitle: Commander of the Continental Army and first president
summary: George Washington commanded the Continental Army through eight years of war, presided over the convention that wrote the Constitution, and served as the first president of the United States. Twice he gave up power when he could have kept it, by resigning his command in 1783 and by retiring after two terms as president, and those choices, more than any battle, made him the “indispensable man” of the founding. A Virginia planter who held hundreds of people in slavery, he arranged in his will to free those he owned, but only after his wife’s death.
thumbAlt: Portrait of George Washington by Gilbert Stuart
aliases: Washington Father of His Country Farewell Address Newburgh Address Mount Vernon
themeText: The presidency War and the military Slavery and emancipation
text: George Washington Westmoreland County, Virginia Mount Vernon, Virginia Virginia militia officer in the French and Indian War Member of the Virginia House of Burgesses (from 1759) Commander in chief of the Continental Army (1775–1783) President of the Constitutional Convention (1787) First president of the United States (1789–1797) Born February 22, 1732 (February 11 by the old calendar), at Popes Creek, Westmoreland County, Virginia Commander in chief Elected by Congress in June 1775; resigned his commission to Congress in December 1783 Elected president Unanimously by the Electoral College in 1789 (69 votes) and 1792 (132 votes), the only president elected unanimously twice Precedents Created the cabinet; retired after two terms, a limit later written into the 22nd Amendment Enslaved people His will freed the people he held in his own right, after Martha Washington’s death Died December 14, 1799, at Mount Vernon, of an acute throat infection Washington’s greatest contribution was his restraint. Americans trusted him with immense power because he had given it up once before, and his conduct as president created the cabinet, the two-term tradition, and the dignity of the office. His slaveholding is the most troubling part of his legacy. He came to see slavery as wrong but freed the people he owned only in his will, and he never spoke against slavery in public. Washington was born on February 22, 1732, at Popes Creek farm in Westmoreland County, Virginia. By the Old Style calendar then used in the British Empire, the date was February 11. His father, Augustine, owned nearly 3,000 acres of tobacco land, and George was the first child of his second wife, Mary Ball. When George was eleven his father died. His older half-brothers inherited most of the estate, including the land that became Mount Vernon, while George received a smaller farm and ten enslaved people. He never had the English schooling his brothers enjoyed, and he later admitted his “consciousness of a defective education.” Through his half-brother Lawrence’s marriage into the powerful Fairfax family, he learned surveying; at sixteen he joined a Fairfax survey of the Shenandoah Valley, and at seventeen he became the official surveyor of Culpeper County. In 1751 he went with Lawrence to Barbados, his only trip outside North America, and survived smallpox there, which left him immune to a disease that would ravage the Continental Army. The Miller Center says the illness probably left him unable to father children, while Encyclopedia Virginia notes that the only modern study found no link between smallpox and male infertility. The French and Indian War. In 1753 Virginia’s lieutenant governor, Robert Dinwiddie, sent the twenty-one-year-old Washington into the Ohio country to order the French out. In May 1754, leading about 140 Virginians and Native allies, he attacked a French party at Jumonville Glen, and its commander, Joseph Coulon de Jumonville, was killed. The French called it an assassination, and the skirmish helped ignite the French and Indian War. Weeks later the French forced him to surrender at Fort Necessity. In 1755 he served as an aide to General Edward Braddock, whose army was routed near the Monongahela River; Washington had two horses shot from under him and four bullets through his coat. He then commanded Virginia’s frontier forces until resigning his commission at the end of 1758. Planter and politician. On January 6, 1759, Washington married Martha Dandridge Custis, a wealthy widow with two young children, and took control of the Custis estate of nearly 20,000 acres. The couple settled at Mount Vernon, which he eventually expanded to nearly 8,000 acres and a mansion of 11,000 square feet. Martha brought 84 enslaved people to the plantation. Elected to the House of Burgesses in 1758, Washington grew frustrated with the British merchants who set the prices for his tobacco and his purchases; he switched from tobacco to wheat and backed boycotts of British goods. In 1769 he wrote to George Mason that “our lordly Masters in Great Britain will be satisfied with nothing less than the deprication of American freedom.” Commander in chief. Washington attended the Second Continental Congress in uniform. On June 15, 1775, the day after it created the Continental Army, Congress chose him as commander in chief; as a Virginian who had never served in the British army, he could unite the colonies. At Cambridge he found a disorganized army of 14,000 men short of powder, tents, and clothing. In March 1776 he forced the British out of Boston by placing cannon hauled from Fort Ticonderoga on Dorchester Heights. Defeated around New York that summer and fall, he retreated across New Jersey. Then, on the night of December 25–26, 1776, he crossed the icy Delaware River and surprised the Hessian garrison at Trenton, and a week later he struck again at Princeton. His record as a battlefield commander was mixed. He lost at Brandywine and Germantown in 1777 and lost Philadelphia, and the Miller Center faults him for battle plans too complicated for his army. But he understood that the cause would survive as long as the army did, and he avoided risking it in a decisive battle, aiming instead to “protract the war.” At Valley Forge in the winter of 1777–1778 some 2,000 of his men died of disease, hunger, and cold, yet the army held together, and Baron von Steuben’s drills made it a disciplined force. After first banning Black soldiers, Washington accepted free Black men in 1776 and later approved the recruitment of Black troops in Rhode Island. In 1781, with the French army under Rochambeau and the French fleet under de Grasse, he trapped General Charles Cornwallis at Yorktown, Virginia. A white flag went up on October 17, and Cornwallis formally surrendered on October 19. Giving up power. In March 1783, when unpaid officers at Newburgh, New York, talked of defying Congress, Washington addressed them. Fumbling for his glasses, he said, “Gentlemen, you must pardon me, for I have not only grown gray but almost blind in service to my country,” and the threat of mutiny dissolved. In December 1783 he returned his commission to Congress at Annapolis. In an age of military dictators and kings, the Miller Center notes, his voluntary surrender of power “was extraordinary.” The Constitution. Alarmed by Shays’s Rebellion and the weakness of the Articles of Confederation, Washington feared that “we are fast verging to anarchy and confusion.” He was elected president of the Constitutional Convention in May 1787 and attended every session, though as presiding officer he did not take part in the debates. Delegates shaped the presidency with him in mind; as Pierce Butler of South Carolina recalled, they defined its powers “by their opinions of his virtue.” His signature and support helped win ratification. The first president. Elected unanimously, Washington took the oath in New York City on April 30, 1789. “I walk on untrodden ground,” he wrote. “There is scarcely any part of my conduct which may not hereafter be drawn into precedent.” When the Senate would not give quick advice on an Indian treaty, he turned instead to his department heads: Secretary of State Thomas Jefferson, Treasury Secretary Alexander Hamilton, War Secretary Henry Knox, and Attorney General Edmund Randolph. On November 26, 1791, he held the first cabinet meeting. He appointed eleven Supreme Court justices. He backed Hamilton’s plans to assume the states’ war debts and create a national bank, which he signed into law on February 25, 1791, over Jefferson’s objections. When western Pennsylvanians rose against the federal whiskey tax in 1794, he called out militias from four states and rode out to inspect them himself. The Whiskey Rebellion collapsed, and he later pardoned the convicted rebels. In the West, after the defeat of Arthur St. Clair’s army in 1791, General Anthony Wayne defeated the Native confederacy at Fallen Timbers in 1794, and its peoples were pushed west. Abroad, Washington kept the young nation out of the war between revolutionary France and Britain. He proclaimed neutrality in April 1793, demanded the recall of the French minister Edmond Genêt, and sent Chief Justice John Jay to London. Jay’s Treaty of 1794 required British troops to leave their western forts but was bitterly unpopular, while Thomas Pinckney’s treaty with Spain opened the Mississippi River to American trade. Reelected unanimously in 1792, he refused a third term in 1796. In his Farewell Address, published on September 19, 1796, he warned Americans “against the baneful effects of the spirit of party” and against entangling their peace “in the toils of European ambition.” Washington believed that the Revolution would be lost if the new nation could not govern itself. “What a triumph for the advocates of despotism,” he wrote in the 1780s, “to find that we are incapable of governing ourselves.” He favored a strong central government, sided with Hamilton against Jefferson on finance, and claimed to stand above party, though his administration became identified with the Federalists. He valued republican virtue (self-sacrifice, decorum, and restraint) and modeled the presidency on it. His views of slavery changed over his life. Before the war he bought and sold enslaved people without apparent hesitation; the service of Black soldiers during the Revolution challenged his ideas about race. Afterward he resolved not to buy or sell more people and to keep families together. By the late 1780s, Encyclopedia Virginia concludes, “a sense of slavery’s injustice began to come over him.” Washington’s slaveholding stands at the center of modern debates about his legacy. As president he lived in Philadelphia, where Pennsylvania law freed enslaved people after six months of residence; he and Martha rotated their enslaved workers back to Virginia to keep them from gaining freedom. When Ona Judge, Martha’s maid, escaped in 1796, and the chef Hercules fled in 1797, the Washingtons tried to recapture them, without success. He never spoke against slavery in public, fearing, the Miller Center suggests, that the South might leave the Union. His other actions drew criticism too. Although he favored protecting Native lands to avoid war, he enforced the Treaty of Fort Harmar, which forced Native nations from their homelands, and his army’s victory at Fallen Timbers opened their lands to white settlers. Jay’s Treaty provoked violent protests and helped divide Americans into rival parties. And in 1798, recalled to command a provisional army during the Quasi-War with France, he forced President John Adams to accept Hamilton as his second in command, a step the Miller Center calls a blow to civilian authority over the army. Washington retired to Mount Vernon in 1797 and devoted himself to scientific farming, crop rotation, mule breeding, and a profitable whiskey distillery. He died on December 14, 1799, of an acute throat infection. “I die hard,” he said, “but I am not afraid to go.” His will freed the people he owned in his own right after Martha’s death. The Miller Center calls it “a forceful statement about the morality of slavery from the grave.” Eulogized as “First in war, first in peace, and first in the hearts of his countrymen,” he remains the preeminent Founding Father. Every president after him followed his example of serving only two terms until Franklin Roosevelt, and the Twenty-second Amendment later made the limit law; every president has also worked with a cabinet. The national capital, the Washington Monument, and Mount Rushmore all honor him. I walk on untrodden ground. There is scarcely any part of my conduct which may not hereafter be drawn into precedent. title: Harriet Tubman
subtitle: Freedom seeker, Underground Railroad conductor, Union scout
summary: Harriet Tubman was born into slavery on Maryland’s Eastern Shore around 1822, escaped in 1849, and then went back again and again to lead family members and friends to freedom, becoming the most famous conductor of the Underground Railroad. During the Civil War she served the Union Army as a nurse, scout, and spy, and in June 1863 she helped plan and lead the Combahee River Raid in South Carolina, which freed more than 700 enslaved people. In her later years in Auburn, New York, she supported women’s suffrage and opened a home for elderly and poor African Americans.
thumbAlt: Photograph of Harriet Tubman seated
aliases: Tubman Araminta Ross Minty Moses General Tubman Combahee River Raid
themeText: Slavery and emancipation African American history Women's history War and the military Reform and protest
text: Harriet Tubman (born Araminta Ross) Dorchester County, Eastern Shore of Maryland Auburn, New York Underground Railroad conductor Union Army scout, spy, and nurse Leader in the Combahee River Raid Women’s suffrage advocate Born About 1822, Dorchester County, Maryland, named Araminta (“Minty”) Ross Escaped Fall 1849, after her enslaver died and she feared being sold Rescues About 13 trips to Maryland between 1850 and 1860, guiding some 70 people to freedom Combahee River Raid June 1–2, 1863: more than 700 people freed (most National Park Service accounts say over 750) Nickname “Moses”; John Brown called her “General Tubman” Died March 10, 1913, in Auburn, New York Tubman turned her own escape into a lifelong campaign against slavery, risking recapture again and again to free others. Her wartime raid made her the first woman in American history to plan and lead an armed military operation, and her later work for suffrage and the poor made her a symbol of courage that reaches far beyond the Underground Railroad. Harriet Tubman was born Araminta Ross around 1822 in Dorchester County, on the Eastern Shore of Maryland, one of nine children of Harriet “Rit” Green Ross and Benjamin Ross. Under slavery the children of an enslaved mother were enslaved too, whatever their father’s status; Ben Ross was free, but Rit and her children were held by a man named Edward Brodess. Brodess broke the family apart. He moved Rit and the children to his farm in Bucktown, away from their father, and sold three of Araminta’s older sisters into the Deep South. At about six she was hired out to other households to care for their children, and she was later made to trap muskrats in the Little Blackwater River, separated from her mother for long periods. She never forgot the pain of those separations. Around the age of thirteen, while she was at the Bucktown village store, she refused to help an overseer stop a man who was running away. The overseer threw a two-pound weight at the fleeing man; it struck Araminta in the head instead and nearly killed her. Her mother nursed her as well as she could, but she was soon sent back to work. For the rest of her life she suffered from severe headaches, seizures, and sudden “sleeping spells,” and she experienced vivid visions that she understood in religious terms. As a young woman Tubman managed to gain a little control over her work. She arranged with Brodess to hire herself out in return for a yearly payment, and she worked in the timber fields at Parson’s Creek alongside her father. There she came to know the marshes and waterways of the Eastern Shore, and she met Black sailors who traveled to Baltimore, Philadelphia, and Delaware and carried news along a hidden network of communication. In 1844 she married a free Black man, John Tubman, and took the name Harriet, perhaps in honor of her mother. In March 1849 Edward Brodess died. To pay his debts, his widow needed to sell some of the people he had held, and Tubman feared being sold away from her family into the even harsher slavery of the Deep South. That fall she fled with two of her brothers; an October 1849 newspaper advertisement offered a reward for “Minty” and her brothers, who turned back. Tubman tried again alone and reached Philadelphia, where she found allies among Black and white abolitionists, including William Still of the Underground Railroad. “I had reasoned this out in my mind,” she later explained; “there was one of two things I had the right to, liberty or death; if I could not have one, I would have the other.” Freedom without her family was not enough. From December 1850 through 1860 she returned to Maryland about thirteen times and led some seventy family members and friends to freedom, and she gave instructions to about seventy more who escaped on their own. The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 made her work far more dangerous, because it empowered the federal government to deputize ordinary citizens to arrest runaways; Tubman therefore often guided people all the way to St. Catharines, Ontario, in Canada. She drew on the skills she had learned in the fields, woods, and wharves, on her knowledge of the stars, and on the secret communication networks of free and enslaved Black people. In 1851 she returned for her husband, only to find that he had remarried, and in 1857 she brought her elderly parents north. William Lloyd Garrison called her “Moses,” and the name stuck. Tubman also became a public figure. In the late 1850s she spoke at antislavery and women’s rights meetings, often introduced under a false name to protect her from the Fugitive Slave Act. She could not read or write, so her speeches survive only in reporters’ brief descriptions. In April 1858 she met the abolitionist John Brown in St. Catharines; he called her “General Tubman,” and she helped him plan and recruit for his attack on Harpers Ferry, though illness kept her from joining the raid itself. In April 1860, visiting Troy, New York, she was credited in some accounts with leading the crowd that freed Charles Nalle, a fugitive from Virginia who had been arrested there. When the Civil War began, Massachusetts Governor John Andrew believed that her knowledge of the Maryland marshes would be useful in the similar coastal lowlands of South Carolina. She arrived at Port Royal in 1862, nursing sick and wounded soldiers and freed people, and soon began scouting and spying behind Confederate lines. She recruited a network of local Black boatmen and scouts, among them men who had escaped from the rice plantations along the Combahee River and knew where the Confederates had placed mines in the water. On June 1, 1863, about three hundred soldiers of the 2nd South Carolina Volunteers, Black troops later known as the 34th U.S. Colored Troops, set out from Beaufort on three gunboats with Colonel James Montgomery and Tubman. Early on June 2 they moved up the Combahee, burned plantation houses, rice mills, and other property, and destroyed seven plantations. Enslaved people in the rice fields ran and swam toward the boats; Tubman helped organize their escape and spread word to nearby plantations that freedom had come. More than 750 people were freed, according to most National Park Service accounts, and in the days that followed Tubman helped recruit more than 150 of them into the Union army. She became the first woman to plan and lead an armed raid in American military history. Tubman’s courage rested on a deep Christian faith. She trusted the visions that came to her during her spells as guidance from God, and she believed she had seen John Brown in a recurring dream before she ever met him. The pain of being separated from her family never left her, and her missions centered on freeing her own relatives and friends so that they could live in freedom together. After the war she carried the same conviction into the campaign for women’s rights. She worked alongside suffragists such as Susan B. Anthony and Elizabeth Cady Stanton and became a co-founder of the National Association of Colored Women, which demanded equality and the vote for Black women. Much of what Americans know about Tubman comes from biographies written in her lifetime, especially Sarah Hopkins Bradford’s Scenes in the Life of Harriet Tubman (1869) and Harriet, the Moses of Her People (1886). These books helped support Tubman financially, but some of their content was embellished, and historians have had to separate fact from legend. The numbers of her journeys and of the people she rescued, for example, vary from one account to another; careful research by historians such as Kate Clifford Larson puts them at about thirteen trips and sixty to seventy people. After the war Tubman also pressed the federal government for recognition of her service, arguing that her work on the Combahee River entitled her to a pension. In 1859 Tubman bought a house in Auburn, New York, from Senator William H. Seward, and it remained her home for the rest of her life. In 1869 she married Nelson Davis, a Civil War veteran, and the couple adopted a daughter, Gertie. She raised money with the African Methodist Episcopal Zion Church and opened a home for elderly and poor African Americans on her land. She died of pneumonia on March 10, 1913, and was buried with military honors in Fort Hill Cemetery in Auburn. Tubman’s memory has only grown since. A ship was named for her during World War II, her portrait has appeared on U.S. postage stamps, and a statue of her stands in Aburi, Ghana. Today she is honored by two national historical parks, in Maryland and in Auburn, and by an Underground Railroad byway through the landscape of her escape. I had reasoned this out in my mind; there was one of two things I had the right to, liberty or death; if I could not have one, I would have the other. Harriet Tubman as told to Sarah Bradford, 1886 I was the conductor of the Underground Railroad for eight years, and I can say what most conductors can’t say — I never ran my train off the track and I never lost a passenger. Harriet Tubman speaking of her rescue missions One of the best and bravest persons on the continent. title: Harry S. Truman
subtitle: Thirty-third president: ended World War II and launched the Cold War containment policy
summary: Harry S. Truman, the thirty-third president of the United States (1945–1953), was a Missouri farmer, artillery captain, and failed shopkeeper who became president when Franklin Roosevelt died in April 1945, after just eighty-two days as vice president. Within months he approved the atomic bombing of Japan; over the next seven years he shaped America’s response to the Soviet Union with the Truman Doctrine, the Marshall Plan and NATO, desegregated the armed forces, and led the country into the Korean War. He left office deeply unpopular, but historians now rank him among the best presidents.
thumbAlt: Official portrait photograph of Harry S. Truman
themeText: The presidency War and the military The Cold War Civil rights and citizenship Foreign policy and diplomacy
text: Harry S. Truman Lamar, Missouri Presiding judge, Jackson County, Missouri U.S. Senator from Missouri (elected 1934) Vice President (1945) Thirty-third president (1945–1953) Presidency April 12, 1945 – January 1953; Democrat Foreign policy Truman Doctrine (1947), Marshall Plan, Berlin Airlift, NATO (1949), Korean War Civil rights Executive Order 9981 (1948) desegregated the armed forces 1948 election Upset victory over Thomas Dewey Died December 26, 1972 Truman was born on May 8, 1884, in Lamar, Missouri, and grew up in Independence, a small town with Southern ways on the old trails to the West. Born with poor eyesight and kept by his mother from rough games, he became a passionate reader of history and a fine pianist who briefly considered a concert career. His eyesight ruled out West Point, and family money troubles ruled out college; after high school he worked in a newspaper mailroom, for a construction company, and as a bank clerk. From 1906 he spent most of a decade on the family farm near Grandview, which he did not enjoy. In 1910 he began courting Bess Wallace, a high school classmate; she turned down his proposal in 1911, but the romance continued. In World War I, Captain Truman took over an artillery battery notorious for unruliness and turned it into a top-notch unit, leading it in the Vosges and the Meuse-Argonne. He married Bess in June 1919 and opened a men’s clothing store in Kansas City with his army friend Eddie Jacobson; it closed in 1922 during the postwar slump, leaving him nearly bankrupt, and he spent years paying off his share of the debts. In 1922 Tom Pendergast, Kansas City’s Democratic boss, backed Truman for county judge, an administrative post. As presiding judge from 1926 he rebuilt Jackson County’s roads and managed its finances in the early Depression, earning a reputation for honesty inside a corrupt machine. Elected to the U.S. Senate in 1934, he was a loyal New Dealer, and from 1941 his “Truman Committee” on wasteful defense spending made him a national figure. Roosevelt chose him as his running mate in 1944. Sworn in on April 12, 1945, Truman later called his first year a “year of decisions.” He saw the war in Europe end, met Allied leaders at Potsdam, and approved dropping atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki on August 6 and 9; Japan surrendered on August 14. As relations with the Soviet Union broke down, he built the policy of containment: the Truman Doctrine of 1947 pledged aid to Greece and Turkey against communism, the Marshall Plan revived Western Europe’s economies, and the North Atlantic Treaty Organization created a military barrier. He recognized the new state of Israel in May 1948, and when North Korea invaded South Korea in June 1950 he responded by waging an undeclared war. At home he steered the economy from war to peace and defended the New Deal, raising the minimum wage and expanding Social Security. In 1948, after Southern senators threatened to filibuster his civil rights proposals, he used executive power instead: Executive Order 9981 ordered equal treatment in the armed forces, and he appointed the first African American federal judge. That November, campaigning relentlessly against the Republican Congress, he beat Thomas Dewey when almost no knowledgeable observer gave him a chance. Truman was a plain-spoken partisan Democrat who described his wartime committee as protecting the “little man” from big business and big labor alike. He believed government should build on the New Deal, and that the United States had to lead the free world against Soviet expansion. Even before Pearl Harbor he had concluded, as he wrote to a Missouri voter, that “the only theory a thug understands is a gun and a bayonet.” Truman rose through the Pendergast machine, and his 1934 Senate primary featured widespread ballot-box stuffing by supporters on both sides. His decision to use atomic bombs — which immediately killed upwards of 100,000 people, with perhaps twice that number dying later from radiation — remains intensely debated. Historians also fault him for accepting General Douglas MacArthur’s misjudgment of Chinese intentions in Korea, for responding too slowly and weakly to Senator Joseph McCarthy’s anticommunist crusade, and for a civil rights record that some call underwhelming. The Korean War and charges of corruption in his administration made him one of the most unpopular politicians in the country by the time he left office in January 1953. Truman’s reputation began to recover soon after he returned home, as Americans came to see him as a feisty everyman from Middle America rather than a Washington partisan. Scholars credit his foreign policy above all: his approach to the Soviet Union guided American policy until the end of the Cold War, and his commitments to NATO, South Korea, and Israel remain pillars of U.S. policy. His order desegregating the military met considerable resistance, but by the end of the Korean War almost all of the military was integrated. Truman made the decisions that ended World War II and set the course of American foreign policy for the next four decades. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ho5AaVHjRrY Harry S.
