title: Malcolm X
subtitle: Black nationalist leader and critic of nonviolence
summary: Malcolm X was the most visible voice of Black nationalism in the 1960s. Born Malcolm Little, he rose from a shattered childhood and a prison cell to become the national spokesman of the Nation of Islam, denouncing white racism and rejecting Martin Luther King Jr.’s nonviolence; he urged Black Americans to seek freedom “by any means necessary.” In 1964 he broke with the Nation, made the pilgrimage to Mecca, and began building bridges to the civil rights movement. He was assassinated in February 1965; his ideas shaped the Black Power movement.
thumbAlt: Photograph of Malcolm X
themeText: Civil rights and citizenship African American history Religion
text: Malcolm X (born Malcolm Little) Omaha, Nebraska Minister and national spokesman, Nation of Islam Founder, Organization of Afro-American Unity (1964) Born May 19, 1925, Omaha, Nebraska, as Malcolm Little Nation of Islam Joined in prison; minister after his 1952 release; national spokesman by the late 1950s Break Left the Nation of Islam in spring 1964; pilgrimage to Mecca Met King Once, at the U.S. Capitol, March 1964 Assassinated February 21, 1965 Malcolm Little was born on May 19, 1925, in Omaha, Nebraska. His parents were active in Marcus Garvey’s movement — his father led a chapter of the Universal Negro Improvement Association — and his father’s activism drew threats from a white supremacist group, the Black Legion. In 1929 the family’s home in Lansing, Michigan, was burned, and two years later his father’s body was found on the town’s trolley tracks; police called both accidents, but the family believed the Black Legion responsible. “Some kind of psychological deterioration hit our family circle,” Malcolm recalled. His mother was later committed to a mental institution, and the children were split among foster homes and reform schools. As a young man in Boston, Malcolm was arrested for burglary in 1946 and sentenced to ten years in prison. There he educated himself, and through his brother Reginald learned the teachings of Elijah Muhammad’s Nation of Islam, which held that white society worked to keep Black people from power. Paroled in 1952 after seven years, he took the name “X” in place of “Little,” which he considered a slave name. Brilliant and charismatic, Malcolm X became a minister and national spokesman of the Nation of Islam, founding mosques in cities such as Detroit and Harlem and using newspaper columns, radio, and television to spread its message. The organization’s membership grew from about 500 in 1952 to some 30,000 by 1963, largely credited to him. A 1959 television documentary, The Hate That Hate Produced, made him famous — so famous that his celebrity began to eclipse that of Elijah Muhammad. He married Betty Shabazz in 1958; they had four daughters. In 1963 he learned that Elijah Muhammad had secretly fathered children with several women in the Nation, and his faith in his mentor collapsed. After he said that President Kennedy “never foresaw that the chickens would come home to roost so soon,” Muhammad silenced him for ninety days, and in March 1964 Malcolm left the Nation. That year his pilgrimage to Mecca transformed him: sharing his beliefs with people of many cultures, he came home saying he had met blond, blue-eyed men he could call his brothers. He founded Muslim Mosque, Inc., and the Organization of African American Unity, reached out to activists of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, and in early 1965 visited Selma, telling Coretta Scott King that he hoped to make her husband’s work easier: “If the white people realize what the alternative is, perhaps they will be more willing to hear Dr. King.” In his Nation of Islam years Malcolm X preached Black pride, self-reliance, racial separation, and self-defense: “I don’t call it violence when it’s self-defense,” he said, “I call it intelligence.” He mocked a revolution built on loving one’s enemy — “That’s no revolution.” After Mecca he returned with a new outlook on integration and a message for all races, while still insisting that Black Americans must fight for their freedom rather than wait for it: “We want freedom now, but we’re not going to get it saying ‘We Shall Overcome.’ We’ve got to fight to overcome.” Malcolm X’s attacks on King and on integration, and his advocacy of separatism, made him one of the most polarizing figures of the era; King called his speeches a “great disservice” and rejected his overtures, and the two men met only once, briefly, in a Capitol hallway in March 1964. His remark about Kennedy’s death drew sharp criticism. The FBI infiltrated the Nation of Islam and watched him closely, and after his break with Elijah Muhammad informants warned that he had been marked for death. On February 14, 1965, his family’s home in East Elmhurst, New York, was firebombed. A week later, on February 21, three gunmen shot him at a speaking engagement at Manhattan’s Audubon Ballroom; he was thirty-nine. Three members of the Nation of Islam were convicted, but in 2021 the Manhattan district attorney moved to vacate the convictions of two of them, finding that prosecutors, the FBI, and the police had withheld key evidence. King called the murder a “great tragedy” and wrote that Malcolm had “the great ability to put his finger on the existence and root of the problem.” Many activists later embraced his message as the Black Power movement grew. Malcolm X gave voice to Black anger and pride and offered a radical alternative to King’s philosophy, and his influence grew after his death. title: Mark Twain
subtitle: Humorist and novelist who turned American speech into literature
summary: Samuel Clemens grew up in Hannibal, Missouri, on the Mississippi River, worked as a printer, riverboat pilot, and frontier journalist, and as “Mark Twain” became the best-loved American writer of his age. Books such as The Adventures of Tom Sawyer and Adventures of Huckleberry Finn drew on his Missouri boyhood, while The Gilded Age and later works attacked corruption, greed, racism, and imperialism. In his time he was considered the funniest man on earth.
thumbAlt: Mark Twain in a white suit, photographed in his later years
aliases: Samuel Clemens Sam Clemens
themeText: Arts and popular culture Slavery and emancipation Foreign policy and diplomacy
text: Samuel Clemens Florida, Missouri Riverboat pilot Journalist and travel writer Novelist and humorist Lecturer Vice president of the Anti-Imperialist League (1901–1910) Pen name “Mark Twain,” a riverboat term — first used while writing for a Nevada newspaper Hometown Hannibal, Missouri, on the Mississippi River Major books The Innocents Abroad (1869), Tom Sawyer (1876), Life on the Mississippi (1883), Huckleberry Finn (1884) Later politics Anti-imperialist; vice president of the Anti-Imperialist League, 1901–1910 Samuel Clemens was born on November 30, 1835, in Florida, Missouri, the sixth of seven children, and at four moved with his family to Hannibal, a small frontier town on the Mississippi River. Missouri was a slave state: his father owned one enslaved person and his uncle several, and Sam spent boyhood summers on his uncle’s farm, listening in the enslaved people’s quarters to the tall tales and spirituals he loved all his life. His father died in 1847, when Sam was eleven, and he left school to become a printer’s apprentice, setting type and reading the news of the world as he worked. At eighteen he went east to work on newspapers in New York and Philadelphia; by 1857 he was back on the river, working as a Mississippi riverboat pilot — until the Civil War stopped river traffic in 1861. He joined a volunteer Confederate unit, the Marion Rangers, and quit after two weeks. That July, at the invitation of his brother Orion, newly appointed secretary of the Nevada Territory, he crossed the frontier by stagecoach, hoping to strike it rich in the silver rush. He failed as a prospector and turned to writing for the Territorial Enterprise in Virginia City, where on February 3, 1863, he first signed himself “Mark Twain,” a riverboat term for “the point where safe water becomes dangerous water.” His comic story about a jumping frog, reprinted in papers across the country in 1865, was his first big break. Sent to report from the Sandwich Islands (Hawaii) in 1866, he came back and launched a career as a stage lecturer. In 1867 he sailed on a steamship tour of Europe and the Holy Land, and his irreverent travel letters became The Innocents Abroad (1869), which made him the best-selling author in the world. On that trip he met Charles Langdon, who reportedly showed him a picture of his sister Olivia; Clemens fell in love at first sight, and they married in 1870. In 1874 the family moved into an elaborate 25-room house in Hartford, Connecticut, that cost $40,000 to $45,000 — just after Twain and Charles Dudley Warner had published The Gilded Age (1873), a satire of political corruption and the national obsession with getting rich. Writing many of his books in summers at his sister-in-law’s farm in Elmira, New York, he produced The Adventures of Tom Sawyer (1876), The Prince and the Pauper (1881), Life on the Mississippi (1883), and A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur’s Court (1889). Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1884), his masterpiece, stripped the romance from slavery and, in attacking it, also railed against the failures of Reconstruction and the treatment of African Americans in Twain’s own day. His own publishing company issued it, and then the memoirs of Ulysses S. Grant, which earned large royalties for Grant’s widow. Twain used humor as a weapon against hypocrisy, greed, and racism, and he turned the way ordinary Americans actually talked into literature. He was a genius on the lecture stage, using pauses and silence to set up his jokes. Traveling the world in the 1890s, he watched European powers exploit weaker nations, and the Boer War, the Boxer Rebellion, and finally the Spanish-American and Philippine wars turned his anger on his own government. Back in the United States in 1900, he declared himself an anti-imperialist and served as vice president of the Anti-Imperialist League from 1901 until his death. “Supposing is good,” he once wrote, “but finding out is better.” Twain grew up in a slaveholding family and briefly served in a Confederate unit. Although he grew rich in Hartford, he kept pouring money into new inventions that failed, and when his publishing company collapsed in 1894 he was bankrupt; he paid back his creditors with a lecture tour around the world. His late attacks on imperialism, including a harshly sarcastic public introduction of Winston Churchill in 1900, led some to call him a traitor, and several of his darker works went unpublished in his lifetime — because magazines would not take them or because he feared for his reputation. Twain’s last years were marked by grief. His son Langdon had died as a toddler; his daughter Susy died of meningitis in 1896, his wife, Livy, in 1904, and his youngest daughter, Jean, in 1909. Twain died four months after Jean, on April 21, 1910, at his last home, Stormfield, in Redding, Connecticut. He is remembered as one of the greatest writers in American history, and his books remain a window into the nineteenth century — slavery, the frontier, the river, the Gilded Age — written by an eyewitness who, in the words of the Ken Burns documentary, could claim with some justification, “I am not an American, I am the American.” Mark Twain gave American literature its own voice — vernacular, funny, and morally serious — and his books remain central to how Americans imagine the nineteenth century, including its racism and its greed. title: Martin Luther King Jr.
subtitle: Minister and leader of the nonviolent civil rights movement
summary: Martin Luther King Jr., a Baptist minister from Atlanta, became the most prominent leader of the civil rights movement. Chosen to lead the Montgomery bus boycott soon after he arrived in the city as a young pastor, he joined the ideals of Christianity to Gandhi’s methods of nonviolent resistance. He led campaigns in Birmingham and Selma, delivered “I Have a Dream” at the March on Washington, and helped win the Civil Rights Act and the Voting Rights Act. At thirty-five he became the youngest man to receive the Nobel Peace Prize. He was assassinated in Memphis in 1968, while supporting a strike of sanitation workers.
thumbAlt: Photograph of Martin Luther King Jr.
aliases: MLK Dr. King Michael Luther King Jr. I Have a Dream Letter from Birmingham Jail
themeText: Civil rights and citizenship African American history Religion Voting rights Reform and protest
text: Martin Luther King Jr. (born Michael Luther King Jr.) Atlanta, Georgia Memphis, Tennessee Pastor, Dexter Avenue Baptist Church, Montgomery (from 1954) President, Montgomery Improvement Association (1955) President, Southern Christian Leadership Conference (from 1957) Co-pastor, Ebenezer Baptist Church, Atlanta (from 1960) Nobel Peace Prize laureate (1964) Born January 15, 1929, Atlanta, Georgia, as Michael Luther King Jr. Education Morehouse College (B.A. 1948); Crozer Theological Seminary (B.D. 1951); Boston University (Ph.D. 1955) Family Married Coretta Scott in 1953; four children Work Between 1957 and 1968 he traveled more than six million miles, spoke more than 2,500 times, and was arrested upwards of twenty times Nobel Peace Prize 1964, at age 35; he gave the prize money to the civil rights movement Assassinated April 4, 1968, at the Lorraine Motel in Memphis, Tennessee King gave the civil rights movement its moral voice and showed how nonviolent mass protest could change American law and conscience. In his last years he pressed the nation to confront poverty and war as well as segregation. King was born in Atlanta on January 15, 1929, as Michael Luther King Jr.; his name was later changed to Martin. Preaching ran in the family. His grandfather led Atlanta’s Ebenezer Baptist Church from 1914 to 1931, and his father, Martin Luther King Sr., led it after him; the younger King would become co-pastor there in 1960. His father also served on the executive committee of Atlanta’s NAACP branch, and in 1944 the teenage King chaired the youth membership committee of its youth council. He attended segregated public schools, finished high school at fifteen, and in 1948 graduated from Morehouse College, as his father and grandfather had. At Crozer Theological Seminary in Pennsylvania, he was elected president of a mostly white senior class and first studied the ideas of Mohandas Gandhi, whom he later called “the greatest Christian of the modern world.” In 1950 he heard Mordecai Johnson, the president of Howard University, describe Gandhi’s techniques of nonviolent resistance after a trip to India. He went on to Boston University, where he earned his doctorate in 1955. In Boston he met Coretta Scott, a student at the New England Conservatory of Music who had joined the NAACP in college. They married on June 18, 1953, at her family’s home near Marion, Alabama, and had four children. In 1954 he became pastor of the Dexter Avenue Baptist Church in Montgomery, Alabama. King was still new to Montgomery when Rosa Parks was arrested on December 1, 1955. On December 5, Black leaders formed the Montgomery Improvement Association and elected him president. Parks later explained that he was “so new to Montgomery” that he had not had time “to make any strong friends or enemies.” That night he told a crowd of several thousand at Holt Street Baptist Church, “If we are wrong, the Supreme Court of this nation is wrong. If we are wrong, the Constitution of the United States is wrong.” During the boycott, which lasted 382 days, his home was bombed and he was convicted of conspiring to interfere with lawful business. When a crowd gathered outside his bombed house, he calmed it: “Be calm as I and my family are.” On December 21, 1956, after the Supreme Court struck down bus segregation, Black and white passengers rode Montgomery’s buses as equals. In 1957 King became president of the new Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC), which coordinated local protest movements across the South through Black churches. In 1959 he and Coretta spent five weeks in India, where they met Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru and Gandhi’s family. Not every campaign succeeded. In Albany, Georgia, in 1961 and 1962, Police Chief Laurie Pritchett jailed hundreds of protesters while avoiding public brutality, and the press called the result “one of the most stunning defeats” of King’s career. King later admitted that he had protested “against segregation generally rather than against a single and distinct facet of it.” He applied that lesson in Birmingham in 1963. Jailed on Good Friday for defying a court order against protest, he wrote his “Letter from Birmingham Jail” in the margins of a newspaper and on scraps of paper, answering eight white clergymen who had called the campaign “unwise and untimely.” When police turned fire hoses and dogs on marching children, the images drew international outrage and forced the city’s business leaders to an agreement. On August 28, 1963, he closed the March on Washington with his “I Have a Dream” speech, telling a crowd that the King Institute counts at more than 200,000 (the Nobel Committee’s biography says 250,000) that America had “defaulted on this promissory note insofar as her citizens of color are concerned.” Time named him its Man of the Year for 1963. In October 1964 he learned that he had won the Nobel Peace Prize, the youngest man ever to receive it, and he gave the prize money of $54,123 to the civil rights movement. In Selma in 1965, he joined SNCC and local activists in the voting rights campaign that led to the Voting Rights Act, which President Lyndon B. Johnson signed in King’s presence on August 6, 1965. King himself summed up the record: “Montgomery led to the Civil Rights Act of 1957 and 1960; Birmingham inspired the Civil Rights Act of 1964; and Selma produced the voting rights legislation of 1965.” Between 1957 and 1968 King traveled more than six million miles, spoke more than 2,500 times, wrote five books, and was arrested upwards of twenty times. In 1966 he took the movement north, moving his family into a Chicago slum to campaign against housing discrimination. During a march through an all-white neighborhood, he was struck by a rock: “I have never seen anything so hostile and so hateful as I’ve seen here today,” he said. He won an open-housing agreement from Mayor Richard Daley, but by 1967 he complained that the city’s agencies had reneged on it. King took the ideals of his movement from Christianity and its methods from Gandhi. “Christ showed us the way,” he said, “and Gandhi in India showed it could work.” He called nonviolence “the only morally and practically sound method open to oppressed people in their struggle for freedom.” The purpose of direct action, he explained in the Birmingham letter, was to create a crisis that would force negotiation, and he defended breaking unjust laws by pointing to the biblical Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego and to the Boston Tea Party. He spoke of the movement’s goal as a “beloved community,” and at Selma he described it as “a society at peace with itself, a society that can live with its conscience.” In his last years King insisted that civil rights were incomplete without economic justice. In 1967 he planned a Poor People’s Campaign to bring poor Americans of all races to Washington to demand jobs, a fair minimum wage, unemployment insurance, and education. He also came to see racism, poverty, and war as connected. In a speech at New York’s Riverside Church on April 4, 1967, he condemned the Vietnam War and called for “a radical revolution of values.” King was attacked from many sides. Segregationists jailed him, bombed his home, and denounced him; Birmingham’s Eugene “Bull” Connor called his Nobel Prize “scraping the bottom of the barrel.” Younger activists in SNCC criticized his leadership style. During the Freedom Rides some asked why he offered only moral and financial support instead of riding himself, and in Albany they worried that his fame would make local people wait for a savior rather than act on their own. At Selma, his decision to turn the marchers back at the Edmund Pettus Bridge on March 9, 1965, angered many of them. As calls for “Black Power” grew after 1966, he was often criticized as too moderate and too dependent on white liberals, while he argued in turn that “effective political power for Negroes cannot come through separatism.” His stand against the Vietnam War cost him allies. The Washington Post wrote that the Riverside Church speech had “diminished his usefulness to his cause, to his country, and to his people,” and the NAACP accused him of linking two separate issues. The federal government treated him as a threat. The FBI monitored King from the Montgomery boycott onward, and Director J. Edgar Hoover, who believed he was influenced by Communists, publicly called him the “most notorious liar in the country.” Attorney General Robert Kennedy authorized wiretaps on his home and SCLC’s offices in 1963. The FBI found no evidence of Communist influence, but it anonymously mailed King a compromising recording and a letter that his staff read as urging him to kill himself. A Senate committee later concluded that the FBI had tried “to discredit the supposed target of Communist Party interest—Dr. King himself.” In the spring of 1968 King went to Memphis to support 1,300 Black sanitation workers who had struck after two of their co-workers were crushed to death by a malfunctioning truck; the strikers marched with signs reading “I Am a Man.” On April 3 he told a rally, “I may not get there with you. But I want you to know tonight that we, as a people, will get to the Promised Land.” The next evening, at 6:05 p.m. on April 4, he was shot on the balcony of the Lorraine Motel. Rioting followed in more than a hundred cities, and more than forty people died. James Earl Ray, an escaped convict, pleaded guilty and was sentenced to ninety-nine years, but soon recanted. In 1997 members of King’s family supported Ray’s request for a new trial, and the Justice Department’s review in 2000 found no evidence that warranted further investigation. The Memphis strike ended in a settlement on April 16, after Coretta Scott King led a silent march of some 42,000 people. SCLC carried on the Poor People’s Campaign, building a tent city called Resurrection City on the National Mall that spring. Coretta Scott King founded the King Center in Atlanta and led the campaign for a national holiday in his honor, first celebrated in January 1986. At his funeral, a recording was played in which King said how he wished to be remembered: “that Martin Luther King, Jr., tried to give his life serving others.” If we are wrong, the Supreme Court of this nation is wrong. If we are wrong, the Constitution of the United States is wrong. If we are wrong, God Almighty is wrong. Martin Luther King Jr. at the first mass meeting of the Montgomery bus boycott, Holt Street Baptist Church, December 5, 1955 For years now, I have heard the word ‘Wait!’ … This ‘Wait’ has almost always meant ‘Never.’ Martin Luther King Jr. Letter from Birmingham Jail, April 1963 The end we seek is a society at peace with itself, a society that can live with its conscience. Martin Luther King Jr. at the end of the Selma to Montgomery march, March 25, 1965 I’ve seen the Promised Land. I may not get there with you. But I want you to know tonight that we, as a people, will get to the Promised Land. title: Muhammad Ali
subtitle: Three-time heavyweight champion who gave up his title rather than fight in Vietnam
summary: Muhammad Ali, born Cassius Clay in segregated Louisville, won Olympic gold at eighteen and the world heavyweight title at twenty-two. That year he announced that he had joined the Nation of Islam and taken a new name. In 1967 he refused induction into the Army during the Vietnam War, citing his faith; he was stripped of his title, convicted, and barred from boxing until the Supreme Court overturned his conviction in 1971. He regained the championship twice, and after Parkinson’s disease ended his public career he became a worldwide symbol of conviction and humanitarian work.
thumbAlt: Portrait photograph of Muhammad Ali in 1967
aliases: Cassius Clay The Greatest Ali The Champ
themeText: Arts and popular culture Civil rights and citizenship African American history Religion War and the military
text: Muhammad Ali (born Cassius Marcellus Clay Jr.) Louisville, Kentucky Olympic gold medalist (Rome, 1960) Three-time world heavyweight champion Conscientious objector to the Vietnam War United Nations Messenger of Peace (2002) Olympic gold Light heavyweight, Rome, 1960, at age eighteen First title Beat Sonny Liston in Miami on February 25, 1964 Refusal Refused induction into the Army in 1967; stripped of his title and convicted Supreme Court Clay v. United States (1971) unanimously reversed his conviction Famous fights Lost to Joe Frazier (1971); beat George Foreman in Zaire, the “Rumble in the Jungle” (1974) Olympic flame Lit the cauldron at the 1996 Atlanta Games Ali joined a champion’s boxing career to the politics of the civil rights movement and opposition to the Vietnam War. By sacrificing his title for his beliefs, he showed that an athlete could take a public stand — and inspired others, including the athletes who protested at the 1968 Olympics. Cassius Marcellus Clay Jr. was born on January 17, 1942, in Louisville, Kentucky, and grew up with his parents, Odessa and Cassius Clay Sr., and his brother, Rudolph, in a house at 3302 Grand Avenue in the city’s West End. He attended mostly Black public schools. When his bicycle was stolen, a city policeman introduced him to boxing; Joe Martin became his first trainer. Boxing soon came before everything; at Central High School his studies suffered. At eighteen he made the 1960 U.S. Olympic team. He was so afraid of flying after a rough flight to the trials that he nearly refused to go to Rome; the story goes that he bought a parachute at an army surplus store and wore it for the whole flight. In Rome he called himself the King of the Olympic Village, became one of its best-liked athletes, and won the light heavyweight gold medal. Later that year he turned professional. On February 25, 1964, in Miami, the young challenger knocked out Sonny Liston in the seventh round to become heavyweight champion of the world. Just before the fight he publicly announced his conversion to the Nation of Islam, and he declared: “Cassius Clay is a slave name. I didn’t choose it, and I don’t want it. I am Muhammad Ali, a free name — it means beloved of God.” He became a close friend of Malcolm X, though he stayed with Elijah Muhammad’s Nation when Malcolm broke with it. In 1967, at the height of the Vietnam War, Ali was drafted. He claimed exemption as a conscientious objector on religious grounds, and when the claim was denied he refused to be inducted. He was stripped of his title, his passport was taken, he was convicted of refusing induction, and he could not box for years at the peak of his career. In June 1971 the Supreme Court, in Clay v. United States, unanimously reversed his conviction because the draft appeal board had given no reason for rejecting his claim. Back in the ring, Ali lost to Joe Frazier in 1971. In 1974 in Zaire he regained the championship by beating George Foreman in the “Rumble in the Jungle.” He lost the title to Leon Spinks early in 1978 and won it back that fall. His last fight, against Larry Holmes in 1980, ended in defeat in the eleventh round. Ali’s faith guided his life. The Nation of Islam promoted Black self-determination and rejected the nonviolent strategy of leaders like Martin Luther King Jr.; Ali insisted on his Muslim name and based his refusal to serve in Vietnam on his religion. Later he devoted himself to humanitarian causes and spoke of six core principles — confidence, conviction, dedication, giving, respect, and spirituality — and of sport as a force that could unite people and treat everyone fairly. Ali’s stand cost him dearly: he was convicted of a federal crime, banned from boxing in his prime, and lost his passport. His loyalty to Elijah Muhammad led him to side against his friend Malcolm X after their split. In the fall of 1984 he was diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease. As his illness advanced, Ali appeared in public less often — which made his surprise appearance at the 1996 Atlanta Olympics, where he lit the Olympic cauldron, all the more moving. In 1980 President Jimmy Carter had sent him to Africa to promote the boycott of the Moscow Olympics, and in 2002 he was named a United Nations Messenger of Peace. The Muhammad Ali Center in Louisville tells his story. When he died in June 2016, his casket was driven past his childhood home and through Louisville’s West End; he is buried in the city’s Cave Hill Cemetery, and in 2019 Louisville’s airport was renamed in his honor. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AIN2Zke74V8 Muhammad Ali Biography: The Greatest Ever? title: Neil Armstrong
subtitle: Test pilot and astronaut who became the first person to walk on the Moon, on July 20, 1969
summary: Neil Armstrong was an Ohio-born engineer and test pilot who flew the X-15 rocket plane to the edge of space, saved his crew during NASA’s first life-threatening emergency in orbit, and on July 20, 1969, as commander of Apollo 11, became the first person to set foot on the Moon. An estimated 650 million people watched him step onto the lunar surface. He left NASA in 1971 to teach engineering.
thumbAlt: Official NASA portrait of Neil Armstrong in his spacesuit, 1969
aliases: Armstrong first man on the Moon One small step Gemini 8 Apollo 11
themeText: Science and technology The Cold War
text: Neil Alden Armstrong Wapakoneta, Ohio Navy pilot in the Korean War NACA/NASA research test pilot (1955–1962) NASA astronaut (selected 1962) Commander of Apollo 11 Professor of engineering, University of Cincinnati (1971–1979) Born August 5, 1930, Wapakoneta, Ohio Korean War 78 combat missions as a Navy jet pilot X-15 Seven flights, 1960–1962; top speed 3,989 mph (Mach 5.74) Gemini VIII March 16, 1966: first docking of two spacecraft in orbit Apollo 11 First person on the Moon, July 20, 1969 Died August 25, 2012, aged 82 Armstrong’s first step on the Moon was the climax of the Space Race and fulfilled the national goal set by President John F. Kennedy. His career as a pilot and engineer, from the X-15 to the Moon, spanned the leap from the jet age to the space age. Armstrong was born on August 5, 1930, in Wapakoneta, Ohio, and was drawn to flight and engineering. He studied aeronautical engineering at Purdue University, but his studies were interrupted by service as a naval aviator from 1949 to 1952; during the Korean War he flew 78 combat missions in F9F-2 jet fighters and earned the Air Medal. He completed his Purdue degree in 1955, later adding a master’s degree in aerospace engineering from the University of Southern California. In 1955 Armstrong joined the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics (NACA), NASA’s predecessor, and became a research test pilot at its flight station at Edwards, California. He flew more than 200 types of aircraft in his career and was one of only twelve pilots to fly the X-15 rocket plane, making seven flights between 1960 and 1962, reaching 207,500 feet and a speed of 3,989 miles per hour. In 1962 NASA chose him for its second group of astronauts. On March 16, 1966, as command pilot of Gemini VIII with David Scott, he performed the first docking of two spacecraft in orbit, linking with an uncrewed Agena target. About half an hour later the joined vehicles began to tumble violently. When Armstrong undocked, the capsule spun even faster — approaching one revolution per second, fast enough for the crew to black out. He regained control by shutting down the maneuvering thrusters and using the reentry thrusters to stop the spin; a thruster had stuck firing. The mission was cut short with an emergency landing in the Pacific, but his cool handling saved both men. On July 16, 1969, Armstrong, Michael Collins, and Edwin “Buzz” Aldrin launched on Apollo 11. On July 20 Armstrong and Aldrin descended in the lunar module Eagle, which Armstrong partly flew by hand to a landing in the Sea of Tranquility. Armstrong then climbed down the ladder and stepped onto the Moon, saying, “That’s one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.” Armstrong spent about two hours and fourteen minutes walking on the surface, collecting samples with Aldrin, before the two rejoined Collins for the trip home. Armstrong’s famous words became the subject of a long debate. He said he had intended to say “one small step for a man” — the version that makes clear sense — and believed he had, but the “a” cannot be clearly heard in the recordings. After decades of audio analysis, the Smithsonian’s National Air and Space Museum quotes the words as it believes he spoke them: “That’s one small step for man.” After Apollo 11 Armstrong left the astronaut corps and served two years as a NASA aeronautics manager at headquarters before leaving the agency in 1971 to become a professor of engineering at the University of Cincinnati, a post he held until 1979. He later served on corporate boards and on a presidential commission on the future of the space program, and in 1986 he was vice chairman of the commission investigating the Challenger disaster. He received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1969 and the Congressional Space Medal of Honor in 1978. He died on August 25, 2012, at 82. In 2014 NASA renamed its flight research center at Edwards, where he had flown the X-15, the Neil A. Armstrong Flight Research Center. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rvmFeJu4maU The moon landing at 50: Neil Armstrong in his own words 60 Minutes 13:59 2026-10-23 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1pQKZc2AXW0 NASA Remembers Neil Armstrong NASA 13:06 2026-10-23

title: Richard Nixon
subtitle: Thirty-seventh president: opened relations with China, then became the only president to resign
summary: Richard Nixon rose from a small California town to the vice presidency in six years, lost the presidency to John F. Kennedy in 1960, and won it in 1968. A lifelong anticommunist, he stunned the world by visiting Communist China in 1972, signed landmark nuclear arms limitation treaties with the Soviet Union, and ended the American ground war in Vietnam; at home he created the Environmental Protection Agency. Reelected in a 49-state landslide, he was brought down by the Watergate scandal and in 1974 became the first and only president to resign.
thumbAlt: Official presidential portrait photograph of Richard Nixon, 1972
aliases: Nixon Tricky Dick RN
themeText: The presidency The Cold War Foreign policy and diplomacy Parties and elections Land and environment
text: Richard Milhous Nixon Yorba Linda, California U.S. Representative from California (1947–1950) U.S. Senator from California (1950–1953) Vice president under Eisenhower (1953–1961) Thirty-seventh president (1969–1974) Presidency January 20, 1969 – August 9, 1974; Republican Opening to China Visited Beijing in February 1972 — “Only Nixon could go to China” Arms control First president to visit Moscow; signed the SALT and Anti-Ballistic Missile treaties in 1972 1972 landslide Won 49 of 50 states, all but Massachusetts At home Signed laws creating OSHA (1970) and the Endangered Species Act (1973); proposed the EPA Resignation August 9, 1974, facing impeachment; pardoned by Gerald Ford a month later Nixon's diplomacy with China and the Soviet Union reshaped the Cold War and set the stage for its end, and his presidency marked the shift from liberal Democratic to conservative Republican dominance. Watergate made him a lasting symbol of the abuse of presidential power and deepened Americans' distrust of their leaders. Nixon was born on January 9, 1913, in Yorba Linda, California, and grew up in another small town, East Whittier. His father, Frank, was argumentative, his mother, Hannah, sweet-tempered. As a young man he lost two brothers, Arthur after a short illness and Harold after a long one. He won debates, school elections, and leading roles in plays, and earned excellent grades at Whittier College and Duke University’s law school — yet the FBI and several prestigious law firms turned him down. Back in Whittier he joined a law firm and a community theater, where he fell for a fellow cast member, Thelma “Pat” Ryan; they married in 1940. During World War II he served in the Navy. In 1946 Southern California Republicans chose him to run for Congress. He beat a five-term New Deal Democrat, Jerry Voorhis, by falsely linking him to a communist-infiltrated labor committee — the start of what the historian Garry Wills called Nixon’s “denigrative method.” On the House Un-American Activities Committee he became a national star by exposing Alger Hiss, a former State Department official who was shown to have passed information to the Soviets. In 1950 he won a Senate seat with a campaign whose “pink sheet” likened his opponent Helen Gahagan Douglas’s voting record to that of a Communist Party–line congressman, earning the lasting nickname “Tricky Dick.” In 1952 Dwight Eisenhower chose Nixon as his running mate. When a newspaper charged that a secret fund kept him in style, he defended himself on national television, promising his little daughter Tricia that he would never return one campaign gift — a cocker spaniel puppy named Checkers. The public response to the “Checkers Speech” was overwhelmingly positive. As vice president he traveled widely: a mob stoned his motorcade in Caracas, Venezuela, and in 1959 he sparred with Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev in the Soviet Union in front of a model American kitchen, the famous “kitchen debate.” After losing to Kennedy in 1960 and in the California governor’s race in 1962, he rebuilt his career by campaigning loyally for Republicans and won the presidency in 1968 by less than one percentage point, with 43 percent of the vote in a three-way race. Foreign policy was his passion. With his national security adviser, Henry Kissinger, he played the Communist rivals against each other. After China invited an American table tennis team in 1971, Kissinger held secret talks, and in February 1972 Nixon made a widely televised visit to Beijing. Later in 1972 he became the first president to visit Moscow, where he and Leonid Brezhnev signed the Strategic Arms Limitation Treaty and the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty. He withdrew American troops from Vietnam gradually under “Vietnamization,” and the Paris Peace Accords of January 1973 ended the participation of U.S. ground forces. At home, his administration imposed more new regulation than any since the New Deal: he signed the law creating the Occupational Safety and Health Administration, proposed the Environmental Protection Agency, and signed the Clean Air Act amendments of 1970, the Endangered Species Act, and the Safe Drinking Water Act. In 1971 he stunned the country with a wage-and-price freeze and closed the “gold window” that let other nations trade dollars for American gold. Nixon was by conviction a conservative and a militant anticommunist, but a supremely flexible tactician — “only as conservative as he could be and only as liberal as he had to be,” in the Miller Center’s phrase. He imposed wage and price controls he believed would not work, for election-year effect, and he took credit for the EPA while privately noting that a Democratic Congress would otherwise have forced stronger laws on him. His steady aim was to move the country to the right and to build a new conservative governing majority, and he did. He believed in concentrating foreign policy power in the White House, and his “Nixon Doctrine” called for aiding allies while expecting them to provide the soldiers for their own defense. Nixon secretly bombed Cambodia in 1969 and in 1970 sent troops into Cambodia, setting off the largest antiwar protests in American history; National Guardsmen killed four students at Kent State University, and police killed two at Jackson State. His own White House tapes later showed that he expected South Vietnam to collapse after American troops left and prolonged the war to postpone that collapse until after his 1972 reelection. During the 1968 campaign his aides had privately urged South Vietnam to stay away from peace talks. After the Pentagon Papers leaked in 1971, he created a secret White House unit, the “Plumbers,” which burglarized the office of the leaker Daniel Ellsberg’s psychiatrist; some of the same men were arrested breaking into the Democratic National Committee’s offices at the Watergate complex on June 17, 1972. Nixon’s effort to cover up these crimes, proven by his own tapes, led the House Judiciary Committee to approve articles of impeachment. Nixon resigned on August 9, 1974; his successor, Gerald Ford, declared that “our long national nightmare is over” and a month later granted him a full pardon. In retirement Nixon slowly rebuilt his reputation as a foreign policy elder: he sold his memoirs, gave a televised interview to David Frost in 1977, wrote books, and was quietly consulted by later presidents. He died on April 22, 1994, and every living president attended his funeral. Historians see his presidency as pivotal — the moment American politics turned from a liberal to a conservative era, and the time when arms control and the opening to China laid groundwork for the end of the Cold War. But his secret tapes, in the Miller Center’s words, make his presidency “an object lesson in the difference between image and reality.” https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MX_HYL6-0Co History vs. Richard Nixon - Alex Gendler TED-Ed 5:40 2026-10-23 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CIqOj0GCTvc The Rise and Fall of Richard Nixon | Full Documentary | American Experience PBS American Experience | PBS 2:48:05 2026-10-23

title: Ronald Reagan
subtitle: Fortieth president and leader of the conservative revival
summary: Ronald Reagan, a former radio announcer, film actor, and governor of California, was elected president in 1980 at a time of economic trouble and setbacks abroad. He cut income taxes, broke an air traffic controllers’ strike, and built up the military as deficits and the national debt soared. After denouncing the Soviet Union, he worked with Mikhail Gorbachev on the 1987 INF Treaty, the first Cold War agreement to reduce nuclear arsenals. Despite the Iran-Contra affair, he left office in 1989 highly popular, having reshaped American conservatism.
thumbAlt: Official portrait of Ronald Reagan
aliases: Dutch The Gipper the Great Communicator Reaganomics Reagan Revolution A Time for Choosing Reagan Doctrine
themeText: The presidency Economy and finance The Cold War Parties and elections Foreign policy and diplomacy
text: Ronald Wilson Reagan Tampico, Illinois Radio sports announcer Film actor (1937–1957) and president of the Screen Actors Guild Host of General Electric Theater Governor of California (1967–1975) Fortieth president (1981–1989) Born February 6, 1911, Tampico, Illinois; grew up in Dixon, Illinois Before politics Sports announcer; about fifty films (1937–1957); president of the Screen Actors Guild; host of General Electric Theater Governor Governor of California, elected 1966 and reelected 1970 Elections 1980: defeated Carter, 489 electoral votes to 49; 1984: defeated Mondale, 525 to 13, carrying 49 states Economic policy Large income-tax cuts (1981), Tax Reform Act (1986); top marginal rate cut from 70 to 28 percent Cold War Four summits with Gorbachev; INF Treaty signed December 1987 Died June 5, 2004, after a decade with Alzheimer’s disease Reagan made conservatism, with its calls for lower taxes, less regulation, a strong military, and firm anticommunism, the dominant force in the Republican Party and a powerful one in American politics. His partnership with Gorbachev helped bring the Cold War toward a peaceful end, while his economic record, with long growth, low inflation, and record deficits, is still debated. Ronald Wilson Reagan was born on February 6, 1911, in an apartment above a general store in Tampico, Illinois. He was the younger son of Jack Reagan, a shoe salesman, and Nelle Wilson Reagan. The family moved from town to town as Jack looked for work and settled in Dixon in 1920. Jack was warm and talkative but an alcoholic. Nelle, a devout member of the Disciples of Christ, taught her sons that alcoholism was a disease and spent much of her time visiting prisoners and hospital patients. Reagan felt he took after her. Jack, a Democrat, refused to let his sons see The Birth of a Nation because it glorified the Ku Klux Klan. During the Depression the New Deal’s Works Progress Administration employed both Jack and Ronald’s brother, Neil. “Dutch” Reagan was a lifeguard for six summers on the Rock River and, according to newspaper reports and later research, saved 77 people from drowning. At Eureka College in Illinois, from 1928 to 1932, he majored in economics with a C average but threw himself into football, drama, and student government. He washed dishes to pay his way. After graduation, with a quarter of Americans out of work, he found a job as a radio sportscaster in Davenport, Iowa, and then at WHO in Des Moines, where he became known for his re-creations of Chicago Cubs games. On a trip to the Cubs’ spring training in California in 1937, he took a screen test at Warner Brothers and won a $200-a-week contract. Over the next twenty years Reagan made about fifty films. The Miller Center gives the total as 52 in one essay and “more than 50” in another. He played the dying football star George Gipp in Knute Rockne—All American (1940), which earned him the nickname “the Gipper,” and his own favorite performance came in Kings Row (1942), whose line “Where’s the rest of me?” became the title of his 1965 autobiography. Nearsightedness kept him out of combat in World War II, and he spent most of the war narrating training films for the Army Air Corps’ First Motion Picture Unit. He married the actress Jane Wyman in 1940; they had a daughter, Maureen, adopted a son, Michael, and divorced in 1948. In 1952 he married the actress Nancy Davis, with whom he had two children, Patti and Ron. Reagan joined the Screen Actors Guild in 1937 and became its president in 1947. (The Miller Center says he served until 1954 and again from 1959; the American Yawp gives 1947 to 1952.) A liberal Democrat and admirer of Franklin Roosevelt, he fought Communist influence in Hollywood. He became a secret FBI informant in 1953 and, as SAG president, helped carry out the studios’ blacklist, though he also worked to clear actors he thought wrongly accused. From 1954 to 1962 he hosted General Electric Theater and toured GE’s 135 plants, giving talks that grew into a standard speech against high taxes and big government. Rising income and high taxes, battles with leftist union leaders, and his GE experiences moved him to the right. He campaigned for Richard Nixon in 1960 and changed his registration to Republican in 1962. A Time for Choosing. On October 27, 1964, Reagan gave a nationally televised speech for the Republican presidential candidate Barry Goldwater. He warned that government was eroding individual freedom and that the country was too weak against the Soviet Union, and told viewers, “You and I have a rendezvous with destiny.” The speech raised $1 million and made him the new hero of the conservative movement. Governor of California. In 1966 Reagan defeated Governor Pat Brown by nearly a million votes, carrying 53 of the state’s 58 counties, and he was reelected in 1970. He proved more pragmatic than expected. To close an inherited deficit he agreed to a record $1 billion tax increase, and he worked with Democrats on welfare reform and property-tax relief. He took a hard line against campus unrest and, at the request of administrators, sent the National Guard to Berkeley in 1969 and Santa Barbara in 1970. He also accepted a Redwood National Park and protected the wild rivers of the north coast. After a half-hearted bid in 1968, he came within a narrow margin of taking the 1976 Republican nomination from President Gerald Ford. The 1980 victory. Running against Carter amid high inflation, unemployment, and the Iranian hostage crisis, Reagan asked voters whether they were better off than four years earlier. He won 51 percent of the vote to Carter’s 41 percent and 489 electoral votes to 49, and Republicans won control of the Senate for the first time since 1954. The hostages in Iran were released as he took the oath on January 20, 1981. In his inaugural address he declared, “In this present crisis, government is not the solution to our problem; government is the problem.” Reaganomics. On March 30, 1981, Reagan was shot and seriously wounded by a would-be assassin. His good humor (“I hope you’re all Republicans,” he told his surgeons) brought a wave of public support. He used it to win a 25 percent cut in income-tax rates over three years, less than the 30 percent he had requested, along with modest spending cuts. His advisers predicted, on supply-side theory, that growth would make up the lost revenue. In 1981 he also fired more than 11,000 striking air traffic controllers, a blow that left organized labor reeling. A severe recession followed as the Federal Reserve under Paul Volcker raised interest rates to break inflation. Unemployment reached 11 percent, and in January 1983 Reagan’s approval fell to 35 percent. Reagan stood by Volcker, inflation fell, and a long expansion began in 1983. He agreed to tax increases in 1982 and 1984, worked with Speaker Tip O’Neill on a 1983 compromise that kept Social Security solvent for a generation, and in his second term won the bipartisan Tax Reform Act of 1986. By the time he left office the top marginal tax rate had fallen from 70 to 28 percent. Reelection. In 1984, with the economy booming and his campaign promising “Morning Again in America,” Reagan defeated Walter Mondale, who had pledged to raise taxes, carrying every state except Minnesota and winning 525 electoral votes to 13. When Mondale raised the issue of his age, Reagan, then 73, joked in their second debate that he would not exploit “my opponent’s youth and inexperience.” Ending the Cold War’s arms race. In his first term Reagan pressed a huge military buildup, called the Soviet Union an “evil empire” in March 1983, and proposed the Strategic Defense Initiative, a space-based missile defense that critics called “Star Wars.” The arrival of Mikhail Gorbachev in 1985 changed the relationship. The two leaders met in Geneva in November 1985 and at Reykjavik in October 1986, where they discussed abolishing nuclear weapons altogether before the talks broke down over SDI. In Berlin on June 12, 1987, Reagan called out, “Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!” In December 1987 the two signed the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces (INF) Treaty, which called for destroying more than 2,600 Soviet and American nuclear weapons, In June 1988 Reagan visited Moscow, met Soviet citizens in Red Square, and spoke to students at Gorbachev’s alma mater. Reagan believed that high taxes and an overgrown federal government stifled economic growth and individual freedom, and that the United States must confront communism and negotiate with the Soviet Union only from strength. He also feared that the doctrine of “mutual assured destruction” could lead to nuclear war, and he pursued the vision of a world without nuclear weapons. He was a pragmatist in practice. As governor he said he preferred partial victories to “going off the cliff with all flags flying,” and many of his main achievements were bipartisan compromises. Reagan’s economic program cut taxes but never balanced the budget. The deficit reached more than $220 billion in 1986, and the national debt roughly tripled, from $914 billion to $2.6 trillion. The Miller Center’s figures on the smallest annual deficit vary slightly, at least $153 billion for 1983–89 in one passage and $149 billion for 1985–89 in another. The gains of the 1980s were unequal. During his first term the incomes of the richest fifth of families rose by 9 percent while those of the poorest fifth fell by 8 percent. Civil rights groups criticized his record. In the summer of 1980, after the Republican convention, he spoke at the Neshoba County Fair in Mississippi, near where three civil rights workers had been murdered in 1964, and spoke in favor of “states’ rights.” The American Yawp argues that his attacks on welfare used thinly veiled racial stereotypes. His administration also backed Bob Jones University’s challenge to the policy of denying tax exemptions to segregated schools, before retreating. Abroad, Reagan supported anticommunist forces from Afghanistan to Central America, a policy called the Reagan Doctrine. His backing of the Contra rebels against Nicaragua’s Sandinista government divided Congress, which restricted aid with the Boland Amendments. In October 1983 a truck bomb killed 241 American servicemen, most of them Marines, at their barracks in Beirut, and the force was withdrawn early in 1984. That same month the United States invaded Grenada. The gravest scandal was the Iran-Contra affair, revealed in late 1986. National Security Council staff had secretly sold arms to Iran to win the release of American hostages in Lebanon and diverted some of the profits to the Contras despite the congressional ban. Reagan at first denied trading arms for hostages. In a speech on March 4, 1987, he took “full responsibility” and admitted that “the facts and the evidence tell me it is not” true. The independent counsel, Lawrence Walsh, concluded in 1993 that there was no credible evidence Reagan knew of the diversion. The Miller Center adds that the inquiries showed “lax management and enormous detachment” on his part. Reagan left office in January 1989 with the highest approval rating of any departing president since Franklin Roosevelt and handed power to his vice president, George H. W. Bush. In a letter of November 5, 1994, he told the nation he had Alzheimer’s disease: “I now begin the journey that will lead me into the sunset of my life. I know that for America there will always be a bright dawn ahead.” He withdrew from public view, and he died on June 5, 2004. After a state funeral he was buried at his presidential library in Simi Valley, California. Historians still debate why the Cold War ended as it did. Some credit Reagan’s military buildup and SDI, others the unrest in Eastern Europe, the war in Afghanistan, or the collapse of the Soviet economy. The Miller Center concludes that there is no consensus, but that Reagan’s policies clearly contributed. Reagan and Gorbachev themselves said that the whole world had won. At home, his landslides pushed the Democrats toward the center, and Republicans for decades presented themselves as his heirs. The Miller Center calls him a transformational president who “casts a long shadow.” You and I have a rendezvous with destiny. I know that for America there will always be a bright dawn ahead. title: Rosa Parks
subtitle: Activist whose arrest sparked the Montgomery bus boycott
summary: Rosa Parks was the seamstress and veteran NAACP activist whose arrest on December 1, 1955, for refusing to give up her seat to a white passenger on a Montgomery, Alabama, bus sparked the Montgomery bus boycott. The thirteen-month protest ended with bus segregation struck down and made Martin Luther King Jr. a national leader. Long remembered as a tired woman who simply wanted to sit down, Parks was in fact a seasoned organizer who had fought Jim Crow for more than a decade. “The only tired I was,” she wrote, “was tired of giving in.”
thumbAlt: Photograph of Rosa Parks
aliases: Rosa McCauley Mother of the civil rights movement
themeText: Civil rights and citizenship African American history Women's history
text: Rosa Louise McCauley Parks Tuskegee, Alabama Secretary of the Montgomery NAACP (1943–1956) Adviser to the NAACP Youth Council Dispatcher for the Montgomery Improvement Association carpool Office assistant to Rep. John Conyers (until 1988) Born February 4, 1913, Tuskegee, Alabama NAACP Joined the Montgomery branch in 1943 and served as its secretary until 1956 Arrest December 1, 1955, charged with “refusing to obey orders of bus driver” The boycott 381 or 382 days, December 1955 to December 1956, by about 17,000 Black residents Later life Moved to Detroit in 1957; worked for Rep. John Conyers until 1988 Honors Congressional Gold Medal (1999); lay in honor in the U.S. Capitol (2005) Died October 24, 2005, age 92 Parks’s refusal became the most famous single act of the civil rights movement, but its power came from years of organizing behind it. Her arrest gave Montgomery’s Black community the rallying point it had been looking for, and the boycott that followed showed that nonviolent mass protest could defeat segregation. Rosa Louise McCauley was born on February 4, 1913, in Tuskegee, Alabama, and spent her first years on a small farm with her mother, grandparents, and brother. As a child she watched the Ku Klux Klan ride at night and listened in fear to news of lynchings near her home. She grew up in Montgomery, attended an industrial school for girls and the laboratory school of Alabama State College, and later enrolled at Alabama State Teachers College, but had to withdraw when her grandmother fell ill. In 1932, at nineteen, she married Raymond Parks, a barber and NAACP member who was then active in the Scottsboro case. In 1943 Rosa Parks joined the Montgomery branch of the NAACP and was elected its secretary, a post she held until 1956; she worked closely with the branch president, E. D. Nixon. Two years later, after being turned away twice, she succeeded in registering to vote. As secretary of the Alabama State Conference of the NAACP, she traveled the state interviewing victims of discrimination and witnesses to lynchings. By 1949 she was adviser to the local NAACP Youth Council, whose members challenged Jim Crow by checking books out of the whites-only library. She had also defied the bus rules before: once a driver put her off a bus for refusing to obey them. In the summer of 1955, with the help of Virginia Durr, she attended a workshop on carrying out the Supreme Court’s school desegregation decision at the Highlander Folk School in Tennessee, where she was encouraged by a fellow participant, Septima Clark. On the evening of December 1, 1955, Parks, then forty-two, boarded a city bus on her way home from the Montgomery Fair department store, where she worked as a seamstress. Montgomery reserved the front ten seats of each bus for white passengers, and Parks sat in the first row behind them. When the bus filled, the driver, James Blake, ordered her and the three other Black passengers in her row to give up their seats. The other three moved; Parks stayed where she was. Blake believed he had the right to move the color line, though the law was unclear on that point, and he called the police. She was arrested, fingerprinted, and charged with “refusing to obey orders of bus driver.” When she called home from jail, her mother’s first question was “Did they beat you?” Parks was not the first. Nine months earlier, fifteen-year-old Claudette Colvin had been arrested for the same offense, and in October eighteen-year-old Mary Louise Smith was arrested too. Neither case moved the city’s Black leaders to act. Parks was different: as King later wrote, she was “one of the most respected people in the Negro community.” E. D. Nixon, with Clifford and Virginia Durr, bailed her out. Jo Ann Robinson and the Women’s Political Council called a one-day boycott for December 5. That day, 90 percent of Montgomery’s Black citizens stayed off the buses, and the boycott grew into a campaign that lasted more than a year. About 17,000 Black citizens took part. Parks was convicted, and her lawyer appealed. During the boycott Parks worked as a dispatcher for the carpool that replaced the buses, and she spoke in churches across the country, including in the North, to raise money for the Montgomery Improvement Association. She was indicted with King and more than eighty others under a 1921 law against conspiracies that interfered with lawful business. Her own appeal was still tied up in the state courts when a three-judge federal court ruled in another case, Browder v. Gayle, that bus segregation was unconstitutional. It did so in June 1956 (on June 4, by the National Archives’ account; on June 5, by the King Institute’s), and the Supreme Court upheld the ruling on November 13, 1956. Copies of Parks’s police report and fingerprint card were entered as evidence in that case. On December 20, 1956, the boycott ended. It had lasted 381 days by the National Archives’ count, or 382 by the Nobel Committee’s. Parks always rejected the story that she had stayed seated simply because her feet hurt. “I was not tired physically, or no more tired than I usually was at the end of a working day,” she wrote in her autobiography. “I was not old, although some people have an image of me as being old then. I was forty-two. No, the only tired I was, was tired of giving in.” Her protest grew out of a lifetime of resistance that began with her childhood memories of Klan terror. She believed in organized, persistent action: she spent years documenting violence for the NAACP, training young activists, and registering voters before the moment that made her famous. She remained modest about her place in history: “I had no idea when I refused to give up my seat on that Montgomery bus that my small action would help put an end to the segregation laws in the South.” Fame brought Parks hardship rather than reward. She lost her job at the department store and received death threats, and harassment continued after the boycott ended. In 1957 she and her husband left Montgomery, first for Hampton, Virginia, and then for Detroit. Shortly before she left, the Montgomery Improvement Association declared August 5, 1957, “Rosa Parks Day” and presented her with $800. Even later in life money was scarce. By 1980, after years of giving her time and money to the movement, the widowed Parks suffered from financial and health troubles, and when she nearly lost her home, neighbors and churches in Detroit came to her aid. Her story has also often been told in a misleading way. News accounts at the time, and many retellings since, presented her as a quiet seamstress who acted on impulse. The National Women’s History Museum argues that this image diminished her role as an established organizer who helped plan the boycott itself. In Detroit, Parks stayed active in the NAACP and in campaigns against inequality in the city. In 1964 she supported John Conyers, a Black lawyer, in his campaign for Congress. After he won, he hired her for his Detroit office, where she worked, among other tasks, helping homeless people find housing, until she retired in 1988. In 1987 she founded the Rosa and Raymond Parks Institute for Self-Development to offer job training and leadership programs for young people. In 1999 Congress awarded her its Gold Medal, and the Southern Christian Leadership Conference gives an annual Rosa Parks Freedom Award. Parks died on October 24, 2005, at the age of ninety-two. On October 30 and 31, 2005, she lay in honor in the U.S. Capitol. I was not tired physically, or no more tired than I usually was at the end of a working day. I was not old, although some people have an image of me as being old then. I was forty-two. No, the only tired I was, was tired of giving in. Rosa Parks in her autobiography Did they beat you? title: Sacagawea
subtitle: The Lemhi Shoshone teenager who traveled with Lewis and Clark’s Corps of Discovery
summary: Sacagawea was a Lemhi Shoshone woman who, at sixteen or seventeen and carrying her newborn son, traveled with the Lewis and Clark Expedition on its journey west and back. The only woman in the Corps of Discovery, she is often remembered as its guide, but the expedition’s journals show something different and arguably more important: her presence told the tribes they met that the party was not a war party, and when the explorers reached her homeland in the Rockies, she helped them find the Shoshone and the horses they needed to cross the mountains.
thumbAlt: Alice Cooper’s statue of Sacagawea at the 1905 Lewis and Clark Exposition in Portland, Oregon
aliases: Sakakawea Sacajawea
themeText: Indigenous history Women's history Territorial expansion
text: Sacagawea Lemhi County, Idaho Fort Manuel Lisa Member of the Corps of Discovery (1805–1806) Interpreter and intermediary People Lemhi Shoshone, from present-day Idaho Captured At about eleven or twelve, by a Hidatsa raiding party With the Corps Left the Mandan and Hidatsa villages in April 1805 with her two-month-old son Role The only woman in the expedition; interpreter with her husband, Toussaint Charbonneau Clark’s words “A woman with a party of men is a token of peace” Sacagawea is one of the most commemorated women in American history and a reminder that the expedition depended on Native people. Her real story — a captive teenager and young mother whose presence and knowledge helped the Corps survive — is both more modest and more remarkable than the legend of the guide who led the way west. Sacagawea was born around 1788 among the Lemhi Shoshone in the mountains of present-day Idaho. When she was about eleven or twelve, a Hidatsa raiding party captured her and carried her east to the Hidatsa villages on the Knife River in present-day North Dakota, where she lived at the Awatixa village. There she became one of the wives of Toussaint Charbonneau, a French-Canadian fur trader. Meriwether Lewis and William Clark met her at the Mandan and Hidatsa villages in 1804 and hired Charbonneau as an interpreter; Sacagawea came too, valued for her knowledge of the tribes and terrain farther west. In February 1805 she gave birth to her first child, a boy — Lewis noted that “one of the wives of Charbono was delivered of a fine boy” — and two months later she set out with the Corps, carrying him. On the journey she dug roots and found other food, and showed the men how to make leather clothing and moccasins. Her presence reassured the tribes they met; as Clark wrote, she “reconciles all the Indians, as to our friendly intentions. A woman with a party of men is a token of peace.” When the expedition reached the Rocky Mountains, everything depended on finding the Shoshone and trading for horses, without which the explorers could not haul their supplies over the mountains. Recognizing landmarks from her childhood, Sacagawea assured the captains that her people were near. When they found the Shoshone, she translated along with her husband, and the Corps secured its horses. Sacagawea left no written words of her own; what is known of her comes almost entirely from the journals of the expedition’s men, which record her actions rather than her thoughts. Popular legend made Sacagawea the guide who led Lewis and Clark across the continent, but the expedition journals offer little evidence of that; historians generally believe she joined because her husband was hired as an interpreter. Even basic facts are disputed. Her name is spelled several ways, and the Mandan, Hidatsa & Arikara Nation’s Sacagawea Project has published its own account, Our Eagle Woman, Sacagawea: They Got It Wrong, challenging the standard story. Accounts of her later life also differ. On the return journey in 1806, Sacagawea and her family left the Corps at the Mandan and Hidatsa villages. Little is known of her life afterward; most historians believe she died of a fever at Fort Manuel Lisa around 1812, when she was not yet thirty. Statues honor her, among them one in Portland, Oregon, and the National Park Service tells her story at Lewis and Clark sites from North Dakota to the Pacific.

title: Sitting Bull
subtitle: Hunkpapa Lakota leader who refused the reservation
summary: Sitting Bull (Tatanka-Iyotanka) was a Hunkpapa Lakota war chief and holy man who led the Lakota who refused to accept life on a reservation. He rejected the 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie and kept his people hunting buffalo on the open plains. In June 1876 his vision of soldiers “falling into camp” came before the Lakota and Cheyenne victory over George Armstrong Custer at the Little Bighorn. Pursued by the army, he led his followers into Canada and surrendered in 1881. He toured briefly with Buffalo Bill’s Wild West and lived at Standing Rock. In December 1890, amid fears of the Ghost Dance, he was killed by Lakota reservation police sent to arrest him.

aliases: Tatanka-Iyotanka Tatanka Iyotake non-treaty Lakota Greasy Grass Battle of the Little Bighorn
themeText: Indigenous history Religion War and the military
text: Sitting Bull (Tatanka-Iyotanka) Near the Grand and Missouri Rivers, present-day South Dakota Standing Rock Reservation Hunkpapa Lakota war leader Leader of the Strong Heart warrior society Spiritual leader Leader of the non-treaty Lakota Performer in Buffalo Bill’s Wild West (1885) Born Between 1831 and 1837, near the confluence of the Grand and Missouri Rivers, present-day South Dakota Nation Hunkpapa band of the Lakota Fort Laramie Treaty (1868) Refused to take part; became leader of the non-treaty Lakota Little Bighorn June 25–26, 1876; his village was attacked by Custer’s 7th Cavalry, which lost five companies under Custer Exile Led followers to Canada in 1877; surrendered at Fort Buford, July 20, 1881 Died December 15, 1890, killed during an arrest at his cabin on the Standing Rock Reservation Sitting Bull became the best-known symbol of Native resistance to American conquest of the Great Plains. His refusal to sign away Lakota land or way of life, and the victory at the Little Bighorn associated with his name, made him famous among white Americans as well as his own people. Sitting Bull was born into a prominent Hunkpapa Lakota family sometime between 1831 and 1837, near where the Grand River meets the Missouri in present-day South Dakota. His father and two of his uncles were chiefs. He killed his first buffalo at ten and counted his first coup, an honor earned in immediate proximity to the enemy, at fourteen. After that he took his father’s name, Tatanka-Iyotanka, Sitting Bull. The National Park Service writes that he already showed the four cardinal Lakota virtues of bravery, fortitude, generosity, and wisdom. He joined the Kit Fox society and the elite Midnight Strong Heart society of warriors, became one of its two Sash Wearers, and then its leader. Sitting Bull was also a holy man. Through the Sun Dance and vision quests he sought guidance from Wakan-Tanka, and many Lakota believed his visions came true. In the 1850s, as the Lakota argued over how to deal with the expanding United States, he spoke for those who wanted to avoid trade and diplomacy with whites altogether. “I have seen nothing that the white man has,” he said, “which is as good as our right to roam and live on the open plains as we choose.” He stayed away from white settlements and forts almost entirely until the 1880s. The non-treaty Lakota. In 1866 the Lakota leader Red Cloud waged a successful war against forts along the Bozeman Trail, and in 1868 he and other leaders signed the Treaty of Fort Laramie. The treaty created the Great Sioux Reservation in the western half of present-day South Dakota, including the Black Hills, which are sacred to the Lakota. Sitting Bull refused to take part and held that those who signed spoke only for themselves. The Lakota split between those who followed Red Cloud and Spotted Tail onto the reservation and the “non-treaty” bands who followed Sitting Bull and kept living as before. (The treaty’s list of signatures, as transcribed by the National Archives, includes a mark for a “Sitting Bull,” while the National Park Service states that Sitting Bull refused to join the negotiations.) The road to war. In 1874 an army expedition under Lieutenant Colonel George Armstrong Custer found gold in the Black Hills, and miners poured onto the reservation in violation of the treaty. The Lakota refused to sell the Black Hills. The government then ordered all Lakota onto the reservation by January 31, 1876, or be treated as “hostiles.” Sitting Bull ignored the deadline and sent word to the reservation Lakota that while they lived on scant rations, his people were feasting on buffalo. In mid-June 1876, at a Sun Dance, he gave fifty pieces of flesh from each arm and went without water for two days and nights. He then saw a vision of soldiers falling upside down into the Lakota camp, “like grasshoppers.” A voice told him, “I give these to you because they have no ears,” which the Lakota understood as a promise of victory. The Little Bighorn. On June 25, 1876, Custer’s 7th Cavalry attacked the great camp of Lakota, Cheyenne, and Arapaho along the Little Bighorn River, which the Lakota called the Greasy Grass. The National Park Service estimates the village at about 7,000 people on its Sitting Bull page and about 8,000 on its battle page, with 1,500 to 1,800 warriors. Sitting Bull, past fighting age, did not fight himself but sent his nephews White Bull and One Bull into battle with his own protective medicine. The warriors drove Major Marcus Reno’s battalion back across the river and destroyed the five companies under Custer’s direct command. The Park Service estimates about 80 Lakota and Cheyenne deaths, and the American Yawp says Custer and 268 of his men were killed. The victory made Sitting Bull internationally famous as the “architect of Custer’s defeat,” whether or not that was accurate. Sitting Bull believed the Lakota should keep their freedom to hunt and live on the open plains, and that no treaty signed by others could bind those who did not consent to it. His authority rested as much on spiritual power as on military skill. He sought visions through the Sun Dance and vision quest, and his followers saw his prophecies fulfilled. After the Little Bighorn, Americans demanded revenge, and the army under Generals George Crook and Nelson Miles pursued the non-treaty bands for a year and a half. The Black Hills were taken by the government without compensation in 1877. The National Archives notes that ownership of the Black Hills is still the subject of a legal dispute between the United States and the Sioux. In the fall of 1877 Sitting Bull led his followers into Canada, which the Lakota called the land of the White Grandmother. Buffalo were scarce there, and sickness and harsh winters wore his people down. One by one his followers drifted back to the reservations, and on July 20, 1881, he surrendered at Fort Buford in Dakota Territory. By then the buffalo herds had been destroyed: the American Yawp says the bison population fell from over ten million at midcentury to only a few hundred by the early 1880s. On the Standing Rock Reservation, Indian agents refused to recognize chiefs. Many Lakota, including Sitting Bull’s protégé Gall, took up farming. In 1885 Sitting Bull was allowed to tour with Buffalo Bill Cody’s Wild West show, where he was the star attraction and became Cody’s friend, but after one season the Standing Rock agent, James McLaughlin, refused to let him go again. The two men clashed for years. In 1890 the Ghost Dance, a religious movement begun by the prophet Wovoka, spread to the Lakota. It promised that if Native people lived justly and danced, their ancestors would return, the buffalo would come back, and whites would vanish from the West. Agents and the army feared an uprising. McLaughlin believed Sitting Bull was involved, and at six in the morning on December 15, 1890, more than forty Lakota Indian police broke into his cabin to take him in for questioning. As they led him outside, a crowd gathered and shouting turned to gunfire. Sitting Bull was killed by a shot to the chest. Two weeks later the 7th Cavalry, Custer’s old regiment, surrounded Spotted Elk’s (Big Foot’s) band at Wounded Knee Creek and, after a shot was fired, massacred them. The American Yawp estimates that between 150 and 300 Lakota men, women, and children were killed. HISTORY puts the toll at almost 150, nearly half of them women and children, and notes that some historians put it twice as high. The American Yawp calls Wounded Knee the end of sustained armed Native resistance on the Plains. Sitting Bull is remembered as a defender of Lakota land and freedom who refused to give up his people’s way of life. The Little Bighorn Battlefield National Monument now presents the battle as a clash between the buffalo-and-horse culture of the northern Plains and the industrial culture of the United States. I have seen nothing that the white man has which is as good as our right to roam and live on the open plains as we choose. Sitting Bull on relations with the United States I give these to you because they have no ears. A voice in Sitting Bull’s vision Sun Dance, June 1876, as recounted by the Lakota I did not think anyone would come and attack us so strong as we were.
