title: Sojourner Truth
subtitle: Abolitionist and women’s rights speaker who escaped slavery in New York
summary: Sojourner Truth was born into slavery in New York as Isabella Baumfree, freed herself in 1826, and became one of the most powerful speakers of the nineteenth century against slavery and for women’s rights. She was the first Black woman to win a lawsuit against a white man, for the return of her son, sold illegally into Alabama. Never formally educated, she dictated a celebrated autobiography and moved audiences with speeches such as the one at Akron in 1851 later known as “Ain’t I a Woman?” In 2009 she became the first Black woman honored with a bust in the U.S. Capitol.
thumbAlt: Photograph of Sojourner Truth
themeText: Slavery and emancipation African American history Women's history Reform and protest Religion
text: Sojourner Truth (born Isabella Bomfree) Ulster County, New York Battle Creek, Michigan Abolitionist and women’s rights lecturer Preacher Recruiter for Black Union troops Freedmen’s relief worker Born About 1797, enslaved in Ulster County, New York; she spoke only Dutch as a child Freedom Escaped with her infant daughter in 1826 Legal victory Sued to recover her son Peter, illegally sold to Alabama, and won New name Took the name Sojourner Truth in 1843 Isabella Baumfree was born about 1797 in Ulster County, New York, one of perhaps ten to twelve children of enslaved parents, James and Elizabeth; all her siblings were sold away. Her first language was the Dutch of her enslavers. At nine she was sold away from her parents, together with a flock of sheep, for $100; she was sold twice more, and from 1810 was held by John Dumont of West Park, New York. There she endured harassment from Dumont’s wife and rape by Dumont. In 1815 she fell in love with Robert, an enslaved man from a neighboring farm, whose owner beat him to death for meeting her. She had five children — James, who died young; Diana, born of the rape; and Peter, Elizabeth, and Sophia, with an older enslaved man named Thomas — and later recalled struggling to feed her own babies because she was made to nurse her enslaver’s white children. New York’s gradual emancipation law promised freedom on July 4, 1827, to those born before 1799. Dumont promised to free her before that date, then reneged. So in 1826 she walked away with her infant daughter Sophia, leaving her older children behind, and found refuge with Isaac and Maria Van Wagenen in New Paltz, who paid Dumont $20 for her labor until emancipation day. When Dumont illegally sold her five-year-old son Peter to an enslaver in Alabama, she took the case to court and, after a long fight, won his return in 1828 — becoming, the National Women’s History Museum notes, the first Black woman to sue a white man and win. A religious awakening followed. She moved to New York City and worked as a housekeeper, and in 1843, feeling called by God to “testify the hope that was in her,” took the name Sojourner Truth and set out to preach across the countryside. At the Northampton Association, a utopian abolitionist community in Massachusetts, she met William Lloyd Garrison and Frederick Douglass. In 1850 Garrison published The Narrative of Sojourner Truth, which she had dictated to Olive Gilbert; she paid for her house in part by selling photographs of herself captioned “I sell the shadow to support the substance.” She spoke at the first National Women’s Rights Convention in Worcester in 1850 and, in May 1851, at the Ohio Women’s Rights Convention in Akron. During the Civil War she recruited Black men for the Union Army — her grandson served in the 54th Massachusetts — and in 1864 she worked for the National Freedmen’s Relief Association in Washington, met President Lincoln, and rode the city’s streetcars to challenge their segregation. After the war she lobbied for federal land grants for freed people and met President Grant. A devout Christian who first learned Bible stories by ear, Truth tied her abolitionism to her faith and to a demand for equality that included women — and Black women in particular. Her speeches exposed how ideals of womanhood excluded Black women and the double burden of race and sex they bore. She also campaigned for prison reform and against capital punishment, and she supported women’s right to vote; in 1872 she went to the polls in Battle Creek and was turned away. Truth’s most famous words are also the hardest to pin down. She spoke without notes at Akron, and the first full account, published within a month, does not contain the phrase “Ain’t I a Woman?” That version appeared twelve years later, written by the suffragist Frances Dana Gage, who put a stereotyped Southern dialect into the mouth of a woman who had grown up speaking Dutch in New York. Gage’s version, reprinted for decades, is the one most people know. Earlier, while working in New York City, Truth had been falsely accused of poisoning and robbing an employer and was acquitted. Truth spent her last decades in Battle Creek, Michigan, where she died on November 26, 1883, at about eighty-six. She is remembered in murals and statues, in the name of NASA’s 1997 Mars rover Sojourner, and, since 2009, in a bust in the U.S. Capitol — the first honoring a Black woman there. Her life story, from the auction block to the lecture platform, made her a lasting symbol of the joined struggles for racial and gender equality. Sojourner Truth made the case, from her own experience, that the struggles against slavery and for women’s rights were one struggle — and that neither could succeed while ignoring Black women. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0sn8CUyvG2k The electrifying speeches of Sojourner Truth - Daina Ramey Berry TED-Ed 4:39 2026-10-23

title: Susan B. Anthony
subtitle: Organizer and public face of the woman suffrage movement
summary: Susan B. Anthony was the best-known organizer of the nineteenth-century woman suffrage movement. For more than fifty years, often in partnership with Elizabeth Cady Stanton, she traveled the country giving speeches, circulating petitions, and building organizations. Raised a Quaker, she began as a temperance and antislavery reformer. After the Civil War she opposed the Fifteenth Amendment because it enfranchised Black men but not women, and she co-founded the National Woman Suffrage Association. In 1872 she was arrested and convicted for voting. She died in 1906. The Nineteenth Amendment, ratified in 1920, was widely called the “Susan B. Anthony Amendment.”

aliases: Susan B. Anthony Amendment The Revolution National Woman Suffrage Association Failure is impossible History of Woman Suffrage
themeText: Women's history Voting rights Reform and protest Labor and work
text: Susan Brownell Anthony Adams, Massachusetts Rochester, New York Teacher Temperance and antislavery reformer; American Anti-Slavery Society agent Co-founder of the National Woman Suffrage Association (1869) Publisher of *The Revolution* President of the National American Woman Suffrage Association (1892–1900) Born February 15, 1820, Adams, Massachusetts, the second of seven children Partnership Met Elizabeth Cady Stanton in 1851; they worked together for the rest of their lives The Revolution Published from 1868; motto “Men, their rights, and nothing more; women, their rights, and nothing less” Arrest Voted in the 1872 presidential election; arrested November 18, 1872; convicted and fined $100 in June 1873 Organizations National Woman Suffrage Association (1869); president of the National American Woman Suffrage Association, 1892–1900 Died March 13, 1906, Rochester, New York; buried in Mount Hope Cemetery Anthony turned woman suffrage into a national, organized movement and kept it focused on a federal constitutional amendment. Her record also includes the racist arguments she adopted after the Civil War, which divided the movement and alienated former allies such as Frederick Douglass. Susan Brownell Anthony was born on February 15, 1820, in Adams, Massachusetts, the second of seven children of Daniel and Lucy Anthony. Her father, a Quaker, built a cotton mill, where Susan worked for a time with one of her sisters. Even as a girl she wondered why he would not make a woman an overseer. He also tried to avoid buying cotton grown by enslaved people. Shortly after she turned thirteen Anthony joined the Society of Friends, whose belief in “the equality of all people before God” guided her life. In 1837 she went to a Friends’ seminary near Philadelphia, but the next year the financial panic bankrupted her father and she had to leave school. Anthony became a teacher. In Canajoharie, New York, in 1848, according to the National Park Service and the National Women’s History Museum, she learned that male teachers earned $10 a month while women earned $2.50. (The Susan B. Anthony Museum dates the start of her Canajoharie post to 1846, at a yearly salary of $110.) In 1845 the family moved to a farm near Rochester, New York, where antislavery Quakers met almost every Sunday, sometimes joined by Frederick Douglass and William Lloyd Garrison. Anthony’s parents and a sister attended the Rochester woman’s rights convention of August 1848. She herself first joined the temperance movement. In 1852, told at a temperance convention that women should “listen and learn,” she turned toward women’s rights. Partnership with Stanton. In 1851, on a street corner in Seneca Falls, Amelia Bloomer introduced Anthony to Elizabeth Cady Stanton, the organizer of the 1848 Seneca Falls convention. Their partnership lasted the rest of their lives. Stanton, raising seven children, often stayed home and wrote speeches, and Anthony, who never married, delivered them across the country. The National Park Service credits a speech by Lucy Stone at the 1852 Syracuse convention with persuading Anthony to commit herself to women’s rights. From 1853 she campaigned for married women’s property rights in New York, collecting signatures, lobbying the legislature, and speaking alone in town after town. Antislavery. By 1856 Anthony was an agent of the American Anti-Slavery Society, arranging meetings and distributing pamphlets. In 1861 her campaign across New York under the slogan “No Union with Slaveholders. No Compromise” met hostile crowds. In Syracuse a mob burned her in effigy and dragged it through the streets, and she later called the period “The Winter of Mobs.” In 1863 she, Stanton, and Lucy Stone formed the Women’s Loyal National League to press for a constitutional amendment abolishing slavery, which came with the Thirteenth Amendment in 1865. The Revolution and the split. In 1868 Anthony and Stanton began publishing The Revolution, under the motto “Men, their rights, and nothing more; women, their rights, and nothing less.” Anthony also organized Working Women’s Associations for women in the printing and garment trades. When Congress proposed the Fifteenth Amendment, which barred denying the vote on account of race but not sex, the old coalition broke apart. Anthony and Stanton opposed the amendment, while Lucy Stone, Frances Ellen Watkins Harper, and Frederick Douglass supported it. In 1869 Anthony called the first woman suffrage convention ever held in Washington, D.C., and she and Stanton founded the National Woman Suffrage Association to work for a federal amendment. Stone and Harper formed the rival American Woman Suffrage Association. Voting in 1872. Anthony urged women to claim the vote under the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments. In November 1872 she and her sisters registered and voted in Rochester for Ulysses S. Grant and two congressmen. On November 18 a U.S. marshal arrested her at home. At her trial in June 1873 at the Ontario County Courthouse in Canandaigua, the judge directed the jury to find her guilty and fined her $100. She refused to pay, and because he did not jail her, she could not appeal to the Supreme Court. The case nonetheless made national headlines. (The sources differ on who voted with her. The National Park Service says her three sisters, while the National Women’s History Museum adds a Quaker friend and eleven other women who registered.) Leading a national movement. With Stanton and Matilda Joslyn Gage, Anthony compiled the History of Woman Suffrage, beginning in 1881. In 1890 the two rival associations merged as the National American Woman Suffrage Association. Stanton was its first president, but Anthony was effectively its leader and became president in 1892. She helped create the International Council of Women and organize the World’s Congress of Representative Women at the 1893 Chicago world’s fair. In 1900 she handed the presidency to Carrie Chapman Catt, “my ideal leader.” The same year she pledged the value of her life insurance so that the University of Rochester would admit women. Anthony’s Quaker faith taught the equality of all people before God, and she argued that the Constitution’s promise of liberty belonged to “we, the whole people … women as well as men.” She believed the vote was the key to every other right for women, and in 1854 she wrote that woman suffrage was “this great central question, which underlies all others.” The Revolution also argued for equal pay and the eight-hour day, and she called for the education of women and Black Americans. Anthony’s opposition to the Fifteenth Amendment led her into racist arguments. The National Women’s History Museum writes that although she had worked for the abolition of slavery, she “adopted the racist positions used by many other white women at that time,” and the National Park Service describes Douglass as hurt by her and Stanton’s “insulting arguments” against African Americans. The quarrel turned ugly at a public meeting of the American Equal Rights Association in New York in 1869. The History of Woman Suffrage she helped write focuses on white suffragists and leaves out suffragists of color. Ida B. Wells, who respected Anthony’s pioneering work, criticized her for not putting Black women’s concerns first in order to keep the support of white women. In 1905 Anthony met President Theodore Roosevelt to urge him to submit a suffrage amendment to Congress. At her eighty-sixth birthday celebration in February 1906 she declared that, with so many women devoting their lives to the cause, “failure is impossible.” She died at her Rochester home on March 13, 1906, of heart failure and pneumonia, and was buried in Mount Hope Cemetery. The National Archives dates the first introduction in Congress of the amendment that became the Nineteenth to 1878. The National Women’s History Museum dates the first proposed federal women’s suffrage amendment to March 1869. Congress passed it in June 1919, and it was ratified on August 18, 1920. It was widely known as the “Susan B. Anthony Amendment.” She was the first non-fictional woman depicted on U.S. currency, on the dollar coin issued from 1979 to 1981 and again in 1999. Her house in Rochester, where she was arrested, is a National Historic Landmark and museum. It was we, the people; not we, the white male citizens; nor yet we, the male citizens; but we, the whole people, who formed the Union. Susan B. Anthony speech after her arrest for voting, 1873 Men, their rights, and nothing more; women, their rights, and nothing less. Motto of The Revolution Anthony and Stanton’s newspaper, 1868 There have been others also just as true and devoted to the cause, … but with such women consecrating their lives, failure is impossible! title: Tecumseh
subtitle: Shawnee leader who built a confederacy of Native nations
summary: Tecumseh was a Shawnee leader who, with his brother Tenskwatawa, “the Prophet,” tried to unite the Native nations between the Great Lakes and the Gulf of Mexico against American expansion. He argued that Native lands belonged to all Native peoples in common and could not be sold by any single nation. His confederacy fought alongside Britain in the War of 1812, and his death at the Battle of the Thames in 1813 ended the last great effort at pan-Native resistance east of the Mississippi.
thumbAlt: Portrait of Tecumseh
themeText: Indigenous history War and the military Territorial expansion
text: Tecumseh Scioto River valley, present-day Ohio Near Moraviantown, Upper Canada (Ontario) Shawnee war leader and diplomat Organizer of a pan-Native confederacy British ally in the War of 1812 Born About 1768, in the Ohio country Brother Tenskwatawa, a religious leader known as “the Prophet” Headquarters Prophetstown, at the junction of the Wabash and Tippecanoe Rivers, Indiana Died October 5, 1813, at the Battle of the Thames Tecumseh was born about 1768 in a Kispoko Shawnee village in the Scioto River valley of present-day Ohio, the son of Pukeshinwau, of the Panther Clan, and Methoataaskee, of the Turtle Clan. His parents had family ties to the Shawnee communities living among the Creeks in present-day Alabama — connections he would later draw on. In 1774, when Tecumseh was six, his father was killed at the Battle of Kanawha near Point Pleasant in present-day West Virginia. He grew up amid constant warfare between the Shawnee and settlers pushing into the Ohio Valley; an older brother who trained him, Cheeseekau, was also killed fighting Americans. Tecumseh fought at the Battle of Fallen Timbers in August 1794, a crushing Native defeat that led to the Treaty of Greenville (1795), in which Native nations ceded much of present-day Ohio and southeastern Indiana. Tecumseh refused to sign it. In the early 1800s, Tecumseh’s brother Tenskwatawa began preaching a spiritual revival that called on Native people to reject American goods and customs and return to their own ways. The brothers founded a village, Prophetstown, in Indiana, which drew followers from many nations. Tecumseh turned the movement into a political and military alliance. When the 1809 Treaty of Fort Wayne required Indiana tribes to sell three million acres to the United States, he protested to Governor William Henry Harrison that no single nation had the right to sell land that belonged to all. He traveled widely to recruit allies; in September 1811 he and Tenskwatawa reached the Creek town of Tukabatchee, in present-day Alabama, urging the southern nations to resist assimilation and join the confederacy. In November 1811, while Tecumseh was in the South, Harrison marched on Prophetstown with about 1,000 men. In the Battle of Tippecanoe on November 7, Harrison’s forces repelled an attack and burned the village. When the War of 1812 began, Tecumseh joined the British and helped capture Detroit in August 1812. After the American victory on Lake Erie in 1813, the British retreated into Upper Canada. Tecumseh insisted on a stand, and on October 5, 1813, at the Battle of the Thames, Harrison’s army defeated the British and their Native allies. Tecumseh was killed. Tecumseh held that the land was the common inheritance of all Native peoples, that cessions by individual chiefs were illegitimate, and that only unity across tribal lines could stop American expansion. He paired this political vision with his brother’s call for spiritual renewal. Not all Native leaders followed Tecumseh; many believed accommodation with the United States offered a better chance of survival, and his movement deepened divisions within nations such as the Creek, where it helped spark civil war. Much of what is known about him comes from American and British sources, and accounts of his speeches and even of his death were often embellished after the fact. Who killed him is still disputed. Tecumseh’s death and the British withdrawal from the region ended organized resistance in the Old Northwest. His opponent, William Henry Harrison, rode the fame of Tippecanoe to the presidency in 1840. Admired even by his enemies, Tecumseh became a symbol of Native resistance and leadership in both the United States and Canada. Tecumseh offered the most ambitious Native answer to American expansion: a confederacy of nations defending their land in common. Its defeat opened the Midwest and South to rapid settlement and Indian removal. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cH-T2aY4DPY Tecumseh and the Native American Resistance Kings and Generals 58:03 2026-10-23

title: Theodore Roosevelt
subtitle: Twenty-sixth president and champion of the “Square Deal”
summary: Theodore Roosevelt became president in 1901, at forty-two, after the assassination of William McKinley. He was the youngest person ever to hold the office. Historians often call him the first modern president, because he made the White House, rather than Congress or the parties, the center of American politics. His “Square Deal” used federal power to regulate big business, protect consumers, and conserve the nation’s forests and wild lands. Abroad he built up the Navy, secured the Panama Canal, and declared the United States the “policeman” of the Western Hemisphere. In 1912 he ran again as the candidate of his own Progressive Party.
thumbAlt: Photograph of Theodore Roosevelt
aliases: TR Teddy Roosevelt Square Deal Rough Riders Bull Moose big stick Roosevelt Corollary bully pulpit
themeText: The presidency Reform and protest Land and environment Foreign policy and diplomacy War and the military
text: Theodore Roosevelt Jr. New York City Oyster Bay, New York New York assemblyman (1882–1884) U.S. Civil Service commissioner President of the New York City Police Board Assistant secretary of the Navy (1897–1898) Rough Rider in the Spanish-American War Governor of New York Vice president (1901) Twenty-sixth president (1901–1909) Progressive (“Bull Moose”) Party candidate (1912) Born October 27, 1858, New York City Presidency 1901–1909; Republican; took office after McKinley’s assassination and was elected in his own right in 1904 Domestic program The Square Deal: the Northern Securities suit, the Hepburn Act, the Meat Inspection and Pure Food and Drug Acts (1906) Conservation 150 national forests, 51 bird reserves, 5 national parks, and 18 national monuments Foreign policy “Speak softly and carry a big stick”; Panama Canal; Roosevelt Corollary to the Monroe Doctrine Nobel Peace Prize For mediating the end of the Russo-Japanese War (1905); the first U.S. president to win it Died January 6, 1919, Sagamore Hill, Oyster Bay, New York Roosevelt changed what Americans expected of a president. He argued that the president could use any power the Constitution did not specifically deny him, and he lent the prestige of the White House to the progressive causes of regulation, consumer protection, and conservation. He also led the United States toward an active, often interventionist role in the world. Theodore Roosevelt was born in New York City on October 27, 1858, the second of four children of Theodore Roosevelt Sr., a wealthy businessman and philanthropist, and Martha “Mittie” Roosevelt, who had grown up on a Georgia plantation. A sickly child with asthma, “Teedie” resolved as a teenager to “make his body” through gymnastics and weight-lifting, and he remained a lifelong champion of exercise and what he called the “strenuous life.” He was taught at home, traveled with his family in Europe and the Middle East, and entered Harvard College in 1876, where he studied natural history and took up boxing and wrestling. In October 1880 he married Alice Hathaway Lee. He enrolled at Columbia Law School but left after a year for politics, and from 1882 to 1884 he served in the New York Assembly. That same year he published his first book, The Naval War of 1812. On February 12, 1884, Alice gave birth to a daughter. Two days later Roosevelt’s mother died of typhoid fever and his wife died of kidney disease, within hours of each other and in the same house. Leaving the baby with his sister, he went to the Dakota Badlands, where he had first come to hunt in 1883. He bought two ranches, herded cattle, and served as a frontier sheriff, and what he saw there of vanishing bison and overgrazed land shaped his later interest in conservation. In 1886 he returned east, ran unsuccessfully for mayor of New York City, and married his childhood sweetheart, Edith Kermit Carow. They settled at Sagamore Hill in Oyster Bay, New York, and had five children, Theodore, Kermit, Ethel, Archibald, and Quentin, besides Alice. Roosevelt kept writing, producing biographies and the four-volume The Winning of the West. He was appointed to the U.S. Civil Service Commission by the Republican Benjamin Harrison and reappointed by the Democrat Grover Cleveland, and he clashed constantly with politicians who wanted jobs handed out as party rewards. In 1895 he became president of the New York City Police Board, where he fought corruption. In 1897 President McKinley made him assistant secretary of the navy, a post that the American Yawp connects to his support for McKinley in 1896. A believer in sea power, influenced by the naval theorist Alfred Thayer Mahan, he put the Navy on alert after the battleship Maine exploded in Havana Harbor in 1898 and told Commodore George Dewey to prepare for war with Spain. When war came, Roosevelt resigned and became commander of the 1st U.S. Volunteer Cavalry, the “Rough Riders,” a mix of Ivy League gentlemen, cowboys, sheriffs, prospectors, police officers, and Native Americans. In Cuba he led them in a charge on foot up San Juan Hill (in fact Kettle Hill) outside Santiago. “I would rather have led that charge and earned my colonelcy than served three terms in the United States Senate,” he wrote. He came home a hero and was elected governor of New York in 1898 by a few thousand votes. In office he refused to give the top patronage jobs to party regulars and backed a tax on utility companies, angering the state Republican boss Thomas Platt. Platt and the national party leader Mark Hanna decided to “kick him upstairs” to the vice presidency in 1900. Roosevelt campaigned tirelessly for McKinley, traveling more than 21,000 miles. When McKinley was shot in September 1901, “that damned cowboy,” as Hanna called him, became president. The Square Deal. Roosevelt believed government had the right to regulate big business for the public good, though he did not want to abolish it. In 1902 his Justice Department sued the Northern Securities Company, a giant railroad combination organized by J. P. Morgan and other financiers, under the Sherman Antitrust Act. In 1904 the Supreme Court ordered it broken up. When an anthracite coal strike threatened the nation’s winter heating in 1902, he called the mine owners and labor representatives to the White House. When the owners refused to negotiate, he threatened to have troops seize and run the mines, and both sides agreed to arbitration. He called the result a “square deal,” and the phrase became the name of his domestic program. The Elkins Act of 1903 banned railroad rebates, and the Hepburn Act of 1906, passed after he took his case directly to the public on a speaking tour, let the Interstate Commerce Commission regulate railroad rates. After reading Upton Sinclair’s The Jungle, he pushed for the Meat Inspection Act and the Pure Food and Drug Act of 1906. Conservation. Roosevelt was, in the Miller Center’s words, the nation’s first conservationist president. He wanted the country to move from exploiting its natural resources to managing them carefully. With Gifford Pinchot he built up the Forest Service. He signed the Newlands Reclamation Act of 1902 for western irrigation and the Antiquities Act of 1906, which let presidents declare national monuments without Congress. He created 150 national forests, 51 bird reserves, five national parks including Mesa Verde, and eighteen national monuments, among them Devil’s Tower and the Grand Canyon, which he protected as a monument when Congress resisted making it a park. The sources give different totals for the land he protected. The Miller Center’s overview says nearly 200 million acres, its domestic-affairs essay says the national forests grew from 42 million to 172 million acres, and the National Park Service says about 230 million acres of public land. The bully pulpit. Roosevelt was the first president to use the press systematically to appeal to the public over the heads of Congress and party bosses. He used the office as a “bully pulpit” to shape public opinion. He also named the investigative reporters of the day “muckrakers,” in a 1906 speech. In 1904 he won the presidency in his own right, defeating Alton Parker 336 electoral votes to 140. He was the first president who had inherited the office to win election to it. He then promised not to seek another term. A world power. Roosevelt’s maxim was “speak softly and carry a big stick.” He made the Navy one of the largest in the world and in 1907 sent sixteen battleships, the “Great White Fleet,” on a fourteen-month voyage around the globe. When Colombia balked at an American canal across Panama, then part of Colombia, the United States backed a Panamanian revolution with money and a naval blockade. The 1903 Hay-Bunau-Varilla Treaty gave it perpetual control of the canal zone. The canal opened in 1914. In 1906 Roosevelt visited the works, the first president to leave the country while in office. As the Russo-Japanese War dragged on, he brought the two sides to peace talks at Portsmouth, New Hampshire, in 1905, and he won the Nobel Peace Prize for it, the first American president to do so. He also helped settle a crisis between France and Germany over Morocco at Algeciras in 1906. Roosevelt believed that the president could use any power not specifically denied him by the Constitution or the laws. He was a reformer but not a radical. He saw big business as a natural stage of economic development and often argued that reform was needed to head off socialism. He distinguished between “good” and “bad” trusts and preferred to regulate corporations rather than break them up. His 1912 program, which he called the “New Nationalism,” cast the federal government as a “trustee” for the people, supervising the economy in the public interest. Abroad he believed that American power and values would benefit the world. He also spoke of a “manly duty” to police the Caribbean and spread what he called the benefits of Anglo-Saxon civilization. Roosevelt’s record on race was, in the Miller Center’s words, “a mixed bag.” He invited Booker T. Washington to dine at the White House in October 1901 and refused to apologize when the Southern press attacked him, but he did little to stop Southern states from taking the vote away from Black citizens, and he believed Black Americans as a race were inferior to whites. In 1906, after a shooting in Brownsville, Texas, was blamed on Black soldiers despite conflicting accounts and no physical evidence, he ordered the dishonorable discharge of three companies, 160 men, without a trial. His foreign policy also drew criticism. In December 1904 he announced what became the Roosevelt Corollary to the Monroe Doctrine. Where Monroe had warned Europe out of the Americas, Roosevelt claimed for the United States the right to intervene in Latin American countries guilty of “chronic wrongdoing.” The policy, the Miller Center notes, created much resentment in Latin America. The sources describe his first use of it in the Dominican Republic differently. The Miller Center says an American collector took over its customs houses, while the American Yawp says Roosevelt sent the Marines to occupy the country in 1905 and imposed financial supervision. Historians have also questioned his reputation as a “trust buster.” The Yawp calls it “wildly exaggerated” and notes that his successor, William Howard Taft, brought more than twice as many breakups in four years as Roosevelt did in seven. Roosevelt chose Taft as his successor in 1908 but soon fell out with him over conservation and appointments. In 1912 he won a series of Republican primaries that put him ahead in the race for delegates, but Taft’s supporters controlled the convention and renominated the president. Roosevelt and his followers formed the Progressive Party. Saying he felt “as strong as a Bull Moose,” he campaigned for a minimum wage for women, an eight-hour day, social insurance, and the direct election of senators. Near the end of the campaign he was shot and insisted on finishing his speech, the bullet slowed by the thick manuscript in his coat. He finished second with 27.4 percent of the vote, ahead of Taft but behind the Democrat Woodrow Wilson. His new party became one of the most significant third parties in American history. After the 1912 defeat Roosevelt explored the River of Doubt in the Brazilian Amazon with his son Kermit and came back weakened by malaria and infection. When World War I began, he argued loudly for military preparedness and attacked Wilson’s neutrality. After the United States entered the war, the War Department turned down his offer to raise a volunteer division. All four of his sons served, and the death of the youngest, Quentin, a pilot shot down over Germany, devastated him. Roosevelt died in his sleep at Sagamore Hill on January 6, 1919. The Miller Center sees Roosevelt’s 1912 platform as a forerunner of nearly every later liberal program, from his cousin Franklin’s New Deal to Lyndon Johnson’s Great Society. He was the first president to give his domestic program a name, a practice later presidents followed. A national park in the North Dakota Badlands, where his interest in conservation began, bears his name. I would rather have led that charge and earned my colonelcy than served three terms in the United States Senate. Theodore Roosevelt on the charge at San Juan (Kettle) Hill, 1898 Chronic wrongdoing, or an impotence which results in a general loosening of the ties of civilized society, may in America, as elsewhere, ultimately require intervention by some civilized nation. Theodore Roosevelt annual message to Congress, December 6, 1904 (the Roosevelt Corollary) Leave it as it is. You cannot improve on it. The ages have been at work on it, and man can only mar it. Theodore Roosevelt on the Grand Canyon We stand at Armageddon, and we battle for the Lord. First Annual Message (December 3, 1901) Miller Center, University of Virginia https://millercenter.org/the-presidency/presidential-speeches/december-3-1901-first-annual-message Roosevelt’s first message to Congress, setting out his views on trusts, labor, conservation, and the Navy. title: Thomas Edison
subtitle: Inventor of the phonograph and a practical electric light, and creator of the modern research laboratory
summary: Thomas Edison, a boy with only a few months of schooling who sold newspapers on a Michigan railroad, became one of the most celebrated inventors in American history. At his Menlo Park, New Jersey, laboratory, the first industrial research lab, he invented the phonograph in 1877 and developed a practical electric light and the whole system needed to power it; in 1882 his Pearl Street station began lighting lower Manhattan. Later, at West Orange, he helped create the recording and motion picture industries. To his countrymen he became a living symbol of American ingenuity.
thumbAlt: Portrait photograph of Thomas Edison, seated, around 1922
aliases: Edison Menlo Park
themeText: Science and technology Economy and finance Everyday life Arts and popular culture
text: Thomas Alva Edison Milan, Ohio West Orange, New Jersey Telegrapher Inventor Industrialist Head of the Naval Consulting Board (World War I) Phonograph 1877: the first machine that could record and play back sound Electric light A carbonized-thread filament burned for 13½ hours; Menlo Park was lit up in December 1879 Power station Pearl Street, lower Manhattan, opened in September 1882 — “the electric age had begun” Laboratories Menlo Park (1876), the first of its kind; West Orange (1887), where up to 10,000 people worked during World War I Honors A special Congressional medal in 1928 Edison did not just invent devices; he built complete systems — power plants, wiring, records, film studios — that turned inventions into industries, and his research laboratory became the model for modern corporate science. Electric light, recorded sound, and movies reshaped everyday American life. Thomas Alva Edison was born on February 11, 1847, in Milan, Ohio, the seventh and last child of Samuel and Nancy Edison; when he was seven the family moved to Port Huron, Michigan. He attended school for only a few months. His mother taught him reading, writing, and arithmetic, and he taught himself the rest from books. At thirteen he went to work selling newspapers and candy on the railroad between Port Huron and Detroit, reading scientific books in his spare time and learning to operate a telegraph. By sixteen he was a full-time telegrapher, drifting from city to city in a booming industry. In Boston in 1868 he began to turn from telegrapher to inventor. His first patent, an electric vote recorder for legislatures, was a commercial failure, and he resolved to invent only things the public would want. In New York his improved stock ticker earned him $40,000 — enough to open his first laboratory and factory in Newark, New Jersey, in 1871. There he improved the telegraph and married Mary Stilwell. In 1876 Edison moved to the village of Menlo Park, New Jersey, and built a laboratory equipped to work on any invention — the first research and development lab anywhere, sometimes called his greatest invention. His first great success there was the tinfoil phonograph of 1877, the first machine that could record and reproduce sound. It made him world famous; he demonstrated it at the White House for President Rutherford B. Hayes in 1878. So great was his fame that when a New York paper ran a fake April Fool’s interview describing an Edison machine that made food out of air, water, and dirt, readers wrote asking when it would be on sale. Next he took on electric light. The idea was not new, but no one had made it practical for the home. After a year and a half, a lamp with a filament of carbonized sewing thread burned for thirteen and a half hours, and in December 1879 Edison lit up the Menlo Park complex. He then built everything else an electric system needed, and in September 1882 his Pearl Street power station began supplying a square mile of lower Manhattan. His electric companies later merged into what became General Electric. In 1887 he opened a much larger laboratory in West Orange, New Jersey, where he could run ten or twenty projects at once. There he turned the phonograph into a home product, creating the recording industry, and developed a device to do “for the eye what the phonograph does for the ear”: motion pictures, first shown in 1891 and filmed from 1893 in a studio called the Black Maria. After ten years of work he produced an alkaline storage battery that became his most profitable product. Edison believed in self-improvement, practical results, and relentless work. After his first patent failed, he insisted on inventing only what people would buy, and he approached each problem by developing the whole system it needed. He favored military preparedness before World War I and headed the Navy’s board of civilian inventors. Edison’s greatest failure was a decade-long attempt in the 1890s to mine iron ore in New Jersey with new methods; he sold all his General Electric stock to pay for it and lost everything he put in. He never controlled the company that bore his name — bankers such as J. P. Morgan financed the electric industry, and in 1892 “Edison” was dropped from General Electric’s name. In motion pictures, many others soon improved on his early work, and by 1918 competition drove him out of the business. His achievements also depended on staffs of skilled assistants and on capital from investment bankers. In later life Edison became a cultural icon, a real-life Horatio Alger hero. Congress voted him a special medal in 1928, and in 1929, for the fiftieth anniversary of the electric light, Henry Ford gave a banquet in his honor at Greenfield Village, where Ford had restored the Menlo Park laboratory; President Herbert Hoover attended. At Ford’s and Harvey Firestone’s request, Edison spent his last years testing thousands of plants as an American source of rubber, settling on goldenrod. He died at his home, Glenmont, in West Orange on October 18, 1931. His laboratory and home are now Thomas Edison National Historical Park. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8k6zyXAXW5o Thomas Edison: His Kaleidoscope Mind Biographics 21:07 2026-10-23

title: Thomas Jefferson
subtitle: Author of the Declaration of Independence and third president
summary: Thomas Jefferson wrote the Declaration of Independence, served as the first secretary of state and the third president, doubled the size of the nation with the Louisiana Purchase, and founded the University of Virginia. He was the leading voice of a republic of independent farmers, limited government, and religious freedom. He was also a lifelong slaveholder who owned more than 600 people over his lifetime, freed only a handful, and most likely fathered six children with Sally Hemings, an enslaved woman in his household. As Encyclopedia Virginia puts it, each generation has claimed him “on both sides of almost every important question.”
thumbAlt: Portrait of Thomas Jefferson by Rembrandt Peale
aliases: Jefferson Monticello Notes on the State of Virginia Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom Jeffersonian Republicans Kentucky Resolutions
themeText: The presidency Political thought Slavery and emancipation Territorial expansion Parties and elections
text: Thomas Jefferson Shadwell, Virginia Monticello, Virginia Principal author of the Declaration of Independence Governor of Virginia (1779–1781) Minister to France (1785–1789) First U.S. secretary of state Vice president (1797–1801) Third president (1801–1809) Founder of the University of Virginia Born April 13, 1743 (April 2, Old Style), at Shadwell, Virginia Party Republican (Democratic-Republican), which he founded with James Madison in the 1790s Elections Lost to John Adams in 1796 (71–68); tied with Aaron Burr in 1800 (73 each) and won in the House on the 36th ballot; reelected easily in 1804 Louisiana Purchase 1803: 828,000 square miles for $15 million, about four cents an acre Enslaved people More than 600 over his lifetime, of whom he freed only a handful Self-chosen epitaph Author of the Declaration of Independence and of the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom, and father of the University of Virginia; he left out the presidency Death July 4, 1826, the fiftieth anniversary of the Declaration, the same day as John Adams Jefferson wrote the creed of the American nation, that “all men are created equal,” and later Americans have used it against the very inequalities he lived with. As president he cut the federal government, doubled the nation’s territory, and built the first opposition party to win power peacefully. As a slaveholder and a theorist of Black inferiority, he embodies the contradiction between liberty and slavery at the heart of the early republic. Jefferson was born on April 13, 1743 (April 2 by the Old Style calendar), at Shadwell, on the Rivanna River in what became Albemarle County, Virginia. His father, Peter Jefferson, was a surveyor and planter who helped make the famous Fry-Jefferson map of Virginia; his mother, Jane Randolph, came from one of the colony’s most powerful families. When his father died in 1757, the fourteen-year-old inherited more than 5,000 acres and about twenty enslaved people. At the College of William and Mary he studied mathematics and science with the Scottish professor William Small and law with George Wythe. He learned Latin, Greek, French, Italian, and Spanish and became perhaps the best-read lawyer in Virginia. In 1769 he began building Monticello, his house on a hilltop overlooking Shadwell. He would remodel it for four decades, and his enslaved craftsmen built much of its fine furniture. On January 1, 1772, he married Martha Wayles Skelton, a young widow. When her father, John Wayles, died in 1773, Jefferson inherited more than 11,000 acres, 135 enslaved people, including the Hemings family, and a large debt. Of their six children only two daughters, Martha and Mary, reached adulthood. Martha Jefferson died in 1782 after a difficult childbirth, on September 6 according to Encyclopedia Virginia (the Miller Center gives November 6), and Jefferson reportedly promised her never to remarry. Revolutionary. A member of the House of Burgesses from 1769, Jefferson won fame in 1774 with A Summary View of the Rights of British America, which argued that Parliament had no authority over the colonies at all. In the Second Continental Congress he was named to the committee to draft a declaration of independence. The other members deferred to him; John Adams admired his writing, and Franklin said he would never write anything for others to edit. Jefferson’s draft, revised by Congress, which struck out his attack on the king for the slave trade, was adopted on July 4, 1776. His authorship did not become widely known until the 1790s. Virginia reformer. Back in Virginia, Jefferson led a revision of the state’s laws. His bills abolished entail and primogeniture, which had kept great estates intact, and his plan for public schools failed. His Statute for Religious Freedom, carried through the legislature by James Madison, passed on January 16, 1786, and separated church and state in Virginia. Wartime governor. Elected governor in 1779, Jefferson had little power under the state constitution, and his term was a series of disasters. In January 1781, partly because Jefferson was slow to call out the militia, Benedict Arnold’s British force occupied Richmond. That June British cavalry raided Charlottesville and Jefferson barely escaped capture at Monticello. Critics accused him of cowardice, charges Encyclopedia Virginia calls “almost certainly unfounded,” but the legislature ordered an inquiry, which later thanked him. Writer and diplomat. In Notes on the State of Virginia, written after his governorship and published in 1785–1787, Jefferson praised farmers as “the chosen people of God,” defended American nature against European claims of inferiority, and denounced slavery as an evil. In the same book he wrote that Black people were “inferior to the whites in the endowments both of body and mind.” (The Miller Center calls Notes his only book; Encyclopedia Virginia calls that description inaccurate.) In Congress in 1784 he drafted a plan for governing the western territories that would admit them as equal states and ban slavery there after 1800. Congress dropped the slavery ban by one vote, but kept the principle of admitting new states as equals. From 1785 to 1789 he served as minister to France, where he became Europe’s leading interpreter of America, designed the Virginia State Capitol on a Roman temple, and urged Madison to add a bill of rights to the new Constitution. Secretary of state and party leader. As Washington’s first secretary of state (1790–1793), Jefferson clashed with Treasury Secretary Alexander Hamilton. He helped broker the compromise that traded federal assumption of state debts for a capital on the Potomac, but he came to believe that Hamilton was a secret monarchist. With Madison he organized the Republican Party, which favored states’ rights, a strict reading of the Constitution, and sympathy for revolutionary France. After finishing second to Adams in 1796 and becoming vice president, he secretly wrote the Kentucky Resolutions of 1798, which claimed a state’s right to nullify the Alien and Sedition Acts. President. In 1800 Jefferson and his running mate, Aaron Burr, tied with 73 electoral votes each, and the Federalist House elected Jefferson only on the thirty-sixth ballot, on February 17, 1801. It was a peaceful transfer of power from one party to another. In his inaugural address he declared, “We are all Republicans, we are all Federalists.” He walked to his inauguration, dressed simply, and sent his messages to Congress in writing. His administration cut the army and navy, repealed internal taxes, pardoned the last prisoners under the Sedition Act, and reduced the national debt from $80 million to $57 million, even after paying for Louisiana. He never vetoed a bill. In 1803 Napoleon offered to sell all of Louisiana. Jefferson’s envoys agreed to pay $15 million for 828,000 square miles, doubling the size of the nation. Jefferson had doubts that the Constitution allowed the purchase, but he set them aside. He sent Meriwether Lewis and William Clark to explore the new lands, and their expedition crossed to the Pacific and back between 1804 and 1806. He also sent the navy against Tripoli in the Barbary War rather than pay higher tribute. Reelected easily in 1804, he struggled in his second term as Britain and France seized American ships. After a British warship fired on the USS Chesapeake in 1807, Jefferson chose economic pressure over war: the Embargo Act of December 1807 banned American foreign trade. It failed. Exports fell from $108 million to $22 million, smuggling flourished, and Congress replaced it as Jefferson left office. Following Washington’s example, he refused a third term. Jefferson believed in a republic of independent landowning farmers, a “wise and frugal Government, which shall restrain men from injuring one another” but otherwise leave them free. He favored strict limits on federal power, freedom of religion, public education, and the spread of property. A deist, he believed in a creator who governed the world through natural laws, and he opposed any official religion. On slavery he wrote eloquently against the institution while holding hundreds of people in bondage. He believed that Black and white Americans could not live together as equals in freedom and that emancipation had to be combined with deportation. In 1820 he called the Missouri crisis “a fire bell in the night” and wrote of slavery, “we have the wolf by the ear, and we can neither hold him, nor safely let him go.” Jefferson’s slaveholding is the central controversy of his reputation. Over his lifetime he owned more than 600 people, mostly through inheritance and natural increase. He sold people to raise money, sold others out of state as punishment, sanctioned whippings, and pursued those who escaped. Beginning in Paris, by the Miller Center’s account, or in the late 1780s or early 1790s, by Encyclopedia Virginia’s, he had a long sexual relationship with Sally Hemings, the enslaved half-sister of his late wife, who had come to Paris at fourteen as a companion to his daughter. In 2000 the Thomas Jefferson Foundation concluded, based on documents, the oral histories of Monticello’s Black families, and DNA studies, that Jefferson “most likely was the father of all six of Sally Hemings’s children.” He freed or allowed to leave all four who survived. Federalists exposed the relationship as a national scandal during his presidency; Jefferson kept a public silence. His presidency had its critics too. Federalists called the Louisiana Purchase unconstitutional. He led attempts to remove Federalist judges by impeachment, succeeding against John Pickering but failing against Samuel Chase. He pressed treason charges against Aaron Burr, who was acquitted in 1807, and his embargo devastated the economy. His Kentucky Resolutions were later invoked in the nullification crisis of the 1830s and by opponents of civil rights enforcement in the 1960s. In retirement at Monticello, Jefferson sold his library of roughly 6,700 volumes to Congress for $23,950 in 1815 to replace the books burned by the British. It became the core of the modern Library of Congress. His last great project was the University of Virginia, chartered in 1819 and opened in 1825. He designed its buildings, chose its faculty and books, and left out a chapel. In 1812 he and John Adams reconciled and began one of the great correspondences in American letters. Jefferson lived beyond his means all his life, and debts left his estate insolvent. At his death he owed $107,273.63, and in 1827 more than 100 enslaved people were sold at auction to pay his creditors. He died at Monticello on July 4, 1826, fifty years to the day after the Declaration was adopted, a few hours before John Adams. He chose his own epitaph, naming only the Declaration, the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom, and the University of Virginia. “If Jefferson was wrong, America is wrong,” the biographer James Parton wrote in 1874. “If America is right, Jefferson was right.” We are all Republicans, we are all Federalists. Thomas Jefferson first inaugural address, March 4, 1801 Those who labour in the earth are the chosen people of God, if ever he had a chosen people, whose breasts he has made his peculiar deposit for substantial and genuine virtue. Thomas Jefferson Notes on the State of Virginia We have the wolf by the ear, and we can neither hold him, nor safely let him go. Justice is in one scale, and self-preservation in the other. title: Thurgood Marshall
subtitle: Civil rights lawyer and first Black justice of the Supreme Court
summary: Thurgood Marshall was the lawyer who led the legal campaign against segregation and, in 1967, became the first African American justice of the Supreme Court. As chief counsel of the NAACP and director of its Legal Defense and Educational Fund, he won nearly thirty Supreme Court cases, above all Brown v. Board of Education (1954), which struck down school segregation. He then served as a federal appeals judge and as solicitor general before joining the Court, where until 1991 he was a forceful liberal voice for individual and civil rights.
thumbAlt: Photograph of Justice Thurgood Marshall
themeText: Civil rights and citizenship African American history Constitution and law
text: Thurgood Marshall Baltimore, Maryland Chief counsel, NAACP (from 1938) Director, NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund (from 1940) Judge, U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit (1961) Solicitor General (1965–1967) Associate Justice of the Supreme Court (1967–1991) Born July 2, 1908, Baltimore Education Lincoln University (B.A. 1930); Howard University Law School (J.D. 1933) Major cases argued Smith v. Allwright (1944), Morgan v. Virginia (1946), Sweatt v. Painter (1950), Brown v. Board of Education (1954) Supreme Court 1967–1991; first African American justice Died January 24, 1993 Marshall was born on July 2, 1908, in Baltimore, the son of a kindergarten teacher and a railroad dining-car waiter. On his days off, his father took the boys to watch trials and then made them argue legal questions at home, challenging every point. Baltimore was segregated — Marshall attended an all-Black grade school and once could not find a restroom he was allowed to use — and as punishment for misbehaving in high school he was sent to read the Constitution, which he came to know backwards and forwards. At Lincoln University in Pennsylvania, a classmate of Langston Hughes, he was suspended for hazing, then found his calling in the debate club and helped desegregate a local movie theater. Rejected by the University of Maryland’s law school because of his race, he went to Howard University; his mother sold her wedding ring to help pay the tuition. There the assistant dean, Charles Hamilton Houston, was training a generation of civil rights lawyers to use the law itself against discrimination. Marshall graduated first in his class in 1933, turned down a scholarship to Harvard, and opened a practice in Baltimore, turning away no one who could not pay. One of Marshall’s first victories forced the University of Maryland’s law school — the school that had rejected him — to admit a Black student. He joined the NAACP’s national staff, succeeded Houston as its chief counsel in 1938, and from 1940 directed the new NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund. He traveled through the South investigating lynchings and the denial of voting rights and fair trials, often at personal risk. In the Supreme Court he won Smith v. Allwright (1944), which opened Texas primaries to Black voters; Morgan v. Virginia (1946), which banned segregation on interstate buses; and Sweatt v. Painter (1950), which required the University of Texas Law School to admit a Black applicant. Then he attacked segregation itself. In 1949 he met Black parents in Clarendon County, South Carolina, whose case, Briggs v. Elliott, became part of Brown. Using social science evidence that segregation harmed Black children, he argued in 1952 and 1953 that separate could never be equal; on May 17, 1954, the Court agreed unanimously. “Equal,” he once said, “means getting the same thing, at the same time and in the same place.” In 1957 his team won the injunction that opened Little Rock’s Central High School to nine Black students. President Kennedy appointed him to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit in 1961; none of his opinions there was reversed by the Supreme Court. In 1965 Lyndon Johnson made him solicitor general, the government’s chief lawyer before the Court, and in 1967 nominated him to the Supreme Court itself. Marshall saw the Constitution as a living document and the courts as the surest road to equality. He respected Martin Luther King Jr. as “a great speaker” and conceded that the protests “reached people’s consciousness,” but he distrusted civil disobedience: “If you want to write a book,” he recalled telling King, who often cited Thoreau, “you go to jail and write it.” On the Court he championed individual rights and civil rights and sought to limit criminal punishment; with Justice William Brennan he argued that the death penalty was unconstitutional in all circumstances. Marshall’s preference for lawsuits over street protest put him at odds with King and younger activists over tactics. As the Court shifted toward conservatism, he found himself increasingly in dissent and frustrated as his influence waned — dissenting, for example, when the Court reversed course on the death penalty in Gregg v. Georgia. Marshall retired in 1991 and was succeeded by Clarence Thomas. He died of heart failure in Bethesda, Maryland, on January 24, 1993. The strategy he and Houston built — case by case, until segregation itself could be challenged — laid the constitutional foundation on which the civil rights movement stood. His career ran from a segregated Baltimore schoolroom to the Supreme Court bench. Thurgood Marshall led the legal assault that dismantled segregation and became a pioneering figure on the nation’s highest court. title: Ulysses S. Grant
subtitle: Union general who won the Civil War and eighteenth president
summary: Ulysses S. Grant was the Union general who won the Civil War and the eighteenth president of the United States (1869–1877). A quiet tanner’s son who failed at farming and business before the war, he rose in four years to command all Union armies, took Vicksburg, wore down Robert E. Lee’s army, and accepted its surrender at Appomattox. As president he fought for the Fifteenth Amendment and sent troops against the Ku Klux Klan, but scandals among his appointees long dominated his reputation, which historians are now reassessing.
thumbAlt: Photograph of Ulysses S. Grant
themeText: War and the military The presidency Civil rights and citizenship
text: Hiram Ulysses Grant Point Pleasant, Ohio Mexican-American War officer Commanding general of the Union armies Eighteenth president (1869–1877) Author of *Personal Memoirs* Education U.S. Military Academy at West Point Civil War victories Forts Henry and Donelson, Vicksburg, Chattanooga, and the final campaign against Lee Presidency 1869–1877 Memoirs Written while dying of throat cancer, completed just before his death in 1885 Hiram Ulysses Grant was born on April 27, 1822, in Point Pleasant, Ohio, the eldest of six children of a tanner. He hated the stinking tannery and swore he would never work in one as an adult. Quiet and small, he was mocked by other children as “Useless,” but he was famous locally for handling unruly horses. His father secured him an appointment to West Point, where a clerical error made him “Ulysses S. Grant” for life. He graduated twenty-first in a class of thirty-nine; though the finest horseman at the academy, he was assigned to the infantry. In the Mexican-American War he served as his regiment’s quartermaster, learning the logistics of war, and was twice cited for bravery — yet he mourned the waste of war. After the war he married Julia Dent, his West Point roommate’s sister; three of his wedding attendants, including James Longstreet, would later fight against him. Posted to the Pacific Coast far from his family, he grew depressed — by some accounts drinking heavily — and resigned from the army in 1854. Over the next several years he failed at farming a plot he called “Hardscrabble” and at a string of other jobs; one Christmas he pawned his watch for $22 to buy his family presents. He freed the one man he was given as a slave rather than sell him. By 1860 he was clerking in his family’s leather shop in Galena, Illinois. When the Civil War began, the Union needed trained officers. Grant turned an unruly Illinois regiment into a disciplined unit and was soon a brigadier general. In February 1862 he captured Forts Henry and Donelson in Tennessee. Donelson, where he took the surrender of an entire Confederate force, was the Union’s first real victory and made him famous overnight as “Unconditional Surrender” Grant. He survived blame for the costly surprise at Shiloh, then in 1863 marched his army down the west bank of the Mississippi, crossed below Vicksburg, cut loose from his supply lines, and won five battles before besieging the city. On July 4, 1863, Vicksburg surrendered with more than 27,000 men, giving the Union control of the Mississippi. “Grant is my man,” Lincoln declared, “and I am his.” In 1864 Lincoln made him lieutenant general and commander of all Union armies. Grant coordinated simultaneous campaigns — Sherman’s march through Georgia, Sheridan’s in the Shenandoah — while he himself fought Lee across Virginia at the Wilderness, Spotsylvania, and Cold Harbor and then besieged Petersburg. On April 9, 1865, at Appomattox Court House, he accepted Lee’s surrender on generous terms: the Confederates could go home if they laid down their arms. Elected president in 1868 under the slogan “Let us have peace,” Grant lobbied hard for the Fifteenth Amendment, guaranteeing the vote regardless of race, and sent the army to protect Black Southerners from the Ku Klux Klan. He presided over the completion of the first transcontinental railroad in 1869, attempted reforms in Native American policy and the civil service, and improved relations with Britain. He was re-elected in a landslide in 1872. Grant disliked politics but shared the Republican creed that had won the war: the Union was perpetual, slavery was dead, and the freedpeople were entitled to the rights of citizens. He sought reconciliation with the white South without abandoning Black Americans. His sense of war was unromantic; he mourned the dead, and from his first fight he took the lesson that the enemy “had as much reason to fear my forces as I had his.” Grant’s relentless fighting in 1864 produced such enormous casualties that Democratic newspapers called him “the Butcher.” As president he chose his cabinet without consulting party leaders and was loyal out of all proportion to friends and associates; some appointees proved incompetent or corrupt. He was never personally implicated in the scandals, but he failed to cut loose those who were, and his reputation suffered. During his second term a depression that spread from Europe brought high unemployment, and many Americans blamed him for the country’s economic troubles. After leaving office Grant lost his fortune in a financial swindle and learned he was dying of throat cancer. To provide for his family, he wrote his Personal Memoirs, working on his porch wrapped in blankets and in terrible pain, and finished them days before his death in 1885. The book was a great success and secured his family’s finances. Long ranked near the bottom of presidential lists because of the scandals, Grant has risen sharply in recent rankings as historians give weight to his defense of African American rights. Grant won the war that ended slavery and, as president, tried — more than most Northern leaders of his time — to secure the rights of the people it had freed. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dkEv515UQ4A Ulysses S. title: Walt Disney
subtitle: Creator of Mickey Mouse, the animated feature film, and Disneyland
summary: Walt Disney grew up on a Missouri farm and in Kansas City, went bankrupt with his first cartoon studio, and moved to Hollywood with almost nothing. With his brother Roy and the animator Ub Iwerks he created Mickey Mouse, who became a star in Steamboat Willie (1928), a cartoon with synchronized music that became the most successful sound cartoon of its day. His studio made Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937), the first full-length animated feature, and later used television to build a new kind of entertainment empire, crowned by Disneyland in 1955. He won more Academy Awards than anyone in history.
thumbAlt: Walt Disney on the Place de la Concorde in Paris in 1935
aliases: Disney Walter Elias Disney Uncle Walt
themeText: Arts and popular culture Science and technology Everyday life Economy and finance
text: Walter Elias Disney Chicago, Illinois Animator and cartoon producer Co-founder of the Walt Disney Studio Film and television producer Creator of Disneyland (1955) Mickey Mouse Debuted in Steamboat Willie (1928); Disney himself was Mickey’s voice First animated feature Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937) Disneyland Opened in 1955 with financial backing from ABC; Main Street, U.S.A. was modeled on Marceline, Missouri Record Holds the record for most Academy Awards won Honors Presidential Medal of Freedom from Lyndon Johnson Disney turned animated cartoons into feature-length art and an industry, and pioneered the merging of film, television, merchandise, and theme parks that defines modern entertainment. His sentimental vision of small-town America shaped how generations of Americans imagined childhood and their own past. Walter Elias Disney was born on December 5, 1901, in Chicago, the son of Elias and Flora Disney; his brother Roy would later run the business side of his company. In 1906 the family moved to a farm near Marceline, Missouri, where Walt began to draw animals. “More things of importance happened to me in Marceline than have happened since,” he wrote in 1938. When the farm failed in 1911, the family moved to Kansas City, and nine-year-old Walt got up at 3:30 every morning, seven days a week, to deliver newspapers before school; on Saturdays he took classes at the Kansas City Art Institute. In 1918, after lying about his age with his mother’s help, he joined the Red Cross Ambulance Corps and spent nine months in France driving ambulances and supply trucks. Back in Kansas City he met the artist Ub Iwerks and learned animation making one-minute advertisements to run before films. In 1922 he started his own studio, Laugh-O-Gram Films, and made Alice’s Wonderland, about a real girl entering a cartoon world. He had good ideas but was not a good businessman: his unpaid staff left, and in July 1923 he declared bankruptcy and left for Hollywood. With $500 borrowed from an uncle, Walt and Roy started the Disney Brothers Studio and sold a series of Alice Comedies. In 1927 they had a hit with Oswald the Lucky Rabbit — until their New York distributor hired away most of the animators and claimed that Universal owned the character. Determined to own his creations from then on, Disney worked with Roy and his one loyal animator, Iwerks, on a new character. Iwerks drew Mickey Mouse, Disney gave him his voice, and Steamboat Willie, with synchronized music, made him famous in 1928. Through the Depression the studio kept experimenting. Disney bought exclusive rights to the new three-color Technicolor process, won his first Academy Award in 1932 for Flowers and Trees, and in 1937 released Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs, the first full-length animated feature. Pinocchio, Fantasia, Dumbo, and Bambi followed in the early 1940s, and during World War II the studio turned to training and patriotic films. In the 1950s Disney moved into live-action movies and television; his Disneyland show’s Davy Crockett episodes set boys everywhere wearing coonskin caps, and The Mickey Mouse Club began on ABC in 1955. That same year, with ABC’s financial backing, he opened Disneyland, a park where visitors could step into his films instead of just watching them. Its Main Street, U.S.A. was modeled on the downtown of Marceline. Disney built his empire on what he considered good, old-fashioned fun and a sentimental picture of small-town America. He had a profound sense of what the public wanted and tapped the moods of each era — the hardships of the Depression, the patriotism of the 1940s, the anticommunism of the 1950s. He insisted on owning everything he created, and he believed great work took a team: “You can dream, create, design, and build the most wonderful place in the world,” he said, “but it requires people to make that dream a reality.” In 1941 his animators went on strike for fair wages and job security; the strike ended that fall, but Disney felt personally betrayed. In 1947 he testified before the House Un-American Activities Committee in its investigation of communist influence in Hollywood, hearings that led to a blacklist barring hundreds of film artists from work. In the 1960s Disney’s “Imagineers” developed new technology such as audio-animatronics, and he began buying land for a second park in central Florida, which opened as Walt Disney World in 1971 — after his death. He helped found the California Institute of the Arts, received the Presidential Medal of Freedom from Lyndon Johnson, and died of lung cancer on December 15, 1966. His studio’s hits of the 1960s included One Hundred and One Dalmatians, Mary Poppins, and The Jungle Book. He still holds the record for most Academy Awards won. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bAtMP73ok78 Walt Disney: Entrepreneur & Producer | Mini Bio | BIO Biography 4:27 2026-10-23

title: W. E. B. Du Bois
subtitle: Scholar, editor, and co-founder of the NAACP
summary: W. E. B. Du Bois was the foremost Black intellectual of the early twentieth century and one of its most uncompromising voices for civil rights. The first African American to earn a PhD at Harvard, he pioneered the sociological study of Black life and wrote The Souls of Black Folk (1903), which challenged Booker T. Washington’s accommodation to segregation. He founded the Niagara Movement in 1905, helped found the NAACP in 1909, and for nearly a quarter century edited its magazine, The Crisis. He was also a leader of the Pan-African movement. He died in Ghana on the eve of the 1963 March on Washington.
thumbAlt: Photograph of W. E. B. Du Bois
aliases: The Souls of Black Folk double consciousness the color line Talented Tenth Niagara Movement The Crisis
themeText: Civil rights and citizenship African American history Political thought
text: William Edward Burghardt Du Bois Great Barrington, Massachusetts Accra, Ghana Sociologist and historian Professor at Wilberforce and Atlanta University Co-founder of the Niagara Movement (1905) and the NAACP (1909) Editor of *The Crisis* (1910–1934) Pan-Africanist Born February 23, 1868, Great Barrington, Massachusetts (one source gives 1869) Education Fisk University; Harvard, where in 1895 he became the first Black American to earn a PhD; graduate study in Germany Major books The Philadelphia Negro (1899), The Souls of Black Folk (1903), Darkwater (1920), Black Reconstruction in America (1935) Organizations Niagara Movement (1905); NAACP (1909), its only Black officer at first The Crisis Founding editor, November 1910 to July 1934 Died August 27, 1963, Accra, Ghana Du Bois insisted that Black Americans demand full civil and political equality without compromise, and he used scholarship, journalism, and organizing to press that demand. His idea of “double consciousness” and his warning that “the problem of the Twentieth Century is the problem of the color-line” remain among the most quoted ideas in American thought. William Edward Burghardt Du Bois was born in Great Barrington, Massachusetts, in 1868, three years after the end of the Civil War. The American Yawp and the Library of Congress give 1868. The Academy of American Poets heads its biography “1868–1963” but gives his birth date in the text as February 23, 1869. He was raised mainly by his mother. His early years were spent in a small farmhouse near the Housatonic River on land his mother’s family had held for more than 150 years. He graduated at the top of his high school class, and as a teenager he reported on the town’s politics as a correspondent for a Philadelphia newspaper. Du Bois went south to Fisk University in Nashville. His years in the South in the 1880s shaped his life’s work, the study of what was then called the “Negro problem,” the system of racial and economic discrimination that he predicted would be the problem of the twentieth century. He then studied at Harvard, did graduate work in Germany, and in 1895 became the first Black American to earn a PhD at Harvard. He taught at Wilberforce University in Ohio and at Atlanta University in Georgia, and his early studies of the Atlantic slave trade and of Black life in Philadelphia, published as The Philadelphia Negro, helped establish sociology as an academic discipline. The Souls of Black Folk. In 1903 Du Bois published The Souls of Black Folk, a collection of essays that combined history, sociology, and literature. It opened with a prophecy: “The problem of the Twentieth Century is the problem of the color-line.” It described the “double-consciousness” of Black Americans, “this sense of always looking at one’s self through the eyes of others,” and the feeling of being “an American, a Negro; two souls, two thoughts, two unreconciled strivings.” In the chapter “Of Mr. Booker T. Washington and Others,” Du Bois criticized Washington’s accommodationism, which, he said later, had “implicitly abandoned all political and social rights.” Du Bois argued instead that a “Talented Tenth” of educated Black leaders should guide the race and press for civil rights immediately and without compromise. The Niagara Movement and the NAACP. In July 1905 Du Bois and William Monroe Trotter gathered twenty-nine Black leaders at Niagara Falls, on the Canadian side because hotels on the American side barred Black guests. Their platform demanded free speech, a free press, manhood suffrage, and the abolition of all distinctions based on race. Washington’s allies, the “Tuskegee Machine,” worked to undermine the movement. In 1909 Du Bois joined white and Black reformers, including veterans of Niagara, in founding the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People. In 1910 he left academia to become its director of publicity and research, at first its only Black officer. The Crisis. In November 1910 the NAACP launched The Crisis, with Du Bois as editor. For its largely Black readers he personified the NAACP. The magazine carried news, editorials, fiction, poetry, art, and reports on the achievements of people of color around the world. In the 1920s, with a circulation of more than 100,000, it became the premier outlet for writers of the Harlem Renaissance. In 1919 he went to France to report on the Paris Peace Conference, investigate the treatment of Black soldiers, and organize a Pan-African Congress. He also wrote novels, poetry, and a historical pageant, The Star of Ethiopia, seen by nearly 30,000 people. Books such as The Souls of Black Folk, The Philadelphia Negro, and Black Reconstruction in America (1935) helped transform the study of African American history. Du Bois believed that Black Americans should demand full equality at once, refusing the compromises Washington accepted. In the Yawp’s words, he urged them “to concede to nothing.” He trusted in the power of social science to expose and defeat white supremacy, and he saw American racism as part of a worldwide color line linked to colonialism. His thinking changed over time. An early socialist, he joined the Communist Party in 1961 and moved to Ghana at the invitation of President Kwame Nkrumah. Du Bois’s rivalry with Booker T. Washington defined Black politics for a generation. Yet he had congratulated Washington on his 1895 Atlanta speech, and he later admitted, “I admired much about him.” Four years after attacking Washington in print, the two men spoke from the same lectern at Philadelphia Divinity School. In the 1920s he and other NAACP leaders traded accusations with the Black nationalist Marcus Garvey, and he criticized Harlem Renaissance writers whose portraits of the “Negro underworld” he feared would harm the civil rights cause. In January 1934 Du Bois published an editorial in The Crisis proposing voluntary segregation as an economic strategy for Black workers and farmers. The NAACP board, led by Walter White, rejected the idea and insisted on the primacy of integration. Amid that conflict, White’s personal rivalry with Du Bois, and the magazine’s financial troubles, Du Bois resigned as editor and from the board in July 1934. He later returned to the NAACP as director of special research, and in 1947 he submitted to the United Nations An Appeal to the World, linking racism in the United States to colonialism abroad. In his last years Du Bois moved to Ghana, where he died on August 27, 1963, on the eve of the March on Washington. The Housatonic Heritage organization calls him the father of both the modern civil rights movement and Pan-Africanism. His boyhood homesite in Great Barrington, purchased in 1967 and dedicated as a memorial in 1969, became a National Historic Landmark in 1979. Washington, he once joked, “died in 1915. A lot of people think I died at the same time.” He lived nearly half a century longer. The problem of the Twentieth Century is the problem of the color-line. W. E. B. Du Bois The Souls of Black Folk, 1903 It is a peculiar sensation, this double-consciousness, this sense of always looking at one's self through the eyes of others, of measuring one's soul by the tape of a world that looks on in amused contempt and pity. W. E. B. Du Bois “Of Our Spiritual Strivings,” The Souls of Black Folk, 1903 One ever feels his twoness,—an American, a Negro; two souls, two thoughts, two unreconciled strivings; two warring ideals in one dark body.
