title: Woodrow Wilson
subtitle: Twenty-eighth president: progressive reformer, wartime leader, and segregationist
summary: Woodrow Wilson, the twenty-eighth president of the United States (1913–1921), was a political scientist who rose within three years from president of Princeton University to the White House. His “New Freedom” reforms created the Federal Reserve and expanded federal regulation of business; he led the nation into World War I and proposed, in his Fourteen Points, a League of Nations to keep the peace. The Senate rejected his treaty, and a stroke left him incapacitated. His vision shaped American internationalism, but he also extended segregation in the federal government and suppressed wartime dissent.
thumbAlt: Photograph of Woodrow Wilson
themeText: The presidency War and the military Foreign policy and diplomacy Reform and protest Civil rights and citizenship
text: Thomas Woodrow Wilson Staunton, Virginia President of Princeton University Governor of New Jersey Twenty-eighth president (1913–1921) Architect of the League of Nations Presidency 1913–1921; Democrat Domestic program The New Freedom: tariff reduction, the Federal Reserve Act (1913), regulation of corporations Foreign policy Neutrality, then war against Germany (1917); the Fourteen Points (1918) Stroke Incapacitated by a stroke in October 1919 for the last seventeen months of his term Thomas Woodrow Wilson was born on December 28, 1856, in Staunton, Virginia, the son of a Presbyterian minister, and grew up in Augusta, Georgia, and Columbia, South Carolina. His earliest memories were of the Civil War: Union soldiers marching into Augusta and his mother nursing wounded Confederates. His father, a leader of the Southern Presbyterian church, taught him to see secession as justified and God as the guide of human destiny. Weak eyesight and possible dyslexia delayed his reading, and with few schools in the war-torn South, his father educated him at home. “The only place in the world where nothing has to be explained to me,” he said later, “is the South.” After a year at Davidson College he entered the College of New Jersey (later Princeton), graduating in 1879. He tried law in Atlanta, found it boring, and earned a PhD in history and political science at Johns Hopkins in 1886. His dissertation, Congressional Government, became a classic: it criticized the weak post–Civil War presidency and admired the British system, in which a prime minister leads both government and Parliament — an early sign of the strong executive he would become. In his last year of graduate school he married Ellen Louise Axson, an artist who encouraged his commitment to reform until her death in 1914. Wilson taught at Bryn Mawr, Wesleyan, and Princeton, publishing books including a five-volume history of the United States. In 1902 he became Princeton’s first president who was not a clergyman and began remaking it into a modern university, introducing small-group “preceptorials.” In 1910 New Jersey’s Democratic bosses, expecting a naive professor, made him their candidate for governor; he promised to be “an unconstitutional governor,” won decisively, and turned on the machine — passing direct primaries, a corrupt-practices act limiting campaign spending, a utility commission, and workers’ compensation. In 1912 Republicans split between President Taft and Theodore Roosevelt, and Wilson won the presidency with just under 42 percent of the vote. His New Freedom lowered tariffs and brought new controls on big business and support for unions; its crowning achievement, the Federal Reserve Act of 1913, created the framework that still regulates the nation’s banks, credit, and money supply. Re-elected narrowly in 1916 on the slogan “He Kept Us Out of War,” he asked Congress for war in April 1917 after Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare and tried to draw Mexico into an alliance against the United States. The government took over the railroads, launched huge shipbuilding programs, and paid for the war with a new income tax and Liberty Bonds. On January 8, 1918, Wilson laid out his Fourteen Points for a just peace — an end to secret alliances and trade barriers, reduced armaments, independence for subject peoples, and a League of Nations. He became the first president to travel to Europe while in office, and at the Paris Peace Conference he attached the League’s Covenant to the Treaty of Versailles. A Presbyterian who believed God was guiding his course, Wilson brought a preacher’s moral certainty to politics. He wanted a strong president who would lead Congress and the public, as a prime minister does; he wanted government to restore economic competition against abusive corporations; and he believed the United States had a duty to help build a new world order of democracy, self-determination, and collective security. Wilson’s democratic ideals had sharp limits. His administration expanded racial segregation in federal offices and the civil service and ignored protests from Black and white opponents, even as violence against African Americans seeking equality reached new heights. His “moral diplomacy” was often high-handed: he intervened militarily in Latin America more often than any predecessor. During the war his administration sponsored the Espionage and Sedition Acts, which outlawed criticism of the government and the war; violators were imprisoned or fined, and even mainstream publications were censored or banned. The Treaty of Versailles departed far from the Fourteen Points. Campaigning for it across the country in September 1919, Wilson collapsed from exhaustion and days later suffered a massive stroke; for the last seventeen months of his term he was largely incapacitated, seeing almost no one but his doctors and his second wife, Edith Bolling Galt Wilson, who became a kind of surrogate president. Refusing to compromise with the Senate, he told his supporters to vote against the amended treaty, and it was defeated twice. The United States never joined the League — but twenty-five years later the United Nations made its home in New York. Most historians rank Wilson among the five most important presidents, while his record on race and civil liberties draws growing criticism. Wilson expanded the federal government’s role in the economy and defined a vision of American internationalism — while his own policies showed the racial limits of Progressive-era democracy. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lbdhxLVlrhI Woodrow Wilson's Fourteen Points | History HISTORY 4:49 2026-10-23 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2YZQZzJMbSs Woodrow Wilson: The Worst Great President? title: Alcatraz Island
subtitle: San Francisco Bay island: a prison, then the site of the 1969–1971 Indian occupation
summary: Alcatraz Island in San Francisco Bay is best known as a former prison, but it is also a landmark of Native American activism. From November 1969 to June 1971, a group calling itself Indians of All Tribes occupied the island, demanding it for an Indian university and cultural center. Their nineteen-month occupation drew national attention to Native rights and helped change federal Indian policy. The island is now part of the Golden Gate National Recreation Area.
location: San Francisco Bay, California (Golden Gate National Recreation Area)
thumbAlt: Alcatraz Island seen from the east
themeText: Indigenous history Civil rights and citizenship
text: West San Francisco Bay, California (Golden Gate National Recreation Area) First claim March 9, 1964: five Sicangu Lakota landed for four hours, citing the 1868 Fort Laramie Treaty Occupation November 20, 1969 – June 11, 1971 Occupiers Indians of All Tribes; about 100 at first, including 80 UCLA students Leader Richard Oakes (Akwesasne Mohawk) Today Golden Gate National Recreation Area, National Park Service Alcatraz is a rocky island in San Francisco Bay. It served for many years as a prison holding both military prisoners and civilians. Today the National Park Service interprets both the prison and the Native occupation. Before the prison. Ohlone people lived around San Francisco Bay for thousands of years; oral history suggests Alcatraz was used to isolate tribal members who had broken laws, to gather bird eggs and sea life, and as a hiding place for Indians escaping the Spanish missions. Prison. Once Alcatraz became a prison, Native Americans were among those held there — in 1895, nineteen Hopi men were imprisoned on the island. The occupations. On March 9, 1964, five Sicangu Lakota led by Belva Cottier and Richard McKenzie claimed the island for four hours, citing the 1868 Fort Laramie Treaty. On November 9, 1969, Richard Oakes and other Native students and Bay Area Indians claimed it symbolically, and on November 20 a full occupation began. The occupiers elected a council, and everyone had a job, from security and sanitation to day care and a school. Over time, leadership fractured, non-Native residents moved in, the government cut off power and water, and a fire destroyed historic buildings. On June 10–11, 1971, federal marshals removed the last fifteen occupiers. Though the occupiers did not win the island, the Park Service concludes that the occupation helped end the federal termination policy and gave birth to a lasting political movement for Indian self-determination. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fW7cG0apZwU Drain Alcatraz: The World's Most Notorious Prison (Full Episode) | Drain the Oceans SPECIAL National Geographic 47:22 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GLXj3Mm-C-k What It Was Like To Be An Inmate At Alcatraz Weird History 13:03 2026-10-22

title: Angel Island Immigration Station
subtitle: The West Coast station built to enforce exclusion, 1910–1940
summary: The immigration station on Angel Island in San Francisco Bay opened in 1910. Unlike Ellis Island, it was designed to detain rather than welcome: under the Chinese Exclusion Act and later laws, Chinese and other Asian immigrants faced long detentions and grueling interrogations to prove their right to enter. Some waited weeks, others years. Detainees carved poems into the barracks walls that survive today.
thumbAlt: The detention barracks at the Angel Island Immigration Station
themeText: Immigration Asian American history Civil rights and citizenship
text: West San Francisco Bay, California Opened January 21, 1910 Operated by U.S. Bureau of Immigration (predecessor of today’s USCIS) Arrivals Immigrants from more than 80 countries, especially China Today National Historic Landmark (1997) with an immigration museum The station stands on Angel Island, the largest island in San Francisco Bay. Immigration officials chose the site for its isolation, believing it would keep detainees from escaping or communicating with relatives in San Francisco. The restored barracks preserve poems carved into the wooden walls by Chinese detainees. Chinese immigrants had come to California since the Gold Rush, but after the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 nearly all Chinese labor immigration was barred. When the 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed immigration records, some Chinese residents claimed children born overseas, creating opportunities for “paper sons” and “paper daughters” — immigrants who entered with purchased identities. To expose them, officials at Angel Island subjected Chinese arrivals to interrogations before a Board of Special Inquiry about their claimed families, neighbors, and villages; any inconsistency could mean rejection or deportation. Some detainees waited weeks, others years, for decisions. Immigrants from more than 80 countries passed through Angel Island, including people from Japan, India, the Philippines, Russia, Mexico, and, in the late 1930s, Jewish refugees fleeing Nazi persecution. In August 1940 the administration building burned, and the remaining detainees were moved to the mainland. Decades later a state park ranger discovered hundreds of Chinese poems carved into the walls of the abandoned barracks; the site became a National Historic Landmark in 1997. Angel Island reveals the exclusionary side of American immigration history — a gateway where race, not merely health or wealth, determined who could enter.

title: Cahokia
subtitle: The largest city in North America north of Mexico before 1492
summary: Around a thousand years ago, Cahokia, near the Mississippi River in present-day Illinois, was the greatest city north of Mexico. Estimates of its population at its height range from about 10,000 to 30,000, comparable to many cities of the time in Europe and the ancient Near East, and its builders raised more than a hundred earthen mounds around great plazas. Cahokia was the leading center of the Mississippian culture, which spread across the Mississippi Valley and the Southeast.
location: Collinsville, Illinois, east of St. Louis
thumbAlt: Earthen mounds at Cahokia Mounds State Historic Site
aliases: Cahokia Mounds Mississippian culture Monks Mound
themeText: Indigenous history Cities and urban life
text: Midwest Collinsville, Illinois, east of St. Louis Peak About 1050–1150 Population Estimates vary: the National Park Service gives 10,000–20,000 for Cahokia proper (40,000–50,000 including nearby centers); the National Library of Medicine’s Native Voices gives 20,000–30,000 Extent The original complex of mounds, homes, and farms covered more than 4,000 acres Status today Illinois state historic site, National Historic Landmark, and UNESCO World Heritage Site (1982) Cahokia Mounds State Historic Site lies a few miles east of the Mississippi River and St. Louis. It preserves the remains of a planned city: neighborhoods of houses, large plazas, public buildings, and more than one hundred earthen mounds, the largest of which is known as Monks Mound. The site is administered by the state of Illinois and is a National Historic Landmark and World Heritage Site. Cahokia was the pre-eminent cultural, religious, and economic center of the Mississippian culture, which flourished across the Mississippi Valley and the southeastern United States between roughly 1000 and 1350. Like other mound builders, Cahokians cleared fields and planted family farms within the city to supply its people with corn, squash, and sunflowers, and satellite towns spread outward from the center. Building the mounds — by carrying earth, basket by basket — required labor organized on a vast scale. The city declined after its peak and was largely abandoned by about 1350. Why remains a subject of research; archaeologists have proposed environmental, economic, and political explanations. Mississippian societies elsewhere in the Southeast continued long after Cahokia’s decline. Cahokia shows that Native North Americans built urban societies with monumental architecture, long-distance trade, and complex political organization centuries before European contact — a powerful corrective to the myth of an untouched wilderness. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ruWuAas8T7Y Why Was Ancient America's Greatest City Abandoned? title: Little Rock Central High School
subtitle: Site of the 1957 desegregation crisis, now a National Historic Site
summary: Little Rock Central High School became a battleground in 1957, when nine Black students, the Little Rock Nine, needed federal troops to attend classes there. Built beginning in 1926, the school is still an operating public high school and is also a National Historic Site managed by the National Park Service, which offers guided tours of the grounds.
thumbAlt: Little Rock Central High School
themeText: Civil rights and citizenship African American history
text: South Little Rock, Arkansas Built Construction began 1926, as Little Rock Senior High School 1957–58 enrollment About 1,800 students in grades 10–12 Today An operating four-year public high school of about 2,500 students Protected site Little Rock Central High School National Historic Site (National Park Service) Address of the visitor center 2120 W. Daisy L. Gatson Bates Drive Central High is an active school, so public access inside the building is limited; National Park Service rangers lead guided tours of the grounds. The street in front of the visitor center is named for Daisy Bates, the NAACP leader who guided the nine students. Construction of Little Rock Senior High School, later renamed Central High, began in 1926. In September 1957 the school became the focus of national and international attention when Governor Orval Faubus used the Arkansas National Guard to block nine Black students from enrolling, and President Eisenhower sent the 101st Airborne Division to protect them. About 1,800 students attended Central during that first year of desegregation. Central High was not the first Arkansas school to desegregate: schools in Charleston and Fayetteville did so in the fall of 1954, Hoxie in 1955, and Bentonville in 1956. But the confrontation at Central made it the symbol of the struggle over Brown v. Board of Education. Central High is a landmark of the civil rights movement — a place where the federal government enforced the Constitution against a state’s resistance. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fPVOO5sugMY Nine from Little Rock, 1964 - Restored US National Archives 18:31 2026-10-22

title: Chaco Canyon
subtitle: Ceremonial center of the ancestral Pueblo world
summary: In a high, dry canyon in northwestern New Mexico, ancestral Pueblo people built a center unlike anything else in North America. Beginning in the mid-800s, they raised multistory stone “great houses” with hundreds of rooms, aligned buildings to the sun and moon, and linked Chaco by roads to more than 150 great houses across the region. By about 1050, Chaco was the ceremonial, administrative, and economic center of the San Juan Basin.
location: San Juan Basin, northwestern New Mexico
thumbAlt: The great kiva plaza at Chetro Ketl in Chaco Canyon
aliases: Pueblo Bonito Chaco Culture
themeText: Indigenous history Religion
text: Southwest San Juan Basin, northwestern New Mexico Flourished Mid-800s to the 1100s Great houses Pueblo Bonito, Una Vida, Peñasco Blanco, Chetro Ketl, Pueblo Alto, and others Reach Roads connected Chaco to more than 150 great houses throughout the region Descendants Pueblo peoples of the Southwest, including the Hopi; Chaco is also central to the origins of several Navajo clans Protected as Chaco Culture National Historical Park Chaco Canyon’s long winters, short growing seasons, and scant rainfall make it an unlikely place for a major cultural center. Yet its great houses were planned from the start and built over decades or centuries with distinctive masonry. They were often oriented to solar, lunar, and cardinal directions, with lines of sight between buildings, astronomical markers, water-control features, and earthen mounds around them. Many researchers think the great houses were not ordinary farming villages but public architecture, used periodically for ceremonies, commerce, and trade when people gathered in the canyon. During the middle and late 800s, Pueblo Bonito, Una Vida, and Peñasco Blanco were built, followed by Hungo Pavi, Chetro Ketl, Pueblo Alto, and others. By 1050, Chaco’s influence extended across the San Juan Basin. Researchers still debate what held this system together — a trading network for turquoise, macaws, copper bells, and shells; a system for sharing food when harvests failed; or a religious “center place.” Pueblo descendants describe Chaco as a special gathering place where many peoples and clans converged to share ceremonies and knowledge. In the 1100s and 1200s, construction slowed and Chaco’s role shifted to other centers, including Aztec and Mesa Verde. People migrated to new areas and reorganized their world. Their descendants are the Pueblo peoples of today, many of whom regard Chaco as a sacred stop along their clans’ migration paths. Chaco is evidence of sophisticated planning, astronomy, and regional organization in North America centuries before Europeans arrived — and it remains a living sacred place for the Native peoples connected to it.

title: Ellis Island
subtitle: The nation’s busiest immigration station, 1892–1924
summary: From 1892 to 1924, Ellis Island in New York Harbor was America’s largest and busiest immigration station, where more than 12 million immigrants were processed. Most passed inspection in a few hours and went on to new lives; for some it was an “Island of Tears,” where families were separated and people were turned away. Today it is part of the Statue of Liberty National Monument and home to a museum of immigration.
thumbAlt: Ellis Island immigration station in 1902
themeText: Immigration Everyday life Cities and urban life
text: Northeast New York Harbor Years of operation as main station 1892–1924 Immigrants processed More than 12 million Inspection time Typically 3–7 hours Today Part of Statue of Liberty National Monument Ellis Island sits in New York Harbor near the Statue of Liberty. Arriving immigrants — especially those traveling in steerage — were ferried to the island for medical and legal inspection. The island is now part of Statue of Liberty National Monument. Ellis Island opened as a federal immigration station in 1892, during an era of mass migration. Between 1870 and 1940 more than 25 million immigrants came to the United States, with arrivals peaking at nearly 900,000 a year in the period 1900–1914. By the turn of the century, newcomers from Southern and Eastern Europe — Italians, Poles, and Eastern European Jews among them — outnumbered the Irish and Germans of earlier decades. For most, the inspection took a few hours; for the vast majority, Ellis Island was an “Island of Hope.” Those who failed medical or legal inspection could be detained or sent back. The Immigration Act of 1924 sharply restricted European immigration and moved inspection to consulates abroad, ending Ellis Island’s role as a major entry point. Its counterpart on the West Coast, Angel Island, operated very differently, under laws designed to exclude Asian immigrants. Ellis Island is the gateway through which a large share of today’s Americans trace their ancestry — a symbol of the nation as a land of immigrants, and of the restrictions that ended the era of mass European migration. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bDNKHWzQiz8 Immigrants at Ellis Island | History HISTORY 4:27 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9UEq2Rm-jV4 Ellis Island: Gateway to the American Dream Geographics 22:54 2026-10-22

title: Harpers Ferry
subtitle: Armory town where John Brown struck at slavery
summary: Harpers Ferry, at the meeting of the Potomac and Shenandoah Rivers, was home to a U.S. armory where interchangeable parts were first successfully used in manufacturing. In October 1859 the abolitionist John Brown seized the armory in a failed attempt to spark a slave uprising. During the Civil War it saw the largest surrender of Union troops of the war. After the war it became home to one of the earliest integrated schools in the country.
location: Harpers Ferry, West Virginia, where the Potomac and Shenandoah Rivers meet
thumbAlt: The armory engine house known as John Brown’s Fort at Harpers Ferry
themeText: Slavery and emancipation Science and technology War and the military
text: South Harpers Ferry, West Virginia, where the Potomac and Shenandoah Rivers meet Industrial first First successful application of interchangeable manufacture, at the U.S. armory John Brown’s raid October 16–18, 1859 Civil War Site of the largest surrender of Federal troops during the war Today Harpers Ferry National Historical Park The town sits on steep ground at the junction of the Potomac and Shenandoah Rivers. Its preserved nineteenth-century streets and buildings are part of Harpers Ferry National Historical Park, which also studies the area’s archeological record going back millennia. The National Park Service describes Harpers Ferry’s history as multilayered. The U.S. armory there pioneered interchangeable manufacture, and the town was reached by one of the first successful American railroads. On October 16, 1859, John Brown and twenty-one followers seized the armory, arsenal, and rifle factory; within thirty-six hours the raid was crushed and Brown captured by Marines under Robert E. Lee. During the Civil War, Harpers Ferry was the site of the largest surrender of Federal troops during the war. After the war, freedpeople were educated in one of the earliest integrated schools in the country. Harpers Ferry concentrates several stories of nineteenth-century America in one small town: industrial innovation, the violent struggle over slavery, the Civil War, and the beginnings of Black education after emancipation. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=G1K57zt5rUE The Raid on Harper’s Ferry - John Brown - US History - Part 4 - Extra History Extra History 11:13 2026-10-22 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=11gevEoaJsk The Raid on Harpers Ferry Smithsonian Magazine 4:07 2026-10-22

title: Independence Hall
subtitle: Where the Declaration and the Constitution were debated and signed
summary: Built as the Pennsylvania State House, Independence Hall is where the Second Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence in 1776 and where the Constitutional Convention wrote the Constitution in 1787. Today it is part of Independence National Historical Park and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
thumbAlt: Independence Hall in Philadelphia
themeText: Constitution and law Political thought
text: Northeast Chestnut Street, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania Construction began 1732 Original purpose Pennsylvania State House, home to the colony’s three branches of government Events here Washington named commander in chief (1775); Declaration adopted (1776); Articles of Confederation took effect (1781); Constitution written (1787) Managed by National Park Service, Independence National Historical Park Independence Hall is a Georgian-style brick building on Chestnut Street in Philadelphia. Its Assembly Room, where the Pennsylvania legislature met, was lent to the Second Continental Congress and later to the Constitutional Convention. The building stands within Independence National Historical Park, which also includes the Liberty Bell and sites associated with Benjamin Franklin. Construction began in 1732 on a building to house all three branches of Pennsylvania’s colonial government. In 1775, in its Assembly Room, the Second Continental Congress appointed George Washington commander in chief of the Continental Army; in July 1776 it voted for independence and adopted the Declaration there. The Articles of Confederation officially took effect in the building in 1781, and in the summer of 1787 delegates to the Constitutional Convention met behind its closed windows to write the Constitution. The building’s later history includes darker chapters: in the nineteenth century, federal hearings under the fugitive slave laws were held here, deciding whether people claimed as escaped slaves would be returned to bondage. Its symbolic status as the “birthplace” of American democracy has made it a place where that democracy’s promises and failures are both remembered. Few buildings anywhere have hosted as many foundational political acts. Independence Hall is the physical center of the American founding. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BK2P1j4dw4o Independence Hall 250 | Exclusive VIP Tour (2026) American Battlefield Trust 28:44 2026-10-22

title: Manzanar
subtitle: A War Relocation Center in California’s Owens Valley, now a National Historic Site
summary: Manzanar was one of ten War Relocation Centers where Japanese Americans were incarcerated during World War II. Built in 1942 on land the Army leased from the city of Los Angeles in California’s Owens Valley, at the foot of the Sierra Nevada, it held families forcibly removed from the West Coast under Executive Order 9066. Today it is a National Historic Site that preserves the camp’s story, and the earlier displacement of the valley’s Paiute people and farm settlers.
location: Owens Valley, Inyo County, California (between Lone Pine and Independence on U.S. 395)
thumbAlt: People exercising at Manzanar with mountains behind
aliases: Manzanar War Relocation Center Manzanar National Historic Site Owens Valley
themeText: Asian American history Civil rights and citizenship Indigenous history War and the military
text: West Owens Valley, Inyo County, California (between Lone Pine and Independence on U.S. 395) Name Spanish for “apple orchard” Camp built 1942, on 6,200 acres leased by the Army from Los Angeles Buildings About 800 during the war; all but three were dismantled or moved afterward Pilgrimage Held each year on the last Saturday of April, sponsored by the Manzanar Committee Today Manzanar National Historic Site, National Park Service Manzanar lies on the floor of the Owens Valley, with Mount Williamson rising directly to the west. Most of the camp’s buildings are gone; the site includes a cemetery, historic orchards, and a visitor center. Photographers including Ansel Adams and Dorothea Lange documented life there during the war. Earlier displacements. People used the Owens Valley for almost 10,000 years, and about 1,500 years ago the Owens Valley Paiute established settlements there, practicing a form of irrigated agriculture. After miners and ranchers moved in during the 1860s, the Army forcibly relocated nearly 1,000 Paiute to Fort Tejon in 1863. From 1910 the farm town of Manzanar grew apples, pears, peaches, and other crops. But Los Angeles bought up the valley’s water rights for its aqueduct, completed in 1913; by 1929 the city owned all of Manzanar’s land and water, and within five years the town was abandoned. The camp. In 1942 the Army leased 6,200 acres at Manzanar from Los Angeles to confine Japanese Americans. Some valley residents opposed the camp; others helped build it and worked there. Families lived there in a fenced and guarded camp. Remembrance. After the war nearly all of the camp’s roughly 800 buildings were removed. Former incarcerees and their descendants return each April on a pilgrimage, and the National Park Service has collected more than 715 oral history interviews about the camp and the valley. Manzanar’s layered history of removal — Paiute, settler, and Japanese American — makes it a powerful place to reflect on who has been forced from the land. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XgmY2P-xT_Y THE NATIONAL PARKS | Manzanar: "Never Again" | PBS PBS 14:21 2026-10-22

title: Mesa Verde
subtitle: Cliff dwellings of the Ancestral Pueblo people
summary: Mesa Verde, in southwestern Colorado, preserves some of the largest and best-preserved cliff dwellings in North America. Ancestral Pueblo people lived on the mesa tops for centuries, then, between about 1180 and 1300, built stone villages tucked into cliff alcoves. Within about a century they had migrated south to join communities in present-day New Mexico and Arizona, where their descendants live today.
thumbAlt: Cliff Palace at Mesa Verde
aliases: Cliff Palace Balcony House
themeText: Indigenous history Land and environment
text: Southwest Southwestern Colorado Cliff dwellings built About 1180–1300 CE Typical size Most average 8–10 rooms; a few, like Cliff Palace, are much larger Why the cliffs Many were built near seep springs as droughts made water scarce Protected Mesa Verde National Park, established June 29, 1906 — the first national park created to preserve cultural heritage The cliff dwellings are built of shaped sandstone set in mud mortar, under overhanging rock. Living rooms can be identified by hearths and grinding bins for corn; narrow rooms served as granaries; circular kivas were used for community and ceremonial life. Most dwellings were small, home to a few families. Balcony House, a mid-sized dwelling, had 38 rooms and two kivas and housed more than thirty people. Cliff Palace is the largest and best known. Ancestral Pueblo people farmed the Mesa Verde region for centuries before the cliff dwellings were built. The move into the alcoves came during a period of extended drought, recorded in tree rings; with mesa-top reservoirs becoming less reliable, families chose homes near cliffside springs. The dwellings were occupied for only about a century. By around 1300 the people had moved south, joining and founding communities in New Mexico and Arizona. The reasons likely combined drought, depleted resources, and social change. Centuries later, President Theodore Roosevelt established Mesa Verde National Park on June 29, 1906 — the first national park created to preserve cultural heritage. Mesa Verde shows how Ancestral Pueblo communities adapted to a demanding environment, and its protection marked the beginning of federal efforts to preserve the archaeological heritage of Native America. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gKDUdEDuIZs Cliff Palace: Colorado’s Pre-Columbian Marvel Geographics 22:28 2026-10-22

title: Mount Rushmore
subtitle: Four presidents carved into the Black Hills, on land sacred to the Lakota
summary: Between 1927 and 1941, sculptor Gutzon Borglum and about 400 workers blasted and carved the faces of George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt, and Abraham Lincoln into a granite mountain in South Dakota’s Black Hills. Meant to represent the nation’s birth, growth, development, and preservation, it draws more than two million visitors a year. But the Black Hills were recognized by treaty as Lakota land and are sacred to many tribes, and the memorial remains a contested symbol.
thumbAlt: The carved faces of Washington, Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt, and Lincoln on Mount Rushmore
aliases: Mount Rushmore National Memorial Shrine of Democracy Six Grandfathers
themeText: National symbols and holidays Indigenous history The presidency
text: Midwest Black Hills, South Dakota Carved 1927–1941; completed October 31, 1941 Sculptor Gutzon Borglum; finished by his son Lincoln Borglum The four presidents Washington (birth), Jefferson (growth), Theodore Roosevelt (development), Lincoln (preservation) Lakota name for the mountain Six Grandfathers Workers About 400; no one died during the 14 years of construction The memorial sits on a granite face of the Black Hills, the easternmost extension of the Rocky Mountains, in Pennington County, South Dakota. Borglum chose each president to stand for an idea: Washington the birth of the United States, Jefferson its growth (through the Declaration of Independence and the Louisiana Purchase), Theodore Roosevelt its development, and Lincoln its preservation. The National Park Service calls the memorial a symbol of freedom and hope; others see in it colonialism and racism. The name Black Hills comes from the Lakota Paha Sapa, “hills of black.” By the late 1700s the Lakota controlled the region after defeating the Cheyenne, and religious ceremonies were held there every year. The 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie recognized the Black Hills as Lakota territory, but the discovery of gold in 1874 drew prospectors and settlers who violated the treaty. The Lakota and Northern Cheyenne fought back in the Great Sioux War of 1876, which included the Battle of the Little Bighorn, but many Lakota were forced onto reservations by the end of the 1800s. In the 1920s South Dakota’s state historian, Doane Robinson, proposed a mountain carving to attract tourists; the first idea was to carve Native Americans and pioneers on granite spires called the Needles. Borglum, fresh from a bitter break with the Confederate memorial at Stone Mountain, Georgia, chose instead a cliff the Lakota called the Six Grandfathers — a choice, the Park Service says, that “completely disregarded” the site’s cultural significance — and the subject became four presidents. Carving began in 1927, with President Calvin Coolidge’s support bringing federal funding. Workers used dynamite to remove about 90 percent of the rock. Borglum died in March 1941, and his son Lincoln oversaw the final work, completed on October 31, 1941. In the 1970s the American Indian Movement held demonstrations at Mount Rushmore, demanding recognition of tribal sovereignty and the restoration of treaty rights. Mount Rushmore is both a celebration of American democracy and a reminder of broken treaties — one of the clearest places to see how a single monument can carry opposite meanings. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Bvj2URpgRc8 Mount Rushmore Was Supposed to Look Very Different Smithsonian Channel 3:58 2026-10-23 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hX4IvoP1HTk The dark history of Mount Rushmore - Ned Blackhawk and Jeffrey D. Means TED-Ed 5:13 2026-10-23

title: The National Mall
subtitle: “America’s Front Yard” in Washington, D.C.
summary: The National Mall is the great open space at the heart of Washington, D.C., stretching from the U.S. Capitol to the Potomac River. Planned as part of Pierre L’Enfant’s design for the capital, commissioned by George Washington, it is lined with the nation’s most famous monuments and memorials, from the Washington Monument and the Lincoln Memorial to the Vietnam Veterans and Martin Luther King Jr. memorials. It has also been the nation’s stage for inaugurations, celebrations, and protests, including the 1963 March on Washington.
location: Washington, D.C., from the U.S. Capitol to the Potomac River
thumbAlt: Aerial view of the National Mall
themeText: Civil rights and citizenship The presidency Cities and urban life
text: Washington, D.C. Washington, D.C., from the U.S. Capitol to the Potomac River Extent From the foot of the U.S. Capitol to the Potomac River Origins Pierre L’Enfant’s plan for the Federal City, commissioned by President George Washington (1791) Managed by National Mall and Memorial Parks, National Park Service — more than 1,000 acres Major memorials Washington Monument; Lincoln, Jefferson, FDR, World War II, Korean War Veterans, Vietnam Veterans, and Martin Luther King Jr. memorials Open 24 hours a day The Mall is a long swath of green lined with monuments and memorials. The National Park Service unit that cares for it manages more than 1,000 acres, including the Washington Monument, the Lincoln and Jefferson memorials, the Franklin Delano Roosevelt Memorial, the World War I and World War II memorials, the Korean War Veterans Memorial (dedicated 1995), the Vietnam Veterans Memorial, the Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial, Constitution Gardens, and Pennsylvania Avenue from the Capitol to the White House. The Mall’s open spaces date to L’Enfant’s plan for the original 1791 Federal City. Over two centuries, memorials were added to honor presidents, wars, and leaders; the Lincoln Memorial’s inscription declares that “the memory of Abraham Lincoln is enshrined forever.” The Mall became the setting for presidential inaugurals and for gatherings exercising First Amendment rights, from civil rights demonstrations — most famously the March on Washington, where Martin Luther King Jr. spoke at the Lincoln Memorial — to annual celebrations and festivals. The National Park Service calls the Mall the premier civic and symbolic space in the nation — the place where Americans gather to remember, celebrate, and protest.

title: Route 66
subtitle: The “Mother Road” from Chicago to Santa Monica
summary: U.S. Highway 66 was created in 1926 to meet the growing demand for automobile travel. Its roughly 2,400 miles from Chicago to Santa Monica linked the main streets of small towns to cities, carried migrants fleeing the Dust Bowl and military convoys in World War II, and fed the boom in postwar road-trip tourism. Decommissioned in 1985, “Route 66” lives on in literature, film, and song as a symbol of mobility, freedom, and the American Dream.
location: Chicago, Illinois, to Santa Monica, California
thumbAlt: A Route 66 highway shield sign
aliases: U.S. Highway 66 Mother Road US 66
themeText: Everyday life Science and technology Arts and popular culture
text: Midwest Chicago, Illinois, to Santa Monica, California Created 1926 Length About 2,400 miles, Chicago to Santa Monica Nickname The “Mother Road” Decommissioned 1985, as a federal highway Historic sites More than 250 buildings, bridges, and road sections on the National Register Route 66 crossed the heart of the country from Chicago to Santa Monica on the Pacific. Along it grew the hotels, filling stations, and restaurants of the automobile age; more than 250 of its buildings, bridges, and road alignments are now listed on the National Register of Historic Places. The highway was created in 1926 to serve the rising number of cars. During the 1930s it carried emigrants out of the Dust Bowl — westward migrants disparagingly called “Okies” by their new neighbors, whose plight John Steinbeck captured in The Grapes of Wrath (1939). In World War II it moved military convoys, and after the war it fed a boom in automobile tourism. The National Park Service credits the road with enabling one of the most comprehensive movements of people in American history, which transformed the West from a rural frontier into a metropolitan region. In 1985 U.S. Highway 66 was decommissioned as a federal highway, but it continues to live on in the American imagination as “Route 66.” Route 66 is the classic American road: a record of migration, war, and the automobile’s remaking of everyday life, and a lasting symbol of freedom and the open road. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y2nLieCOCxI Why Route 66 became America’s most famous road Vox 17:42 2026-10-23 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uZneA_hg8_c Route 66: The Asphalt Soul of America Geographics 14:16 2026-10-23

title: St. Augustine
subtitle: The oldest continuously occupied European-founded city in the United States
summary: Spanish forces under Pedro Menéndez de Avilés founded St. Augustine on September 8, 1565, at the site of a Timucua village called Seloy. Built to guard the route of Spain’s treasure fleets and to drive out a French Protestant colony nearby, it began a Spanish presence in Florida that lasted, with one interruption, for more than two centuries. It was founded decades before the English reached Jamestown.
thumbAlt: Aerial view of the Castillo de San Marcos and the town of St. Augustine, Florida, 1965
themeText: Colonial encounters Religion Latino history
text: Southeast St. Augustine, Florida Founded September 8, 1565, by Pedro Menéndez de Avilés Original site The Timucua village of Seloy First conflict Spanish destruction of French Fort Caroline and the killing of shipwrecked French Huguenots at Matanzas Inlet, 1565 Landmark Castillo de San Marcos, a Spanish stone fort, now a national monument St. Augustine lies on Florida’s Atlantic coast. Its historic district includes the Castillo de San Marcos, a stone fortress built by Spain and now a national monument, and the nearby Fort Matanzas. The city’s Spanish street plan and buildings make it one of the few places in the United States where the Spanish colonial era is still visible in the landscape. When King Philip II of Spain learned that French Protestants (Huguenots) under René de Laudonnière had built Fort Caroline on Spanish-claimed land in Florida — a perfect base for attacks on Spanish treasure fleets — he sent General Pedro Menéndez de Avilés to remove them. Menéndez arrived in August 1565 with some 800 people and, on September 8, came ashore at the Timucua village of Seloy, naming his settlement St. Augustine. A French fleet under Jean Ribault sailed to attack, but a hurricane wrecked it. Menéndez then captured Fort Caroline, killing most of its men. Learning from Timucua informants that shipwrecked Frenchmen were on the beach to the south, he twice met them at an inlet, accepted their surrender, and had most of them killed — 111 men in the first group and 134 in the second, including Ribault. The inlet has been called Matanzas, “slaughters,” ever since. The massacre secured Spanish control of Florida for some 235 years. St. Augustine is a reminder that the European colonization of what became the United States began with Spain, in the South, and that the colonial story was shaped as much by Spanish and Indigenous peoples as by the English. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AwmFDWXz1eI The Legacy of St. Augustine: Myth, History & the Story of America's Oldest City Library of Congress 56:41 2026-10-23

title: Statue of Liberty
subtitle: France’s gift to the United States, and a welcome to generations of immigrants
summary: The Statue of Liberty, officially Liberty Enlightening the World, was a gift from the people of France, designed by sculptor Frédéric-Auguste Bartholdi with an iron framework by Gustave Eiffel, on a pedestal paid for by Americans. Dedicated on October 28, 1886, in New York Harbor, it was meant to celebrate American independence and French-American friendship. Next to Ellis Island, and later inscribed with Emma Lazarus’s poem “The New Colossus,” it became a symbol of welcome to immigrants.
thumbAlt: The Statue of Liberty on its pedestal, holding up her torch
aliases: Liberty Enlightening the World Lady Liberty
themeText: Immigration National symbols and holidays Foreign policy and diplomacy
text: Northeast Liberty Island, New York Harbor Dedicated October 28, 1886, by President Grover Cleveland Creators Bartholdi (sculptor), Eiffel (framework), Richard Morris Hunt (pedestal) Height 151 feet; about 305 feet including the pedestal Tablet JULY IV MDCCLXXVI — July 4, 1776 National monument Since October 15, 1924; cared for by the National Park Service since 1933 The statue stands on Liberty Island (formerly Bedloe’s Island) in New York Harbor, on a pedestal set within Fort Wood, an 11-point Army fort built in the early 1800s. Lady Liberty holds a torch in her right hand and, in her left, a tablet inscribed with the date of the Declaration of Independence. Her crown’s spikes evoke rays of light, and a broken shackle and chains — symbols of the end of slavery — lie at her feet, invisible from below. Her copper skin is only 3/32 of an inch thick. In 1865 the French historian and abolitionist Édouard de Laboulaye proposed a monumental gift from the people of France to the people of the United States — to mark the centennial of American independence and to celebrate the recent abolition of slavery. Sculptor Bartholdi took up the idea. France paid for the statue; Americans were to pay for the pedestal. The Franco-Prussian War delayed the work, and when the first engineer died in 1879, Gustave Eiffel designed the internal framework. To raise money, the torch-bearing arm was displayed in Philadelphia in 1876 and in New York’s Madison Square from 1877 to 1882. France formally presented the statue on July 4, 1884. Fundraising for the pedestal lagged until Joseph Pulitzer used his newspaper, the New York World, to appeal to the public, promising to print every donor’s name; about 120,000 people gave more than $100,000. The statue crossed the Atlantic in 214 crates, arriving on June 17, 1885, and was dedicated on October 28, 1886. President Grover Cleveland promised, “We will not forget that Liberty has here made her home.” Emma Lazarus had written “The New Colossus” in 1883 for a fundraising auction; in 1903 a plaque with the poem — “Give me your tired, your poor, Your huddled masses yearning to breathe free” — was placed in the pedestal. Because the statue stood next to the immigration station at Ellis Island, it became a symbol of welcome, and in 1965 President Lyndon B. Johnson signed a major immigration act at its base. It was restored for its 1986 centennial, when a replica of Bartholdi’s original torch replaced the much-altered original. The Statue of Liberty is perhaps the best-known symbol of the United States — a monument to independence and the end of slavery that came to stand above all for the promise America offered immigrants. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HGkqh-iwS28 What "Lady Liberty" and Ellis Island Mean Today | National Geographic National Geographic 4:15 2026-10-23

title: The White House
subtitle: The president’s home and office since 1800, built partly by enslaved workers, burned in 1814 and rebuilt more than once
summary: The White House has been the home and workplace of every American president since John and Abigail Adams moved in, in November 1800. Designed by the Irish-born architect James Hoban, it was built between 1792 and 1800 by free workers and by enslaved people hired out by their owners. British troops burned it in 1814, and Hoban rebuilt it. Long called the “President’s House” or “Executive Mansion,” it got its official name from Theodore Roosevelt in 1901. Today it is a residence, an office, a stage for ceremonies, and a museum visited by hundreds of thousands of people a year.
thumbAlt: The north front of the White House, with its columned portico, seen across the lawn
aliases: President’s House Executive Mansion 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue West Wing Oval Office James Hoban
themeText: The presidency National symbols and holidays Slavery and emancipation
text: Washington, D.C. 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue NW, Washington, D.C. Architect James Hoban, winner of a 1792 design competition Cornerstone October 13, 1792 First residents John and Abigail Adams, November 1800 Burned By British troops, August 24, 1814; rebuilt by 1817 Official name “White House” adopted by Theodore Roosevelt, October 1901 Major rebuildings 1792, 1817, 1902, 1952 — the dates on a marker in the Entrance Hall The White House stands on Pennsylvania Avenue in Washington, D.C., in President’s Park, on a site chosen by George Washington and the city’s planner, Peter Charles L’Enfant. The main house, faced with sandstone from a quarry on Virginia’s Aquia Creek, is flanked by the West Wing, with the president’s offices, and the East Wing. It serves at once as a family home, the president’s office, a ceremonial stage for the nation’s most important visitors, and a museum. In March 1792 the commissioners of the new federal city announced a national design competition for the President’s House; Thomas Jefferson himself submitted a design, but in July the commissioners, with Washington’s approval, chose Hoban’s. The cornerstone was laid at a Masonic ceremony on October 13, 1792. Enslaved people worked on every stage of construction from 1792 to 1800 — quarrying stone, cutting timber, making bricks, and working as carpenters, sawyers, and laborers — alongside free white workers and craftsmen. Because the new capital had few residents, the commissioners hired enslaved people from slave owners in Maryland, Virginia, and the District of Columbia, and the owners collected their wages. Hoban himself owned enslaved carpenters — payrolls from 1794 to 1797 list four of them, Ben, Daniel, Harry, and Peter — and he grew rich building the new capital. In 1798 the stone walls were coated with a lime whitewash to protect them from freezing; contrary to legend, the house was white long before the British burned it. On August 24, 1814, during the War of 1812, British troops set the house on fire. Hoban rebuilt it by 1817, again partly with enslaved labor. Presidents kept changing it: Jefferson added colonnades, James Monroe the South Portico, and Andrew Jackson the North Portico in 1829–30. In 1902 Theodore Roosevelt replaced the old glass conservatories with the West Wing, separating the president’s offices from the family’s home; Franklin Roosevelt added the East Wing in 1942. By the late 1940s, decades of careless alterations had left the house in danger of collapse. From 1948 to 1952, while Harry Truman’s family lived across the street at Blair House, workers tore out everything inside the outer stone walls and rebuilt the interior on a steel frame with deep new concrete foundations. The project cost $5.7 million and changed the house more than the fire of 1814 had. Some of Hoban’s old pine beams were milled into paneling for the ground-floor rooms. The White House is one of the best-known symbols of the American presidency and of the nation itself. Its history also holds a contradiction that the White House Historical Association now highlights: the home of the leader of a nation founded on liberty was built in part by people held in slavery.

title: Yellowstone National Park
subtitle: The world’s first national park, set aside in 1872 on top of an active volcano
summary: On March 1, 1872, President Ulysses S. Grant signed a law that set aside more than two million acres of the Rocky Mountains, mostly in what is now Wyoming, as “a public park or pleasuring-ground for the benefit and enjoyment of the people.” Yellowstone became the world’s first national park. It sits on one of the world’s largest volcanic calderas and holds more than half of all the geysers on Earth. People had lived in and traveled through the region for more than 11,000 years before it became a park.
thumbAlt: Thomas Moran’s 1872 painting of the Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone, with the Lower Falls between golden cliffs
aliases: Yellowstone Old Faithful first national park National Park Service Yellowstone National Park Protection Act
themeText: Land and environment National symbols and holidays Indigenous history Territorial expansion
text: West Wyoming, Montana, and Idaho Established March 1, 1872, signed by President Ulysses S. Grant Size About 2.2 million acres (3,472 square miles) — larger than Rhode Island and Delaware combined Location 96% in Wyoming, 3% in Montana, 1% in Idaho Geysers More than 500 active — over half the world’s total — among 10,000+ hydrothermal features Volcano A caldera about 45 by 30 miles Visits 4.74 million in 2024 Yellowstone lies in the northwest corner of Wyoming, reaching into Montana and Idaho. About 80 percent of the park is forest, mostly lodgepole pine. Beneath it is an active volcano whose caldera is one of the largest in the world, and its heat powers more than 10,000 hot springs, mud pots, steam vents, and geysers. The park is home to 67 species of mammals, including bison, elk, and grizzly bears; the Lower Falls of the Yellowstone River plunge 308 feet. More than 1,800 archeological sites record the long human presence there. For thousands of years many tribes and bands, among them the Tukudika (“Sheep Eaters”), lived in, hunted in, and traveled through the region. In the years before 1872 the Washburn and Hayden expeditions explored it, and William Henry Jackson’s photographs and Thomas Moran’s paintings captured the imagination of Congress. Members of the expeditions, including Nathaniel Langford, lobbied for a bill modeled on the 1864 law that had given Yosemite Valley to California to protect. Closing so large an area to settlement broke with the government’s usual policy of transferring public land to private owners, but Congress agreed, and Grant signed the act six months after the Hayden Expedition. Because the area lay across three territories, it became a federal park rather than a state one. The early park had little money and no laws to protect it. Langford served as an unpaid superintendent; his successor, Philetus Norris, built the first roads, but he also spread a myth that Native Americans had avoided the area out of fear of the geysers, to reassure tourists during the wars between the United States and Native nations. Poachers, squatters, and vandals ravaged the park until the U.S. Army took charge in 1886. When soldiers caught a poacher killing bison in 1894 and could only expel him, a national outcry pushed Congress to pass a law giving the Army real power to protect the park. Yellowstone’s experience helped lead to the creation of the National Park Service in 1916, and rangers replaced the Army in 1918. After World War II visitors poured in — a million a year by 1948 — and the Park Service’s Mission 66 program rebuilt roads and visitor facilities. Yellowstone established a new idea: that some land should belong permanently to the whole public and be protected for its natural wonders rather than sold. That idea grew into the national park system — today more than 80 million acres in all fifty states and several U.S. territories. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RCYSEDqPv4o A Brief History of Yellowstone National Park | National Geographic National Geographic 4:22 2026-10-23

title: The American Revolution
subtitle: The war for independence from Britain, 1775–1783, and the revolution in ideas that made a new nation
summary: In little more than a decade after 1763, colonists who had been proud to be British came to see Parliament’s taxes and controls as a threat to their liberty, and in 1776 they declared independence. The war that followed, from the first shots at Lexington and Concord in April 1775 to the Treaty of Paris in September 1783, pitted the new United States, with France as its ally from 1778, against the world’s largest military. The Revolution created a republic founded on the idea that government rests on the consent of the governed, but it left slavery in place and opened Native lands to settlement, contradictions that shaped the nation for generations.
location: The thirteen colonies, the Atlantic, and battlefields from Canada to Georgia
thumbAlt: John Trumbull’s painting of the British surrender at Yorktown
aliases: Revolutionary War War of Independence War for Independence Patriots Loyalists Continental Army Saratoga Valley Forge Treaty of Paris
themeText: War and the military Political thought Foreign policy and diplomacy African American history Indigenous history Women's history
text: The thirteen colonies, the Atlantic, and battlefields from Canada to Georgia Belligerents United States and allies France (from 1778), Spain, and the Dutch Republic vs. Great Britain, Loyalists, German auxiliaries, and allied Native nations Commanders George Washington (Continental Army); Thomas Gage, William Howe, Henry Clinton, Charles Cornwallis (Britain) Key battles Lexington and Concord (1775), Bunker Hill (1775), Trenton (1776), Saratoga (1777), Yorktown (1781) Independence declared Resolution passed July 2, 1776; Declaration approved July 4, 1776 Ended by Treaty of Paris, signed September 3, 1783 Black Americans An estimated 5,000–6,000 fought for independence; about 20,000 joined the British On one side stood the Patriots, colonists who came to support independence, organized first in local committees and provincial congresses and then in the Continental Congress and the Continental Army under George Washington. From 1778 France was their ally, and Spain and the Dutch Republic also went to war with Britain, turning the rebellion into a global conflict. On the other side stood Great Britain, its regular army and navy, tens of thousands of hired German soldiers, usually called Hessians, and the Loyalists, colonists of every rank who remained faithful to the king. Many Americans were neither. A good number of colonists tried to stay neutral. The roughly 250,000 Native Americans in British North America, in more than eighty nations east of the Mississippi, mostly tried at first to stay out of the conflict; when they took sides, they did so to protect their lands and sovereignty. Many, including Shawnee, Creek, Cherokee, and most of the Six Nations of the Haudenosaunee, sided with Britain, while the Oneida and Tuscarora supported the Americans. Black Americans, free and enslaved, also weighed which side offered freedom: an estimated 5,000 to 6,000 fought for independence, while about 20,000 fought for the British. Seen from 1763, nothing would have seemed less likely than an American revolution. Colonists had just helped Britain win the Seven Years’ War, and most had never been prouder to be British. Over the previous century they had grown used to running their own affairs. Each colony had an elected assembly that taxed residents and paid royal officials, and because land was easier to get than in England, a larger share of colonial men could vote. Many colonists embraced the ideology of republicanism, which warned that power corrupts and that a free people must be virtuous and watchful against conspiracy and tyranny. The ideas of John Locke and the religious revivals of the Great Awakening both encouraged ordinary people to question inherited authority. Victory left Britain in control of North America east of the Mississippi, but it also doubled the national debt and left the empire with expensive new frontiers to defend. King George III’s government set out to bring the colonies under firmer control. The Royal Proclamation of 1763 forbade settlement west of the Appalachian Mountains, hoping to avoid costly wars with Native nations after Pontiac’s War, and colonists who had fought for that land protested. The imperial crisis, 1764–1774. Parliament’s attempts to raise revenue set off a decade of escalating resistance. The Sugar Act of 1764 tightened enforcement of duties on molasses and sent smugglers to courts without juries, and the Currency Act restricted colonial paper money in the middle of a postwar recession. The Stamp Act of 1765, the first direct tax Parliament had ever laid on the colonies, required stamps on newspapers, legal documents, diplomas, and even playing cards. Colonists resisted in three ways: assemblies passed resolutions such as the Virginia Resolves, and nine colonies sent delegates to a Stamp Act Congress; merchants organized boycotts of British goods; and crowds burned effigies and drove every stamp distributor to resign. Parliament repealed the act in 1766 but declared its full power to bind the colonies “in all cases whatsoever.” The Townshend Acts of 1767 placed duties on everyday imports such as lead, glass, paint, and tea and used the money to pay royal officials, freeing governors from the assemblies’ control. Resistance now drew in colonists of every rank. Merchants and consumers signed nonimportation and nonconsumption agreements, committees policed them, and women organized spinning clubs so that families could wear homespun instead of British cloth. Troops sent to Boston in 1768 clashed with townspeople until the Boston Massacre of March 1770. Parliament then repealed every Townshend duty except the one on tea. When the Tea Act of 1773 tried to rescue the East India Company by selling its tea in America, Bostonians dumped 342 chests into the harbor at the Boston Tea Party. Parliament answered with the Coercive Acts of 1774, which closed Boston’s port, took over Massachusetts’s government, and allowed troops to be quartered in colonists’ houses. Rather than isolating Massachusetts, the acts united the colonies. The First Continental Congress met in September 1774 and adopted the Continental Association, a continent-wide boycott enforced by local committees of ordinary colonists. From war to independence, 1775–1776. Fighting began on April 19, 1775, at Lexington and Concord, and some twenty thousand militiamen soon besieged the British in Boston. At Bunker Hill (actually Breed’s Hill) in June, the British took the colonists’ fortifications but suffered twice as many casualties as the Americans. The Second Continental Congress adopted the army besieging Boston and made George Washington its commander, while still sending the king an Olive Branch Petition; George III instead proclaimed the colonies in rebellion. In the opening months of 1776 Thomas Paine’s pamphlet Common Sense attacked monarchy itself and turned independence into a popular cause. On July 2, 1776, Congress voted for Richard Henry Lee’s resolution that the colonies “are, and of right ought to be, Free and Independent States,” and on July 4 it approved the Declaration of Independence, drafted by Thomas Jefferson. The war in the North, 1776–1778. That summer the largest expeditionary force in British history landed at New York, and the Continental Army, badly beaten in Brooklyn and Manhattan, retreated across New Jersey. With morale collapsing and enlistments expiring, Washington crossed the icy Delaware River on Christmas night 1776 and surprised a garrison of 1,500 Hessians at Trenton, then won again at Princeton a week later. In 1777 the British took Philadelphia, but a British army marching south from Canada under General John Burgoyne was surrounded and forced to surrender at Saratoga, New York. The Continental Army suffered through the winter of 1777–1778 at Valley Forge, where more than 2,500 men died of disease and exposure. Washington learned that his untrained army could not win head-on battles against British professionals; as long as he kept it intact, the war would go on, however many cities the British captured. The war in the South and the world, 1778–1783. In 1778 Britain shifted its effort to the South, where it expected more Loyalist support. British campaigns captured major cities from Georgia to Virginia, but Britain lacked the troops to hold the countryside, and bitter fighting between local Patriots and Loyalists made the Southern war a true civil war. In 1781 Washington and the French army marched south and, with a French fleet blocking the coast, trapped General Charles Cornwallis at Yorktown, Virginia, forcing his surrender in 1781. Saratoga (1777) was the decisive turning point. The surrender of an entire British army convinced the French government that the American cause could succeed. France had already been sending secret aid; when news of Saratoga reached Foreign Minister Vergennes in December 1777, he decided for an alliance, and the Treaty of Alliance and the Treaty of Amity and Commerce were signed on February 6, 1778. The war became a global conflict that stretched British forces from Europe to India. Yorktown (October 1781) left Britain with no new strategy and no public support for continuing the war. By then Britain was also fighting France, Spain, and the Netherlands, and the capture of a second army brought the government to the peace table. Peace talks opened in Paris in September 1782. Benjamin Franklin, John Adams, and John Jay insisted on British recognition of independence and refused a separate peace without France. Two months of hard bargaining produced preliminary articles in which Britain accepted American independence and the new nation’s boundaries and settled questions of fishing rights off Newfoundland, prewar debts, and Loyalist property. The final Treaty of Paris was signed on September 3, 1783. Three months later, on December 23, 1783, Washington resigned his command, a gesture that ensured civilian rule over the new republic. The Revolution’s most immediate result was a wave of constitution writing. In 1776 and 1777 the new states drafted written constitutions based on popular sovereignty, the idea that government’s authority comes from the people; several, following Virginia, included a bill of rights. Pennsylvania’s constitution allowed all free men to vote, and Massachusetts’s 1780 constitution, debated in town meetings, created a government of three branches with checks and balances. The Articles of Confederation, ratified in 1781, joined the states in a weak union whose Congress could not tax or regulate trade. Politics became more democratic and society less deferential, and the end of British trade restrictions opened new markets and manufacturing. The Revolution’s promise of equality also had sharp limits. Women had organized boycotts and run farms and shops during the war, but they gained no political rights; instead they were praised as “republican mothers” responsible for raising virtuous citizens. About sixty thousand Loyalists left the country, many for Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Quebec, and states kept seizing Loyalist property despite the peace treaty. For enslaved people, the war was the largest flight from slavery before the Civil War: historians estimate that as many as 80,000 to 100,000 escaped their Patriot enslavers, and 8,000 to 10,000 Black Loyalists left with the British in 1783 to begin new lives across the Atlantic world. Several Northern states passed gradual emancipation laws, but in the South slavery endured, and the Declaration’s words about equality became a challenge the nation would face again and again. For Native nations, American victory brought a rush of settlers into the West and governments hostile to their land claims, and Native peoples would continue to be pushed west throughout the next century. The American Revolution created the United States and launched what historians call the age of democratic revolutions, followed by revolutions in France, Haiti, and South America. Its ideals, above all the Declaration’s claim that “all men are created equal,” became the shared language that later movements, from abolitionists to suffragists and civil rights activists, used to demand that the nation live up to its founding. There is something absurd, in supposing a continent to be perpetually governed by an island.
